For Java records, the canonical constructor and its property mappings are automatically detected, so this annotation is not required. It can still be used to specify a non-canonical constructor if needed, for example to provide default values for certain components: @BeanType(properties="name") public record WithBeanCtor(String name, int age) { @BeanCtor(properties="name") public WithBeanCtor(String name) { this(name, 0); // Default age to 0 } } When using @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor on a record, use @BeanType(properties) to limit the visible properties to match the constructor parameters. See Also @BeanType Annotation - Class-level bean-modeling annotation. @BeanProp Annotation - Property-level bean-modeling annotation. Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support.

While parsing into beans, Juneau attempts to determine the class types of bean properties through reflection on the bean property getter or setter. Often this is insufficient if the property type is an interface or abstract class that cannot be instantiated. This is where bean names and dictionaries come into play. Bean names and dictionaries are used for identifying class types when they cannot be inferred through reflection. Bean classes are given names through the @Marshalled(typeName) annotation. These names are then added to the serialized output as virtual _type properties (or element names in XML). On the parsing side, these type names are resolved to classes through the use of bean dictionaries. For example, if a bean property is of type Object, then the serializer will add _type attributes so that the class can be determined during parsing. @Marshalled(typeName="foo") public class Foo { // A bean property where the object types cannot be inferred since it's an Object[]. @MarshalledProp(dictionary={Bar.class,Baz.class}) public Object[] x = new Object[]{new Bar(), new Baz()}; } @Marshalled(typeName="bar") public class Bar {} @Marshalled(typeName="baz") public class Baz {} When serialized as JSON, _type attributes would be added when needed to infer the type during parsing: { x: [ {_type:'bar'}, {_type:'baz'} ] } Type names can be represented slightly differently in different languages. For example, the dictionary name is used as element names when serialized to XML. This allows the typeName annotation to be used as a shortcut for defining element names for beans. When serialized as XML, the bean is rendered as: <foo> <x> <bar/> <baz/> </x> </foo> Bean dictionaries are registered through the following: MarshalledPropdictionaryMarshalleddictionaryMarshallingContext.BuilderbeanDictionary(Class...) The bean dictionary setting can consist of any of the following types: Any bean class that specifies a value for @Marshalled(typeName). Any subclass of BeanDictionaryList containing a collection of bean classes with type name annotations. Any subclass of BeanDictionaryMap containing a mapping of type names to classes without type name annotations. Any array or collection of the objects above. // Create a parser and tell it which classes to try to resolve. ReaderParser parser = JsonParser .create() .beanDictionary(Foo.class, Bar.class) .build(); // Use the predefined HTML5 bean dictionary which is a BeanDictionaryList. ReaderParser parser = HtmlParser .create() .beanDictionary(HtmlBeanDictionary.class) .build(); The _type property name can be overridden through the following: MarshalledtypePropertyNameMarshallingContext.BuildertypePropertyName(String) When using the annotation, you'll typically want to define it on an interface class so that it can be inherited by all subclasses. @Marshalled(typePropertyName="mytype", dictionary={MyClass1.class,MyClass2.class}) public interface MyInterface {...} @Marshalled(typeName="C1") public class MyClass1 implements MyInterface {...} @Marshalled(typeName="C2") public class MyClass2 implements MyInterface {...} MyInterface[] x = new MyInterface[]{ new MyClass1(), new MyClass2() }; // Produces "[{mytype:'C1',...},{mytype:'C2',...}]" String json = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(x); note Type names do not need to be universally unique. However, they must be unique within a dictionary. The following reserved words cannot be used as type names: object, array, number, boolean, null. Serialized type names are DISABLED by default. They must be enabled on the serializer using the Serializer.Builder.addBeanTypes() setting.

The @BeanIgnore annotation (org.apache.juneau.commons.bean) excludes a class, field, method, or constructor from bean introspection — the model-side decision about whether something participates in bean detection at all. This is the model-side annotation. Format-side concerns — skipping a type entirely at the wire-format layer regardless of whether it's a bean — live on the sibling annotation @MarshalledIgnore (org.apache.juneau.marshall), described at the end of this page. The two annotations are independent and may be combined.

When applied to a field or method, @BeanIgnore excludes it from bean property discovery. public class MyBean { // Not a bean property! @BeanIgnore public String foo; // Not a bean property! @BeanIgnore public String getBar() {...} }

When applied to a constructor, @BeanIgnore excludes it from constructor detection (i.e. it won't be considered a candidate bean constructor). public class MyBean { public MyBean() {...} // Excluded from constructor detection. @BeanIgnore public MyBean(String foo) {...} }

When applied to a class, @BeanIgnore marks the class as not a bean for modeling purposes. The marshaller falls through to its other type-detection logic (object swaps, @BeanType-style hints, @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING), etc.) instead of treating the class as a bean — it does not by itself suppress output the way @MarshalledIgnore does. // Not treated as a bean for modeling purposes. // The marshaller still tries to render it, e.g. via toString() or an installed swap. @BeanIgnore public class MyType {...} Migration In versions prior to 10.0, @BeanIgnore on a class caused the object to be serialized via toString() rather than as a bean — that historical behavior is what the current @BeanIgnore-on-class semantics above describe. If you specifically want the wire format to render null for a type regardless of bean-modeling status, use @MarshalledIgnore (see below) instead. If you want the explicit toString() serialization behavior, use @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING): // Serialize as toString() value. @Marshalled(as=MarshalledAs.STRING) public class MyType { @Override public String toString() { return "my-value"; } }

By default, @BeanIgnore on a field only excludes that field from field-based bean discovery. Public (or otherwise visible) getters/setters can still expose the same logical property — for example when beanFieldVisibility is NONE and only methods are used. That matches patterns such as @BeanIgnore on private f5…f8 with public getF5() while still serializing f5 via the getter. To also exclude the matching JavaBean accessor pair from metadata (so the property does not appear in serialization or parsing), set ignoreAccessors = true on the field annotation: public class MyBean { public String visible = "ok"; // Hidden from Juneau bean metadata: no "foo" in serialization/parsing @BeanIgnore(ignoreAccessors = true) private String foo = "secret"; public String getFoo() { return foo; } public void setFoo(String value) { foo = value; } } The logical property name is derived from the field the same way as for visible fields: @BeanProp / @Name on the field, if present, otherwise the marshalling context's PropertyNamer applied to the field name. That name must match the accessor-derived property name (e.g. field foo with getFoo/setFoo).

Ignoring individual record components is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. Applying @BeanIgnore to a record component's accessor method or field will exclude it from serialization output, but the parser will be unable to instantiate the record if the component value is missing from the input. If you need to omit components during parsing, use @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor that provides defaults for the omitted components.

@MarshalledIgnore (org.apache.juneau.marshall) is a type-level-only annotation (it has no field/method target and no ignoreAccessors attribute). Serializers output null for instances of the annotated type, and parsers return null when asked to instantiate it — this is a wire-format concern independent of whatever the bean-modeling layer would otherwise do with the type. // Suppressed entirely at the wire-format layer — serializes as null. @MarshalledIgnore public class MyType {...} Because the two annotations are independent, they combine as follows: @MarshalledIgnore alone — the class still participates in bean detection (it may be treated as a bean by the modeling layer), but the marshaller emits null. @BeanIgnore alone — the class is not a bean for modeling purposes, but the marshaller still tries to render it (typically via toString() or an installed swap). Both — the class is not a bean and the marshaller emits null. See Also Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support. @BeanType Annotation - The model-side/format-side split pattern this page follows.

The @BeanProp annotation is applied to bean fields, getter/setter methods, and constructor parameters to control bean introspection and property modeling. This is the model-side annotation in juneau-commons. It carries the attributes that describe the bean property itself — its name, accessibility (read/write only), concrete type, generic type parameters, element type, and the bean factory used to instantiate its value. Format-side concerns (wire-format overrides, dictionary) live on @MarshalledProp in juneau-marshall. Migration This annotation was previously named @Beanp. Usages of @Beanp should be updated to @BeanProp (in org.apache.juneau.commons.bean).

The @BeanProp(name) annotation overrides the name of the bean property. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(name="Bar") public String getFoo() {...} } The @Name annotation is a shortcut for specifying a bean property name: public class MyBean { @Name("Bar") public String getFoo() {...} } The @BeanProp(value) annotation is a synonym for name. Use it when you are only specifying a name so the annotation is more concise: // These two annotations are equivalent: @BeanProp(name="foo") @BeanProp("foo") If the beanFieldVisibility setting on the marshalling context excludes this field (e.g. the visibility is set to the default of PUBLIC but the field is PROTECTED), this annotation can be used to force the field to be identified as a property. public class MyBean { @BeanProp protected String getFoo() {...} }

The bean property named * is the designated "dynamic property" which allows for "extra" bean properties not otherwise defined. This is similar in concept to the Jackson @JsonGetterAll and @JsonSetterAll annotations but generalized for all supported marshall languages. The primary purpose is for backwards compatibility in parsing newer streams with additional information into older beans. The following shows various ways of using dynamic bean properties. // Option #1 - A simple public Map field. // The field name can be anything. public class BeanWithDynaField { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> extraStuff = new LinkedHashMap<>(); } // Option #2 - Getters and setters. // Method names can be anything. // Getter must return a Map with String keys. // Setter must take in two arguments, a String and Object. public class BeanWithDynaMethods { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> getMyExtraStuff() { ... } @BeanProp(name="*") public void setAnExtraField(String name, Object value) { ... } } // Option #3 - Getter only. // Properties will be added through the getter. public class BeanWithDynaGetterOnly { @BeanProp(name="*") public Map<String,Object> getMyExtraStuff() { ... } } note If you're not interested in these additional properties, you can use the ignoreUnknownBeanProperties setting to ignore values that don't fit into existing properties.

The @BeanProp(type) annotation identifies a specialized class type for a generalized property. Normally the type is inferred through reflection of the field type or getter return type. However, specify this value if you're parsing beans where the bean property class is an interface or abstract class to identify the bean type to instantiate. Otherwise, you may cause an InstantiationException when trying to set these fields. This property must denote a concrete class with a no-arg constructor. public class MyBean { // Identify concrete type as a HashMap. @BeanProp(type=HashMap.class) public Map p1; }

The @BeanProp(params) annotation is for bean properties of type map or collection. It identifies the class types of the contents of the bean property object when the general parameter types are interfaces or abstract classes. public class MyBean { // Identify concrete map type with String keys and Integer values. @BeanProp(type=HashMap.class, params={String.class,Integer.class}) public Map p1; }

The @BeanProp(ro) annotation identifies a property as read-only. Serializers will serialize such properties as usual, but parsers will silently ignore them. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(ro="true") public float price; } Java Records Marking record components as read-only is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor.

The @BeanProp(wo) annotation identifies a property as write-only. Parsers will parse such properties as usual, but serializers will silently ignore them. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(wo="true") public float price; }

Specifies the element type for properties of type Stream, BeanSupplier, BeanConsumer, or BeanChannel when type erasure prevents the framework from inferring the generic type argument at runtime. public class OrderCollection { // Stream property - element type cannot be inferred at runtime due to erasure @BeanProp(elementType=Order.class) public Stream<Order> getOrders() { ... } }

Specifies a BeanFactory class to use when instantiating the value of this specific bean property, overriding the class-level @BeanType(factory) if present. public class MyBean { @BeanProp(factory=ItemChannelFactory.class, elementType=Item.class) public BeanChannel<Item> getItems() { ... } }

info @BeanProp and @Name annotations are automatically inherited when bean property methods (getters, setters, extraKeys) are overridden in subclasses. This feature is particularly useful for fluent APIs where you want to override setters to change the return type without needing to re-annotate every method. // Parent class with annotated property public class Parent { private List<String> children; @BeanProp("c") // Custom property name public List<String> getChildren() { return children; } public Parent setChildren(List<String> children) { this.children = children; return this; } } // Child class with fluent setter override public class Child extends Parent { @Override public List<String> getChildren() { return super.getChildren(); } @Override public Child setChildren(List<String> children) { // Automatically inherits @BeanProp("c") from parent. // Property name remains "c" — no re-annotation needed. super.setChildren(children); return this; // Return type changed for fluent chaining } } If you want to override a method and use a different property name, re-annotate explicitly: public class Child extends Parent { @Override @BeanProp("childList") // Explicit new name takes precedence public Child setChildren(List<String> children) { super.setChildren(children); return this; } } See Also @BeanType Annotation - Class-level bean-modeling annotation. Java Beans Support - Overview of bean property detection.

In addition to the bean type name support, Juneau provides simplified support for bean subtypes via the @Marshalled(dictionary=…) attribute declared on a parent bean class. Bean subtypes are similar in concept to bean type names, with two convenience differences: You declare the list of possible subclasses through an annotation on the parent bean class, rather than registering them individually. You do not need to register the subtype classes on the bean dictionary of the parser — the parser discovers them from the parent class's dictionary.

In the following example, the abstract superclass declares its two concrete subclasses, and each subclass declares its _type name: // Abstract superclass declares its subtypes. @Marshalled( dictionary={A1.class, A2.class} ) public abstract class A { public String f0 = "f0"; } // Subclass 1 @Marshalled(typeName="A1") public class A1 extends A { public String f1; } // Subclass 2 @Marshalled(typeName="A2") public class A2 extends A { public String f2; } When serialized, the concrete subtype is emitted as a virtual _type property: A1 object = new A1(); object.f1 = "f1"; String json = Json5.of(object); assertEquals("{_type:'A1',f1:'f1',f0:'f0'}", json); When parsed back into the abstract type, the _type property is used to instantiate the correct concrete subclass: A object = Json.to(json, A.class); assertTrue(object instanceof A1);
The _type property name is the default type-discriminator key. It can be changed globally via MarshallingContext.Builder.typePropertyName(String), or per-class via @Marshalled(typePropertyName=…).
Bean Dictionaries — the general bean-dictionary mechanism. @Marshalled(typeName) Annotation — declaring type names.

The @BeanType annotation is applied to classes to control bean introspection and modeling. This is the model-side annotation in juneau-commons. It carries the attributes that describe the bean itself — which properties to include or exclude, how to name them, what stop class to use, and so on. Format-side concerns (wire format, type names, dictionary, interceptors, implementation class) live on @Marshalled in juneau-marshall. This split lets a class participate in the bean model without dragging in any marshalling concerns, and lets the bean-modeling layer live in juneau-commons independent of juneau-marshall. Migration Prior to the 10.0 refactor, @BeanType's members were part of @Marshalled. @BeanType (in org.apache.juneau.commons.bean) is now the correct annotation for all bean-modeling attributes listed below. The old @Bean annotation has been removed.

Bean property inclusion and ordering can be controlled using @BeanType(properties|p). // Address class with only street/city/state properties (in that order). // All other properties are ignored. @BeanType(properties="street,city,state") public class Address { ... } p is a shortened synonym for properties: @BeanType(p="street,city,state") public class Address { ... }

Bean properties can be excluded using @BeanType(excludeProperties|xp). // Address class with all properties except city and state. @BeanType(excludeProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } xp is a shortened synonym for excludeProperties: @BeanType(xp="city,state") public class Address { ... } Java Records Excluding record components is not supported during parsing. Because records are immutable, all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. Excluded components will be omitted from serialization output, but the parser will be unable to instantiate the record if the excluded component values are missing from the input.

Specifies one or more properties that are serialized normally but silently ignored during parsing. // city and state are serialized but not parsed. @BeanType(readOnlyProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } ro is a shortened synonym for readOnlyProperties.

Specifies one or more properties that are parsed normally but silently ignored during serialization. // city and state are parsed but not serialized. @BeanType(writeOnlyProperties="city,state") public class Address { ... } wo is a shortened synonym for writeOnlyProperties.

Bean properties are sorted alphabetically by default. To opt a specific bean out of this default sorting, use @BeanType(unsorted): // Opt this bean out of the default alphabetical property ordering. @BeanType(unsorted=true) public class MyBean { ... } Sorting can also be disabled globally for all beans via MarshallingContext.Builder.unsortedProperties(): WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .unsortedProperties() // disable sorting for all beans .build(); Or for individual classes without modifying the bean class itself: WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .unsortedProperties(MyBean.class) // disable sorting for MyBean only .build();

The @BeanType(propertyNamer) annotation is used to provide customized naming of properties. Property namers transform bean property names from standard form to some other form. For example, PropertyNamerDLC converts property names to dashed-lowercase, and these will be used as attribute names in JSON and element names in XML. // Define a class with dashed-lowercase property names. @BeanType(propertyNamer=PropertyNamerDLC.class) public class MyBean { ... }

The @BeanType(interfaceClass) annotation limits the properties of a bean to those declared on a specific interface class. When specified, only the list of properties defined on the interface class will be used during serialization. Additional properties on subclasses will be ignored. // Parent class @BeanType(interfaceClass=A.class) public abstract class A { public String f0 = "f0"; } // Child class public class A1 extends A { public String f1 = "f1"; } A1 a1 = new A1(); String result = Json5.of(a1); assertEquals("{f0:'f0'}", result); // Note f1 is not serialized. Note that this annotation can be used on the parent class so that it filters to all child classes. Or can be set individually on the child classes.

The @BeanType(stopClass) annotation limits which properties are included by halting class hierarchy traversal. It is identical in purpose to the stop class specified by Introspector.getBeanInfo(Class,Class). Any properties in the stop class or in its base classes will be ignored during analysis. For example, in the following class hierarchy, instances of C3 will include property p3 but not p1 or p2: public class C1 { public int getP1(); } public class C2 extends C1 { public int getP2(); } @BeanType(stopClass=C2.class) public class C3 extends C2 { public int getP3(); }

When true, fluent setters are detected as writable bean properties. @BeanType(findFluentSetters=true) public class MyBean { public int getId() { ... } public MyBean id(int id) { ... } // detected as fluent setter for "id" } Fluent setters must be public, non-static, take exactly one parameter, and return the bean itself.

Specifies a BeanFactory class to use for instantiating the bean instead of relying on a no-arg constructor or static getInstance() method. @BeanType(factory=MyBeanFactory.class) public class MyBean { ... }

Attributes that affect wire format — type names, dictionary, interceptors, implementation class, examples, and locale/timezone formats — live on @Marshalled (per-class) and @MarshalledConfig (bulk application via on/onClass on REST classes and methods). The interceptor attribute on @Marshalled can be used to intercept and modify bean getter and setter calls at the marshalling layer: // Interceptor that strips out sensitive information on Address beans. public class AddressInterceptor extends BeanInterceptor<Address> { @Override public Object readProperty(Address bean, String name, Object value) { if ("taxInfo".equals(name)) return "redacted"; return value; } @Override public Object writeProperty(Address bean, String name, Object value) { if ("taxInfo".equals(name) && "redacted".equals(value)) return TaxInfoUtils.lookup(bean.getStreet(), bean.getCity(), bean.getState()); return value; } } // Register interceptor on bean class. @Marshalled(interceptor=AddressInterceptor.class) public class Address { public String getTaxInfo() {...} public void setTaxInfo(String value) {...} }

When using @BeanType with Java records, note the following: @BeanType(properties) can be used to control property order, but all record components should be included. Omitting components will prevent parsing since all components must be provided to the canonical constructor. @BeanType(excludeProperties) will exclude components from serialization output, but excluded components will cause parsing to fail if their values are missing from the input. @BeanType(readOnlyProperties) will cause parsing to fail for the same reason. If you need to omit components during parsing, use @BeanCtor with a non-canonical constructor that provides defaults for the omitted components. See Also Java Beans Support - Overview of bean property detection. Java Records Support - Full documentation on Java records support.
The following guidelines help you get the most out of the Juneau marshalling APIs in terms of performance and maintainability.

Serializers and parsers are immutable and thread-safe, and they maintain internal caches of bean metadata. Reusing a single instance across requests (rather than rebuilding one per call) lets those caches do their job and avoids the cost of re-analyzing the same bean classes repeatedly. // Good — build once, reuse everywhere (e.g. a static field or injected singleton). static final JsonSerializer SERIALIZER = JsonSerializer.create().ws().build(); String json = SERIALIZER.write(myBean); The predefined DEFAULT instances (JsonSerializer.DEFAULT, JsonParser.DEFAULT, …) are already reusable singletons — prefer them when you don't need custom settings. When you do need a variant, use copy() on an existing instance so the derived instance shares the same construction path.

In general, JSON serialization and parsing is roughly 20% faster than XML, and JSON output is more compact. MessagePack is the fastest and most compact of the built-in formats — prefer it for high-throughput or bandwidth-sensitive machine-to-machine traffic where human readability isn't required. RDF has very different performance characteristics from the core marshallers — node traversal in RDF models is inefficient, so building tree structures out of large RDF graphs is comparatively slow. RDF is documented separately in the RDF section; the guidance on this page applies to the core juneau-marshall formats.
documents.s: Choose the right format for the job

documents.t: The MarshallingTraverseContext.Builder.detectRecursions() option adds a performance penalty of around 20% because every object on the traversal stack has to be checked for cycles. Enable it only when serializing models that can actually contain recursive references. See Non-Tree Models and Recursion Detection. The MarshallingContext.Builder.validateSchema() option validates bean property values against their @Schema-declared constraints during parsing and serialization. This adds per-property validation overhead and is disabled by default — turn it on only on the boundaries where you actually need input/output validation (typically inbound parsing), not on every internal marshalling operation.
documents.s: Enable optional features only when needed

documents.t: The Parser methods that take a ClassMeta parameter are slightly faster than the overloads that take a Class or Object, because the latter must perform a hash lookup to resolve the target type to its ClassMeta. On tight loops that repeatedly parse the same type, resolve the ClassMeta once (via BeanContext.getClassMeta(...)) and reuse it.
documents.s: Prefer ClassMeta parse overloads on hot paths

documents.t: For large collections or continuous feeds, don't build a giant in-memory POJO and serialize it in one shot. Juneau's streaming APIs let you emit or consume records one at a time with a bounded memory footprint — see Token & Record Streaming and Large-Dataset Streaming.
documents.s: Stream large datasets instead of buffering

documents.t: The MarshallUtils class provides concise static shortcuts (json(...), xml(...), msgPack(...), …) that are ideal for one-off serialization/parsing, tests, and scripts — especially with static imports. Because they delegate to the shared DEFAULT marshaller instances, they carry no extra construction cost. Reach for an explicit serializer/parser instance instead when you need custom settings (whitespace, quotes, swaps, dictionaries, etc.), since MarshallUtils always uses default configuration.
Marshallers — the marshaller API overview. Serializers and Parsers Token & Record Streaming

Entries can also be accessed as binary data. Binary data can be represented in 3 formats: Format Example BASE-64 (default) Zm9vYmFycw== Hexadecimal 666F6F62617273 Spaced hexadecimal 66 6F 6F 62 61 72 73 The binary data format is controlled via the following setting: Config.BuilderbinaryFormat(BinaryFormat) Example key = Zm9vYmFycw== byte[] bytes = config.get("key").asBytes().orElse(null); Binary lines can be split up into separate lines for readability: key = Zm9vYm Fycw== Binary data line wrapping can be controlled via the following setting: Config.BuilderbinaryLineLength(int)

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from BSON (Binary JSON) using native serializers and parsers. BSON is the binary serialization format used by MongoDB, extending JSON with typed integers (int32/int64), native datetime, decimal128, and binary data. It uses little-endian byte order and length-prefixed documents. The BsonSerializer converts POJOs directly to BSON format, and the BsonParser creates POJOs directly from BSON. BSON support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a bean to BSON Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); byte[] bson = Bson.of(alice); // Parse BSON into a bean Person parsed = Bson.to(bson, Person.class);

// Parse BSON into a bean Person p = Bson.to(bson, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Bson.to(bson, JsonMap.class); // Parse into a typed map Map<String, Object> m = Bson.to(bson, Map.class, String.class, Object.class); // Parse a list (root must be document; use wrapped {"value": [...]} for standalone arrays) List<Person> people = Bson.to(bson, List.class, Person.class);

// Use the default serializer byte[] bson = BsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience byte[] bson = Bson.of(someObject); // Custom serializer: write dates as ISO 8601 strings instead of BSON datetime BsonSerializer s = BsonSerializer.create().writeDatesAsDatetime(false).build(); byte[] bson = s.write(someObject);

Java Type BSON Type Notes Bean, Map Document (0x03) Nested structures Collection, array Array (0x04) Document with "0", "1", ... keys String, Enum String (0x02) int, short, byte Int32 (0x10) 4 bytes little-endian long Int64 (0x12) 8 bytes little-endian float, double Double (0x01) IEEE 754 Date, Calendar, Instant Datetime (0x09) When writeDatesAsDatetime=true Duration String ISO 8601 duration byte[] Binary (0x05) Subtype 0x00 BigDecimal, BigInteger Decimal128 (0x13) IEEE 754-2008 null Null (0x0A) Local java.time types with no instant (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, LocalTime, Year, etc.) are always written as ISO 8601 strings. BSON datetime has millisecond resolution, so sub-millisecond precision of Instant, OffsetDateTime and ZonedDateTime is truncated when writeDatesAsDatetime is true; use writeDatesAsDatetime(false) for lossless ISO 8601 output. BigDecimal / BigInteger values outside the Decimal128 range (34 significant digits, exponent -6176..6111) cannot be represented and fail with a SerializeException.

Instance Description BsonSerializer.DEFAULT / BsonParser.DEFAULT Default settings; raw BSON bytes. BsonSerializer.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX / BsonParser.DEFAULT_SPACED_HEX binaryFormat(SPACED_HEX). BsonSerializer.DEFAULT_BASE64 / BsonParser.DEFAULT_BASE64 binaryFormat(BASE64). The binary format setting only affects the stream-to-string conveniences (such as writeToString); the serializer always emits native BSON bytes from write(...).

Configured through BsonSerializer.create() (see BsonSerializer.Builder). Builder method Default Description addBeanTypesBson(boolean) false Add _type properties to beans whose type cannot be inferred through reflection. writeDatesAsDatetime(boolean) true Write Date / Calendar / Instant as BSON datetime (0x09); when false, write ISO 8601 strings. nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" Field name used for null map keys (BSON field names cannot be null). binaryFormat(BinaryFormat) NOT_SET Text rendering (SPACED_HEX, HEX, BASE64, BASE64_URL) used by string conveniences. The defaults can also be set with the BsonSerializer.addBeanTypesBson, BsonSerializer.nullKeyString and BsonSerializer.writeDatesAsDatetime environment settings.

Configured through BsonParser.create() (see BsonParser.Builder). Builder method Default Description nullKeyString(String) "<NULL>" A field with this name is stored with a null key in the target map. Must match the serializer value. trimStrings(boolean) false Trim whitespace from parsed string values (inherited from Parser). binaryFormat(BinaryFormat) NOT_SET Binary text-format hint (SPACED_HEX, HEX, BASE64, BASE64_URL); see BinaryFormat. BsonSerializer s = BsonSerializer.create() .writeDatesAsDatetime(false) .nullKeyString("~null~") .build(); BsonParser p = BsonParser.create().nullKeyString("~null~").build(); byte[] bson = s.write(someMap); Map<?,?> m = p.read(bson, Map.class);
Produces: application/bson Accepts: application/bson

// BSON support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated BSON-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } // RestClient with BSON RestClient client = RestClient.create().uri("http://localhost:8080").bson().build(); byte[] response = client.get("/api/data").bson().run().body();

Root must be a document: BSON requires a top-level document. Standalone scalars, collections, and arrays are wrapped as {value: x}. Map keys must be strings: Non-string keys use toString(). Null keys use a configurable placeholder. ObjectId is read-only: BSON ObjectId (0x07) is parsed as a 24-character hex string; Juneau does not generate ObjectIds. Deprecated types skipped: Undefined, DBPointer, Symbol, JS with Scope are silently skipped during parsing. MongoDB-internal types unsupported: JavaScript, Timestamp, MinKey, MaxKey are not supported.

@BsonConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Attributes are strings: Attribute Description addBeanTypes Add _type properties to beans whose type can't be inferred through reflection (default false). writeDatesAsDatetime Write Date/Calendar/Instant as the BSON datetime type (0x09); if false, write ISO-8601 strings. maxLength Maximum wire-declared length (bytes) for strings, binary payloads and document/array size prefixes when parsing; guards against malicious size prefixes. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @BsonConfig(writeDatesAsDatetime="true", maxLength="1048576") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Bson is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @BsonApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations). See Also BSON Specification for the full format definition. Marshallers for the marshaller API overview. MessagePack Basics for another binary JSON format.

This is the end-to-end tutorial for adding a page to an admin console built on Juneau: a resource that serves the chrome, a navigation tree, a sortable and searchable table backed by a server-side data endpoint, and a test that pins the page contract. The example is a pet inventory page; substitute your own bean. The reference pages cover each piece in depth. Read them when a step here raises a question. Admin-Console Chrome: directives, themes and the page contract. Rich Table Views: what a table card can do. DataTables Server-Side Processing and BeanQuery: the data endpoint.

The result looks like the petstore's pets page: the chrome's header and navigation around one table card fed by a server-side data endpoint. A console page is four cooperating parts: Part Provided by The chrome template (header, navigation, footer) <@console> and <@navigation> in one shared FreeMarker template. The page template (its cards) <@page> with one or more <@card> elements. The data endpoint A REST operation returning DataTablesResults<T>, backed by BeanQuery. The assets (CSS, JavaScript) The mixins ConsoleChromeMixin, ViewsMixin and DataTablesMixin. <@page> is the outermost directive in a page template. It captures its body (the cards), then includes the chrome template, which must contain <@console>. The server never renders the chrome as HTML; it writes a JSON page contract into the document and the shell script juneau-console.js draws the header, navigation, cards and footer in the browser.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-console-ui-freemarker</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-views</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-datatables</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The module table in Admin-Console Chrome explains what each one adds. juneau-rest-server-datatables is optional, but you need it for any server-mode table, which is the common case. juneau-rest-server-datatables also brings in the jQuery and DataTables WebJars.

The host resource composes every asset-serving mixin. Each one serves scripts and stylesheets relative to the resource's own path, so all of them must be on the resource that serves the page. @Rest( path="/console", mixins={ FreemarkerMixin.class, // renders .ftlh views ConsoleChromeMixin.class, // chrome.css, theme CSS, juneau-console.js ViewsMixin.class, // the views toolkit scripts and CSS DataTablesMixin.class, // juneau-datatables.js WebJarsMixin.class // /webjars/*: jQuery and DataTables } ) public class PetConsole extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean public FreemarkerMixin freemarker() { // Typed as FreemarkerMixin: the return type is load-bearing. return ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .chromeTemplate("console/chrome.ftlh") .build(); } @RestGet(path="/pets") public View pets() { return FreemarkerView.of("console/pets.ftlh"); } } Compose DataTablesMixin and WebJarsMixin A datatables card loads juneau-datatables.js (served by DataTablesMixin) and the jQuery and DataTables files (served by WebJarsMixin) before juneau-views.js. If either mixin is missing, those URLs 404 and the table fails loudly in the browser console. See Card Asset Dependencies. To set a theme for the whole console, build the mixin with ConsoleChromeMixin.create().theme("gray").build(), or pick one per page with <@console theme="gray">.
documents.s: Step 2: The host resource and its mixins

documents.t: One template holds the chrome and is shared by every page. It contains <@console> exactly once, with the navigation tree and <@main/>, which marks where each page's cards go. <#-- templates/console/chrome.ftlh --> <@console brand="Pet Store Console" chrome="true"> <@navigation> <@node id="catalog" label="Catalog" href="/console/pets"/> <@node id="orders" label="Orders" href="/console/orders"/> <@node id="admin" label="Admin" visible=user.admin> <@node id="users" label="Users" href="/console/users"/> </@node> </@navigation> <@main/> <@footer text="Pet Store"/> </@console> Node ids must match ^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]{0,63}$. Set visible= to a boolean to gate a node on a permission check. The page names its active node with <@page tab="catalog">.

<#-- templates/console/pets.ftlh --> <@page tab="catalog" toolkit="views"> <@card type="html">

Pets

<@card type="datatables" id="pets" title="Inventory"> { dataUrl: '/console/pets/data', dataMode: 'server', defaultOrder: [[0, 'asc']], columns: [ { key: 'name', label: 'Name', searchType: 'text' }, { key: 'status', label: 'Status', searchType: 'enum' }, { key: 'price', label: 'Price', searchType: 'numeric' } ] } toolkit="views" asks for the views toolkit pack. A datatables card also loads jQuery, DataTables and the glue, without any toolkit= entry. A datatables card requires an id, and its body is a JSON5 catalog with dataUrl and columns. Do not write a contract version in the catalog; the chrome stamps the current one. src= is the alternative to a body: it points the card at a resource instead of carrying inline content. The body is a JSON5 catalog only. A bare-URL body is rejected (E-25). The reserved card types are html, datatables, run-view, terminal, chart and job-log. See Chart Cards and Job-Log Card. Besides dataUrl and columns, the chrome passes these catalog keys through: copyLink, rowActions, rowClassRules and pausePollingWhileEditing onto the view, and selection and bulk onto the slot. See Catalog and Columns for every catalog key, the search types and the operator sets. Adopters can add their own card types. On the server, implement a CardTypeHandler and register it through ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.Builder.cardType(...) or META-INF/services. In the browser, call JuneauConsole.registerCard(type, {render}), or push onto window.JuneauConsoleCards before the shell loads. A PageSpec.card(...) card of your type runs the same handler: the card's body map (or the markup passed to card(spec, markup)) is the authored body, so the handler validates it and shapes the fragment as it does for <@card>, and a bad body fails the render with the same message.
documents.s: Step 4: The page template with a table card

documents.t: The table's dataUrl points at a REST operation that takes the DataTables request and returns results. It runs the request through BeanQuery. private final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Pet> ctx = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Pet.class).build(); @RestPost(path="/pets/data", parsers=JsonParser.class) public DataTablesResults<Pet> petData(@Content DataTablesRequest req) { try (var s = ctx.getSession(petService.all())) { return DataTablesQuery.run(req, s); } } Restrict the operation to JSON with parsers=JsonParser.class. DataTablesQuery.toBeanQuery lets you add a guard, such as a tenant filter, before the query runs. The full contract is in DataTables Server-Side Processing; the query language is in BeanQuery. Because the table posts JSON, the state-changing checks of the loopback boundary apply if you use it; see Security Model.

You do not write the script tags. The parts of the order you can rely on: The theme stylesheet comes first, then the CSS of any library packs, then css= stylesheets from <@page>, then the toolkit CSS and any <@theme> token overrides. Library packs that the cards need (for a datatables card: jQuery, DataTables, then the glue) load first. The toolkit pack scripts then load in the pack's fixed order: renders, icons, search, pagestate, urlstate (shareable-URL state and the View Settings Copy link button), ribbon, views, config, regions, helpers. Full list on JavaScript API. Any init= scripts from <@page> load after the toolkit scripts, in the order given, and <@scripts phase="after-toolkit"> content is placed immediately after the toolkit scripts. The console shell, juneau-console.js, mounts the cards from the page contract. It hands a datatables card to JuneauViews.regions.mount on DOMContentLoaded, so the views scripts may load after it. The load order is a contract: juneau-views.js must come before juneau-regions.js, and the library packs load before the toolkit. If you add your own scripts, list them in init= so they land after the toolkit.
documents.s: Step 6: What the page loads, and in what order

documents.t: Because the chrome exists only as the contract, assert on the contract rather than on rendered HTML. PageContractAssert lives in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.console.test and has no JUnit dependency. import static org.apache.juneau.rest.server.console.test.PageContractAssert.*; @Test void petsPage() throws Exception { var html = client.get("/pets").run().getContent().asString(); assertPage(html) .isValid() .hasActiveNav("catalog") .hasCard("pets", "datatables"); } Also lint your templates without rendering them: var findings = ConsoleTemplateValidator.create() .templateRoot(Path.of("src/main/resources/templates")) .chromeTemplate("console/chrome.ftlh") .validateAll(); assertTrue(findings.isEmpty(), findings::toString); Set ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create().devMode(true) while developing to validate every rendered contract against the schema.

A template mistake fails the render with an HTTP 500 and a message naming the directive and the fix. The usual ones: Symptom Cause 500, "<@card type=\"datatables\"> requires 'dataUrl' and 'columns'" The catalog is missing one of them. 500 naming the known paths <@page tab=...> names a node that is not in the navigation. 500, duplicate card id Two cards share an id. Blank table and a console warning about the DataTables glue The host does not compose DataTablesMixin or WebJarsMixin. .jc-console-error banner in the browser The contract failed a check in the shell, such as an unsupported page contractVersion or a missing template.

Add row actions, selection and bulk mutation: Row Actions and Bulk Mutation. Add row-detail panels or card bodies drawn by a function: Regions. Let users save and share table layouts: View Settings and Shareable Links. Restyle the console: the theme and token sections of Admin-Console Chrome.

The following URL parameters have special meaning and can be passed in through the URL of the request: GET Parameter Description &plainText=true Response will always be Content-Type: text/plain and the returned text will be human-readable (WriterSerializer.Builder.useWhitespace() enabled). Useful for debugging. &method=X Overload the HTTP method as a GET parameter (e.g. OPTIONS or HEAD). The name is matched case-insensitively and read from the query string only. On a safe request (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) the override is honored only for another safe method or an operation declared @RestOp(read=true); anything else is refused with 405. On a POST any admitted method is honored. Must be enabled via @Rest(allowedMethodParams) setting. &Header-Name=headerValue Specify a header value as a GET parameter (e.g. &Accept=text/json). Must be enabled via @Rest(allowedHeaderParams) setting. &content=X Pass in the HTTP body content on PUT and POST methods as a UON-encoded GET parameter (e.g. ?content=(name='John%20Smith',age=45)). Honored on PUT/POST only. Can be disabled via @Rest(disableContentParam) setting. &x-response-headers=X Pass-through headers to the response. Must be a UON-encoded map of key-value pairs. &juneauSerializerOptions=X Override serializer session options for this request. Must be a UON-encoded map; keys must be in the @Rest(allowedSerializerOptions) allowlist or the request fails with 400 Bad Request. &juneauParserOptions=X Override parser session options for this request. Must be a UON-encoded map; keys must be in the @Rest(allowedParserOptions) allowlist or the request fails with 400 Bad Request. note Earlier releases documented &debug=true and &noTrace=true URL parameters. These no longer exist. Request debugging is now driven by the JUL logger level (see Logging / Debugging), and the /echo endpoint must be enabled explicitly via EchoMixin.

The following methods can be used to bulk-load configuration values: ConfigsetSection(String,List,Map)load(Map)load(Reader,boolean)load(String,boolean) Changes can then be committed using the Config.commit() method.

Juneau serializers treat instances of Readers and InputStreams special by simply serializing their contents directly to the output stream or writer. This allows you to embed fully customized serializer output. public class MyBean { // A bean property that produces raw JSON. public Reader f1 = new StringReader("{'foo':'bar'}"); } // Produces "{f1:{'foo':'bar'}}" String json = Json5.of(new MyBean()); Note that if you're serializing Readers and InputStreams, it's up to you to make sure you're producing valid output (in this case JSON). A more typical scenario where this is useful is by using swaps to convert POJOs to Readers whose contents are determined via the MarshallingSession.getMediaType() method. In the following example, we're customizing the JSON output for a particular bean type but leaving all other renditions as-is: @Swap(MyBeanSwapSometimes.class) public class MyBean {...} // A swap that produces specialized output for JSON but default serialization for // all other media types. public class MyBeanSwapSometimes extends ObjectSwap { public Object swap(MarshallingSession session, MyPojo object) throws Exception { MediaType mediaType = session.getMediaType(); if (mediaType.hasSubType("json")) return new StringReader("{myPojo:'foobar'}"); // Custom JSON output return object; // Otherwise serialize it as a normal bean } } warning Due to the nature of the RDF serializers, Readers and InputStreams are serialized as literals, not as RDF text. This is due to the fact that the RDF serializers use a DOM for serialization so we don't have access to the underlying stream.

A console card can need scripts and stylesheets beyond the views toolkit. A datatables card needs jQuery, DataTables and Juneau's glue script. The card declares that need, and <@page> loads each asset once, in dependency order, after the body has rendered.

A toolkit pack is a named list of CSS and JS assets. A pack can depend on other packs, and it has a kind: VENDOR packs are libraries and their glue. Their CSS comes before the page css=, and their JS comes before every runtime script. RUNTIME packs are Juneau UI runtimes. They keep the position the views pack always had. Pack Kind Loads Depends on jquery VENDOR jquery.min.js (WebJar org.webjars:jquery) datatables VENDOR dataTables.min.js, dataTables.dataTables.min.css (npm WebJars datatables.net, datatables.net-dt) jquery datatables-glue VENDOR juneau-datatables.js (served by DataTablesMixin) datatables datatables-buttons VENDOR dataTables.buttons.min.js, buttons.html5.min.js, buttons.dataTables.min.css datatables views RUNTIME the views runtime calendar RUNTIME juneau-calendar.js, juneau-calendar.css xterm VENDOR xterm.js, xterm.css (npm WebJar @xterm/xterm) terminal RUNTIME juneau-terminal.js, juneau-terminal.css (served by TerminalMixin) views, xterm charts RUNTIME juneau-charts.js (served by ConsoleChromeMixin) joblog RUNTIME juneau-joblog.js (served by ConsoleChromeMixin) datatables-buttons gives copy and CSV export. Excel and PDF export need JSZip and pdfmake, which aren't included; register your own pack for them (below).

<@page> loads the packs in toolkit=, plus the packs its cards require: Card Requires type="datatables" datatables-glue, plus joblog when its detail.region is a job-log region type="html" nothing type="run-view" nothing extra (its runtime ships in the views pack) type="terminal" terminal (which pulls in views and xterm) type="chart" charts type="job-log" joblog A card adds more with requires=: <@card type="datatables" id="rel" requires="datatables-buttons">{ ... }</@card> A card type can also require packs from the card's body: a CardTypeHandler overrides requiredPacks(JsonMap body) (empty by default), and the page unions what it returns with the type's packs and requires=. That is how a datatables card with a job-log detail region gets joblog without a requires=. requires= takes a comma-separated string or a sequence. An unknown pack name fails the render with a 500 that names the card. Each pack loads after the packs it depends on, and each asset loads once, however many cards need it. Markup outside a card records nothing. jcHasToolkit reports only toolkit=.

Compose WebJarsMixin (from juneau-rest-server) into the resource that serves the page. It serves /webjars/* from the classpath with a one-year immutable Cache-Control, and the URLs carry the WebJar version. juneau-rest-server-datatables brings the WebJars in as dependencies. @Rest(mixins={FreemarkerMixin.class, ViewsMixin.class, DataTablesMixin.class, WebJarsMixin.class}) public class PetConsole extends BasicRestServlet { ... } If the host doesn't compose WebJarsMixin, the library URLs 404 and the table doesn't start.

All of this is on ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.Builder, and build() checks it: an unknown pack name, a cycle, or a VENDOR pack that depends on a RUNTIME pack fails the build. ConsoleFreemarkerMixin.create() .registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack.create("datatables-export") .js("/app/jszip.min.js", "/app/pdfmake.min.js", "/app/vfs_fonts.js") .dependsOn("datatables-buttons") .kind(ToolkitPack.Kind.VENDOR) .resolver((req, path) -> req.getUriResolver().resolve("servlet:" + path)) .build()) .cardRequires("datatables", "datatables-export") // every datatables card .providedPacks("jquery") // the chrome already loads jQuery .build(); registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack) adds a pack. A pack with a built-in name replaces it, including its dependencies, so registerToolkitPack(ToolkitPack.create("datatables")...) swaps in your own DataTables build. The (name, css, js) form registers a RUNTIME pack with no dependencies. cardRequires(type, packs...) adds packs to every card of a type. providedPacks(names...) names packs your chrome already loads. A provided pack loads nothing; its dependencies still load unless they're provided too. If a page already loads a file through init= or css=, a pack asset with the same file name is skipped, and the log gets a WARN naming the template. A copy loaded through init= is not a bridge: it is skipped only when the file name matches, and the pack's other assets still load. An app that has its own copies of the libraries names the packs in providedPacks(...), or mounts WebJarsMixin and lets the packs load them.

<@head phase="before-page-css">, then VENDOR CSS, then the page css=, then RUNTIME CSS. juneau-console.js, then VENDOR JS (for a datatables card: jQuery, DataTables, juneau-datatables.js), then RUNTIME JS, then <@scripts phase="after-toolkit">, then init=.
Building a Console Page Admin-Console Chrome Rich Table Views DataTables Server-Side Processing

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from CBOR (Concise Binary Object Representation) per RFC 8949 using native serializers and parsers. CBOR is a compact binary format designed for extremely small code size, very small message size, and extensibility. It is widely used in IoT, constrained environments, COSE (CBOR Object Signing and Encryption), and WebAuthn. The CborSerializer converts POJOs directly to CBOR format, and the CborParser creates POJOs directly from CBOR. CBOR shares the same data model as JSON: maps, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, and null. Compared to MsgPack, CBOR follows a different specification (RFC 8949) with different encoding rules and a larger ecosystem (IETF standards, COSE, WebAuthn). CBOR support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a bean to CBOR Person alice = new Person("Alice", 30); byte[] cbor = Cbor.of(alice); // Parse CBOR into a bean Person parsed = Cbor.to(cbor, Person.class);

// Parse CBOR into a bean Person p = Cbor.to(cbor, Person.class); // Parse into a map JsonMap map = Cbor.to(cbor, JsonMap.class); // Parse from InputStream try (InputStream is = new FileInputStream("data.cbor")) { Person p = Cbor.to(is, Person.class); }

// Use the default serializer byte[] cbor = CborSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience byte[] cbor = Cbor.of(someObject); // Serialize to OutputStream try (OutputStream os = new FileOutputStream("data.cbor")) { Cbor.of(someObject, os); }

Java Type CBOR Encoding Notes Bean, Map Map (major type 5) Nested structures Collection, array Array (major type 4) Definite-length String, Enum Text string (major type 3) UTF-8 int, long (positive) Unsigned integer (major type 0) Compact encoding int, long (negative) Negative integer (major type 1) -1-n encoding float Float32 (0xFA) IEEE 754 single double Float64 (0xFB) IEEE 754 double boolean Simple value 20/21 (0xF4/0xF5) null Simple value 22 (0xF6) byte[] Byte string (major type 2) Native binary Date, Instant, etc. Text string ISO 8601 Duration Text string ISO 8601 duration

For debugging and text-based transport, CBOR provides SpacedHex and Base64 variants: // Spaced-hex output: "A2 61 78 01 61 79 02" String hex = CborSerializer.SpacedHex.DEFAULT.write(bean); JsonMap parsed = CborParser.SpacedHex.DEFAULT.read(hex, JsonMap.class); // Base64 output String b64 = CborSerializer.Base64.DEFAULT.write(bean); JsonMap parsed = CborParser.Base64.DEFAULT.read(b64, JsonMap.class);
Produces: application/cbor Accepts: application/cbor
// CBOR support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated CBOR-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

BigInteger/BigDecimal: Cast to long/double; precision loss for values exceeding range. Use ObjectSwap for string serialization if needed. Indefinite-length: Parser does not support indefinite-length arrays/maps from external producers. Half-precision float: Serializer always uses float32/float64; parser accepts float16 from external producers. Semantic tags: Parser ignores tag numbers; tagged value is parsed normally. Tag output deferred to future release.

CBOR is a FULL-capability streaming format. The CborParser implements TokenReadable and ArrayRecordReadable; the CborSerializer implements TokenWritable and ArrayRecordWritable. This means you can read and write CBOR using fine-grained structural token cursors in O(1) memory, without materializing the entire document. // Read CBOR tokens one at a time try (TokenReader r = CborParser.DEFAULT.readTokens(cborBytes)) { while (r.next() != TokenType.END_OF_STREAM) { // inspect r.getCurrentToken(), r.getString(), etc. } } // Write CBOR tokens directly ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); try (TokenWriter w = CborSerializer.DEFAULT.writeTokens(baos)) { w.startObject(); w.fieldName("name"); w.string("Alice"); w.endObject(); } See Token-Streaming Basics for the full capability matrix and API overview, Token Streaming for the TokenReader/TokenWriter API, and Array-Record Streaming for element-by-element streaming over top-level arrays (CBOR uses indefinite-length arrays on write, so the array-record writer needs no element count).

@CborConfig sets serializer/parser properties on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Attributes are strings: Attribute Description addBeanTypes Add _type properties to beans whose type can't be inferred through reflection (default false). useTags Use CBOR semantic tags for dates and other typed values (default false). maxLength Maximum wire-declared length for byte/text strings and array/map element counts when parsing. rank Ordering relative to other config annotations. @Rest @CborConfig(useTags="true", maxLength="1048576") public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Cbor is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @CborApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations).
RFC 8949 (CBOR) Cbor marshaller org.apache.juneau.marshall.cbor package

A chart card draws a line, bar or donut chart from rows of JSON. Juneau draws it as inline SVG with no third-party chart library. The script is juneau-charts.js, and <@page> loads it for you when a page has a chart card.

<@card type="chart" id="orders-trend" title="Orders" src="/console/store/stats/daily"> { kind: 'line', x: { field: 'day', label: 'Day' }, series: [ { field: 'placed', label: 'Placed' }, { field: 'delivered', label: 'Delivered', tone: 'ok' } ] } </@card> The endpoint returns an array of flat rows, or an object with a rows array: [ { "day": "Mon", "placed": 3, "delivered": 1 }, { "day": "Tue", "placed": 5, "delivered": 2 } ] From Java, build the same card with ChartDef: page.card(ChartDef.line("orders-trend").title("Orders").src("/console/store/stats/daily") .x("day", null, "Day") .series("placed", "Placed") .series("delivered", "Delivered", "ok") .toCardSpec());

Kind Needs Options line x, one or more series y, legend, height bar x, one or more series stacked, orientation: 'horizontal', y, legend, height donut label, value center ('total' or literal text) x is a field name, or { field, type, label } where type is category, time or number. A series is a field name, or { field, label, tone }. A tone is danger, ok or warning, or a palette index from 1 to 8; colors come from the --jc-chart-1 to --jc-chart-8 theme properties when a theme sets them. A donut folds two or more slices under 2% into one "Other" slice.

Key Meaning src= / data Exactly one. data is an inline array of rows. refreshMs Re-fetch src= every N ms, at least 5000; needs src= (inline data never refreshes). If a refresh fetch fails, the last chart stays, dimmed, and polling continues. height Plot height in pixels, at least 120 (default 240). legend bottom (default), right or none. emptyText Shown when there are no rows (default "No data."). onClick.href A same-origin path template (no scheme, no // prefix, no .. segment); {field} is replaced with the clicked row's URL-encoded value. A cross-origin href fails the page in Java (ChartDef and the card check); if one still reaches the browser, juneau-charts.js logs E-JS-79 and ignores the click. Clicking a point, bar or slice fires a juneau:chart-click event with detail = { card, row, series } (series is null for the built-in kinds), whether or not onClick.href is set. (A donut's folded "Other" slice stands for several rows, so it doesn't click.)

A chart can follow a table on the same page through the params subscription role. The chart's src= carries a {token}, the subscription maps a field of the published payload to that token, and the chart re-fetches whenever the payload changes. A datatables card publishes filter:<id> with the search box text in search, so this chart follows the search box of the table changes: <@card type="datatables" id="changes" title="Changes"> { dataUrl: '/api/changes', columns: [ { key: 'id' }, { key: 'owner' } ] } </@card> <@card type="chart" id="byOwner" title="Open changes by owner" src="/api/changes/by-owner?q={q}" subscribes=[{"topic": "filter:changes", "as": "params", "map": {"q": "search"}}]> { kind: 'bar', x: 'owner', series: [ { field: 'open', label: 'Open' } ] } </@card> From Java, wire the card you get from toCardSpec(); ChartDef itself rejects subscribes because wiring is card-level: page.card(ChartDef.bar("byOwner").title("Open changes by owner").src("/api/changes/by-owner?q={q}") .x("owner").series("open", "Open") .toCardSpec() .subscribes(Subscription.to(Topics.filter("changes")).as("params").map("q", "search"))); Until the first payload arrives, the chart waits instead of fetching a URL with an unfilled {q}. params is the only role a chart accepts: a chart does not publish, and any other as: value on a chart subscription fails the page (E-44 in Java, E-JS-47 in the browser).

The chart is an SVG with role="img", or role="group" when the card is clickable (onClick.href is set, so the marks inside it are interactive). Either way it is labelled through aria-labelledby by a caption that summarizes it, for example "Line chart, 2 series, 7 points, Day from 'Mon' to 'Sun'", so a screen reader reads the summary once. The legend swatches are decorative, and the legend lists each series (or slice) by name. A Show data button (it becomes Hide data, and reports aria-expanded) reveals the same rows as a table, which is the accessible alternative to the drawing. Keyboard focus applies only when onClick.href is set. Then each point (line and bar) or slice (donut) is a focusable role="button" with a label such as "Mon: Placed 3, Delivered 1". On a line or bar chart the points form one tab stop and the arrow keys move between them; on a donut each slice is its own tab stop and the arrow keys do nothing. Enter or Space follows the link. Without onClick.href the marks are not focusable and not buttons; use the data table instead. If a refresh cannot redraw the chart (the renderer throws, or a series field has disappeared from the rows), the card shows the error once as an alert, polling stops, and the card fails. A refresh whose fetch fails keeps the last chart, dims it, and tries again on the next tick.

JuneauCharts.register("spark", function (plot, rows, card, c) { const svg = c.svg(plot); // draw with c.node(svg, tag, cls, attrs), c.scaleLinear(...), c.tone(series, i) return { update(rows) { /* redraw */ }, destroy() { /* clean up */ } }; }); A script that loads before juneau-charts.js can queue its kinds instead: (window.JuneauConsoleCharts = window.JuneauConsoleCharts || []).push(["spark", renderer]);. A kind name is lowercase letters, digits and hyphens, starting with a letter, at most 32 characters (^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,31}$); ChartDef and the card check reject any other name. A card whose kind isn't registered yet waits; if the kind still isn't there when the page has loaded, the card shows E-JS-60.

Code When E-JS-60 The card's kind is not registered. E-JS-62 The src= fetch failed. On a refresh the error is only logged and the last chart stays, dimmed. E-JS-63 A series field is missing from the rows. E-JS-64 A kind was registered twice. E-JS-75 refreshMs was below 5000; the minimum is used. E-JS-79 onClick.href resolved to a URL that isn't same-origin. E-JS-80 A kind's renderer threw. It is shown once; a failed refresh also stops polling. Java checks the card body when the page renders: a missing or malformed kind, both or neither of src= and data, a line or bar without x and a series, a series with no field, a donut without label and value, refreshMs below 5000 (or without src=), height below 120, and an onClick.href that isn't a same-origin path all fail the page.

Child Resources are REST servlets or objects that are linked to parent resources through the @Rest(children) annotation. Example /** Parent Resource */ @Rest( path="/parent", children={MyChildResource.class} ) public MyRootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup {...} /** Child Resource */ @Rest( path="/child" // Path relative to parent resource. ) // Note that we don't need to extend from RestServlet. public MyChildResource extends BasicRestResource {...} The path of the child resource gets appended to the path of the parent resource. So in the example above, the child resource is accessed through the URL /parent/child. One advantage of using child resources is that they do not need to be declared in the JEE web.xml file. Initialization of and access to the child resources occurs through the parent resource. Children can be nested arbitrary deep to create complex REST interfaces with a single top-level REST servlet. As explained earlier, child REST objects typically extend from BasicRestResource or BasicRestResourceGroup and not from one of the servlet classes. They also technically don't even need to extend from those classes and can instead just be a normal class annotated with the bare-minimum @Rest and @RestOp annotations.

In addition to declaring children statically via @Rest(children=…), parent resources that extend BasicRestServletGroup or BasicRestResourceGroup can add and remove child resources at runtime. This is useful for plug-in architectures, integration tests, and other scenarios where the set of mounted endpoints is not known ahead of time. The convenience methods on the group classes delegate to RestChildren, which holds children in a thread-safe, copy-on-write snapshot — reads on the request hot path are lock-free, while mutations are serialized through a write lock. Example @Rest(path="/root") public class MyServer extends BasicRestServletGroup {} @Rest(path="/alpha") public class AlphaChild extends BasicRestResource { @RestGet("/ping") public String ping() { return "alpha-pong"; } } var server = new MyServer(); // ... bootstrap into Jetty / Spring Boot / MockRestClient ... // Add by class — path is derived from the child's @Rest(path) annotation. server.addChild(AlphaChild.class); // Add by instance — useful when the child is hand-constructed or comes from a bean store. var beta = new BetaChild(); server.addChild(beta); // Add with an explicit path override. server.addChild("/gamma", new AlphaChild()); // Remove by path or by class. server.removeChild("/alpha"); server.removeChild(AlphaChild.class); // Inspect what is currently mounted. var keys = server.getChildResources().asMap().keySet();

Method Description addChild(Class<?>) Instantiate from the bean store (or via no-arg constructor) and mount at the child's @Rest(path). addChild(Object) Mount an existing instance at the child's @Rest(path). addChild(Object, boolean replace) Same as above but, when replace=true, atomically destroys any existing child mounted at the same path. addChild(String path, Object) Mount an existing instance at an explicit path, ignoring any @Rest(path) on the resource. addChild(String path, Object, boolean replace) Explicit-path variant with replace semantics. removeChild(String path) Remove the child mounted at the given path. Returns the removed RestContext (or null). removeChild(Class<?>) Remove the child whose resource is an instance of the given class. Returns the removed RestContext (or null). getChildResources() Returns the underlying RestChildren for direct inspection.

When a child is added, its @RestInit, @RestPostInit, and @RestPostInitChildFirst hooks run before addChild returns. When a child is removed, its @RestDestroy hooks run and the resource's Servlet.destroy() is invoked (if applicable) — including for any grandchildren mounted underneath. Mutations are atomic: route matching either sees the full pre-add state or the full post-add state, never a partially-mounted child. Adding a second child at the same path without replace=true throws IllegalStateException to prevent silent route shadowing.

By default, all children declared via @Rest(children=...) are constructed eagerly at parent startup. For resource trees with many rarely-touched children (admin panels, diagnostic endpoints, heavyweight integration bridges), this can add significant startup cost. The 10.0 lazy-children feature defers construction until first access.

@Rest( path="/root", lazyChildren="true", children={ HeavyAdminResource.class, DiagnosticsResource.class } ) public class RootResources extends BasicRestServletGroup {} Programmatic equivalent via AbstractRestBuilder: MyRest.builder().lazyChildInit(true).build();

Aspect Description URL matching Routing entries are registered immediately; URLs are reachable from the first request. Construction The full RestContext for each lazy child — including bean-store setup, lifecycle hooks, and memoizers — is built on the first inbound request to that child's URL prefix. Concurrency Concurrent first-requests to the same lazy child are serialized via double-checked locking. Only one thread runs construction; others block until it completes. Never-invoked children A lazy child that receives zero requests is never constructed. Its @RestDestroy / shutdown hooks are skipped at parent destruction time.

Large microservice trees: dozens of rarely-touched admin, debug, or compatibility endpoints that don't need to be materialized unless an operator actually navigates to them. Expensive integration children: a child that initializes a database connection pool or external API client only pays that cost on first use.

The first request to a lazy child pays the full construction cost, which can be significant for heavyweight children. If predictable first-request latency is required, do not opt in — keep the default eager behavior.

Children are deliberately isolated from the host's resolution chain (see Mixin-vs-child divergence) — a child's serializers, parsers, guards, call logger, etc. are resolved against the child's own RestContext only, never walked through the parent. @Rest(childrenDefs=@Child(...)) doesn't change that isolation; it gives the host an explicit, opt-in way to seed a curated set of settings onto a specific child's otherwise-isolated context, at the point the host declares it: @Rest( childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, callLogger = StructuredJsonLogger.class, guards = AdminBearerGuard.class) ) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/items") public List<Item> items() { ... } } AdminResource's endpoints now log through StructuredJsonLogger and require AdminBearerGuard — as declared by the host — without editing AdminResource itself and without those settings leaking into ApiResource's own /items resolution chain. childrenDefs is additive to and coexists with children: bare-class entries in children= and rich @Child entries in childrenDefs= are discovered together (bare entries first, then childrenDefs entries). A @Child(type=X.class) with no seed members is the exact equivalent of a bare children=X.class entry; if both name the same class, the rich entry wins (the bare entry is upgraded in place) — the same equivalence rule @Mixin establishes for mixins/mixinDefs.

Unlike a host @Mixin override — which wins over the mixin class's own declarations — a @Child seed can only add to or fill gaps in the child's own configuration. It never lets the child weaken or discard something the host imposed, and it never masks something the child explicitly declared for itself. Every seed member falls into exactly one of two buckets: Bucket Members Behavior Additive-security guards, converters, roleGuard, rolesDeclared The host's contribution is added alongside whatever the child declares — the child can never remove or weaken it. Child-wins scalars callLogger, partSerializer, partParser, debug, defaultCharset, maxInput The seed is a fallback/default. If the child's own @Rest chain explicitly declares the same setting, the child's value wins; the seed applies only when the child is silent. Additive-security, list-shaped (guards, converters) — PREPEND. The host-seeded entries run first (outermost), then the child's own declared entries. A seeded guard degrades to a plain "set" when the child declares no guards of its own, and the child's own guards/converters are never dropped: @Rest(path = "/admin", guards = AdminOwnGuard.class) // the child's own guard public class AdminResource { @RestGet(path = "/threads") public String threads() { ... } } @Rest(childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, guards = HostGateGuard.class)) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } A request to /admin/threads must satisfy both HostGateGuard (seeded, runs first) and AdminOwnGuard (the child's own, runs second) — neither is optional. Additive-security, role-based (roleGuard/rolesDeclared) — AND-STACK. A host-seeded roleGuard/rolesDeclared and the child's own explicit value both apply as independent, ANDed role checks, rather than one overriding the other. If the host seeds roleGuard="admin" and the child declares its own roleGuard="on-call", a request must satisfy both roles. Child-wins scalars — fallback only. If the child leaves partSerializer (or any other child-wins member) undeclared, the host's seeded value takes effect. If the child declares its own @Rest(partSerializer=...), the child's value wins outright and the seed is ignored for that property — same "does this property have an explicit value anywhere more-derived?" resolution the framework already uses everywhere else.
documents.s: The unifying principle: seeds never remove or override the child's own config

documents.t: defaultAccept and defaultContentType are not @Child seed members. They're resolved through the framework's shared default-request-headers mechanism (HttpHeaderList.setDefault(...)), which keeps the first value set while walking the annotation chain least-derived-first — independently of @Child, this already resolves in favor of the least-derived declaration in any class hierarchy. Seeding these two through @Child would therefore make the host's seed win over the child's own explicit value, the opposite of the child-wins contract every other scalar in this bucket honors. Rather than ship that contract violation, they're deferred until HttpHeaderList's first-wins resolution is revisited.

@Child itself has no noInherit() member — there's no inherited chain to cut in an isolated context. But a child's own @Rest(noInherit="<property>") does cut the corresponding host seed too, for any seedable property, additive-security or child-wins-scalar alike: @Rest(path = "/admin", noInherit = "guards") // opts out of the host's seeded guard entirely public class AdminResource { @RestGet(path = "/threads") public String threads() { ... } } @Rest(childrenDefs = @Child(type = AdminResource.class, guards = HostGateGuard.class)) public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } With noInherit = "guards" on AdminResource, HostGateGuard is not applied at all — the child stays fully in control, exactly as if the host had never seeded it. This falls out of the same generic noInherit cutoff the framework already applies uniformly to every @Rest property; there's no special-casing for seeded vs. non-seeded values.
A @Child seed survives deferred construction under @Rest(lazyChildren="true") — a lazily materialized child receives its seed on first request exactly as an eagerly-built child would.

REST Server — Children vs Mixins — the same-vs-different matrix for choosing children (isolation) vs mixins (inheritance). REST Server — Mixin Sub-Contexts — the inheritance-based alternative composition primitive, including the host-side @Mixin override this page's @Child section mirrors.

Juneau 10 ships two REST client stacks in the same release. Both are supported; they differ in which HTTP library they are built on and how much of the Juneau API surface they expose. Next-Generation (NG) client Classic client Maven artifact juneau-rest-client juneau-rest-client-classic Package org.apache.juneau.rest.client org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic HTTP library Pluggable transport; JDK HttpClient by default (no third-party dependencies) Apache HttpClient 4.5 only Extends HttpClient No Yes (implements org.apache.http.client.HttpClient) HTTP types org.apache.juneau.http.* org.apache.juneau.http.classic.* (HttpCore-based) Mock client org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.MockRestClient org.apache.juneau.rest.mock.classic.MockRestClient SSRF guard for @Remote / @Url Yes, with per-hop redirect re-validation (NG Security) Yes (classic guard classes) Stability Canonical; marked beta until the next major release Stable, unchanged from 9.x

You are starting a new project. You want zero third-party dependencies (the JDK HttpClient transport is the default), or you want to pick OkHttp, Jetty, or Apache HttpClient 4.5/5 per deployment without changing application code.
