The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: CsvParserDEFAULT

Target Type Parsing Strategy Collection<Bean> / Bean[] Header row → property names; each data row → one bean. Collection<Map> / Map[] Header row → map keys; each data row → one map. Collection<SimpleType> / SimpleType[] value column; each row → one value coerced to element type. Single Bean Header row + one data row → one bean. Single Map Header row + one data row → one map. Object Returns a JsonList of JsonMap entries (all values as strings).

Cell values are strings in CSV. The parser automatically coerces them to the target property/element type using the same type conversion machinery used by all Juneau parsers: Primitive types and their wrappers (int, long, double, boolean, etc.) String Enum types (by name) BigDecimal, BigInteger Date/time types (Date, Calendar, Temporal subtypes) — as ISO 8601 strings Duration — as ISO 8601 duration strings (e.g. PT1H30M) Any type whose ClassMeta supports convertToType(String)
The unquoted literal string null in a CSV cell is parsed as Java null. A quoted "null" cell is parsed as the Java String "null".

The parser handles all RFC 4180 quoted field constructs: "hello, world" → hello, world (comma inside quoted field) "line1\nline2" → line1\nline2 (newline inside quoted field) "say ""hi""" → say "hi" (doubled quotes → single quote)

By default, CSV columns that do not match any bean property are silently ignored (the ignoreUnknownBeanProperties parser setting applies). To throw on unknown properties, configure the parser: CsvParser p = CsvParser.create() .disableIgnoreMissingSetters() .build();

Object swaps registered on the parser are applied during cell value conversion: CsvParser p = CsvParser.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build(); List<Event> events = p.read(csv, List.class, Event.class);
CsvParser consumes input of media type text/csv.

The CsvSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into CSV. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderWriterSerializer.BuilderCsvSerializer.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: CsvSerializerDEFAULT

// Serialize a list of beans to CSV List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String csv = CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); // Creates a custom serializer CsvSerializer s = CsvSerializer.create() .swaps(DateSwap.class) .build(); String csv = s.write(people); // Use the Csv marshaller for convenience String csv = Csv.of(people);

Beans are serialized as a header row followed by one data row per bean: public class Person { public String name; public int age; } List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); name,age Alice,30 Bob,25 Maps are serialized using the keys of the first map as the header row: List<Map<String,Object>> rows = List.of( Map.of("city", "Seattle", "pop", 750000), Map.of("city", "Portland", "pop", 640000) ); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(rows); city,pop Seattle,750000 Portland,640000 Simple values are serialized with a single value column: List<String> values = List.of("alpha", "beta", "gamma"); CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(values); value alpha beta gamma

Values that contain commas, double-quote characters, or newlines are automatically enclosed in double quotes. Double-quote characters inside a quoted value are escaped by doubling them: List.of(new Person("Smith, John", 40)); // name contains a comma // Produces: name,age // "Smith, John",40 List.of(new Person("say \"hi\"", 40)); // name contains quotes // Produces: name,age // "say ""hi""",40

Java null is serialized as the unquoted literal null. A Java String with the value "null" is serialized as the quoted string "null" to distinguish it: new Bean(null, "null") // Produces: a,b // null,"null"
CsvSerializer produces output of media type text/csv.

The org.apache.juneau.marshall.csv package provides a fully-implemented CSV (Comma Separated Values) serializer and parser. CSV support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

CSV is an inherently tabular format: each row represents one entry and each column represents one field. Juneau models this as: Input type CSV output Collection<Bean> or Bean[] Header row = property names; one data row per bean. Collection<Map> or Map[] Header row = keys of the first map; one data row per map. Collection<SimpleType> or SimpleType[] Single value column header; one data row per value. Single Bean Header row + one data row. Single Map Header row + one data row.

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a list of beans to CSV List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String csv = CsvSerializer.DEFAULT.write(people); // Produces: // name,age // Alice,30 // Bob,25 // Parse it back List<Person> parsed = CsvParser.DEFAULT.read(csv, List.class, Person.class); Or use the convenience marshaller: String csv = Csv.of(people); List<Person> parsed = Csv.to(csv, List.class, Person.class);

The serializer and parser comply with RFC 4180: Fields containing commas, double-quote characters, or newlines are enclosed in double quotes. Double-quote characters inside a quoted field are escaped by doubling them ("" → "). Both CRLF and LF line endings are accepted on input. The Java null value serializes as the unquoted literal null.

Java null is serialized as the unquoted string null and is parsed back as Java null. A Java String with the value "null" is serialized as a quoted "null" to distinguish it. name,value null,"null" The first row's name cell parses back to Java null. The value cell parses back to the Java String "null".

Object swaps registered via .swaps(...) work exactly as with other Juneau serializers/parsers. Swap classes transform bean property values before serialization and unswap them during parsing. CsvSerializer s = CsvSerializer.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build(); CsvParser p = CsvParser.create().swaps(DateSwap.class).build();

@CsvConfig applies to both CsvSerializer and CsvParser on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Its only attribute today is rank. @Csv is a class/method/field marker (its only attribute is description), and @CsvApply applies it to other classes/members via on()/onClass() (see Dynamically Applied Annotations).
CSV Serializers CSV Parsers Token-Streaming Basics — CSV is a PARTIAL streaming format (record cursor only); a CSV row isn't a clean structural token sequence.

The RestCallHandler interface provides the ability to provide custom handling of requests. RestClient.BuildercallHandler(Class<? extends RestCallHandler>)RestCallHandlerrun(HttpHost,HttpRequest,HttpContext) Example // Our custom call handler. public class MyRestCallHandler implements RestCallHandler { private final RestClient client; public MyRestCallHandler(RestClient client) { this.client = client; } @Override public HttpResponse run(HttpHost target, HttpRequest request, HttpContext context) throws IOException { // Insert any special handling here. // The following is the default behavior: if (target == null) return client.execute((HttpUriRequest)request, context); return client.execute(target, request, context); } } // Create a client that uses our custom handler. RestClient client = RestClient .create() .json() .callHandler(MyRestCallHandler.class) .build(); Note that there are other ways of accomplishing this such as extending the RestClient class and overriding the RestClient.run(HttpHost,HttpRequest,HttpContext) method or by defining your own HttpRequestExecutor. Using this interface is often simpler though.

Setter methods that take in a Serializer can be used to provide custom serialization of entries instead of using the predefined serializer. // Set an XML value instead of JSON. config.set("key1", myAddress, XmlSerializer.DEFAULT_SQ_READABLE); key1 = 123 Main Street Anywhere NY 12345 The value can then be retrieved using the equivalent parser: Address myAddress = config.get("key1").as(XmlParser.DEFAULT, Address.class).orElse(null);
Custom error messages allow you to provide contextual information when BCT assertions fail. This makes test failures more informative and helps identify issues faster during debugging.

BCT supports custom error messages through a Supplier<String> parameter in all assertion methods. This provides: Lazy evaluation - Messages are only generated when assertions fail Format support - Use Shorts.fs() for convenient formatted messages with arguments Flexible composition - Combine custom messages with default assertion messages

// Simple static message assertBean(() -> "User validation failed", user, "email", "john@example.com"); // More descriptive context assertBean(() -> "Expected user to be active but was inactive", user, "isActive", "true"); // Test context information assertBean(() -> "Order status check for order #12345", order, "status", "PENDING");

The Shorts.fs() method provides a convenient way to create message suppliers with format arguments: import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; // Single placeholder String testName = "validateUser"; assertBean(fs("Test %s failed", testName), result, "status", "SUCCESS"); // Multiple placeholders String userName = "Alice"; int iteration = 5; assertBean(fs("User %s validation failed on iteration %s", userName, iteration), user, "isValid", "true"); // Contextual information String orderId = "ORD-123"; String expectedStatus = "COMPLETED"; assertBean(fs("Order %s expected status %s", orderId, expectedStatus), order, "status", expectedStatus);

// Lazy evaluation for expensive computation assertBean(() -> "Test failed at " + Instant.now(), user, "lastLogin", expectedTime); // Complex context information assertBean(() -> { return String.format("Test failed in %s on thread %s", Thread.currentThread().getName(), Thread.currentThread().getId()); }, result, "status", "SUCCESS"); // Conditional message generation assertBean(() -> { if (isDebugMode()) { return "Debug: Full stack trace available"; } else { return "Test failed - enable debug for details"; } }, user, "email", "john@example.com");

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testMultipleOrders() { List<Order> orders = getOrders(); for (int i = 0; i < orders.size(); i++) { Order order = orders.get(i); assertBean(fs("Order validation failed at index %s", i), order, "status,total", "PENDING,99.99"); } }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testUsersByRole() { Map<String, User> usersByRole = getUsersByRole(); for (Map.Entry<String, User> entry : usersByRole.entrySet()) { String role = entry.getKey(); User user = entry.getValue(); assertBean(fs("User validation failed for role: %s", role), user, "role,isActive", role + ",true"); } }
@Test void testOrderProcessing() { Order order = processOrder(); assertBean(() -> String.format("Order processed at %s, validation failed", LocalDateTime.now()), order, "status", "COMPLETED"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testConfiguration() { Config config = loadConfig(); String environment = System.getProperty("env", "unknown"); assertBean(fs("Config validation failed in environment: %s", environment), config, "database.host,database.port", "localhost,5432"); }

Use custom messages when: Testing in loops or with multiple iterations Test failures need additional context Debugging complex test scenarios Testing with dynamic or generated data Running tests in different environments Testing concurrent or parallel scenarios Avoid custom messages when: The test is simple and self-explanatory The assertion failure message is already clear Adding message overhead provides no value

Be specific: Include relevant context (IDs, names, indices) Be concise: Keep messages short but informative Include values: Add expected/actual values when helpful Add context: Include loop indices, test phases, environment info Use suppliers for expensive operations: Defer message generation until needed Avoid sensitive data: Don't include passwords, tokens, or PII in messages

// Bad - expensive computation always executed String heavyComputation = performExpensiveOperation(); assertBean(() -> "Test failed with: " + heavyComputation, user, "status", "ACTIVE"); // Good - computation only happens on failure assertBean(() -> "Test failed with: " + performExpensiveOperation(), user, "status", "ACTIVE");

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; // Set custom converter in @BeforeEach @BeforeEach void setUp() { var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); setConverter(converter); } // Use custom message with the converter assertBean(fs("Date validation failed for user %s", userId), user, "birthDate", "1990-01-15"); @AfterEach void tearDown() { resetConverter(); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @ParameterizedTest @ValueSource(strings = {"alice@example.com", "bob@example.com", "carol@example.com"}) void testUserEmails(String email) { User user = findUserByEmail(email); assertBean(fs("User validation failed for email: %s", email), user, "email,isVerified", email + ",true"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @TestFactory Stream<DynamicTest> testOrders() { return orders.stream() .map(order -> DynamicTest.dynamicTest( "Test Order #" + order.getId(), () -> assertBean( fs("Order %s validation failed", order.getId()), order, "status", "PENDING"))); }

org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: Order ORD-123 expected status COMPLETED Expected: COMPLETED Actual: PENDING

@Test void testOrderProcessing() { Order order = createOrder(); // Process order processOrder(order); // Validate with detailed context assertBean(() -> String.format( "Order validation failed:
" + " Order ID: %s
" + " Customer: %s
" + " Processing Time: %s
" + " Thread: %s", order.getId(), order.getCustomer().getName(), Duration.between(order.getCreatedAt(), Instant.now()), Thread.currentThread().getName() ), order, "status,isPaid,isShipped", "COMPLETED,true,true"); } Output on failure: org.opentest4j.AssertionFailedError: Order validation failed: Order ID: ORD-123 Customer: John Doe Processing Time: PT2.5S Thread: main Expected: COMPLETED Actual: PENDING

@Test void testUserLifecycle() { // Creation phase User user = createUser(); assertBean(() -> "User creation phase failed", user, "status", "NEW"); // Activation phase activateUser(user); assertBean(() -> "User activation phase failed", user, "status", "ACTIVE"); // Verification phase verifyUser(user); assertBean(() -> "User verification phase failed", user, "status,isVerified", "ACTIVE,true"); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testBatchProcessing() { List<Order> orders = loadOrders(); for (int i = 0; i < orders.size(); i++) { Order order = orders.get(i); processOrder(order); assertBean(fs( "Batch processing failed at index %s of %s, Order ID: %s", i, orders.size(), order.getId()), order, "status", "PROCESSED"); } }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.fs; @Test void testUserPermissions() { User user = loadUser(); String expectedRole = user.isAdmin() ? "ADMIN" : "USER"; assertBean(fs( "Permission check failed for %s user (expected role: %s)", user.isAdmin() ? "admin" : "regular", expectedRole), user, "role,hasAccess", expectedRole + ",true"); }

The ConfigStore API has been written to allow easy development of custom configuration storage classes. The example below shows a starting point for an implementation based on polling a relational database. The source can be found here: SqlStore. Completing it is left as an exercise: Example Store Class public class SqlStore extends ConfigStore { private final String jdbcUrl; private final String tableName, nameColumn, valueColumn; private final Timer watcher; private final ConcurrentHashMap cache = new ConcurrentHashMap(); protected SqlStore(ConfigStore.Builder builder) { super(builder); this.jdbcUrl = builder.jdbcUrl; this.tableName = builder.tableName; this.nameColumn = builder.nameColumn; this.valueColumn = builder.valueColumn; int pollInterval = builder.pollInterval; TimerTask timerTask = new TimerTask() { @Override public void run() { SqlStore.this.poll(); } }; this.watcher = new Timer("MyTimer"); watcher.scheduleAtFixedRate(timerTask, 0, pollInterval * 1000); } synchronized void poll() { // Loop through all our entries and find the latest values. for (Map.Entry e : cache.entrySet()) { String name = e.getKey(); String cacheContents = e.getValue(); String newContents = getDatabaseValue(name); // Change detected! if (! cacheContents.equals(newContents)) update(name, newContents); } } // Reads the value from the database. protected String getDatabaseValue(String name) { // Implement me! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public boolean exists(String name) { // Implement me! return false; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String read(String name) { String contents = cache.get(name); if (contents == null) { contents = getDatabaseValue(name); update(name, contents); } return contents; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized String write(String name, String expectedContents, String newContents) { // This is a no-op. if (StringUtils.eq(expectedContents, newContents)) return null; String currentContents = read(name); if (expectedContents != null && StringUtils.ne(currentContents, expectedContents)) return currentContents; update(name, newContents); // Success! return null; } @Override /* ConfigStore */ public synchronized SqlStore update(String name, String newContents) { cache.put(name, newContents); super.update(name, newContents); // Trigger any listeners. return this; } @Override /* Closeable */ public synchronized void close() { if (watcher != null) watcher.cancel(); } }

BCT provides flexible customization options through the @BctConfig annotation and the BctConfiguration class. These tools allow you to configure assertion behavior, customize property access, and extend BCT's capabilities to match your testing needs.
@BctConfig Annotation BctConfiguration Class Configuration Properties Custom Bean Converters Thread Safety Advanced Customization Topics

The @BctConfig annotation provides a declarative way to configure BCT settings for your tests. It can be applied at both the class level and method level, with method-level annotations taking precedence over class-level annotations.

import org.apache.juneau.test.bct.BctConfig; import org.apache.juneau.commons.lang.TriState; @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) void testSomething() { // sortMaps=true (from class), sortCollections=true (from method) assertBean(order, "items{0{name}}", "{{Laptop}}"); } }

Controls whether map entries are sorted by key before comparison in assertions. @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void testMap() { // Map entries will be sorted before comparison Map<String, String> map = Map.of("zebra", "animal", "apple", "fruit"); assertBean(map, "apple,zebra", "fruit,animal"); } } Values: TriState.TRUE - Enable map sorting TriState.FALSE - Disable map sorting TriState.UNSET - Inherit from class-level annotation (default for method-level)

Controls whether collection elements are sorted before comparison in assertions. @BctConfig(sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void testList() { // List elements will be sorted before comparison List<String> list = Arrays.asList("zebra", "apple", "banana"); assertList(list, "apple", "banana", "zebra"); } } Values: TriState.TRUE - Enable collection sorting TriState.FALSE - Disable collection sorting TriState.UNSET - Inherit from class-level annotation (default for method-level)

Specifies a custom bean converter class to use for all assertions in the test. public static class MyCustomConverter extends BasicBeanConverter { public MyCustomConverter() { super(BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, date -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build()); } } @BctConfig(beanConverter=MyCustomConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test void testWithCustomConverter() { // All assertions use MyCustomConverter assertBean(event, "date", "2023-12-01"); } } Requirements: The converter class must have a no-arg constructor The constructor will be made accessible if needed (for nested classes, etc.) If instantiation fails, the test will fail with a descriptive error message

Method-level annotations override class-level annotations for the same property. Properties not specified in the method annotation inherit from the class annotation. @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE, beanConverter=MyConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.FALSE, sortCollections=TriState.TRUE) void testMethod() { // sortMaps=false (from method, overrides class) // sortCollections=true (from method) // beanConverter=MyConverter (from class, inherited) } @Test void testAnotherMethod() { // sortMaps=true (from class) // sortCollections=UNSET (default, not set) // beanConverter=MyConverter (from class) } }

To explicitly use the default converter when a class-level converter is set, use BasicBeanConverter.class: @BctConfig(beanConverter=MyConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test @BctConfig(beanConverter=BasicBeanConverter.class) void testWithDefaultConverter() { // Uses default converter, not MyConverter } }
The BctConfiguration class provides a programmatic API for configuring BCT settings. It's useful when you need dynamic configuration or want to set up converters in test setup methods.

import static org.apache.juneau.test.bct.BctConfiguration.*; @BeforeEach void setUp() { // Enable map sorting set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Enable collection sorting set(BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS, true); // Set custom converter var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, date -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); set(converter); } @AfterEach void tearDown() { // Clear all thread-local settings clear(); }

// Get a setting with a default value boolean sortMaps = BctConfiguration.get(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Get a setting object (can check if set) StringSetting setting = BctConfiguration.get(BCT_SORT_MAPS); if (setting != null && setting.asBoolean()) { // Map sorting is enabled }

Settings can be set globally (affecting all threads) or thread-locally (affecting only the current thread). Thread-local settings take precedence. // Set global setting (affects all threads) BctConfiguration.setGlobal(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Set thread-local setting (overrides global for this thread) BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Clear thread-local settings BctConfiguration.clear(); // Clear global settings BctConfiguration.clearGlobal();

Property name: "Bct.sortMaps" When enabled, map entries are sorted by key before comparison, ensuring consistent assertion results regardless of map implementation or insertion order. BctConfiguration.set(BctConfiguration.BCT_SORT_MAPS, true);

Property name: "Bct.sortCollections" When enabled, collection elements are sorted before comparison, ensuring consistent assertion results regardless of collection implementation or insertion order. BctConfiguration.set(BctConfiguration.BCT_SORT_COLLECTIONS, true);
Bean converters control how objects are accessed and converted to strings for comparison. BCT uses BasicBeanConverter.DEFAULT by default, but you can provide custom converters for specialized needs.

public static class MyCustomConverter extends BasicBeanConverter { public MyCustomConverter() { super(BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() // Add custom stringifier for LocalDate .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) // Add custom stringifier for Money .addStringifier(Money.class, (conv,money) -> money.getAmount().toPlainString()) .build()); } }
@BctConfig(beanConverter=MyCustomConverter.class) class MyTest { @Test void testWithCustomConverter() { assertBean(order, "date,total", "2023-12-01,99.99"); } }

@BeforeEach void setUp() { var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addStringifier(LocalDate.class, (conv,date) -> date.format(DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE)) .build(); setConverter(converter); // BctAssertions.setConverter(...) - a thin passthrough to BctConfiguration.set(...) } @AfterEach void tearDown() { resetConverter(); // BctAssertions.resetConverter() - a thin passthrough to BctConfiguration.clear() }

Must have a no-arg constructor Constructor will be made accessible if needed (for nested classes, private constructors, etc.) If instantiation fails, a RuntimeException is thrown with a descriptive message

All configuration in BCT is thread-safe and uses thread-local storage. This ensures that: Parallel test execution doesn't interfere with each other's settings Each test thread has its own isolated configuration Settings are automatically cleared after each test when using @BctConfig
// Thread 1 BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, true); // Thread 2 (running in parallel) BctConfiguration.set(BCT_SORT_MAPS, false); // Each thread has its own setting - no interference

When using @BctConfig, settings are automatically cleared after each test method: @BctConfig(sortMaps=TriState.TRUE) class MyTest { @Test void test1() { // sortMaps is enabled } @Test void test2() { // sortMaps is still enabled (from class annotation) // But if test1 had method-level annotation, it would be cleared } }

For more advanced customization options, see: Stringifiers - Define how objects are converted to strings for comparison Listifiers - Convert collection-like objects to lists for testing Swappers - Transform objects before processing (unwrap Optional, Supplier, etc.)
Bean-Centric Testing Basics - Main BCT documentation Custom Error Messages - Enhanced error reporting Property Extractors - Custom property access logic

Several methods are provided for customizing the underlying HTTP client and client builder classes: RestClient.BuilderhttpClientBuilder(HttpClientBuilder) - Set the client builder yourself.createHttpClientBuilder() - Override to create the client builder.createHttpClient() - Override to create the client.createConnectionManager() - Override to create the connection management. Additionally, all methods on the HttpClientBuilder class have been extended with fluent setters. Example // Create a client with customized HttpClient settings. MyBean bean = RestClient .create() .disableRedirectHandling() .connectionManager(myConnectionManager) .addInterceptorFirst(myHttpRequestInterceptor) .build(); Refer to the HttpClientBuilder docs for more information.

juneau-rest-server-datatables is an opt-in add-on (not bundled in juneau-distrib, the same precedent as juneau-rest-server-management-logging) that wires a DataTables grid's server-side processing contract onto BeanQuery — the request/response envelope, the query-building rules, and a first-party browser glue script. DataTables itself, jQuery, and their CSS remain caller-provided: they are not vendored (their license is not ASF category-A). <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-datatables</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

A DataTables-backed endpoint takes @Content DataTablesRequest and returns DataTablesResults<T> (or DataTablesResults<List<Object>> for array rows — see "Array rows" below). DataTablesMixin serves the browser glue script; the resource's own data endpoint is plain @RestOp: @Rest(path="/releases", mixins=DataTablesMixin.class) public class ReleaseResource extends BasicRestServlet { private final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Release> ctx = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Release.class).build(); @RestOp(method=POST, path="/query") public DataTablesResults<Release> query(@Content DataTablesRequest req) { try (var s = ctx.getSession(releases())) { return DataTablesQuery.run(req, s); } } } Restrict the endpoint to JSON Declare parsers=JsonParser.class on the data endpoint, e.g. @RestPost(path="/query", parsers=JsonParser.class). Under BasicUniversalConfig a form-urlencoded body would otherwise also bind to DataTablesRequest, but JuneauDataTables.ajax only ever sends JSON. DataTablesQuery.run(req, session) builds a BeanQuery from the request (via the public DataTablesQuery.toBeanQuery(req, ctx), usable standalone if you need to inspect or adjust the query before running it — for example to add a tenant guard with query.copy().eq("tenant", id).build()), executes it against the session, and maps the Page result onto the DataTables envelope (recordsTotal/recordsFiltered/data). The caller owns the session, so the same adapter works over the in-memory engine or a SQL-backed one.

JuneauDataTables.ajax(url, extra?) builds a DataTables ajax option object that POSTs the DataTables draw state as a JSON body (not DataTables' default form-encoded request) — matching @Content DataTablesRequest. extra is shallow-merged over the defaults (except contentType, which is always application/json). An extra.data object is merged into the outgoing body, and an extra.data function receives the draw state and may mutate it or return a replacement object — useful for a CSRF token or an active-filter toggle, without rebuilding the whole ajax option yourself. Any top-level body property that is not part of the DataTables request — one merged in through extra.data, or one a DataTables extension adds (SearchBuilder's searchBuilder, SearchPanes' searchPanes) — does not fail the parse: it is collected into DataTablesRequest.getExtra(), where the handler can read it. The adapter itself ignores it, so those extensions have no server-side effect unless your handler applies them. The same goes for DataTables 2's search.fixed() terms: they are parsed (Search.getFixed()) but not applied. For a table that needs no extra wiring at all, skip the inline JuneauDataTables.initAll() (already wired into the page's auto-init pass) sees data-juneau-datatable-ajax on a table whose options carry no ajax key, defaults serverSide: true, and installs ajax: JuneauDataTables.ajax(url) for you. A table that relies on a instead of declared columns (for example a server-rendered DataTablesTable) makes DataTables send integer data values, so pair it with runArrays (see "Array rows"), and keep the header order identical to the context's columns() order.

Each DataTablesRequest.Column.data resolves against the context's declared columns (BeanQueryContext.columns(), in declaration order): data value Resolves to A declared column name That column, as-is. All digits (e.g. "2") The n-th declared column, 0-based. null or "" Always skipped — no error, regardless of searchable/orderable. A dotted path or an unknown name, on a column with a non-blank per-column search or an order[] entry BeanQuerySyntaxException: Unknown column 'name'. A dotted path or an unknown name, on a column that is only a candidate for the global search, or never used No error — resolution is lazy; the column is simply left out. A column with searchable: false is ignored for both per-column and global search, and a column with orderable: false is ignored for sorting. Two DataTables columns resolving to the same key are merged (search terms are ANDed; a duplicate sort key keeps its first occurrence).

A per-column search box (columns[i].search.value) is a raw BeanQuery search expression for that one column ($eq(...), $in(...), $contains(...), …), parsed exactly like a server-side BeanQueryRequest.search term for that column. The global search box (search.value) has no column context, so it expands to an $or of one leaf per searchable, resolvable column, chosen by that column's SearchType: SearchType Global-search leaf TEXT, ID $contains VERSION $prefix ENUM $eqic (case-insensitive exact match) NUMERIC $eq, only when the term parses as a decimal number BOOLEAN $eq, only when the term is true or false (case-insensitive) TIMESTAMP $eq, only when the term is an ISO-8601 instant (e.g. 2026-09-30T00:00:00Z) A NUMERIC, BOOLEAN or TIMESTAMP column whose type the term does not parse as is left out of the $or — it is never an error. Java-only numeric spellings such as 1d, NaN, Infinity and hex floats are not treated as numeric. If only one column is eligible the $or collapses to a single leaf, and if none is eligible the global search adds nothing. Every column type participates, not just text. Column and sort-key counts are capped by the context's getMaxSearchClauses()/getMaxSortKeys() (checked against columns.size() and order.size() before any column is resolved). Exceeding either cap is a BeanQuerySyntaxException — raise the cap on the BeanQueryContext if a table legitimately needs more columns or sort keys than the default allows. Paging maps start/length onto the query's page window: length=-1 means all rows, and a negative start is clamped to 0.

DataTablesQuery.runArrays(req, session) is the run sibling for a table whose columns[i].data are integers. The query's view is set to every declared column in BeanQueryContext.columns() order and each row is flattened to a List<Object> in that same order, so data: n and the n-th array cell refer to the same column.

A malformed request (an unknown column referenced by a search or sort, a cap exceeded, a bad search expression, a disallowed operator or restricted column) throws BeanQuerySyntaxException, which DataTablesQuery.run/runArrays let propagate. The central RestContext.convertThrowable mapping turns it into HTTP 400 with an X-BeanQuery-Error: <CODE> header and the exception's message in the body, the same as every other BeanQueryRequest endpoint. DataTablesResults.error(draw, message) and the response's error field remain available as public API but the adapter no longer uses them. On the client, JuneauDataTables.ajax installs an xhr.dt listener. When a request fails with a status of 400 or more and carries the X-BeanQuery-Error header, the listener reads the server's message from the response body (falling back to Invalid query (<status>).), fires DataTables' error.dt event and honors DataTable.ext.errMode (default: a browser alert; 'none', 'throw' or a function also work) instead of showing the generic "Ajax error". Other failures keep DataTables' default handling. An unexpected failure in your bean accessors or query execution (BeanQueryExecutionException) is not caught here; it propagates to the central RestContext.convertThrowable mapping (HTTP 500), the same as every other BeanQueryRequest endpoint. Counts are always requested as CountRequest.BOTH, but the context's own CountPolicy still wins. recordsTotal and recordsFiltered are the long forms of the session's Page.total()/Page.matched(); when a count is absent, recordsFiltered is left unset and recordsTotal falls back to Page.matched() if that is present. DataTables' own protocol has no concept of an absent count, so there is no CountPolicy opt-out at this layer.

BeanQuery — the query bean, builder, and session this adapter sits on top of. Admin-Console Chrome — <@card type="datatables"> (see Building a Console Page) renders a DataTablesTable, and (server-side mode) wires the same data-juneau-datatable-ajax attribute this page describes. Worked example: the petstore Pets page (a server-mode table over BeanQuery) and Audit page.

The View Settings dialog lets a user tailor a datatable view (the juneau-rest-server-views table card) and keep those choices across reloads. This page covers the dialog's tabs, how settings persist and are applied, the Sort tab, auto-refresh, the per-column search announcer and the Copy link button. For the catalog keys that configure a view see Rich Table Views; for the page-state store and the ?state= URL codec see View Settings and Shareable Links.

The dialog has four tabs: View (columns: visibility, order, label, format), Search (which columns take part in the search box), Sort and Options. The tabs follow the WAI-ARIA tabs pattern: each tab carries aria-selected and aria-controls, only the active tab is in the Tab order, and Left, Right, Home and End move between tabs. Every per-row control (visible, move up/down, label, format and so on) has an aria-label that names its column.

A view can show fewer tabs with columnConfig.tabs in its catalog: { "columnConfig": { "tabs": ["columns", "sort"] } } The names are columns, search, sort and options; columns is the tab shown on screen as View. An empty or unknown list falls back to all four tabs. Settings that belong to a hidden tab are not read from, applied from or written to the stored settings for that view.

Apply writes one settings blob per table into the page-state store (browser localStorage by default). The blob carries a schemaVersion, currently 2. When the stored blob has a different (older, newer or missing) schemaVersion, or the sort is in the old string-array form, the runtime deletes it, falls back to the catalog defaults and shows a one-time notice ("your saved settings were reset"). It never tries to migrate a blob it does not recognise. A stored blob is used only by tables whose catalog has columnConfig; it is ignored for any other table.

Stored settings take effect when the page loads, not only when the dialog is opened. On the first draw the runtime restores the View (visible columns, order, labels, formats), Search membership, Sort, and the Options (page size, wrap, density, auto-refresh), each gated on the tabs the view exposes. A column a user hid stays hidden after a reload, in both client and server data modes. The dialog itself opens seeded from the restored settings, so pressing Apply without touching anything does not overwrite them with the catalog defaults.

The Sort tab is an ordered priority list. Each entry names a column and a direction (Asc or Desc); the first entry is the primary sort key. The draft starts from the view's defaultOrder, so an untouched Apply keeps the default order instead of persisting an ascending sort over every column. Sort is stored as a list of {column, direction} entries.

Besides page size, wrap and density, the Options tab has an Auto-refresh choice: Off (the default), 30 seconds, 1 minute, 5 minutes or 15 minutes. It is stored as autoRefreshMs (0 for Off), and a blob written before the option existed reads as Off. Auto-refresh re-draws the table from the server using the same path as the manual refresh. It does not run while: the View Settings dialog is open, a row-detail region is open, a request is already in flight, or the browser tab is hidden. The timer is cleared when the table is torn down or re-initialised. Behavior change The suspension check used by polling, isPollSuspended, now also returns true while the View Settings dialog is open. A view declared with pausePollingWhileEditing therefore pauses its polling while the dialog is open.

Every header cell of a searchable column has a search icon that opens a small popover (it replaces the old ribbon-level columnSearchToggle button). The popover shows a one-line help text for the column's SearchType. The table has a polite aria-live region that announces results to screen readers. When the popover is dismissed with text that has not been applied, it announces "Search for 'x' not applied." so the typed text is not lost silently.

The Copy link button sits beside the settings gear. It copies the shareable ?state= URL described in View Settings and Shareable Links and announces "Link copied." or, if the clipboard is unavailable or denied, "Could not copy link." The button is shown when the table is primary: true, or when it is the only top-level view table on the page. Set primary: false to hide it for a table, or copyLink: false to hide only the button. It is not rendered when juneau-urlstate.js is not loaded. When a page opens with ?state=, the tab is found by matching the value against the data-juneau-strip-tab attribute of the page's tab elements; a value that matches no tab is ignored.
Rich Table Views and its JavaScript API 10.66 DataTables Server-Side Processing v10.0 Migration Guide for the breaking changes to columnSearchToggle, schemaVersion and readViewSettings

juneau-rest-server-widgets is a small, optional module of declarative widget beans: plain Java objects that describe a dialog, a form, a calendar, a row of stat tiles or a badge, plus the first-party browser scripts that paint them. A bean carries data and a fail-closed validate(); it carries no HTML-emitting code. The server-side emitters live in juneau-rest-server-views, which composes these beans, and the dialog/form/bar runtime ships with that module's juneau-views.js. Not the same thing as $W{...} widgets Juneau has two unrelated things called "widget": This page 10.31.2 Widgets / 10.31.3 Predefined Widgets Module juneau-rest-server-widgets juneau-rest-server Package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widgets (plural) org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widget (singular) Core type Widget — a marker interface with validate() Widget — an abstract class with getHtml() / getStyle() / getScript() What it is Typed, data-only beans (modal, form, calendar, badges) Code that emits raw HTML/CSS/JS into an @HtmlDocConfig page via $W{Name} Safety model Typed fields painted with textContent; never an HTML sink Raw markup authored by the application The two share nothing but a simple class name, and a Widget in your imports is ambiguous if you use both. Import one by its fully-qualified name. <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-widgets</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The module depends only on juneau-rest-server and juneau-commons. It deliberately has no dependency on juneau-rest-server-views, so a widget bean can never import a views type. The runtime lives next to the views module The script this module ships (juneau-calendar.js) resolves its icons through the views module's juneau-icons.js and pushes its popovers onto the single layer stack that juneau-views.js publishes. A page that loads it must load both of those too. See the WidgetsMixin section below.

Widget is a one-method marker interface: public interface Widget { void validate(); // throws IllegalArgumentException if not well-formed } Implementers: ModalDef, FormDef, CalendarDef, BarSlot and ServerValues. Every one of them is fail-closed. validate() rejects a malformed bean rather than repairing it, and the REST serving path calls it for you (see the validation gate). Beans that ride the wire also carry a CONTRACT_VERSION string that the browser runtime compares against a literal it bakes in; a mismatch refuses to paint rather than painting something subtly wrong. Bean CONTRACT_VERSION ModalDef "2" FormDef "2" CalendarDef "2" BarSlot "1" ServerValues "1" (Java-only, never on the wire) ModalDef and FormDef move in lockstep with each other and with the runtime; bumping any two of the three makes every form-bearing dialog refuse to open.

Group Types Dialogs and forms ModalDef (+ Field, ChildAction), FormDef (+ Input, Input.Option, Section) Calendar CalendarDef (+ CalendarView, WeekStart), CalendarEvent, EventCategory (+ CategoryColor) Bar slot BarSlot, BarWidget (sealed), BarBadge, BarText Badges and menus Badge, StatusTone, MenuItem Actions ActionBarItem, ActionRef (+ Emphasis, EnabledRule), SafeAction, Behavior, Op Server values ServerValues, ServerValuesValue, ServerValuesRegistry Serving WidgetsMixin (+ WidgetValidationProcessor)

ModalDef is the payload a row action with present=dialog opens: the response to the modal-open confirmation fetch. It is a REST response body, so you return one from an ordinary @RestGet. Example @RestGet("/incidents/{id}/ack-dialog") public ModalDef ackDialog(@Path("id") String id) { var incident = incidents.get(id); return ModalDef.create("Acknowledge this incident?") .field("Incident", incident.number()) .field("Title", incident.title()) .field("Service", incident.service()) .codeField("Correlation id", incident.correlationId()) .form(FormDef.create() .field(FormDef.Input.of("comment", "Comment", "textarea").maxLength(500))) .idempotencyKey(keys.mint("ack", id)); }

The confirmation body is typed fields, not markup. Each ModalDef.Field is a label and a value, painted by the runtime with textContent, never innerHTML. Live data (an incident title anyone can edit) is attacker-influenceable and the page's origin holds the CSRF token, so an HTML sink here would be stored XSS leading to arbitrary writes. There is no way to express one. Field.kind is "text" (the default) or "code" (monospaced and copyable — an id, a URL, a token). Use .field(label, value) and .codeField(label, value) respectively.

Property Meaning contractVersion Always "2" from construction. title The prompt / title. Required, non-blank. fields The typed confirmation fields, in display order. form Optional FormDef. Omit for a confirm-only dialog. idempotencyKey A server-minted key, bound to the action and target, that the runtime echoes verbatim on submit so a double-click or retry collapses to one effect. selfTargeted Opt-in: the key targets itself (a dialog with no row, whose submit creates the thing). See the warning below. keepOpenOnSubmit Opt-in: do not close at confirm-click; paint the write's result into the open dialog as a receipt. childActions A catalog of actions scoped to this one open dialog, for action inputs that open a stacked step. barSlot An optional BarSlot painted immediately after the title. Additive; does not bump the contract version. selfTargeted discards the real target Set selfTargeted(true) only on a modal whose key came from the self-targeted mint helper. On a modal carrying an artifact-bound key it silently replaces the real target with the key itself, which makes the server's binding check vacuous. It defaults to unset, and a dialog that leaves it unset keeps sending the row's real id.

By default the runtime closes a dialog at confirm time and then submits, so the dialog is gone before the result exists. keepOpenOnSubmit suppresses the close and paints the result into the open dialog. A receipt dialog is non-submittable by construction (it has no confirm control, and the runtime refuses to paint one whose payload carries a form), and it is reached only after a committed write. A dialog synthesized from a confirm string alone cannot opt in; a receipt-bearing action must serve a real ModalDef. An older runtime that ignores the flag closes the dialog and drops the receipt; the write still happens.

A type="action" form input names an action id, which the runtime normally resolves against the enclosing view's row-action catalog. A step reached from inside an open dialog (a Review step in a wizard) is not a row action, and publishing it as one would surface it in every row's menu. ModalDef.ChildAction is that missing catalog, scoped structurally to one open dialog because it rides on the per-open payload. The existing row-action lookup runs first and unchanged, so a served payload can never shadow a declared row action. ModalDef.create("Create rule") .form(FormDef.create().field(FormDef.Input.of("review", "Review", "action").actionId("review"))) .childAction(ModalDef.ChildAction.of("review", "Review") .form("/rules/review-form") .endpoint("/rules") .method("POST") .carryDrafts(true)); ChildAction has id, label, form (the child's form-source URL), endpoint, method, onSuccess and carryDrafts. carryDrafts sends the parent dialog's current values to the child's form GET as one URL-encoded juneauDrafts query parameter, so a Review step does not open empty. It requires both a form on the parent and a form URL on the child. Drafts land in access logs and browser history Never carry a secret through carryDrafts.

FormDef is the input form of a modal. A form is either a flat fields list or an ordered list of sections, never both (the flat list is the single-section case). Sections render as a strip above one visible pane; they are a layout of one dialog, not a stack of dialogs, and a value typed into one section survives a trip through another. Example var form = FormDef.create() .field(FormDef.Input.of("resolution", "Resolution comment", "textarea").required().maxLength(1000)) .field(FormDef.Input.of("severity", "Severity", "select") .option("low", "Low").option("high", "High").value("low")) .field(FormDef.Input.of("notify", "Notify owner", "toggle")); // Sectioned: var wizard = FormDef.create() .section(FormDef.Section.of("basics", "Basics") .field(FormDef.Input.of("name", "Name", "text").required())) .section(FormDef.Section.of("advanced", "Advanced") .field(FormDef.Input.of("retries", "Retries", "text").pattern("[0-9]+")));

The type allowlist is the XSS bound: hostile prefill cannot become an element. The client paints native controls with createElement, uses textContent for labels and options, and .value / .checked for prefills. type Notes text, textarea The default is text. Only these two accept pattern and maxLength. password A masked, write-only input (<input type="password" autocomplete="new-password">). It is never pre-filled, so it is blank on edit and on re-open; validate() rejects a value on a password input, and it does not accept pattern or maxLength. Its typed value is excluded from the carryDrafts draft query, so it never lands in a URL. checkbox, toggle Boolean inputs. select Requires at least one Option; a prefilled value must match an option. options is legal only here. action A button that opens the row action (or child action) named by actionId. actionId is required here and illegal elsewhere. Use .action(ActionRef) or .actionId(String). Input properties: name (the submit-body key, required), label (required), type, required, value, options, pattern, maxLength, help, actionId. pattern is capped at 256 characters and must compile (ReDoS defense in depth); maxLength must be positive. FormDef.template names an optional server-side template for authors and is ignored by the client (not an HTML sink). Create such a form with FormDef.ofTemplate(String). validate() additionally rejects duplicate field names (across all sections of a sectioned form), duplicate section ids, and an empty sections list.

CalendarDef describes a month calendar with navigation, categories and a display-only legend. The emitter (CalendarTable) is in the views module; the page mounts an empty data-juneau-calendar marker and juneau-calendar.js hydrates it. The server paints the initial month and seed events (progressive enhancement); the runtime computes later months client-side and fetches their events from a same-origin, data-only per-month GET. Example var cal = CalendarDef.create() .id("oncall") .endpoint("servlet:/oncall/events/{year}/{month}") .categories( EventCategory.create().id("primary").label("Primary").color(EventCategory.CategoryColor.BLUE), EventCategory.create().id("backup").label("Backup").color(EventCategory.CategoryColor.AMBER)) .events( CalendarEvent.create().id("e1").title("Alice").start("2026-03-02").end("2026-03-04").categoryId("primary"), CalendarEvent.create().id("e2").title("Deploy window").start("2026-03-05T09:00").end("2026-03-05T10:00")) .weekStart(CalendarDef.WeekStart.MONDAY) .maxPerDay(4); Property Meaning id Required; must match [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*. Emitted as data-juneau-calendar. endpoint Same-origin path template containing both {year} and {month}. null makes the calendar seed-only and disables month navigation. categories Legend entries in display order. A seed event's categoryId must be declared here. events Optional initial-month seed events. view CalendarView.MONTH is the only value (default). weekStart SUNDAY (default) or MONDAY. initialYear / initialMonth Set together with .initial(year, month), or neither (the server clock decides). Month is 1–12. maxPerDay Chips per day before "+N more". Default 3, minimum 1. Spanning bars occupy lanes, with a budget equal to maxPerDay clamped to a hard ceiling of 8 per week row. The two caps are separate: a bar crossing a cell does not consume that cell's chip budget.

CalendarEvent has id, title, start, end, allDay, categoryId, href and tooltip. start/end are ISO-8601 local values: yyyy-MM-dd or yyyy-MM-ddTHH:mm. A trailing offset or Z is ignored rather than rejected, and the time renders in the server's clock zone. end is layout-significant, with split inclusivity: Shape end is Example All-day (date-only) inclusive start=2026-03-02, end=2026-03-04 fills three day cells Timed (date-time) exclusive 09:00 to 10:00 is [09:00, 10:00) on the start day; crossing midnight makes a spanning bar Omitted start-only, valid an all-day event fills the start day; a timed one is a zero-width chip A timed event whose end equals its start, or any end before start, is malformed. So is an allDay/end disagreement (for example allDay=true with a date-time end). A malformed seed event is dropped, not fatal: it neither fails the definition nor the whole month payload, and a per-month GET handler should apply the same rule with CalendarEvent.retainWellFormed(...). Event titles, tooltips and labels are painted with textContent. href must be a same-origin document URL.

EventCategory has id, label, color and description. color is one of the fixed CategoryColor values BLUE, GREEN, AMBER, RED and NEUTRAL (the default). There is no author-supplied inline color, so the emitted class is built only from a sanitized id and a fixed token — no CSS-injection surface. An unknown categoryId on a wire event paints as NEUTRAL. Why the contract is "2" end became layout-significant, and the constant doubles as the data-juneau-calendar-contract handshake stamp, so a v1 runtime cannot silently draw a multi-day event as one chip.

Badge is an overlay on a header action (a bell count) or inside a BarBadge. It is exactly one of a count badge or a dot badge, never both. Badge.count(7).max(99).tone(StatusTone.ERROR).label("unread notifications"); // "7"; 120 would show "99+" Badge.dot().tone(StatusTone.INFO); // presence only Property Rule count >= 0. Mutually exclusive with dot. dot Presence badge, no number. max >= 1; a larger count renders as max+. tone A StatusTone (INFO, SUCCESS, WARNING, ERROR, NEUTRAL); null keeps the default color. A tone outside that palette fails closed: nothing is painted. label Visually hidden screen-reader context. Counts are painted with textContent. Badge is a plain bean, not a Widget; its validate() is called by the enclosing bean.

BarSlot is an additive trailing region beside the subtab ribbon — a small row of BarWidgets such as "3 changes pending". It is a Widget with id, widgets (at least one, ids unique) and an optional same-origin refreshUrl for demand-refreshing the counts. BarWidget is sealed over two types: BarBadge.of(id).label("change pending").badge(Badge.count(3).tone(StatusTone.WARNING)) BarText.of(id, "Last synced 10:42") var slot = BarSlot.create("pending") .widgets(BarBadge.of("chg").label("changes pending").badge(Badge.count(3).tone(StatusTone.WARNING)), BarText.of("env", "prod")) .refreshUrl("/pending/count"); A BarSlot can be attached to a ModalDef (barSlot(...), anchored right after the title) and, in the views module, to a page and to a Detail View. On the modal it is carried on the wire, because the modal is itself the wire payload.

Type Role ActionBarItem Marker for one item in an action bar: an ActionRef or a SafeAction. ActionRef An opaque id naming a write action on the enclosing view. The action's existence is checked in the views module, not here. SafeAction A client-only action with no endpoint. The one constant is COLLAPSE (collapse the child row), which stays enabled even during an in-flight or failed expand so the user can dismiss it. Behavior How a header or menu action acts when activated: LINK (same-origin href), SAFE (dispatch a format-validated client event token that the host app interprets) or MENU. MenuItem One row of a header or avatar menu: a link (MenuItem.link(id, label, href)), a safe item (MenuItem.safe(id, label, token)) or a divider (MenuItem.divider()). Behavior.MENU is not functional yet The menu manager has not shipped. Until it does, a MENU trigger is disabled and its list is omitted. MenuItem.validate() requires exactly one of href/safe on a non-divider, a same-origin href, and a safe token matching ^[a-z][a-z0-9-]{0,63}$. Dividers are exempt from every id/label/target rule.

ActionRef.of("resolve") .emphasis(ActionRef.Emphasis.PRIMARY) .enabledWhen("status", Op.EQ, "open", "Only open incidents can be resolved.") .enabledWhen("owner", Op.PRESENT, "Assign an owner first."); Op is the shared single-field comparison vocabulary: EQ and NE take a value, PRESENT and ABSENT do not (Op.requiresValue() discriminates; the wrong overload throws). The rules obey a few deliberate constraints: Presentation only, never authorization. The server re-reads the row and refuses on its own authority. Prefer disabled; hide only when irrelevant. An action that is merely impossible right now stays visible and disabled with a reason. A detail-panel action has no visibleWhen; to drop an action from a whole view, omit it from that view's list. (Row actions in a table view can also declare visibleWhen for the case where the action does not apply to a row at all.) The first-declared failing rule wins, and its reason is shown via a tooltip and aria-describedby. Declaration order is the priority mechanism. Fail closed. A rule on a field the panel never declares is rejected at startup; if the field is missing from a row at runtime the rule fails and the action disables (even ABSENT). ActionRef.Emphasis is PRIMARY (solid accent; at most one per bar) or SECONDARY (the default). Both emphasis and enabledWhen are Java-only and never marshalled.
documents.s: Gating an action on row state: ActionRef.enabledWhen

documents.t: ServerValues declares named scalar providers and interpolates them into widget chrome text (titles, labels) as $FV{name} or $FV{name,default} at serve time. It is a thin typed facade over the SVL engine, not a second templating language, and it is Java-only (lambda providers are never serialized). ServerValues sv = ServerValues.create() .value("failedCount", session -> metrics.failed()) .value("env", session -> "prod"); // Column title "Failures ($FV{failedCount})" resolves at serve time. A provider returns a String, Number, Boolean or null. Anything else is rejected at resolve time; collections are not joined. A name that is not declared, or a null result, falls through to the $FV{name,default} default. A provider that throws propagates (fail-closed). Providers are session-aware (Function<VarResolverSession,?>) and re-run on every reference unless the value is declared cacheable through ServerValuesValue.of(name, provider, true). Cache only values that are stable across a whole response. $FV is not $W: $W emits raw widget HTML, while $FV resolves plain, serializer-encoded text and never injects markup. The $FV variable itself (ServerValuesVar) lives in juneau-rest-server-views.

Compose the mixin to serve the three first-party assets: @Rest(mixins=WidgetsMixin.class) public class MyRest extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Path constant Served at Purpose CALENDAR_JS_PATH /juneau-calendar.js Calendar runtime CALENDAR_CSS_PATH /juneau-calendar.css Calendar stylesheet (declares --jc-* token fallbacks) Assets are cacheable for one day and carry a content-sensitive cache-buster. Reference them from a page with WidgetsMixin.widgetAssetUrl(path) (a servlet:-prefixed URL that Juneau's own HTML serializer resolves) or, for a template engine that never sees that rewrite, WidgetsMixin.widgetAssetUrl(req, path) (an absolute, browser-fetchable URL). Load order is a contract juneau-calendar.js must come after the views module's juneau-views.js. The calendar defines no stack of its own and fails loudly if the shared one is absent. The mixin also exposes the handshake stamps the runtimes bake in: CALENDAR_CONTRACT_VERSION ("2", alias of CalendarDef), BAR_CONTRACT_VERSION ("1", alias of BarSlot) and HEADER_CONTRACT_VERSION ("1"). They are deliberately independent, so a calendar-envelope change never forces a bar or header bump. The views module keeps deprecated accessors at the paths it served these assets from before they moved; they read the same bytes from this module, so existing applications keep working.

WidgetsMixin.WidgetValidationProcessor is a ResponseProcessor that calls validate() on any REST response whose content is a Widget, and answers a failure with HTTP 500 (a malformed widget is a server defect, not a client error). It returns NEXT, so it never claims the response or perturbs the chain. It is registered twice, on purpose: through ServiceLoader (so it applies to every resource on a classpath that carries the module, with no opt-in) and through the mixin's own @Rest(responseProcessors=...) (so a host that composes the mixin is covered even if a shading step drops the services file). Things to know: Top level only. It tests getContent() itself. A Widget nested in a List or Map is not walked; nested widgets inside a ModalDef are covered by that bean's own recursive validate(). Non-REST producers are not gated. A direct Json.of(modal) has no processor in front of it. Call validate() or the chaining ModalDef.checked() / FormDef.checked() yourself. Double validation is intentional. A modal that already called checked() is validated again by the processor; validate() is cheap and idempotent. Escape hatch. To serve a deliberately invalid widget, replace the whole chain with a @Bean ResponseProcessorList factory method. There is no narrower opt-out.

10.31.2 Widgets and 10.31.3 Predefined Widgets — the unrelated $W{...} HTML header widgets 10.64 Admin-Console Chrome — the themeable chrome these widgets are painted with 10.65 Markdown View Rendering org.apache.juneau.rest.server.widgets

By default, HTTP parts that don't have value (such as missing query parameters) end up with null values: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query("p1") int p1, @FormData("f1") MyBean f1, @Header("Accept-Language") AcceptLanguage h1 ) { if (p1 == null) p1 = -1; if (f1 == null) f1 = DEFAULT_BEAN; if (h1 == null) h1 = AcceptLanguage.of("en"); } You have several options to provide default values for HTTP parts. The most common is to simply use Optional parameters and handle default values programmatically: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query("p1") Optional<Integer> p1, @FormData("f1") Optional<MyBean> f1, @Header("Accept-Language") Optional<AcceptLanguage> h1 ) { int _p1 = p1.orElse(-1); MyBean _f1 = f1.orElse(DEFAULT_BEAN); AcceptLanguage _h1 = h1.orElse(AcceptLanguage.of("en")); } You can also specify default values on the annotations: @RestPost("/example") public String doGetExample1( @Query(name="p1", def="-1") int p1, @FormData(name="f1", def="foo=bar,baz=qux") MyBean f1, @Header(name="Accept-Language", def="en") AcceptLanguage lang ) { ... } A third option is to specify default values via the Rest and RestOp annotations. RestdefaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestHeaders defaultResponseHeadersRestOpdefaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestFormData defaultRequestHeaders defaultRequestQueryData defaultResponseHeaders Example // Servlet with default headers @Rest( // Assume "text/json" Accept value when Accept not specified defaultRequestHeaders={"Accept: text/json"}, // Add a version header attribute to all responses defaultResponseHeaders={"X-Version: 1.0"} ) public MyRestServlet extends BasicRestServlet { ... } Default parts can also be supplied programmatically via named beans using @Bean (for example name="defaultRequestHeaders", name="defaultResponseHeaders", name="defaultRequestAttributes", name="defaultRequestFormData", name="defaultRequestQueryData"). In 10.0+, prefer annotation attributes and @Bean-named beans over the legacy builder APIs.

By default, all serializers and parsers have built in ObjectSwaps defined for the following common data types: note As of 10.0.0, Iterator, Iterable, Stream, and Enumeration types are serialized natively without swaps. The IteratorSwap and EnumerationSwap classes have been removed. See Release 10.0.0 for details. note As of 10.0.0, date/time types (Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes, XMLGregorianCalendar) and Duration are serialized and parsed natively as ISO 8601 strings without swaps. The default swap registrations for these types have been removed from this list. The old swap classes (TemporalCalendarSwap, TemporalDateSwap, CalendarSwap, DateSwap, TemporalSwap) have been removed; to customize the output format (e.g. RFC 1123 instead of ISO 8601) use @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=...) / @Marshalled(calendarFormat=...) / MarshallingContext.Builder.calendarFormat(CalendarFormat...), or register your own ObjectSwap. See Release 10.0.0 for details. Locale Class TimeZone ZoneId The following types are now handled natively (built-in ISO 8601 support, no swap required): Calendar Date Instant ZonedDateTime LocalDate LocalDateTime LocalTime OffsetDateTime OffsetTime Year YearMonth Temporal XMLGregorianCalendar Duration Various other swaps are provided in the org.apache.juneau.marshall.swaps package.

VarResolver.DEFAULT is a reusable, thread-safe VarResolver instance pre-configured with the most commonly-needed source variables. Because it is immutable and shared, you can reference it directly from anywhere without constructing your own resolver.

Variable Class Resolves against $S{key[,default]} SystemPropertiesVar Java system properties (System.getProperty) $E{key[,default]} EnvVariablesVar OS environment variables (System.getenv) $EF{key[,default]} EnvFileVar A .env-style env file on the filesystem $DE{key[,default]} DotenvVar A .env dotenv file $A{key[,default]} ArgsVar JVM command-line arguments $MF{key[,default]} ManifestFileVar Classpath META-INF/MANIFEST.MF entries Each variable accepts an optional comma-separated default that is returned when the key cannot be resolved.

// Resolve a single system-property variable. String s = VarResolver.DEFAULT.resolve("The Java home directory is $S{java.home}"); Variables can be arbitrarily nested — the resolved value of one variable can itself contain variables, and a variable's default can be another variable: // Look up a value in priority order: // 1) the MYPROPERTY environment variable, // 2) the 'my.property' system property if the env var is not set, // 3) the literal 'not found' if neither is set. String s = VarResolver.DEFAULT.resolve("$E{MYPROPERTY,$S{my.property,not found}}"); Resolving a string that contains no variables is a no-op that returns the input unchanged, so it is safe (and cheap) to run arbitrary text through the resolver.

VarResolver.DEFAULT is a starting point, not a dead end. Use copy() to derive a new resolver that inherits its variables and adds your own: // Derive a resolver that also supports a custom $MY{...} variable. VarResolver vr = VarResolver.DEFAULT.copy() .vars(MyCustomVar.class) .build();

Simple Variable Language — the full SVL reference, including the #{...} function-call syntax. VarResolvers — creating and configuring your own resolvers. SVL Other Notes — escaping and recursion caveats.

Apache Juneau ships two packaging aids that make it easy to depend on a coherent, version-aligned slice of the framework without hand-maintaining a long list of <version> tags: A Bill of Materials (BOM) — org.apache.juneau:juneau-bom — for version alignment. A small set of curated dependency bundles — one per deployment shape — that transitively pull a coherent module set. Both are deliberately dependency-only aids. They register nothing and discover nothing at runtime (see Explicit over magic below).

Import juneau-bom (scope import, type pom) in your <dependencyManagement> and then drop the explicit versions from every Juneau dependency — the BOM supplies them: <dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-bom</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> <type>pom</type> <scope>import</scope> </dependency> </dependencies> </dependencyManagement> <dependencies> <!-- No <version> needed - the BOM aligns it. --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server</artifactId> </dependency> </dependencies> The BOM enumerates the consumer-facing Juneau modules (juneau-core marshalling/config, juneau-rest, juneau-microservice, juneau-bean, juneau-sc), the test-support modules (juneau-test, juneau-microservice-test, juneau-rest-mock), and the curated *-bundle POMs themselves. It excludes aggregate/non-library artifacts (juneau-shaded/*, juneau-examples, juneau-petstore, juneau-distrib) and the juneau-run build tooling.

Every module below is version-managed by juneau-bom. See the Ecosystem Overview for what each one does and what it requires. Area Managed artifacts Core juneau-commons, juneau-config, juneau-marshall, juneau-marshall-rdf, juneau-beanquery-sql, juneau-beanquery-postgres, juneau-test Secrets juneau-secret-macos-keychain Beans
