A missing required field shows an error banner and focuses the field; nothing is sent. submit.submitLabel The button text (default "Run"). height The log pane height in pixels, at least 80 (default 240). urlParam Mirror the running job id into this URL query parameter (a name matching [A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_-]*). clearOnSubmit Clear the previous run's log on a new submit: true (default) or false. output Write a value from the result into the card (see Output).

While a job runs, the button becomes Cancel, which posts to the job's cancelUrl; it is disabled when the AsyncJobRef has no cancelUrl. Whichever ends the job first, the cancel response or the stream's result, sets the banner. A cancel that fails shows its message in an error banner and leaves the job running. The card remembers the running job in the browser's local storage. A fresh attach to a job stream is live-only, so the card always connects with ?lastEventId=0 added to the streamUrl and gets the progress so far, both straight after a submit and after a reload. Every progress event carries an SSE id; when the browser reconnects a dropped stream by itself it sends Last-Event-ID, and the server resumes after the last line shown. The card shows every progress line it receives and does no client-side de-duplication, so a server that repeats a line shows a visible repeat rather than hiding it. With urlParam, it reconnects only when the URL names the same job. A job the server no longer knows (or any stream that closes before delivering a single event, which includes a 429 or 5xx on attach) shows "Job not found; it may have finished or the server restarted." in the log pane and returns the form to its idle state, and the stored job and URL parameter are cleared. If the stream drops for good after it had delivered events, a warning banner says the job may still be running and to reload to reattach. A browser without EventSource shows a warning that live progress is unavailable. New run forgets the finished job and shows the form again.

The same card can live inside a table row's detail panel, where it runs a job for that row. Declare it as the detail's region with populate: 'job-log'; the region's config takes the card's body keys plus submit.keyUrl and an optional detail grid: <@card type="datatables" id="species">{ dataMode: 'client', dataUrl: '/console/ops/jobs/species', columns: [ { key: 'species', label: 'Species' }, { key: 'available', label: 'Available' } ], detail: { endpoint: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}', region: { id: 'restock-species', populate: 'job-log', config: { submit: { endpoint: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/restock', action: 'restock-species', keyUrl: '/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/key', submitLabel: 'Restock', fields: [ { name: 'count', label: 'How many', type: 'number', default: 1, required: true }, { name: 'species', type: 'hidden', source: 'row.species' } ] }, detail: { renderer: 'fieldGrid', fields: [ { data: 'available', label: 'Available' } ] }, output: { target: { field: 'available' }, from: 'row.available' } } } } }</@card> From Java, build the same region with JobLogRegion and hand it to the row detail: RowDetail.create("/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}") .region(JobLogRegion.create("restock-species") .submit(JobLogRegion.Submit.create("/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/restock", "restock-species", "/console/ops/jobs/species/{id}/key") .submitLabel("Restock") .field(JobLogRegion.Field.of("count").label("How many").type("number").defaultValue(1).required(true)) .field(JobLogRegion.Field.of("species").type("hidden").source("row.species"))) .detail(JobLogRegion.Detail.of("fieldGrid", RegionDef.Field.of("available").label("Available"))) .output(JobLogRegion.Output.field("available").from("row.available")) .toRegion()); In a region: The envelope is always action, and targetId is the row's own id, read from the panel's row stamp. It never comes from a field or from row data. envelope may be omitted; any value other than action fails the page. The key comes from the server. When the panel opens, the card posts to submit.keyUrl (with {id} replaced) and keeps the submit button disabled until a key for this row and action arrives. A refused or mismatched key shows E-JS-109 and a Retry button. A key is reused only until the server answers; the next run fetches a fresh one. {id} is the only token in submit.endpoint and submit.keyUrl, and both are same-origin path templates. urlParam is rejected. source: 'row.<field>' fills a field from the row's data: an own property of the parent row only, never another row, the page or the DOM. The name matches [A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]{0,63}, with no paths. A hidden field binds at submit, from the row as of the click; a visible field is prefilled when the panel renders and the user's edit wins. Only strings, finite numbers, booleans and null are allowed: anything else falls back to the field's default, and with no default the submit is refused with E-JS-110 and nothing is sent. detail paints a field grid above the form with the named JuneauViews.helpers renderer and the row's detail payload. Its data-juneau-field slots are what output.target.field addresses, so a result can update the panel's own values. One job per row. While the row's job runs, the row is marked and its row actions are disabled; a row action activated anyway (from a menu, a pill or a detail button) is refused with row-job-running and sends nothing. Collapsing the panel leaves the job running; expanding it again re-attaches and replays the log from the start. The re-attached view has no submit until the job ends. While it runs, it shows Cancel when the job has a cancelUrl, and a cancel from either view goes through JuneauViews.jobs.cancel. The outcome still comes from the job's stream. A job can be watched from one re-attached view at a time; a second collapse and re-expand during the same job may not re-attach. A page reload does not re-attach. The table's poll waits. While the open panel's job runs, the table's timer reload is held and the staleness pill shows Paused, so the panel isn't redrawn under the log. The card registers its job-log populator whatever the script order. An app that registers its own job-log populator first keeps it, and one registered later replaces the card's. A page that declares a job-log region without juneau-views.js and juneau-regions.js logs E-JS-111. A datatables card with a job-log region pulls the joblog asset pack on its own; you don't add requires. window.JuneauJobLog.mount(el, config, {signal}) mounts the same row-bound card programmatically into any element inside a view table row or its detail panel, from a region config. It returns {destroy, cancel, phase}; aborting signal removes the view but never cancels the job. It throws E-JS-111 when JuneauViews.jobs is missing. The row-job runtime, helpers.jobButton, and the server side (JobKeyLedger, RowJobSubmit) are covered in Row Jobs.

The streamUrl and cancelUrl of the returned AsyncJobRef must resolve to the page's own origin, because the cancel request carries the console's CSRF token. A ref from another origin is refused with E-JS-77. The same check applies to a job ref read back from local storage after a reload, except that a bad stored ref is silently ignored (no E-JS-77) and the card starts idle. submit.endpoint is checked at render by the same same-origin-path rule as ChartDef hrefs, and again in the browser before each submit, because that request carries the CSRF token too: an endpoint that resolves to another origin, contains a backslash or starts with a space is refused with E-JS-81 and nothing is sent. In a row-detail region the server's key binding is what makes the request row-bound. The key endpoint issues a key bound to the action, the row id and the caller, and the submit endpoint verifies all three; a key issued for one row is refused for any other with the same 409 used for an unknown or expired key. Presets from source and hidden fields are ordinary request data that the user can edit, so the server must never decide which row to act on, or whether the caller may act, from them. Use the verified targetId. The key endpoint must apply the same authorization as the action it keys.

The log pane is role="log" with aria-live="polite" and takes keyboard focus, so a screen reader reads new lines as they arrive. Errors, including a rejected submit, a missing required field and a failed job, appear in a banner with role="alert", so they are announced at once, and again if the same error comes back. The ok and warning banners (a successful job, an interrupted stream, a browser without EventSource) have no role and are announced politely through the console's status region instead. When the Run/Cancel button changes or disappears, keyboard focus moves to the control that replaces it, or to the log pane, rather than falling back to the page.

Code When E-JS-77 The submit response is not a valid AsyncJobRef: jobId or streamUrl is missing, or streamUrl or cancelUrl is not same-origin. Shown in an alert banner above the form, which stays usable. E-JS-78 The stream's result event could not be parsed, or has no outcome. Shown in the alert banner. E-JS-81 submit.endpoint is not a same-origin path. Shown in the alert banner; nothing is sent. E-JS-109 Region mode: the key endpoint refused, or answered with a body whose contractVersion, action, targetId or key doesn't match this row and action. Shown in the alert banner with a Retry button; submit stays disabled. E-JS-110 A source: 'row.<field>' preset didn't resolve to a string, finite number, boolean or null, and the field has no default; or a hidden field has neither a source nor a default (the message then names only the missing default, since a page card has no row). Nothing is sent. E-JS-111 A job-log region, JuneauJobLog.mount or helpers.jobButton was used without window.JuneauViews.regions or window.JuneauViews.jobs. E-JS-112 output.target was not found inside the card (or region), or output.target.selector is not a valid selector. Nothing is written. E-JS-113 A JuneauViews.jobs hook threw. It is logged and the job's stream carries on. Java checks the card body when the page renders: a missing submit.endpoint, an unknown key in the body, in submit or in a field, a cross-origin submit.endpoint, a submit.method other than POST or PUT, a field without a name or with a type other than text, textarea, number or hidden, a height below 80, a malformed urlParam, a clearOnSubmit that isn't a boolean, a field named idempotencyKey in the flat envelope, an envelope: 'action' without submit.action, a source on the page card, a malformed output, and a src= or template= on the card all fail the page. A job-log region's config is checked by the same rules (the shared JobLogChecks), plus a required keyUrl, {id}-only templates and no urlParam. A rejected submit (for example a job limit) shows the server's message above the form.

Juneau has no ORM module (no analog of Jackson's jackson-datatype-hibernate). The supported path is DTO-first: map persistence entities to marshallable beans inside the service layer, with the persistence session still open, and return the DTO from REST. This page covers Hibernate 6/7 with jakarta.persistence only. Hibernate 5 / javax.persistence is not documented here.

Keep @Entity types and EntityManager / Session out of serializers. public class UserDto { public String id; public String name; } public UserDto toDto(User entity) { var dto = new UserDto(); dto.id = entity.getId(); dto.name = entity.getName(); return dto; // session still open if you read lazy associations here } The REST method returns UserDto, not User.

Juneau will still bind a JSON object onto a matching bean via the no-arg constructor and setters if you pass an entity class to a parser. That instance is detached and unmanaged. It is not in a persistence context. The service must find the managed entity, copy fields, and merge. Never persist the object the parser just constructed. This is a documentation warning, not a parser feature Juneau will add.

Initialize (or project) the graph you intend to emit so the serializer never walks an uninitialized lazy association. Bidirectional associations: put @MarshalledIgnore / @BeanIgnore on one side, or enable detectRecursions() — see Recursion. jakarta.persistence.Transient is not java.beans.Transient. Juneau ignores java.beans.Transient and Java transient fields by default. JPA @Transient is ignored only if you also mark @MarshalledIgnore / @BeanIgnore (or exclude the property). Bytecode-enhanced entities keep the entity class name. The $HibernateProxy$ unwrap below does not apply. Uninitialized enhanced attributes still throw LazyInitializationException if the serializer reads them. PersistentBag / PersistentSet serialize as collections once initialized. An uninitialized lazy collection is a LazyInitializationException, not null.
documents.s: If you serialize an entity anyway

documents.t: ClassUtils.getProxyFor recognizes Hibernate lazy association proxies whose class name contains $HibernateProxy$ and returns the immediate superclass. getClassMetaForObject uses that class for every marshalling format (JSON, XML, HTML, CSV, YAML, …), not JSON only. Other types getProxyFor already knew (JDK dynamic proxies, $$EnhancerBySpringCGLIB$$, Javassist, $ByteBuddy$) unwrap the same way. JDK proxies — including annotation instances — resolve to the first interface. Subclass proxies resolve to the immediate superclass, which is the entity for a typical Hibernate association proxy but may be a mapped superclass under @Inheritance. Not unwrapped: Spring 6 names that contain only $$SpringCGLIB$$ (that infix is logger-name-only today). Bytecode-enhanced entities with no $HibernateProxy$ in the class name.

If a type is both a Juneau bean and a JPA entity: no-arg constructor, mutable properties. Do not persist @MarshalledIgnore fields you still need in the database, and do not marshall fields that must stay persistence-only without an ignore annotation.

No juneau-marshall-hibernate module, no force-load / id-only lazy knobs, and no EntityManager inside the marshaller. If LazyInitializationException or N+1 still hurts after mapping to DTOs, that is a follow-up — not hidden settings on the serializer.
documents.s: What this release does not ship

documents.t: The Json5Serializer class can be used to serialized POJOs into JSON 5 notation. JSON 5 is similar to JSON except for the following: JSON attributes are only quoted when necessary. Uses single-quotes for quoting. Examples // Some free-form JSON. JsonMap map = JsonMap.of( "foo", "x1", "_bar", "x2", " baz ", "x3", "123", "x4", "return", "x5", "", "x6" ); // Serialized to standard JSON { "foo": "x1", "_bar": "x2", " baz ": "x3", "123": "x4", "return": "x5", "": "x6" } // Serialized to JSON5 { foo: 'x1', _bar: 'x2', ' baz ': 'x3', // Quoted due to embedded spaces. '123': 'x4', // Quoted to prevent confusion with number. 'return': 'x5', // Quoted because it's a keyword. '': 'x6' // Quoted because it's an empty string. } The advantage to JSON 5 is you can represent it in a Java String in minimal form with minimal escaping. This is particularly useful in cases such as unit testing where you can easily validate POJOs by simplifying them to JSON 5 and do a simple string comparison. WriterSerializer serializer = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT; assertEquals("{foo:'bar',baz:123}", serializer.toString(myPojo));

For indented, multi-line JSON5 output, use the dedicated Json5R variant marshaller (backed by Json5Serializer.DEFAULT_READABLE). It is a first-class Json5 facade, so it exposes the same static of(...) / to(...) shortcut surface as Json5 itself: // Compact (default): String compact = Json5.of(myPojo); // {foo:'bar',baz:123} // Readable (indented, multi-line): String pretty = Json5R.of(myPojo); (This replaces the former Json5.DEFAULT_READABLE constant, removed in 10.0.0.) See Also Json5SerializerJson5Parser JSON5L Basics — JSON5 combined with newline-delimited (one document per line) framing.
documents.s: Readable output — the Json5R variant marshaller

documents.t: Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from JSON5L — a combination of the relaxed JSON5 dialect and JSONL's newline-delimited framing (one document per line). JSON5L is a good fit for human-edited line-delimited config and data files: it keeps JSONL's "one record per line" streaming model while tolerating comments, unquoted keys, single-quoted strings, and trailing commas on each line. The Json5lSerializer converts POJOs to JSON5L, and the Json5lParser creates POJOs from JSON5L by parsing each line as a JSON5 value. JSON5L support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a list of beans to JSON5L List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String json5l = Json5l.of(people); By default the output is strict RFC-8259 JSON per line — byte-identical to JSONL: {"name":"Alice","age":30} {"name":"Bob","age":25}

The serializer emits strict JSON per line by default, keeping output maximally portable (any JSONL or JSON consumer can read it). Enable json5Sugar() to emit JSON5 sugar — single-quoted strings and unquoted field names where safe: Json5lSerializer s = Json5lSerializer.create().json5Sugar().build(); String json5l = s.write(people); Produces: {name:'Alice',age:30} {name:'Bob',age:25}
documents.s: Strict by default, JSON5 sugar opt-in

documents.t: JSON5L follows JSON5 comment rules line-by-line: A line that is blank or contains only a comment (// ... or a single-line /* ... */) is skipped, like a blank line. Inline comments within a record's JSON are tolerated (e.g. {a:1} // note). A /* ... */ block comment must open and close on the same physical line — block comments cannot span record boundaries, since each line is parsed independently.

Produces: application/json5l Accepts: application/json5l, application/json5lines (alias), text/json5l, and (at a reduced q-value) the JSONL family application/jsonl, application/jsonlines, application/x-ndjson, text/jsonl.
// JSON5L is included in BasicUniversalConfig @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

No pretty-printing: Each value must fit on a single line; useWhitespace() is always suppressed. First-line-only for single-object targets: When parsing to a single non-collection type, only the first non-blank, non-comment line is parsed; trailing lines are ignored. No record-spanning block comments: A /* ... */ comment must begin and end on the same line.

@Json5lConfig applies to both Json5lSerializer and Json5lParser on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Its only attribute today is rank; JSON5L has no @Json5l data annotation or @Json5lApply. See Also JSONL Basics — the strict line-delimited sibling format. JSON5 — the relaxed JSON dialect JSON5L parses per line. JSON Lines Specification and JSON5 Specification for the underlying formats. Token-Streaming Basics — JSON5L is a FULL streaming format; each line maps cleanly onto the token cursor.

The @Json annotation is used to override the behavior of JsonSerializer on individual bean classes or properties. The annotation can be applied to beans as well as other objects serialized to other types (e.g. strings). JsonwrapperAttr The @Json(wrapperAttr) annotation can be used to wrap beans inside a JSON object with a specified attribute name. Example: @Json(wrapperAttr="personBean") public class Person { public String name = "John Smith"; } The following shows the JSON representation with and without the annotation present: Without annotation With annotation { "name": "John Smith" } { "personBean": { "name": "John Smith" } }

The JsonMap and JsonList classes are generic Java representations of JSON objects and arrays. These classes can be used to create "unstructured" models for serialization (as opposed to "structured" models consisting of beans). If you want to quickly generate JSON/XML/HTML from generic maps/collections, or parse JSON/XML/HTML into generic maps/collections, these classes work well. tip In v10.0, JsonMap / JsonList were re-parented onto a new neutral base — MarshalledMap / MarshalledList — which carries all the marshaller-agnostic surface (typed accessors, fluent setters, getAt/putAt path navigation, bean integration, etc.) with no language coupling. JsonMap / JsonList are now strictly the strict-JSON flavor (toString() returns RFC 8259 JSON; the bare-string constructor defaults to JsonParser). The JSON5 flavor lives in the new sibling pair Json5Map / Json5List (toString() = JSON5; bare-string constructor defaults to Json5Parser). Most of the API on this page works the same on all three — they share the neutral base. These classes extend the following JCF / Juneau classes: java.util.LinkedHashMaporg.apache.juneau.marshall.collections.MarshalledMaporg.apache.juneau.marshall.collections.JsonMapjava.util.LinkedListorg.apache.juneau.marshall.collections.MarshalledListorg.apache.juneau.marshall.collections.JsonList The JsonMap and JsonList classes are very similar to the JSONObject and JSONArray classes found in other libraries. However, the names were chosen because the concepts of Maps and Lists are already familiar to Java programmers, and these classes can be used with any of the serializers or parsers. These object can be serialized in one of three ways: Using the provided JsonMap.writeTo(java.io.Writer) or JsonList.writeTo(java.io.Writer) methods. Passing them to one of the Serializer serialize methods. Simply calling the JsonMap.toString() or JsonList.toString() methods which will serialize it as strict RFC 8259 JSON. (Use Json5Map / Json5List when JSON5 output is wanted, or call toJson5() on the existing JsonMap / JsonList.) Any valid JSON can be parsed into an unstructured model consisting of generic JsonMap and JsonList objects. (Any valid XML can also be parsed into an unstructured model) // Parse an arbitrary JSON document into an unstructered data model // consisting of JsonMaps, JsonLists, and java primitive objects. String json = "{a:{name:'John Smith',age:21},b:{name:'Joe Smith',age:42}}"; JsonMap map = Json.to(json, JsonMap.class); // Use JsonMap API to extract data from the unstructured model. int johnSmithAge = map.getMap("a").getInt("age"); // Convert it back into JSON. json = Json.of(map); // Or convert it to XML. String xml = Xml.of(map); // toString() / toJson() return strict RFC 8259 JSON. String strict = map.toString(); // {"a":{"name":"John Smith","age":21}, ...} String strict2 = map.toJson(); // synonym for toString(). // toJson5() returns the historical unquoted-key / single-quoted-string form. String json5 = map.toJson5(); // {a:{name:'John Smith',age:21}, ...} The JsonMap and JsonList classes have many convenience features: // Convert the map to a bean. MyBean myBean = map.cast(MyBean.class); // Find entries by multiple keys. MyBean myBean = map.find(MyBean.class, "key1", "key2"); // Fluent-style appenders. map.append("key1", "val1").append("key2", "val2"); // REST-like functions for manipulating nodes in the data structure using URL-like notation. map.getAt("foo/bar/myBean", MyBean.class); map.putAt("foo/bar/myBean", MyBean.class); map.postAt("foo/bar/myListOfBeans", MyBean.class); map.deleteAt("foo/bar/myBean"); // Copy with inclusion or exclusion. JsonMap map2 = map.include("key1", "key2", "key3"); JsonMap map3 = map.exclude("key1", "key2", "key3"); // Serialize using another serializer. String xml = XmlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(map); // Nested maps. map.inner(anotherMap); note As a general rule, if you do not specify a target type during parsing, or if the target type cannot be determined through reflection, the parser generates a flavored map/list whose runtime type matches the parser: JsonParser produces JsonMap / JsonList. Json5Parser produces Json5Map / Json5List. All other parsers (XmlParser, YamlParser, UonParser, HoconParser, MsgPackParser, CborParser, BsonParser, HtmlParser, JsonlParser, HjsonParser, MarkdownParser, CsvParser, RDF parsers, etc.) currently produce the neutral MarshalledMap / MarshalledList. Callers that need a specific runtime type — for example to keep an explicit (JsonMap) cast working — should pass an explicit target class to the parser, e.g. parser.read(text, JsonMap.class). The flavor hook is only consulted for unbound Object / Map<String,Object> / Collection<Object> targets; explicit target classes always win.

The JSON data type produced depends on the Java object type being serialized. Primitives and primitive objects are converted to JSON primitives. Beans and Maps are converted to JSON objects. Collections and arrays are converted to JSON arrays. Anything else is converted to JSON strings.

POJO type JSON type Example Serialized form String String serialize("foobar"); 'foobar' Number Number serialize(123); 123 Boolean Boolean serialize(true); true Null Null serialize(null); null Beans with properties of any type on this list Object serialize(new MyBean()); {p1:'val1',p2:true} Maps with values of any type on this list Object serialize(new TreeMap()); {key1:'val1',key2:true} Collections and arrays of any type on this list Array serialize(new Object[]{1,"foo",true}); [1,'foo',true] Date/time types (Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes, Duration) are serialized natively as ISO 8601 strings. Swaps can be used to convert non-serializable POJOs into serializable forms (such as byte[] arrays to Base-64 encoded strings) or to override the default format for types that already have built-in support.

The JsonParser class is used to parse JSON into POJOs. The class hierarchy for the builder of this parser is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderParser.BuilderReaderParser.BuilderJsonParser.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured parsers are provided for convenience: JsonParserDEFAULTJson5ParserDEFAULT The JsonParser strictly enforces RFC 8259 JSON: Double-quoted strings only (single quotes throw ParseException). No comments, trailing commas, or unquoted keys. JSON fragments (string, numeric, or boolean primitive values). For JSON5 syntax (single quotes, comments, trailing commas, unquoted keys), use Json5Parser.

Juneau provides the JsonSchemaSerializer class for generating JSON-Schema documents that describe the output generated by the JsonSerializer class. This class shares the same properties as JsonSerializer. For convenience the JsonSerializer.getSchemaSerializer() method has been added for creating instances of schema serializers from the regular serializer instance. When you want a typed schema DTO instead of raw map output, use JsonSchemaBeanGenerator from juneau-bean-jsonschema: import org.apache.juneau.bean.jsonschema.*; JsonSchema schema = JsonSchemaBeanGenerator.DEFAULT.generate(Person.class); // Equivalent convenience: JsonSchema<?> schema2 = JsonSchema.of(Person.class);

Parsers and serializers can also enforce @Schema constraints at parse/serialize time by enabling MarshallingContext.Builder.validateSchema(). Validation is powered by JsonSchemaValidator in juneau-bean-jsonschema, which implements JSON Schema Draft 2020-12 semantics over the typed JsonSchema bean. See juneau-bean-jsonschema for details and supported keywords.

public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted } The code for creating our POJO model and generating JSON-Schema is shown below: // Get the one of the default schema serializers. JsonSchemaSerializer serializer = JsonSchemaSerializer.DEFAULT_SIMPLE_READABLE; // Get the JSON Schema for the POJO. String jsonSchema = serializer.write(new Person()); // This also works. jsonSchema = serializer.write(Person.class);

{ type: 'object', description: 'org.apache.juneau.sample.Person', properties: { name: { type: 'string', description: 'java.lang.String' }, birthDate: { type: 'string', description: 'java.util.Calendar' }, addresses: { type: 'array', description: 'java.util.LinkedList', items: { type: 'object', description: 'org.apache.juneau.sample.Address', properties: { street: { type: 'string', description: 'java.lang.String' }, city: { type: 'string', description: 'java.lang.String' }, state: { type: 'string', description: 'java.lang.String' }, zip: { type: 'number', description: 'int' }, isCurrent: { type: 'boolean', description: 'boolean' } } } } } }

The @Schema annotation supports a summary field (alias su) for short, single-line descriptions intended for AI / LLM consumption, compact docs, and tooltips. Unlike description, which can be multi-line and detailed, summary should be a single sentence or phrase that captures the essential meaning. @Schema( summary="A pet available for adoption", description={ "Represents a pet in the store's inventory.", "Includes details such as name, species, breed, age, and adoption status." } ) public class Pet { @Schema(summary="The pet's display name") public String name; } The summary value is emitted under the JSON Schema key "summary" and is also propagated through JsonSchemaBeanGenerator (accessible via JsonSchema.getSummary()) and into generated Swagger / OpenAPI documents. The companion annotations @Marshalled, @BeanProp, @Response, @Header, @Query, @Path, @FormData, and @Content expose a matching summary field.

The JsonSerializer class is used to serialize POJOs into JSON. The class hierarchy for the builder of this serializer is: Context.BuilderMarshallingContextable.BuilderMarshallingTraverseContext.BuilderSerializer.BuilderWriterSerializer.BuilderJsonSerializer.Builder Refer to the builder javadocs for configurable settings. The following pre-configured serializers are provided for convenience: JsonSerializerDEFAULTDEFAULT_READABLEJson5SerializerDEFAULTDEFAULT_READABLE

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from JSON using ultra-efficient serializers and parsers. The JsonSerializer converts POJOs directly to strict RFC 8259 JSON (double quotes) without intermediate DOM objects. The JsonParser creates POJOs from strict JSON only. For JSON5 syntax (single quotes, comments, etc.), use Json5Serializer and Json5Parser. The following example shows JSON for a typical bean:

public class Person { // Bean properties public String name; @MarshalledProp(calendarFormat=CalendarFormat.ISO_INSTANT) public Calendar birthDate; public List addresses; // Getters/setters omitted } public class Address { // Bean properties public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; public boolean isCurrent; // Getters/setters omitted }

Person person = new Person() .name("John Smith") .birthDate("1946-08-12T00:00:00Z") .addresses( new Address() .street("100 Main Street") .city("Anywhereville") .state(NY) .zip(12345) .isCurrent(true) );
{ "name": "John Smith", "birthDate": "1946-08-12T00:00:00Z", "addresses": [ { "street": "100 Main Street", "city": "Anywhereville", "state": "NY", "zip": 12345, "isCurrent": true } ] }
{ name: 'John Smith', birthDate: '1946-08-12T00:00:00Z', addresses: [ { street: '100 Main Street', city: 'Anywhereville', state: 'NY', zip: 12345, isCurrent: true } ] }

Juneau supports converting arbitrary POJOs to and from JSONL (JSON Lines, also called NDJSON) using native serializers and parsers. JSONL is a text format where each line is a valid JSON value, separated by newlines. It is the standard format for LLM fine-tuning datasets, streaming AI inference, log aggregation, and bulk data pipelines. The JsonlSerializer converts POJOs directly to JSONL format, and the JsonlParser creates POJOs directly from JSONL by parsing each line as a JSON value. JSONL support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency>

// A simple bean public class Person { public String name; public int age; public Person() {} public Person(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } // Serialize a list of beans to JSONL List<Person> people = List.of(new Person("Alice", 30), new Person("Bob", 25)); String jsonl = Jsonl.of(people); Produces: {"name":"Alice","age":30} {"name":"Bob","age":25}

// Parse JSONL into a list of beans List<Person> parsed = Jsonl.to(jsonl, List.class, Person.class); // Parse into an array Person[] array = Jsonl.to(jsonl, Person[].class); // Parse a single line Person p = Jsonl.to("{\"name\":\"Alice\",\"age\":30}", Person.class); // Parse into a list of maps List<JsonMap> maps = Jsonl.to(jsonl, List.class, JsonMap.class);
// Use the default serializer String jsonl = JsonlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(someObject); // Use the marshaller for convenience String jsonl = Jsonl.of(someObject);

The conversion follows the JSONL specification: Collections and arrays → One JSON value per line (no wrapping brackets) Single bean or map → One JSON line Strings → JSON string literals, one per line Numbers → JSON number literals, one per line Booleans → true / false, one per line Null → null, one per line Nested objects → Stay compact on a single line per outer element ObjectSwaps → Applied for non-JSON-primitive types (e.g. byte arrays, dates)
Produces: application/jsonl Accepts: application/jsonl, application/jsonlines (the JSON Lines spec's suggested type; alias), application/x-ndjson, text/jsonl
// JSONL support is included via BasicUniversalConfig (there is no dedicated JSONL-only config interface). @Rest public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... }

No pretty-printing: Each JSON value must fit on a single line; useWhitespace() is always suppressed. First-line-only for single-object targets: When parsing JSONL to a single non-collection type, only the first non-empty line is parsed; trailing lines are ignored. No multi-line JSON input: Each JSON value must be on a single line; pretty-printed JSON will cause parse errors.

@JsonlConfig applies to both JsonlSerializer and JsonlParser on a REST class or method (see Context Annotations). Its only attribute today is rank; JSONL has no @Jsonl data annotation or @JsonlApply, so bean-level behavior comes from the @Json family and the shared bean annotations. @Rest @JsonlConfig public class MyResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } See Also JSON Lines Specification for the full format definition. JSON5L Basics — the relaxed-dialect sibling that tolerates comments, unquoted keys, and single quotes per line. Marshallers for the marshaller API overview. Token-Streaming Basics — JSONL is a FULL streaming format because each line is itself a JSON value that maps cleanly onto the token cursor.

The juneau-rest-server-view-jsp module adds JSP (JavaServer Pages) view-rendering to juneau-rest-server without bleeding the JSP-engine dependency (Apache Jasper) into the core. This page covers the JSP-specific bridge. For the engine-agnostic View interface itself, see the 10.0.0 release notes under the juneau-rest-server section. Sibling view modules Thymeleaf, Mustache, and FreeMarker ship the same shape in 10.0.0.

JSP is niche but real for legacy migrations into Juneau — particularly internal admin consoles and reporting tools that already have a tested .jsp template library and don't want to rewrite to React / Thymeleaf. Before juneau-rest-server-view-jsp, integrating a JspServlet alongside Juneau's RestServlet meant fighting servlet-mapping precedence; the mixin packaging makes this clean.

Class Role View (in juneau-rest-server core) Engine-agnostic contract: getTemplateName(), getAttributes(), getResponseHeaders(). JspMixin Mixin. Mounts /jsp/* for raw .jsp requests; registers JspViewRenderer on the response-processor chain. Builder: basePath(String) (default /), cacheTemplates(boolean) (accepted for ViewMixinBuilder conformance; no-op — see below). JspView View implementation. Immutable; fluent: JspView.of("hello.jsp").attr("name", name).header("Cache-Control", "no-store"). JspViewRenderer ResponseProcessor that detects JspView returns and dispatches via ServletContext.getRequestDispatcher(...).forward(...).
juneau-rest-server-view-jsp ships only the JSP API + JSTL impl in provided scope. No JSP engine is bundled with the bridge module. Consumers add the engine matching their deployment container.

Container Recommended engine Maven coordinates Jetty 12 EE11 — juneau-microservice-jetty, Spring Boot embedded Jetty Eclipse Jetty's repackaged Jasper bundle org.eclipse.jetty.ee11:jetty-ee11-apache-jsp Embedded Tomcat — Spring Boot default Apache Tomcat's embedded Jasper org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-jasper External WAR deploy — Tomcat / JBoss / WildFly / etc. Container-supplied no additional dependency When no JSP engine is on the classpath, the renderer surfaces a clear diagnostic naming the missing dependency: No JSP engine is available on the classpath. Add one of: - org.eclipse.jetty.ee11:jetty-ee11-apache-jsp (Jetty 12 EE11) - org.apache.tomcat.embed:tomcat-embed-jasper (embedded Tomcat / Spring Boot default) - Or rely on the deployment container's bundled engine (Tomcat / JBoss / WildFly / ...) See https://juneau.apache.org/docs/topics/JspViewSupport for the full matrix. The underlying JSP engine in all cases is Apache Jasper (the Tomcat project's); Jetty's artifact is just a repackaged Jasper bundle aligned with a specific Jakarta EE generation.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-view-jsp</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- pick ONE engine --> <dependency> <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty.ee11</groupId> <artifactId>jetty-ee11-apache-jsp</artifactId> <version>12.1.8</version> </dependency>

src/main/resources/ META-INF/resources/WEB-INF/views/ hello.jsp The META-INF/resources/ prefix is the Servlet 3.0 convention that lets embedded containers (Jetty, Spring-Boot-embedded-Tomcat) discover servlet resources from a JAR. The same layout works under microservice deployments and Spring Boot fat-jar deployments.
<%@ page contentType="text/html; charset=UTF-8" %> Hello, ${name}!

import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.jsp.*; import org.apache.juneau.http.*; @Rest(path="/app", mixins=JspMixin.class) public class AppResource extends RestServlet { @Bean JspMixin jsp() { return JspMixin.create() .basePath("/WEB-INF/views/") .build(); } @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return JspView.of("hello.jsp").attr("name", name); } } GET /app/hello/world returns Hello, world! — JspViewRenderer intercepts the JspView return, copies the name attribute onto the request, and forwards to the JSP engine at /WEB-INF/views/hello.jsp.

To use JspView from a host-class @RestGet without adopting the full mixin, add JspViewRenderer.class directly to the host's responseProcessors: @Rest(responseProcessors={JspViewRenderer.class}) public class AppResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return JspView.of("hello.jsp").attr("name", name); } } The ResponseProcessorList partition pass (added in 10.0.0) automatically repositions JspViewRenderer to run before SerializedPojoProcessor, so JspView-returning methods reach the renderer rather than being bean-serialized. The complementary negative case — a host without the renderer bean-serializes the JspView — is verified by JspView_TypedHandler_Test#a05. JSP note: Full template rendering (${name} substitution) requires a real servlet container with a JSP engine. Under MockRest the dispatcher is absent so the renderer reaches a 500; the invariant tested is that the renderer was reached (response body does not contain "templateName" as a bean-serialized field).

The mixin also installs a default /jsp/* mount that forwards raw .jsp requests under the configured base path. With basePath("/WEB-INF/views/"), a request for GET /app/jsp/hello.jsp renders /WEB-INF/views/hello.jsp directly — no Java handler required. The greedy /* handler is excluded from the generated Swagger / OpenAPI spec via @OpSwagger(ignore=true) since the path isn't API-meaningful.

Spring Boot's reference docs explicitly recommend Thymeleaf / FreeMarker / Mustache over JSP for embedded servlet containers — JSP works under embedded Tomcat / Jetty but has notable sharp edges. Plan for the following:

A Spring Boot fat jar (spring-boot-maven-plugin repackaged) does not place .jsp files where the embedded JSP engine expects them by default. Put .jsp resources under src/main/resources/META-INF/resources/WEB-INF/views/.... spring-boot:run (Maven plugin) reads from src/main/resources/ and src/main/webapp/ directly; the deployed jar reads from the classpath via META-INF/resources/. Both modes must work. The META-INF/resources/WEB-INF/views/ layout is the canonical layout that works under both — use it everywhere.

@Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean public JspMixin jsp() { return JspMixin.create() .basePath("/WEB-INF/views/") .build(); } } The Spring BeanStore adapter resolves the bean through ApplicationContext.getBean(JspMixin.class); no additional plumbing is required.

End-to-end integration tests for the bridge module under embedded Tomcat surface two known constraints that aren't bridge-module bugs but worth documenting up front: Servlet-mapping conflicts. Juneau's RestServlet is mapped at /*, which can intercept RequestDispatcher.forward(...) calls intended for the container's JSP servlet. Register the JSP servlet at *.jsp with higher precedence, or mount Juneau at a sub-path such as /api/*. Response-processor ordering (previously a known limitation, resolved in 10.0.0): JspViewRenderer now implements ViewRenderer and is automatically positioned before SerializedPojoProcessor by the ResponseProcessorList partition pass. A @RestOp method returning JspView reaches the renderer without any extra configuration — JspMixin declares @Rest(mergeResponseProcessorsIntoHost=true), so a plain @Rest(mixins=JspMixin.class) folds JspViewRenderer into the host's own chain and the framework ensures ordering. See REST Server — Mixin Sub-Contexts for the opt-in model.

Some apps want /views/ for the public site and /admin/views/ for the admin console. Register two JspMixin beans, each in its own subclass with its own paths override: @Rest(paths={"/views/*"}) public class PublicViewsResource extends JspMixin { public PublicViewsResource() { super(JspMixin.create().basePath("/WEB-INF/views/public/")); } } @Rest(paths={"/admin/views/*"}) public class AdminViewsResource extends JspMixin { public AdminViewsResource() { super(JspMixin.create().basePath("/WEB-INF/views/admin/")); } } Both subclasses mount independently and each resolves templates against its own basePath.

JspMixin.Builder implements ViewMixinBuilder, the minimal contract shared by all four view-engine mixin builders (basePath(String) + cacheTemplates(boolean)): import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; ViewMixinBuilder<?> anyEngineBuilder = JspMixin.create(); anyEngineBuilder.basePath("/WEB-INF/views/").cacheTemplates(false); cacheTemplates(boolean) is accepted and reported back (isCacheTemplates()) purely for conformance with the shared contract — it has no effect on this bridge. JSP recompilation is delegated entirely to the servlet container via RequestDispatcher.forward(...); there is no bridge-owned template cache to disable. Configure hot-reload through your container instead (e.g. Tomcat/Jasper's development / modificationTestInterval servlet-init-params).

JSF / Facelets — not planned. JSF is a separate concern; if ever requested, ships as a sibling juneau-rest-server-view-jsf module. Custom tag libraries beyond JSTL — users supply their own taglibs via classpath dependencies; the bridge module doesn't bundle them. Server-side includes (SSI) — separate concern, not commonly mixed with JSP. Pre-compiled JSP classfile loading — bypassing the JSP engine entirely is a performance optimization deferred to a future release. RequestDispatcher.forward() resets the response output stream. A @RestPreCall-hook that has already written response headers/body before the renderer runs may break the forward. The renderer runs at response-resolution time so this is rarely hit by accident; document it for any caller relying on RestPreCall.

Predefined POJOs for generating commonly-used document types.
The juneau-bean libraries contain several predefined POJOs for generating commonly-used document types that are designed to be used with the Juneau Marshaller APIs for both serializing and parsing.

The juneau-bean group is split into one module per document type. Every module depends only on juneau-marshall, so its beans round-trip through any Juneau serializer/parser. Module Description juneau-bean-html5 HTML5 DOM element beans for building HTML fragments and documents as POJOs. juneau-bean-atom Atom syndication feed beans (RFC 4287). juneau-bean-jsonschema JSON Schema (Draft 2020-12) beans, generator bridge, and validator. juneau-bean-openapi-v3 OpenAPI 3.0 document and UI beans. juneau-bean-common Shared general-purpose DTOs (LinkString, ResultSetList). juneau-bean-swagger-v2 Swagger 2.0 document and UI beans. juneau-bean-mcp-v20250618 Model Context Protocol (MCP) 2025-06-18 wire beans (JSON-RPC envelope lives in juneau-bean-jsonrpc). juneau-bean-mcp-v20260728 Model Context Protocol (MCP) 2026-07-28 wire beans (package org.apache.juneau.bean.mcp.v20260728): request/result metadata, cache hints, multi-round-trip requests, elicitation, sampling, and subscriptions. Documented alongside the 2025-06-18 beans on the same page. juneau-bean-jsonrpc Revision-neutral JSON-RPC 2.0 envelope beans (JsonRpcRequest, JsonRpcResponse, JsonRpcError, McpException). juneau-bean-rfc7807 RFC 7807 Problem Details (application/problem+json) beans. juneau-bean-hal HAL hypermedia (application/hal+json) beans. juneau-bean-jsonapi JSON:API v1.1 (application/vnd.api+json) beans. juneau-bean-jsonpatch JSON Patch (RFC 6902) beans. The sections below highlight a few of these modules; see each module's page for full coverage.

The Juneau HTML5 DTO beans are simply beans with fluent-style setters that allow you to quickly construct HTML fragments as Java objects. These objects can then be serialized to HTML using one of the existing HTML serializers, or to other languages such as JSON using the JSON serializers. The HtmlBuilder class is a utility class with predefined static methods that allow you to easily construct DTO bean instances in a minimal amount of code. Examples import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; // An HTML table Object mytable = table( tr( th("c1"), th("c2") ), tr( td("v1"), td("v2") ) ); String html = Html.of(mytable);
c1 c2
v1 v2
See Also HTML5 for more information.

The juneau-bean-common module provides a small set of general-purpose Data Transfer Object (DTO) beans in the org.apache.juneau.bean package that don't belong to any single wire-format module.

Unlike the format-specific bean modules (juneau-bean-atom, juneau-bean-hal, and so on), this module isn't a base library that the other juneau-bean-X modules build on — each of those depends directly on juneau-marshall, not on this module. Instead, juneau-bean-common ships a couple of reusable DTOs that are consumed by higher-level modules such as juneau-rest-server and the Juneau examples. Its only runtime dependency is juneau-marshall.

Class Purpose LinkString A simple hyperlink bean. Renders as an HTML name anchor when serialized with the HTML serializer, and as a plain bean in all other formats. ResultSetList Transforms a JDBC ResultSet into a List> for easy serialization. Reads the entire result set into memory and closes it.

LinkString is annotated with @HtmlLink, so the HTML serializer converts it into a hyperlink while every other serializer treats it as an ordinary two-property bean (name and uri). import org.apache.juneau.bean.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.html.*; LinkString link = new LinkString("Apache Juneau", "https://juneau.apache.org"); // HTML output: Apache Juneau String html = HtmlSerializer.DEFAULT.write(link); The uri accepts printf-style (String.format) arguments for parameterized links: LinkString view = new LinkString("View", "/items/%s", itemId);

ResultSetList extends LinkedList<Map<String,Object>>, giving you a directly-serializable snapshot of a SQL query result: import org.apache.juneau.bean.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; try (ResultSet rs = statement.executeQuery("SELECT id, name FROM users")) { // Load rows starting at position 1, with no cap, and no synthetic row-number column. ResultSetList rows = new ResultSetList(rs, 1, Integer.MAX_VALUE, false); String json = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(rows); // [{"id":1,"name":"..."},{"id":2,"name":"..."}] } Large binary/character columns (BLOB, CLOB, LONGVARBINARY, etc.) are summarized rather than fully materialized.
Runtime: juneau-marshall External: None Used by: juneau-rest-server and the Juneau examples (not by the other juneau-bean-X modules)

The juneau-bean-hal module provides Java beans for the HAL (Hypertext Application Language) hypermedia format, also described in draft-kelly-json-hal-08. HAL is a JSON-based wire format that lets a REST API describe its resources alongside the links and embedded sub-resources that surround them.

HAL standardises two reserved members on every resource: _links (a map of relation name to one or more HalLink objects) and _embedded (a map of relation name to one or more sub-resources). Everything else in the object is the resource's own payload. This module brings that wire format to Juneau as typed @Marshalled POJOs that round-trip through the default JsonSerializer / JsonParser — no custom marshaller required.

Typed beans for the full HAL spec — HalResource, HalLink, HalLinkArray, HalResourceArray, with all eight Link Object fields per draft-kelly-json-hal-08. Spec-correct single-or-array handling — _links and _embedded map values can be either a single object or a JSON array per the spec. Per-property ObjectSwaps (HalLinkOrArraySwap / HalResourceOrArraySwap) handle the union both directions. Open-ended payload via @BeanProp("*") — Arbitrary resource fields are added via set(String, Object) and read back via get(String) / extraKeys(). They serialise flat at the top level alongside _links and _embedded. Fluent ergonomics for the single-or-array shapes — addLink(rel, link) sets a single-link entry; addLinks(rel, links...) promotes the entry to a HalLinkArray (creating one or extending an existing array as needed). Same pattern is mirrored for _embedded. No external dependencies — Only depends on juneau-marshall.

Class Notes HalResource Top-level HAL resource. Reserved _links and _embedded maps + open payload. HalLink Link Object with href, templated, type, deprecation, name, profile, title, hreflang. HalLinkArray LinkedList<HalLink> — multi-link branch inside an _links map. HalResourceArray LinkedList<HalResource> — multi-resource branch inside an _embedded map. HalLinkOrArraySwap Per-property ObjectSwap resolving each _links value to single HalLink or HalLinkArray. HalResourceOrArraySwap Per-property ObjectSwap resolving each _embedded value to single HalResource or HalResourceArray.

import org.apache.juneau.bean.hal.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; HalResource order = new HalResource() .addLink("self", new HalLink("/orders/123")) .addLink("warehouse", new HalLink("/warehouse/56")) .addLink("invoice", new HalLink("/invoices/873")) .addLinks("curies", new HalLink("https://acme.example/{rel}").setName("acme").setTemplated(true)) .set("currency", "USD") .set("status", "shipped") .set("total", 30.00) .addEmbedded("customer", new HalResource() .addLink("self", new HalLink("/customers/7")) .set("name", "Kelsey")); String wire = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(order); HalResource back = JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(wire, HalResource.class);

HAL allows a relation in _links to map to either a single Link Object or an array of them. The convenience methods make the choice explicit at the call site: addLink(rel, link) — sets a single-link value at rel, replacing any existing value. addLinks(rel, links...) — promotes the entry under rel to a HalLinkArray. If the existing value is a single HalLink, it is wrapped into a new array; if it is already an array, the new links are appended; if absent, a fresh array is created. HalResource r = new HalResource() .addLink("self", new HalLink("/orders/123")) // _links.self ⇒ object .addLinks("curies", new HalLink("https://acme.example/{rel}").setName("acme").setTemplated(true), new HalLink("https://acme.example/v2/{rel}").setName("acme2").setTemplated(true) ); // _links.curies ⇒ array The same pattern is mirrored on _embedded via addEmbedded(rel, res) and addEmbedded(rel, res...). The HalLinkOrArraySwap / HalResourceOrArraySwap swaps make both wire shapes round-trip cleanly through the default JSON parser.

Arbitrary resource fields are added via set(String, Object) and read back via get(String) / extraKeys(). They serialise flat into the top-level object, alongside (and not nested under) _links and _embedded. HalResource r = new HalResource() .addLink("self", new HalLink("/orders/123")) .set("total", 99.50) .set("currency", "USD"); // {"_links":{"self":{"href":"/orders/123"}},"total":99.5,"currency":"USD"}

Per the spec, _embedded represents tree-shaped containment, not arbitrary graphs. Juneau's BeanTraverseContext throws on cyclic object references by default — which is the right behaviour here, so leave it on.
documents.s: _embedded is a tree, not a graph

The Juneau HTML5 DTO beans are simply beans with fluent-style setters that allow you to quickly construct HTML fragments as Java objects. These objects can then be serialized to HTML using one of the existing HTML serializers, or to other languages such as JSON using the JSON serializers. The HtmlBuilder class is a utility class with predefined static methods that allow you to easily construct DTO bean instances in a minimal amount of code. The following examples show how to create common HTML DOM objects. Java code HTML import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; Object mytable = table( tr( th("c1"), th("c2") ), tr( td("v1"), td("v2") ) ); String html = Html.of(mytable);
c1 c2
v1 v2
import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; Object mydiv = div().align("center").onmouseover("alert(\"boo!\");") .children( p("Juneau supports ", b(i("mixed")), " content!") ); String html = Html.of(mydiv);

Juneau supports mixed content!

import static org.apache.juneau.bean.html5.HtmlBuilder.*; Object myform = form().action("/submit").method("POST") .children( "Position (1-10000): ", input("number").name("pos").value(1), br(), "Limit (1-10000): ", input("number").name("limit").value(100), br(), button("submit", "Submit"), button("reset", "Reset") ); String html = Html.of(myform);
Position (1-10000):
Limit (1-10000):
Using the HTML5 DTO beans, you should be able to construct any valid HTML5 from full document bodies to any possible fragments. The HtmlParser class can be used convert these HTML documents back into POJOs. Other serializers and parsers (e.g. JsonSerializer) can be used to represent these POJOs in languages other than HTML.

The juneau-bean-jsonapi module provides Java beans for the JSON:API v1.1 wire format, used by APIs that serve application/vnd.api+json. JSON:API standardises a document shape, resource objects, relationships, errors, and link semantics so clients and servers can interoperate without ad-hoc per-API conventions.

This module models the JSON:API wire format as typed @Marshalled POJOs that round-trip through the default JsonSerializer / JsonParser — no custom marshaller required. The bean shapes mirror the spec one-for-one, including the document-level mutual-exclusion rule between data and errors and the per-spec union types on data and links.

Full spec coverage — Document, resource, resource identifier, relationship, error, error source, link, and the jsonapi version object. Document-level invariants — A validate() helper enforces the spec rule that a document MUST contain at least one of data / errors / meta, and that data and errors MUST NOT coexist. Polymorphic data member — Top-level data can be null, a single JsonApiResource, or a list of them; modelled as Object with typed setter overloads. String-or-link map values — Every links map (on JsonApiDocument, JsonApiResource, JsonApiRelationship, JsonApiError) accepts either a JSON string URL or a JsonApiLink JSON object per the spec, via the JsonApiLinkOrStringSwap ObjectSwap. No external dependencies — Only depends on juneau-marshall.

Class Spec members JsonApiDocument data, errors, meta, jsonapi, links, included JsonApiResource type, id, attributes, relationships, links, meta JsonApiResourceIdentifier type, id, meta JsonApiRelationship data (linkage), links, meta JsonApiError id, links, status, code, title, detail, source, meta JsonApiErrorSource pointer, parameter, header JsonApiLink href, rel, describedby, title, type, hreflang, meta JsonApiVersion version, meta (the jsonapi member) JsonApiLinkOrStringSwap Per-property swap applied to every links map

JSON:API uses type on a resource object as an open-ended entity-type string ("articles", "people", etc.) chosen by the API — not as a closed Java class hierarchy. The Juneau bean intentionally models type as a plain String and is not annotated with @Marshalled(typePropertyName="type", dictionary=...). Conflating JSON:API resource typing with Juneau bean dispatch would: Break round-tripping of any type value the JVM doesn't know about up front, and Force every API to enumerate its resource types in a Java dictionary at compile time. If you want a per-API typed resource hierarchy, build one on top of JsonApiResource in your application code rather than baking it into the wire bean.
documents.s: Why JsonApiResource.type is a plain String

documents.t: import org.apache.juneau.bean.jsonapi.*; import org.apache.juneau.collections.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json.*; JsonApiResource article = new JsonApiResource("articles", "1") .setAttributes(JsonMap.of("title", "JSON:API paints my bikeshed!")) .putRelationship("author", new JsonApiRelationship().setData(new JsonApiResourceIdentifier("people", "9"))); JsonApiDocument doc = new JsonApiDocument() .setJsonapi(new JsonApiVersion("1.1")) .setData(article); String wire = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.write(doc); JsonApiDocument back = JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(wire, JsonApiDocument.class);

JsonApiResource author = new JsonApiResource("people", "9") .setAttributes(JsonMap.of("firstName", "Dan", "lastName", "Gebhardt")); JsonApiResource comment1 = new JsonApiResource("comments", "5") .setAttributes(JsonMap.of("body", "First!")); JsonApiResource comment2 = new JsonApiResource("comments", "12") .setAttributes(JsonMap.of("body", "I like XML better")); JsonApiResource article = new JsonApiResource("articles", "1") .setAttributes(JsonMap.of("title", "JSON:API paints my bikeshed!")) .putRelationship("author", new JsonApiRelationship().setData(new JsonApiResourceIdentifier("people", "9"))) .putRelationship("comments", new JsonApiRelationship().setData(java.util.List.of( new JsonApiResourceIdentifier("comments", "5"), new JsonApiResourceIdentifier("comments", "12")))); JsonApiDocument doc = new JsonApiDocument() .setJsonapi(new JsonApiVersion("1.1")) .setData(article) .addIncluded(author, comment1, comment2);

Every links map accepts both shapes the spec allows. The JsonApiLinkOrStringSwap walks the map on parse and converts each JSON-object value to a JsonApiLink, leaving string values as String. On serialize, String values come out as JSON strings and JsonApiLink values come out as JSON objects. JsonApiRelationship rel = new JsonApiRelationship() .setLinks(new java.util.LinkedHashMap<>(java.util.Map.of( "self", "/articles/1/relationships/author", // string URL "related", new JsonApiLink("/articles/1/author").setTitle("Author") // full link object )));
documents.s: String-or-link values inside a links map

documents.t: JsonApiDocument doc = new JsonApiDocument().addErrors( new JsonApiError() .setStatus("422") .setTitle("Invalid Attribute") .setDetail("Title must contain at least three characters.") .setSource(new JsonApiErrorSource().setPointer("/data/attributes/title")) );

JsonApiDocument doc = new JsonApiDocument(); doc.validate(); // throws IllegalStateException: at least one of data/errors/meta required doc.setData(article).addErrors(new JsonApiError()); doc.validate(); // throws IllegalStateException: data and errors must not coexist

The matching Content-Type constant lives in juneau-rest-common and has been available since 9.2.x: import org.apache.juneau.http.header.ContentType; ContentType.APPLICATION_VND_API_JSON; // "application/vnd.api+json"
