The juneau-commons module is the foundational layer of the Juneau ecosystem. It has no framework dependencies — just Java — and provides the low-level utilities, collections, I/O helpers, reflection tools, settings management, and dependency-injection support that all other Juneau modules build on top of. Because every other Juneau module depends on it transitively, its classes are always on the classpath whenever you use Juneau. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-commons</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> Jar juneau-commons-10.0.0.jar OSGi org.apache.juneau.common_10.0.0.jar Links Maven Central · Javadocs · Source

The juneau-commons module provides common utilities and APIs used across the Juneau ecosystem. Key Packages: Utils (org.apache.juneau.commons.utils): General utility classes for strings, collections, classes, dates, files, and more Collections (org.apache.juneau.commons.collections): Enhanced collection utilities including fluent collections, multi-maps, filtered collections, and caching utilities Lang (org.apache.juneau.commons.lang): Language utilities including value wrappers, version management, string formatting, and state enums Reflection (org.apache.juneau.commons.reflect): Comprehensive reflection utilities for working with classes, methods, fields, and annotations Beans (org.apache.juneau.commons.bean): The format-independent bean-modeling layer — annotations and the introspection engine describing how Java beans are recognized, read, written, and mapped Settings (org.apache.juneau.commons.settings): Thread-local and global settings management with support for functional sources and stores Function (org.apache.juneau.commons.function): Functional programming utilities including higher-arity and checked-exception functional interfaces, tuples, and lazy/nullable suppliers Conversion (org.apache.juneau.commons.conversion): A lightweight, pluggable type-conversion engine that converts objects between types without a full marshalling context I/O (org.apache.juneau.commons.io): File and stream utilities, console support, MIME type detection, and path builders Inject (org.apache.juneau.commons.inject): JSR-330–aligned bean store + Spring-lite injection layer (@Inject, @Named, @Qualifier, @Singleton, @Primary, @Order, @Bean, @Configuration, @Conditional, @PostConstruct, @PreDestroy, and Provider<T>) without compile-time dependencies on jakarta.inject-api or jakarta.annotation-api Simple Variable Language (org.apache.juneau.commons.svl): Recursive $var{key} variable resolution with a built-in function catalog and reusable compiled templates Http (org.apache.juneau.commons.http): Lightweight, dependency-free primitives for parsing and modeling HTTP header values — media types, content-negotiation ranges, and name/value parameters Http-Part (org.apache.juneau.commons.httppart): Shared enumerations and exception describing HTTP parts (query, path, header, form-data, body) for OpenAPI-schema-based serialization and parsing Concurrent (org.apache.juneau.commons.concurrent): Concurrency utilities including auto-closeable simple locks, read-write locks, and nullable atomic references Logging (org.apache.juneau.commons.logging): RichLogger-based JUL extensions with configurable message generation, hierarchical capture propagation, and in-memory log capture for testing Runtime (org.apache.juneau.commons.runtime): Lean accessors for command-line arguments and JAR manifest files Time (org.apache.juneau.commons.time): Time utilities for granular, precision-aware date/time handling

The org.apache.juneau.commons.beanquery package is a protocol-agnostic API for searching, sorting, projecting and paging rows of beans. The same query runs over an in-memory collection or, through the juneau-beanquery-sql module, a database table.

A query engine has two halves: A context is built once, is immutable, and is safe to share. Its builder fixes the queryable columns, the operators, the limits and a server-side guard. A session is opened per request and closed with try-with-resources. It can narrow the columns, override the limits, and add a per-request guard, but it can never widen what the context allows.

Queries an in-JVM collection. create(Class) derives the columns and their search types from the bean's readable Juneau bean properties: getters, public fields and record components, with @BeanIgnore, @BeanProp and the property namer applied; write-only properties are excluded. create(Class, BeanConfigContext) and create(BeanMeta) do the same under a custom bean configuration. create() (no class) is for Map rows and needs explicit column(...) declarations. // Once, at startup. static final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Person> PEOPLE = InMemoryBeanQueryContext .create(Person.class) .exclude("passwordHash") // Never searchable, sortable or viewable. .guard(p -> ! p.isDeleted()) // Server-only filter a request cannot remove. .defaultLimit(50) .maxLimit(500) .build(); // Per request — binding straight from raw request parameters. try (InMemoryBeanQuerySession<Person> session = PEOPLE.getSession(people)) { BeanQuery query = new BeanQuery() .setSearch("age=$gt(21),name=$prefix(Al)") .setSort("name,age-") .setLimit(20) .setOpts("counts=both"); Page<Person> page = session.find(query); page.rows().forEach(this::render); page.total().ifPresent(total -> renderFooter(page.matched().orElse(0) + " of " + total)); } A session builder adds per-request rules: try (InMemoryBeanQuerySession<Person> session = PEOPLE.createSession() .rows(people) .guard(p -> p.getTenant().equals(tenant)) // This request's tenant only. .restrictColumns("name", "age") // Narrow only. .build()) { Counts counts = session.count(query); } Use copy() to derive a variant of a built context: InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Person> admin = PEOPLE.copy().maxLimit(5000).build();

Renders each validated query into parameterized SQL for a SqlDialect (Juneau ships PostgresDialect in juneau-beanquery-postgres). Columns are always declared explicitly; the class only fixes the row type. static final SqlBeanQueryContext<Person> PEOPLE = SqlBeanQueryContext .create(Person.class) .dialect(PostgresDialect.INSTANCE) .table("person") .column("name", SearchType.TEXT) .column("age", SearchType.NUMERIC) .columnSql("name", "full_name") // Column name -> SQL column. .guard(SqlFragment.of("\"deleted\" = false")) .rowMapper((rs, cols) -> new Person(rs.getString("full_name"), rs.getInt("age"))) .dataSource(dataSource) .queryTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)) .build(); // A session takes a connection from the data source and gives it back on close. try (SqlBeanQuerySession<Person> session = PEOPLE.getSession()) { Page<Person> page = session.find(query); } // Or run on a caller-owned connection (and transaction), which the session never closes. try (SqlBeanQuerySession<Person> session = PEOPLE.createSession() .connection(connection) .guard(SqlFragment.of("\"tenant\" = ?", tenant)) .build(); Stream<Map<String,Object>> rows = session.streamValues(exportQuery)) { rows.forEach(csv::write); } renderRows(...) and renderCount(...) return the SQL and binds without opening a connection, which is useful in tests. Streams read rows on demand; closing the stream, or the session, closes the cursor. A closed SqlBeanQuerySession throws IllegalStateException on further queries.

Both BeanQueryContext and BeanQuerySession expose a few read-only accessors so callers can introspect the active settings instead of hard-coding them: BeanQueryContext.getColumnType(String) — the SearchType of a declared column. BeanQueryContext.getMaxSearchClauses() / getMaxSortKeys() — the context's caps. BeanQuerySession.getContext() — the context that opened the session. BeanQuerySession.getMaxSearchClauses() / getMaxSortKeys() — the session's caps (the context's value, or this session's override). SqlBeanQueryContext.getType() — the row type passed to create(Class).

A BeanQuery carries only raw strings, so it binds straight from request parameters: Field Example Meaning search age=$gt(21),name=Al* Comma-separated column=expression clauses, AND-ed. A bare value on a text or id column is a case-insensitive substring or * wildcard match; on other types it is an exact match (prefix for versions). sort name,age- Sort keys; a trailing - (or :desc) sorts descending. view name,age Columns to return from findValues / streamValues, in order. position / limit 40 / 20 The page window. A missing limit means defaultLimit; a negative one means maxLimit; one above maxLimit is clamped to it. opts counts=both Options. Under CountPolicy.IF_REQUESTED: counts=matched asks for the matched count only; counts=both or counts=true asks for both. Operators include $eq, $ne, $in, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $between, $contains, $prefix, $blank, and the combinators $and, $or and $not. $regex is enabled by default; allowRegex(false) disables it. In memory, each call's regex matching shares one regexTimeout deadline (default 50 ms). For a TIMESTAMP or duration column, $gt/$gte/$lt/$lte/$eq/$ne/$between also accept a RelativeDuration value — a signed [+-]<n>(ms|s|m|h|d) literal (or the equivalent ISO-8601 duration such as -PT24H) relative to the time the request is evaluated. BeanQuery.create().gte("lastSeen", RelativeDuration.ofHours(-24)).build() renders as lastSeen=$gte("-24h"), meaning "the last 24 hours." Building a query through BeanQuery.create()/GroupBuilder is forgiving about repeats: a second condition on a column already present at the same level no longer overwrites the first, it merges with it into an implicit $and(...), e.g. BeanQuery.create().gt("age", 21).lt("age", 65) renders as age=$and($gt("21"),$lt("65")). A hand-written search string binding straight from request parameters is stricter: a column repeated at the top level is rejected with BeanQuerySyntaxException, telling the caller to combine the conditions with $and(...) explicitly rather than guessing which one should win.

The juneau-rest-server-datatables module's DataTablesQuery adapter maps a DataTables request bean onto a BeanQuery via BeanQuery.Builder, runs it on a BeanQuerySession, and copies the result onto the DataTables response envelope (total → recordsTotal, matched → recordsFiltered, each read from the independently-optional Page.total()/Page.matched()). Each searchable column's own, non-blank per-column search box becomes one column=expression clause, AND-ed across columns by the engine. The table's single global search box is different: a non-blank global search term synthesizes a top-level $or of one leaf per searchable column, and the leaf's operator depends on that column's declared SearchType on the session's BeanQueryContext (an undeclared or unknown column is treated as TEXT): SearchType Global-search leaf TEXT, ID $contains VERSION $prefix ENUM $eq (standing in for a future $eqic) NUMERIC, BOOLEAN, TIMESTAMP $eq, only when the term parses as that type — otherwise the column is skipped An AND-ed per-column term on the same column as the global search is intentional, not a bug: the column's own leaf and the global $or group narrow independently, matching DataTables' own column-search-plus-global-search UX.

The juneau-rest-server module binds BeanQuery to HTTP two ways. BeanQueryRequest. Take a BeanQueryRequest as a @RestOp argument. It is a BeanQuery subclass annotated @Request, so it binds straight from the request and can be passed to a session without an adapter. Every wire name equals the property name: Parameter Type Meaning search string column=expression clauses view string Columns to return, in order (a column projection, not a saved-view id) sort string Sort columns; :desc or - for descending position integer, minimum=0 0-based index of the first row (negative is rejected by part validation, HTTP 400) limit integer Maximum rows; the context applies defaultLimit and clamps to maxLimit opts string key=value options, e.g. counts=true private static final InMemoryBeanQueryContext<Person> PEOPLE = InMemoryBeanQueryContext.create(Person.class).build(); @RestGet("/people") public List<Person> getPeople(BeanQueryRequest q) { try (var s = PEOPLE.getSession(people)) { return s.find(q).rows(); } } Each getter carries a @Schema description, so the operation is documented in Swagger automatically. To use different parameter names, subclass BeanQueryRequest and redeclare the getter with your own @Query name. Saved-view endpoints that use view as an id must not take a BeanQueryRequest. A concrete @Request class needs a public no-arg constructor and a public setter for every annotated getter; a violation throws IllegalArgumentException when the resource's operation table is built (at startup with @Rest(eagerInit=true), otherwise on the first request). Queryable. For a response that is already a Collection or array of beans or maps, register @Rest(converters=Queryable.class) (or @RestOp(converters=...)). It builds and caches a context per element class, applies any QueryableSettings bean (defaultLimit, maxLimit, allowRegex, regexTimeout, countPolicy and the caps), runs the request, and returns the rows. ?opts=counts=true adds X-BeanQuery-Total and X-BeanQuery-Matched headers, each only when that count was computed. See Converters.

RestContext.convertThrowable maps BeanQuery exceptions thrown from any operation or converter: Exception HTTP Body Header BeanQuerySyntaxException 400 The message. With problem details on, a "code" member too X-BeanQuery-Error: <Code name>, e.g. UNKNOWN_COLUMN, BAD_VALUE, REGEX_DISABLED BeanQueryExecutionException 500 Query execution failed. none (the cause is logged, never sent) GET /people?search=pasword=x&sort=name,age:desc&view=name,age HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request X-BeanQuery-Error: UNKNOWN_COLUMN { "status": 400, "title": "Bad Request", "detail": "Unknown column 'pasword' in search.", "code": "UNKNOWN_COLUMN" } Without problem details, the body is the plain message and the header is the only machine-readable code. The DataTables adapter (DataTablesQuery) follows the same mapping: it lets the exception propagate, so a syntax error is HTTP 400 with the X-BeanQuery-Error header, and JuneauDataTables.ajax shows the server's message to the user.

Every query is validated into a ResolvedQuery before any engine sees it. session.resolve(query) exposes that step on its own. Unknown columns, operators the column does not allow, and anything over a cap (clauses, sort keys, expression depth) are rejected, never silently dropped. A page limit above maxLimit is clamped to maxLimit. maxSearchLength caps the raw string length of all four query fields — search, sort, view and opts — not just the search string. A $regex pattern is also capped at 256 characters, rejected before it is ever matched. regexTimeout only bounds the in-memory engine's regex matching; it has no effect on SqlBeanQueryContext, which pushes $regex down to the database's own regex operator with no engine-side time limit. If a SQL context allows $regex, set SqlBeanQueryContext.Builder#queryTimeout (default: none) so a pathological pattern cannot run unbounded. Setting Default Per-session override defaultLimit / maxLimit 100 / 1000 (null = uncapped) yes maxSearchClauses / maxSortKeys 64 / 8 yes maxSearchLength / maxExpressionDepth 4096 / 16 yes countPolicy IF_REQUESTED yes regexTimeout 50 ms yes allowRegex, operators, columnOperators on, standard set no Session overrides are for trusted server-side callers, such as a CSV export. They should never be driven by request data. CountPolicy decides which counts a Page carries: NONE: no counts. MATCHED: only matched(), the rows that pass the guards and the search. BOTH: matched() and total() (the rows that pass the guards). IF_REQUESTED: whatever the query's opts ask for. session.count(query) always returns both counts.

SqlBeanQueryContext renders a validated query through a SqlDialect. Juneau ships one, PostgresDialect, in its own module and package (org.apache.juneau.beanquery.postgres): <dependency><groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId><artifactId>juneau-beanquery-sql</artifactId></dependency> <dependency><groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId><artifactId>juneau-beanquery-postgres</artifactId></dependency> import org.apache.juneau.beanquery.postgres.PostgresDialect; SqlBeanQueryContext<Task> ctx = SqlBeanQueryContext.create(Task.class) .dialect(PostgresDialect.INSTANCE) .table("tasks") .column("name", SearchType.TEXT) .column("status", SearchType.ENUM) .dataSource(dataSource) .build();

During query resolution every literal that belongs to a value operator (a bare token, $eq, $ne, $in, $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte, $between) is parsed once with SearchType.parse(String). Both engines then see the same typed value (SearchExpression.typedValue()): Column type Parsed value NUMERIC BigDecimal BOOLEAN Boolean (true/false, case-insensitive) TIMESTAMP OffsetDateTime (explicit offset, or epoch milliseconds as UTC), LocalDateTime (no offset), or LocalDate (date only) TEXT, ID, ENUM, VERSION String, unchanged A value that does not parse for its column type (age=$gt(abc) on a NUMERIC column) fails with BeanQuerySyntaxException code BAD_VALUE (HTTP 400), the same in the in-memory and SQL engines. It is never "no match" and never a database error. TIMESTAMP offsets A value with an explicit offset (2026-09-30T12:00:00Z) is one absolute instant. A local form (date-time without offset, or a bare date) is UTC in the in-memory engine but is interpreted in the database session time zone in SQL. Use offset forms, or epoch milliseconds, in any search that must behave identically everywhere.

A NUMERIC or TIMESTAMP literal may be a relative duration, [+-]<n>(ms|s|m|h|d) (lowercase units), for example -24h, or the equivalent signed ISO-8601 duration (PT24H, -PT24H, +PT30M, P1D), which has identical semantics (-24h and -PT24H are interchangeable). Only days, hours, minutes and (fractional) seconds are accepted, with a single leading sign; years, months, weeks and per-component signs such as PT-1H are BAD_VALUE, and fractions of a millisecond are floored. ISO durations go through the same code path and typed binds in the in-memory and SQL engines, so a SQL dialect never sees the text. It resolves against one requestTime taken once per query, so every clause sees the same "now". A TIMESTAMP becomes requestTime plus the signed amount, as an OffsetDateTime at UTC. A NUMERIC becomes the signed amount in milliseconds. A bare signed number such as -5 is never a duration. A total that overflows is BAD_VALUE; on BOOLEAN a duration is BAD_VALUE; TEXT, ID, ENUM and VERSION keep it as literal text. Instant now = Instant.parse("2026-09-30T12:00:00Z"); SearchType.TIMESTAMP.parse("-24h", now); // 2026-09-29T12:00Z (OffsetDateTime) SearchType.NUMERIC.parse("-24h", now); // BigDecimal("-86400000") SearchType.NUMERIC.parse("-PT24H", now); // BigDecimal("-86400000"), same as -24h

A SqlRowMapper<T> turns the current ResultSet row into a bean for find and stream. findValues, streamValues and count never need one. Two are built in: SqlRowMapper.map(): each row becomes a LinkedHashMap<String,Object> keyed by column name in SELECT order. SQL NULL is null. SqlRowMapper.bean(Class): each row becomes a record (canonical constructor) or a class with a public no-arg constructor and public single-argument setX methods (fluent setters are fine). Columns match properties by exact name; unmatched columns are ignored; properties with no column (or a NULL for a primitive) keep the type default. bean(...) plans the class once and throws IllegalArgumentException for an unmappable type (interface, abstract class, enum, no no-arg constructor, overloaded setter). A read failure throws BeanQueryExecutionException naming the column, never the SQL. record Task(String name, int age) {} SqlRowMapper<Task> beans = SqlRowMapper.bean(Task.class); SqlRowMapper<Map<String,Object>> maps = SqlRowMapper.map(); When rowMapper(...) is not called, build() chooses from the row type T: a Map type that LinkedHashMap is assignable to gets map(); any other type bean(T) can plan gets bean(T); Object, other Map types (such as TreeMap) and unplannable types get none, and find/stream then throw IllegalStateException with the reason. An explicit rowMapper(...) always wins.

A custom operator carries a SearchSqlRenderer as a typed extension. The renderer receives the dialect, the quoted column, the column's SearchType and List<Object> args, and returns a SqlFragment (SQL plus ordered binds). Always bind values; never concatenate them into SQL. By default the args are the literal Strings; call typedArgs(true) to receive the parsed values from the table above (built-in value operators always get typed args). SearchOperator divisibleBy = SearchOperator .create("$divby", "Matches multiples of N. Example: $divby(3)") .types(SearchType.NUMERIC) .minArgs(1).maxArgs(1) .typedArgs(true) // args.get(0) is a BigDecimal, bound as-is .extension(SearchSqlRenderer.class, (dialect, col, type, args) -> SqlFragment.of("(" + col + " % ? = 0)", args.get(0))) .build();

The two engines must agree on which rows match. Where a dialect cannot express a feature with the in-memory meaning, it rejects the query with BeanQuerySyntaxException code BAD_VALUE (HTTP 400) instead of silently returning different rows: An operator the dialect does not support, such as $regex on a dialect with no regular-expression operator, is BAD_VALUE. A dialect that does not order VERSION values as dotted-integer tuples (it does not declare supportsVersionOrdering()) rejects the VERSION range operators $gt, $gte, $lt, $lte and $between. PostgresDialect declares supportsVersionOrdering() and renders $regex, so it supports both, with the differences listed below.

ENUM. Compared as text; the column is cast (col::text) wherever a text function applies, so a native Postgres enum column behaves like text, including bare */? wildcards (case-insensitive, whole constant name). VERSION. Stored as dotted text (10.0.1) and compared as an integer tuple (10.9 sorts before 10.10), like the in-memory engine. A stored value that is not a dotted sequence of integers never matches. Differences from in-memory: each part is limited to 9 digits, and a trailing empty part (10.) or signed part (+1) is rejected. $regex. Rendered with the POSIX operators ~ (case-sensitive) and ~* (case-insensitive), anchored to the full string; flags=i|m|s map to the Postgres embedded options. This is Postgres (ARE) regex syntax, not Java regex: possessive quantifiers and \p{L} style classes are Java-only, and the server can reject a pattern the in-memory engine accepts, failing the query. Set a statement_timeout on connections that run user-supplied patterns. $not and NULL. $not(x) renders as NOT COALESCE(x, FALSE), so a NULL cell matches $not(...) exactly as in memory. $blank means NULL or ASCII-only whitespace. Binds. Values are always ? parameters, never SQL text.

Exception Cause Typical HTTP mapping BeanQuerySyntaxException The query breaks a rule (unknown column or operator, malformed expression, over a limit). 400 BeanQueryExecutionException The engine failed (a getter, guard or rowMapper threw, a row was null, SQL failed, a connection could not be opened). The message names no SQL or bind values. 500 IllegalArgumentException / IllegalStateException Author misconfiguration or API misuse (for example a closed session, or reading a count that was not computed). n/a — a deployment bug to fix, not a request to reject try (var session = PEOPLE.getSession(people)) { return session.find(query); } catch (BeanQuerySyntaxException e) { throw new BadRequest(e, "Invalid query: %s", e.getMessage()); }

A clause's right-hand side is either an operator call, $name(arg,...), or a bare pattern with no operator at all, e.g. age=$gt(21) or name=Al*. A literal $ in a bare pattern or an operator argument is written $$ — $$ is always a literal $, so $$eq(x) is the literal text $eq(x), while $eq(x) is the operator call.

$eq, $in and $ne are exact and case-sensitive. $eqic is the case-insensitive exact-match counterpart to $eq — same exact-match semantics, just ignoring case. Bare patterns and $contains / $prefix / $regex are case-insensitive, as before. Operator names are themselves case-insensitive: $EQ(...) and $eq(...) are the same operator.

A bare pattern supports two wildcards: * (any run of characters) and ? (exactly one character), e.g. name=Al* or name=Al?n. Quoting a token with double quotes bypasses wildcard interpretation entirely and matches the quoted text literally — name="a*b" matches the literal string a*b, not a wildcard pattern.

A regex argument is quoted the same as any other operator argument whenever it contains a , or ) that would otherwise be read as argument punctuation, e.g. name=$regex("a,b\)"). $regex also accepts an optional second argument, flags=X, where X is one or more of i (case-insensitive), m (multiline) or s (dot-all): e.g. name=$regex(^A.*,flags=im). A second argument that is not prefixed flags= is ignored. With no flags= argument, $regex matches case-insensitively by default. Passing flags= replaces that default rather than adding to it — $regex(^A.*,flags=m) is case-sensitive, not case-insensitive-and- multiline. To keep case-insensitivity alongside another flag, include i explicitly, e.g. flags=im.

SearchOperator is immutable. Register a new operator through its builder: SearchOperator startsWithIgnoreCase = SearchOperator.create("$starts", "Matches a case-insensitive prefix.") .types(SearchType.TEXT, SearchType.ID) .predicate((cell, args) -> cell != null && String.valueOf(cell).toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).startsWith(args.get(0).toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))) .build(); .build() is required — the intermediate builder stages returned by .types(...) / .predicate(...) are not themselves usable as a SearchOperator. Use copy() on an existing SearchOperator to get a pre-filled builder for a variant.

A malformed search expression (the right-hand side of one clause) throws BeanQuerySyntaxException with a specific Code naming the exact grammar problem, rather than a generic parse failure, so a request-facing adapter can show a specific message: UNKNOWN_OPERATOR MALFORMED_OPERATOR BAD_ARG_COUNT UNBALANCED EMPTY_ARGUMENT EMPTY_EXPRESSION TRAILING_TEXT UNTERMINATED_QUOTE INVALID_OPERATOR_NAME Code has further values beyond these nine, covering problems the expression grammar itself can't detect — an unknown or duplicate column name, a search string or option string over its length limit, too many sort keys or $and/$or clauses, nesting too deep, a disabled or too-long regex, a regex that exceeds its matching-time budget, and $and/$or/$not called with the wrong number of arguments. Those are thrown during query resolution rather than expression parsing, and are outside the scope of this grammar reference.

juneau-search.js, the client-side datatable search box, mirrors every rule above byte-for-byte — this is verified by running a shared JSON test corpus against both the Java engine and the JavaScript engine.

SearchType.bareHelp() returns a one-sentence, per-type explanation of what a bare (operator-less) value means for a column of that type. This is the text a search-bar popover shows next to each searchable column: SearchType bareHelp() TEXT, ID Matches any value containing this text (case-insensitive). Use $eq(...) for an exact, case-sensitive match. ENUM Matches one value exactly, case-insensitive. NUMERIC Matches a number exactly. Use $gt / $gte / $lt / $lte / $between for a range, or a duration such as -24h or -PT24H (= -86400000 ms). TIMESTAMP Matches an exact instant; a bare date means UTC midnight exactly, so for a whole day use $between(d, d+1). Also accepts a duration such as -24h or -PT24H, relative to the request time. VERSION Matches any version starting with this prefix, e.g. 250 matches 250.1 and 250.2.3. BOOLEAN Matches true or false exactly. Porting searches from another $-operator syntax Some existing $-operator search syntaxes treat $eq(...) as case-insensitive; Juneau's $eq(...) is exact and case-sensitive. The direct port of such an $eq(...) call is Juneau's $eqic(...), not $eq(...). A bare (operator-less) search value behaves per the grammar above: a case-insensitive substring match on TEXT/ID, a dotted-tuple prefix on VERSION, and an exact match on NUMERIC/TIMESTAMP/ENUM/BOOLEAN. For TIMESTAMP specifically, a bare date is an exact UTC-midnight instant, not "that whole day" — use $between(d, d+1) for a day range. There is no linter or automated check for a case-insensitive-style $eq(...) call site carried over from another syntax; this callout is the whole mitigation.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.bean package provides Juneau's bean-modeling layer — the annotations and introspection engine that describe how Java beans are recognized, read, written, and mapped, independently of any particular marshalling format. The marshalling modules build on this layer through a small set of SPI seams so the bean model stays decoupled from serialization concerns.
Annotations that control how classes and their properties are introspected.

Applied to a class to control bean introspection and modeling — property inclusion/order, read-only/write-only properties, a custom PropertyNamer, a stop class, and more. @BeanType(properties="id,name,city", propertyNamer=PropertyNamerDLC.class) public class Address { public String id, name, city; }

Applied to fields, getters/setters, or constructor parameters to control property modeling — most commonly to override the property name via its value()/name(). public class Person { @BeanProp("full-name") public String getName() { ... } }

Maps constructor arguments to property names on beans with read-only properties. public class Point { public final int x, y; @BeanCtor(properties="x,y") public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } }

Excludes a class, field, method, or constructor from bean introspection. public class Account { public String username; @BeanIgnore public String getPasswordHash() { ... } // never treated as a bean property }
Specifies the parameter name used for bean property mapping (e.g. on a constructor parameter). public Point(@Name("x") int x, @Name("y") int y) { ... }
Specifies bean-modeling config properties (visibility rules, property-namer, not-bean packages/classes, etc.) on REST classes and methods.
The runtime types that hold and expose bean metadata.
Encapsulates all access to the properties of a bean class (like a souped-up java.beans.BeanInfo). Obtained via the static factory. BeanMeta<Address> bm = BeanMeta.of(Address.class);
SPI seam exposing the type-classification surface (is-bean, element/key/value types, instantiation) that the bean-runtime types need without coupling the bean-modeling layer to the marshalling layer.

A Map-style wrapper around a Java bean, exposing its properties as map entries backed by BeanMeta. BeanMap<Address> m = BeanMap.of(new Address()); m.put("city", "Portland"); Object city = m.get("city");
Represents a single entry in a BeanMap.
Contains metadata about a single bean property.
Represents a simple bean property value together with the metadata associated with it.
The minimum runtime surface the bean-modeling layer needs from a marshalling session.
Immutable runtime configuration for the bean-modeling layer, built via its nested Builder.
Converts conventional bean property names into other conventions.
Defines the API for converting a conventional bean property name to some other form. public interface PropertyNamer { String getPropertyName(String name); }
The default namer — returns property names unchanged.
Converts property names to dashed-lower-case format (fooBar → foo-bar).
Converts property names to dashed-upper-case-start format.
Converts property names to underscore-lower-case format (fooBar → foo_bar).
Optional schema-driven validation of bean-property values.
Validates a bean-property value against a schema, throwing SchemaValidationException on failure. void validate(Object value) throws SchemaValidationException;
Builds PropertyValidator instances from a JSON-Schema-shaped map of constraints.
Discovery helper that locates a PropertyValidatorFactory via ServiceLoader.
Seams that let the marshalling layer plug into the bean model without the bean-modeling package depending on marshalling.
Intercepts bean property reads and writes, allowing values to be transformed during introspection. BeanInterceptor.Void is the non-existent (no-op) placeholder.
Exposes the per-class filter surface the bean-runtime types need, decoupled from the marshalling-side filter.
Exposes marshalling-aware BeanMeta construction hooks.
Applies marshalling-side post-processing to a BeanPropertyMeta.Builder after its validation succeeds.
Exposes the dictionary-lookup surface the bean-runtime types need, decoupled from the marshalling-side bean registry.
Exposes the type-resolution operations that the bean-property validation pass needs from the marshalling layer.
Marks an object that represents (wraps) another object.
Provides an InvocationHandler for creating dynamic proxy instances of bean interfaces.
org.apache.juneau.commons.bean

The org.apache.juneau.commons.collections package provides enhanced collection utilities that extend the standard Java Collections Framework with fluent APIs, specialized collection types, and caching capabilities.

Fluent builder for constructing List instances with various configuration options. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.CollectionUtils.*; // Basic usage List<String> list = listBuilder(String.class) .add("apple", "banana", "cherry") .build(); // With sorting List<Integer> sorted = listBuilder(Integer.class) .add(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6) .sorted() .build(); // Conditional elements List<String> filtered = listBuilder(String.class) .add("always") .addIf(includeOptional, "optional") .build(); // Immutable list List<String> immutable = listBuilder(String.class) .add("read", "only") .unmodifiable() .build();

Fluent builder for constructing Map instances. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.CollectionUtils.*; // Basic usage Map<String, Integer> map = mapBuilder(String.class, Integer.class) .add("one", 1) .add("two", 2) .add("three", 3) .build(); // Using pairs Map<String, String> props = mapBuilder(String.class, String.class) .addPairs("host", "localhost", "port", "8080") .build(); // With sorting by key Map<String, Integer> sorted = mapBuilder(String.class, Integer.class) .add("zebra", 3) .add("apple", 1) .add("banana", 2) .sorted() .build();

Fluent builder for constructing Set instances with automatic deduplication. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.CollectionUtils.*; // Basic usage Set<String> set = setBuilder(String.class) .add("apple", "banana", "cherry") .build(); // Automatic deduplication Set<Integer> unique = setBuilder(Integer.class) .add(1, 2, 3, 2, 1) // Duplicates ignored .build(); // Contains: 1, 2, 3

A fluent wrapper around an arbitrary map that provides convenient methods for adding entries. FluentMap<String, String> map = new FluentMap<>(new LinkedHashMap<>()); map .a("key1", "value1") .a("key2", "value2") .ai(true, "key3", "value3") // Added .ai(false, "key4", "value4"); // Not added // Add all entries from another map Map<String, String> other = Map.of("key5", "value5", "key6", "value6"); map.aa(other);

A fluent wrapper around a list for convenient element addition. FluentList<String> list = new FluentList<>(new ArrayList<>()); list .a("item1") .a("item2") .ai(true, "item3") // Added .ai(false, "item4"); // Not added
A fluent wrapper around a set for convenient element addition. FluentSet<String> set = new FluentSet<>(new LinkedHashSet<>()); set .a("item1") .a("item2") .ai(true, "item3"); // Added

A composite map that presents multiple maps as a single unified map. Map<String, String> map1 = Map.of("key1", "value1", "key2", "value2"); Map<String, String> map2 = Map.of("key3", "value3", "key2", "value2b"); Map<String, String> map3 = Map.of("key4", "value4"); MultiMap<String, String> multiMap = new MultiMap<>(map1, map2, map3); // Access entries by key multiMap.get("key1"); // Returns "value1" from map1 multiMap.get("key2"); // Returns "value2" from map1 (first match wins) multiMap.get("key3"); // Returns "value3" from map2

A composite list that presents multiple lists as a single unified list. List<String> list1 = List.of("a", "b", "c"); List<String> list2 = List.of("d", "e"); List<String> list3 = List.of("f", "g", "h"); MultiList<String> multiList = new MultiList<>(list1, list2, list3); // Access elements multiList.get(0); // Returns "a" from list1 multiList.get(3); // Returns "d" from list2 multiList.size(); // Returns 8 (total elements)

A composite set that presents multiple sets as a single unified set. Set<String> set1 = Set.of("a", "b", "c"); Set<String> set2 = Set.of("c", "d", "e"); // "c" is duplicate Set<String> set3 = Set.of("f", "g"); MultiSet<String> multiSet = new MultiSet<>(set1, set2, set3); // Access elements (duplicates handled automatically) multiSet.contains("c"); // Returns true multiSet.size(); // Returns 7 (unique elements: a, b, c, d, e, f, g)

A bidirectional map that allows lookup by both key and value. BidiMap<String, Integer> bidiMap = new BidiMap<>(); bidiMap.put("one", 1); bidiMap.put("two", 2); bidiMap.put("three", 3); // Forward lookup bidiMap.get("one"); // Returns 1 // Reverse lookup bidiMap.getKey(1); // Returns "one" bidiMap.getKey(2); // Returns "two"

A map that filters entries based on a predicate. FilteredMap<String, Integer> filtered = new FilteredMap<>( new HashMap<>(), (k, v) -> v > 0 // Only keep positive values ); filtered.put("a", 5); // Added filtered.put("b", -1); // Filtered out filtered.put("c", 10); // Added

A list that filters elements based on a predicate. FilteredList<Integer> filtered = new FilteredList<>( new ArrayList<>(), v -> v > 0 // Only keep positive values ); filtered.add(5); // Added filtered.add(-1); // Filtered out filtered.add(10); // Added

A set that filters elements based on a predicate. FilteredSet<Integer> filtered = new FilteredSet<>( new LinkedHashSet<>(), v -> v > 0 // Only keep positive values ); filtered.add(5); // Added filtered.add(-1); // Filtered out filtered.add(10); // Added

Simple in-memory cache for storing and retrieving objects by key. // Create a cache with default supplier Cache<String, Pattern> patternCache = Cache .of(String.class, Pattern.class) .maxSize(100) .supplier(Pattern::compile) .build(); // Retrieve using default supplier Pattern pattern1 = patternCache.get("[a-z]+"); // Or override the supplier Pattern pattern2 = patternCache.get("[0-9]+", () -> Pattern.compile("[0-9]+", Pattern.CASE_INSENSITIVE));

A composite key composed of multiple values, suitable for use as a key in hash-based collections. // Create a composite key from multiple values HashKey key = HashKey.of( "config1", "config2", true, 42 ); // Use as a key in a cache or map Map<HashKey, MyObject> cache = new HashMap<>(); cache.put(key, myObject); // Retrieve using an equivalent key HashKey lookupKey = HashKey.of("config1", "config2", true, 42); MyObject cached = cache.get(lookupKey); // Returns myObject

An ArrayList that maintains elements in sorted order. SortedArrayList<String> sorted = new SortedArrayList<>(); sorted.add("zebra"); sorted.add("apple"); sorted.add("banana"); // Elements are automatically sorted // Contains: ["apple", "banana", "zebra"]

A LinkedList that maintains elements in sorted order. SortedLinkedList<Integer> sorted = new SortedLinkedList<>(); sorted.add(3); sorted.add(1); sorted.add(4); // Elements are automatically sorted // Contains: [1, 3, 4]

A list that presents a reversed view of another list. List<String> original = List.of("a", "b", "c", "d"); ReversedList<String> reversed = new ReversedList<>(original); reversed.get(0); // Returns "d" reversed.get(1); // Returns "c" reversed.get(2); // Returns "b" reversed.get(3); // Returns "a"

The org.apache.juneau.commons.concurrent package provides small concurrency helpers that make locks and atomic references work cleanly with try-with-resources and Optional-style APIs.

An AutoCloseable wrapper around a java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock that acquires the lock on construction and releases it on close(), so it can be used directly in a try-with-resources block. The SimpleLock.NO_OP constant is a do-nothing lock. try (SimpleLock ignored = new SimpleLock(myLock)) { // critical section — lock released automatically }

An extension of ReentrantReadWriteLock whose read() and write() methods return auto-closeable SimpleLock instances. SimpleReadWriteLock.NO_OP is a do-nothing variant. SimpleReadWriteLock rw = new SimpleReadWriteLock(); try (SimpleLock ignored = rw.read()) { // read-locked section } try (SimpleLock ignored = rw.write()) { // write-locked section }

A thread-safe reference that combines AtomicReference with Optional-like convenience methods (isPresent(), map(), flatMap(), filter(), of()/ofNullable()/empty()). NullableReference<String> ref = NullableReference.of("hello"); boolean present = ref.isPresent(); NullableReference<Integer> len = ref.map(String::length);

An SPI for detecting reuse ("replay") of a one-time-use identifier, such as a nonce or a single-use token. checkAndRecord(String, long) atomically checks whether an identifier has been seen before and records it as seen, as one indivisible operation — of any two concurrent calls with the same identifier, at most one returns true (first-seen). When the backing store can't answer (for example a remote store is unreachable), the consumer decides how the failure is resolved by passing a ReplayCache.FailMode to checkAndRecord(String, long, ReplayCache.FailMode, Consumer): ReplayCache.FailMode.FAIL_CLOSED (the safe default) — treats a store failure as a replay (reject). ReplayCache.FailMode.FAIL_OPEN — treats a store failure as first-seen (allow), degrading to the multi-use-tolerant behavior a consumer would have with no ReplayCache wired at all. ReplayCache.FailMode is a nested enum declared on ReplayCache itself — it is unrelated to any other FailMode class that may exist elsewhere in the framework. ReplayCache cache = new InMemoryReplayCache(); long expiresAtMs = System.currentTimeMillis() + 60_000L; boolean firstUse = cache.checkAndRecord(nonce, expiresAtMs, ReplayCache.FailMode.FAIL_CLOSED); if (!firstUse) { throw new SecurityException("Replayed nonce detected"); }

The built-in, zero-config ReplayCache implementation: a per-process ConcurrentHashMap-backed seen-identifier set, with self-eviction bounded by each record's own expiresAtMs. Eviction sweeps are throttled to at most once per InMemoryReplayCache.DEFAULT_SWEEP_INTERVAL_MS (1000 ms by default) to keep checkAndRecord() cheap under load. Because it's per-process memory, InMemoryReplayCache only enforces single-use within one JVM — two instances behind a load balancer will not see each other's recorded identifiers. Consumers who need cross-node single-use enforcement must supply their own ReplayCache backed by a store shared across every node. InMemoryReplayCache cache = new InMemoryReplayCache();
The org.apache.juneau.commons.conversion package provides a lightweight, pluggable type-conversion engine for converting objects between types without requiring a full marshalling context or session.

The primary interface for converting objects between types. Use BasicConverter.INSTANCE for a ready-made singleton that handles a wide range of common conversions. Converter converter = BasicConverter.INSTANCE; Integer i = converter.to("123", Integer.class);

A concrete CachingConverter supporting common type conversions (numbers, booleans, dates, collections, arrays, and more) without a MarshallingContext. Exposes the shared BasicConverter.INSTANCE singleton. long[] a = BasicConverter.INSTANCE.to("1,2,3", long[].class);
An abstract Converter that lazily discovers conversion functions on first use for a given input/output type pair and caches them for subsequent calls.
A BasicConverter subclass that accepts one or more ConversionFinder strategies, consulted in order before the built-in conversions.
A functional interface representing a single type conversion. The args parameter carries any type arguments needed for parameterized output types.
A pluggable strategy for discovering Conversion functions between type pairs; passed to the ConfigurableConverter constructor.
Provides contextual objects to Conversion functions at call time.
Unchecked exception thrown by Converter.to(Object, Class) when no conversion path exists between two types. Callers unsure whether a conversion is possible can test first rather than catch.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.function package extends the standard java.util.function toolkit with higher-arity functional interfaces, checked-exception–friendly variants, small immutable tuples, and lazy/nullable suppliers used throughout the framework.
Two-to-five argument extensions of the standard Consumer and Function patterns.
An operation that accepts two arguments and returns no result. Higher-arity siblings: Consumer3, Consumer4, Consumer5.
A function that accepts two arguments and produces a result. Higher-arity siblings: Function3, Function4, Function5.
Functional interfaces whose functional method is allowed to throw checked exceptions — useful for passing exception-throwing code where the JDK interfaces would force a try/catch.
Identical to Runnable but its run() method may throw a checked exception.
A Consumer whose acceptThrows(T) may throw a checked exception. Higher-arity siblings: ThrowingConsumer2, ThrowingConsumer3, ThrowingConsumer4, ThrowingConsumer5.
A Function whose functional method may throw a checked exception. Higher-arity siblings: ThrowingFunction2, ThrowingFunction3, ThrowingFunction4, ThrowingFunction5.
A Supplier whose get() may throw a checked exception.
A Supplier whose value may be null, with Optional-like null-safe query methods. NullableSupplier<String> s = NullableSupplier.ofNullable(computeOrNull());

A thread-safe supplier that caches the result of its first call and can be reset. Memoizer<Config> config = new Memoizer<>(() -> loadExpensiveConfig()); Config c = config.get(); // computed once config.reset(); // next get() recomputes

Static factory methods for creating memoizing suppliers, without needing to call the NullableSupplier/Memoizer constructors directly. Suppliers.memoize(Supplier) — wraps a Supplier in a thread-safe, non-resettable memoizing NullableSupplier. The underlying supplier is invoked at most once (races are tolerated — if multiple threads call get() before the first result is cached, the supplier may be invoked more than once, but every caller ends up with the same cached value). Suppliers.memoizer(Supplier) — wraps a Supplier in a resettable Memoizer, equivalent to new Memoizer<>(supplier). // One-shot memoization - no reset needed NullableSupplier<Config> config = Suppliers.memoize(() -> loadExpensiveConfig()); Config c = config.get(); // computed once and cached // Resettable memoization - equivalent to new Memoizer<>(supplier) Memoizer<Config> config2 = Suppliers.memoizer(() -> loadExpensiveConfig()); config2.reset(); // next get() recomputes
Immutable value tuples with content-based equals()/hashCode() — handy as composite map keys.
A single-value tuple. Wider tuples: Tuple2, Tuple3, Tuple4, Tuple5. Tuple2<String,Integer> key = Tuple2.of("foo", 42); String a = key.getA(); Integer b = key.getB();
Lifecycle-aware source/target interfaces that let the marshalling layer stream beans one at a time without buffering an entire document.
A lazy, one-at-a-time producer used as a serializer source (extends Iterable).
A one-at-a-time consumer used as a parser target (extends ThrowingConsumer).
Combines BeanSupplier and BeanConsumer for round-trip use on the same property or class. ListBeanChannel is a simple ArrayList-backed implementation.
A universal factory interface used with @Marshalled(factory=...) as the single DI hook for framework-instantiated classes. BeanFactory.Void is the sentinel default meaning "no factory specified".

The org.apache.juneau.commons.http package provides lightweight, dependency-free primitives for parsing and modeling HTTP header values — media types, content-negotiation ranges, and name/value parameters — as defined by RFC 2616.
Describes a single media type used in content negotiation (e.g. text/html;charset=UTF-8). Provides constants for the common types Juneau supports. MediaType json = MediaType.JSON; // application/json
Describes a single range within an Accept-style header, including its quality (q) metric and extension parameters.

A parsed Accept (or similar) header — a list of MediaRange values sorted most-acceptable first, with a match(...) method for selecting the best available media type. MediaRanges accept = MediaRanges.of("text/json;q=0.8, text/*;q=0.6, */*;q=0.0"); int best = accept.match(List.of(MediaType.JSON, MediaType.XML));
Like MediaRange but for plain comma-delimited header values with an optional quality metric (e.g. Accept-Encoding).
A parsed Accept-Encoding (or similar) header — a sorted list of StringRange values.
Represents a parsed element from an HTTP header value — a name plus zero or more parameters (RFC 2616).
A lightweight parser that splits comma-delimited header values into HeaderElement objects with semicolon-delimited parameters.
A name/value pair parameter, typically used in HTTP headers and request parameters.
A simple immutable implementation of NameValuePair.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.httppart package provides the shared enumerations and exception used to describe HTTP "parts" (query parameters, path variables, headers, form data, and request/response bodies) for OpenAPI-schema-based serialization and parsing.
The possible HTTP part types (e.g. query, header, path, form-data, body).
Valid values for a schema's type field (string, number, integer, boolean, array, object, etc.).
Valid values for a schema's format field (int32, int64, date-time, byte, binary, etc.).
Valid values for a schema's collectionFormat field (csv, ssv, tsv, pipes, multi, etc.).
Thrown when an HTTP part fails schema validation.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.io package provides file and stream utilities, console support, MIME type detection, and path builders for working with files and I/O operations.

Represents a file that can be located either on the classpath or in the file system. // Classpath file LocalFile classpathFile = new LocalFile(MyClass.class, "config.properties"); InputStream is = classpathFile.read(); // File system file LocalFile fsFile = new LocalFile(Paths.get("/path/to/file.txt")); InputStream is2 = fsFile.read(); // With caching for repeated access LocalFile cachedFile = new LocalFile(MyClass.class, "template.html"); cachedFile.cache(); // Cache contents in memory InputStream is3 = cachedFile.read(); // Fast - uses cache // Check existence without triggering an exception if (fsFile.exists()) { InputStream is4 = fsFile.read(); }

Represents a directory that can be located either on the classpath or in the file system. // Classpath directory LocalDir classpathDir = new LocalDir(MyClass.class, "templates"); LocalFile file = classpathDir.resolve("index.html"); // File system directory LocalDir fsDir = new LocalDir(Paths.get("/var/config")); LocalFile file2 = fsDir.resolve("app.properties"); // Package directory (null or empty path) LocalDir packageDir = new LocalDir(MyClass.class, null); LocalFile file3 = packageDir.resolve("resource.txt");

Fluent builder for creating Reader instances from files. FileReaderBuilder builder = FileReaderBuilder.create() .file(Paths.get("file.txt")) .charset(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) .allowNoFile(true); // Don't throw if the file doesn't exist Reader reader = builder.build();

Fluent builder for creating Writer instances for files. FileWriterBuilder builder = FileWriterBuilder.create() .file(Paths.get("output.txt")) .charset(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) .append(true) .buffered(true); Writer writer = builder.build();

Fluent builder for creating Reader instances from Path objects. PathReaderBuilder builder = PathReaderBuilder.create() .path(Paths.get("file.txt")) .charset(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) .allowNoFile(true); // Don't throw if the file doesn't exist Reader reader = builder.build();
Utility for printing formatted (printf-style) messages to the console. Console.out("Hello %s, you have %s items", "John", 5); Console.err("Something went wrong: %s", errorMessage);

Utility for detecting MIME types from file extensions. // Use the default, pre-populated instance String mimeType = MimeTypeDetector.DEFAULT.getContentType("file.pdf"); // "application/pdf" // Or build a customized instance MimeTypeDetector detector = MimeTypeDetector.builder() .addDefaultMappings() .build(); String mimeType2 = detector.getContentType("image.jpg"); // "image/jpeg"
A Reader implementation that reads from a CharSequence. CharSequenceReader reader = new CharSequenceReader("Hello World"); int ch = reader.read(); // 'H'

An InputStream implementation that reads from a Reader. Reader reader = new StringReader("Hello World"); ReaderInputStream inputStream = new ReaderInputStream(reader, StandardCharsets.UTF_8); byte[] bytes = inputStream.readAllBytes();

A Writer implementation that writes to a StringBuilder. StringBuilderWriter writer = new StringBuilderWriter(); writer.write("Hello"); writer.write(" World"); String result = writer.toString(); // "Hello World"

An OutputStream wrapper that prevents the underlying stream from being closed. OutputStream original = new FileOutputStream("file.txt"); NoCloseOutputStream wrapped = new NoCloseOutputStream(original); wrapped.close(); // Does not close the original stream

A Writer wrapper that prevents the underlying writer from being closed. Writer original = new FileWriter("file.txt"); NoCloseWriter wrapped = new NoCloseWriter(original); wrapped.close(); // Does not close the original writer

// Try classpath first, then file system - use exists() to check without // relying on exception handling for control flow. LocalFile file = new LocalFile(MyClass.class, "config.properties"); LocalFile fsFile = new LocalFile(Paths.get("/etc/myapp/config.properties")); LocalFile resolved = file.exists() ? file : fsFile; try (InputStream is = resolved.read()) { // Read file contents }
documents.s: Reading Files from Classpath or File System

documents.t: // Cache file for repeated access LocalFile template = new LocalFile(MyClass.class, "template.html"); template.cache(); // Load into memory // Multiple reads use cached content for (int i = 0; i < 100; i++) { try (InputStream is = template.read()) { // Fast - uses cached content } }

// Resolve files within a directory LocalDir templates = new LocalDir(MyClass.class, "templates"); LocalFile index = templates.resolve("index.html"); LocalFile about = templates.resolve("about.html");

// Read file with specific charset, using a Path try (Reader reader = FileReaderBuilder.create() .file(Paths.get("file.txt")) .charset(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) .build()) { // Read from file } // Write file with append mode try (Writer writer = FileWriterBuilder.create() .file(Paths.get("output.txt")) .charset(StandardCharsets.UTF_8) .append(true) .buffered(true) .build()) { writer.write("New content"); }
