The org.apache.juneau.commons.inject package provides Juneau's lightweight injection model. The framework is JSR-330–aligned (jakarta.inject / javax.inject) and layers a small set of Spring-flavored conveniences (@Bean, @Configuration, @Primary, @Order, @Conditional) on top — all under Juneau-owned annotations, and without a compile-time dependency on jakarta.inject-api or jakarta.annotation-api. Juneau supports JSR-330 (jakarta.inject / javax.inject) annotations as closely as our lightweight model allows. Where Spring conventions add value to the lightweight model, we adopt them under our own annotations.

Goal Non-goal Lightweight, predictable bean lookup with constructor / field / method injection. Become a full JSR-330 / CDI provider. FQN-based recognition of jakarta.inject / javax.inject / Spring @Autowired so user code that already uses those annotations Just Works. Become a Spring replacement. Spring-lite conveniences (@Bean, @Configuration, @Primary, @Order, @Conditional) under Juneau annotations. Pull jakarta.inject-api onto the compile classpath of juneau-commons or downstream modules. JSR-250 lifecycle (@PostConstruct / @PreDestroy) honored on framework-instantiated beans. Provide a JVM-wide singleton scope, AOP, proxying, or scopes beyond @Singleton.
documents.s: What this package is — and is not

documents.t: All FQN-based — Juneau picks them up transparently whether the user wrote the Juneau-owned annotation, the JSR-330 equivalent, or the Spring equivalent. Concern Juneau type JSR-330 / Spring equivalents recognized Injection point org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Inject jakarta.inject.Inject, javax.inject.Inject, org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired Named qualifier org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Named jakarta.inject.Named, javax.inject.Named Qualifier marker org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Qualifier jakarta.inject.Qualifier, javax.inject.Qualifier Singleton scope org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Singleton jakarta.inject.Singleton, javax.inject.Singleton Provider org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Provider<T> (single T get()) jakarta.inject.Provider, javax.inject.Provider (resolved via java.lang.reflect.Proxy) Post-construct hook org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.PostConstruct jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct, javax.annotation.PostConstruct Pre-destroy hook org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.PreDestroy jakarta.annotation.PreDestroy, javax.annotation.PreDestroy Juneau-only extensions: Annotation Purpose @Bean(name, value, priority) Marks a method or field on a framework-instantiated host as a provider of a bean. @Configuration(imports={...}) Marks a type that hosts @Bean declarations. imports chains additional configuration classes. Members declared on superclasses are inherited. @Primary Disambiguates when multiple candidates of the same type exist. Unqualified getBean(type) prefers a @Primary candidate; multiple primaries throw BeanCreationException. @Order(int) Bean ordering for getBeansOfType(Class) — lower is higher precedence. When both @Order and @Bean#priority() are present, @Order wins. @Conditional(Class<? extends Condition>) Generic predicate-driven registration guard. @ConditionalOnClass("fqn") Skip registration when a class is not on the classpath. @ConditionalOnMissingBean(Class, name) Skip when a matching bean is already in the store. @ConditionalOnProperty(name, havingValue, matchIfMissing) Skip / register based on a Settings property. Condition and ConditionContext are the SPI for custom predicates.

beanStore.getBean(MyService.class); // unnamed (or @Primary among candidates) beanStore.getBean(MyService.class, "name"); // qualified by name beanStore.getBeansOfType(MyService.class); // all candidates, ordered by @Order / priority beanStore.hasBean(MyService.class);

WritableBeanStore store = new BasicBeanStore(null); store.addBean(MyService.class, new MyService()); // unnamed store.addBean(MyService.class, new MyService(), "name"); // named store.addSupplier(MyService.class, MyService::new); store.addDefaultSupplier(MyService.class, () -> defaultInstance); // framework default, lowest priority store.registerConfiguration(MyConfig.class); // @Configuration with @Bean members registerConfiguration is idempotent at the store level — registering the same class twice (directly or transitively via imports) is processed only once per store.

WritableBeanStore extends AutoCloseable. Calling close(): Invokes @PreDestroy on all beans that were resolved through getBean(...) / getBeansOfType(...), in LIFO order (most-recently resolved first). Aggregates per-bean destroyer failures as suppressed exceptions on a single BeanCreationException. Marks the store closed; subsequent mutating operations throw IllegalStateException. Is idempotent — a second close() is a no-op. RestContext.destroy() calls beanStore.close() after the existing @RestDestroy hooks fire.

public class MyService { private final Repo repo; private final Notifier notifier; @Inject // org.apache.juneau.commons.inject.Inject — or jakarta / javax / Spring @Autowired public MyService(Repo repo, @Named("email") Notifier notifier) { this.repo = repo; this.notifier = notifier; } }

@Configuration(imports = { CommonConfig.class }) public class AppConfig extends BaseConfig { @Bean public Repo repo() { return new JdbcRepo(); } @Bean @Primary public Notifier emailNotifier() { return new EmailNotifier(); } @Bean @ConditionalOnClass("redis.clients.jedis.Jedis") public Cache cache() { return new RedisCache(); } } AppConfig inherits @Bean members declared on BaseConfig. The Cache bean only registers if Jedis is on the classpath.

public class LazyConsumer { @Inject jakarta.inject.Provider<HeavyService> provider; void onRequest() { var svc = provider.get(); // resolved from the bean store per-call } } Juneau resolves the jakarta.inject.Provider<T> parameter via a java.lang.reflect.Proxy over a Supplier<T> from the bean store — no Spring or jakarta.inject-api jar required at compile time.

public class CacheService implements AutoCloseable { @Inject Settings settings; @PostConstruct public void start() { /* warm up */ } @PreDestroy public void shutdown() { /* flush + close */ } } @PreDestroy fires only on beans that were resolved from the store, in LIFO order, when WritableBeanStore.close() is called.

REST resources have @Inject-annotated fields and methods populated from the resource's bean store during context initialization, immediately before @PostConstruct callbacks fire. @Rest public class MyResource { @Bean public Repo repo() { return new JdbcRepo(); } @Inject Repo repo; // populated by RestContext @jakarta.inject.Inject Notifier notifier; // also populated (FQN match) @PostConstruct void init() { /* fields are ready here */ } }

When BeanInstantiator constructs a bean (including a @Configuration class), it searches declared constructors in this order, taking the most-specific resolvable constructor at each level: public protected package-private (default access) private constructors are deliberately excluded — they signal "do not instantiate". The same ladder is used for builder discovery on the bean's builder type. In practice this means a @Configuration class (or any other bean type instantiated through the framework) does not need to expose a public constructor purely to satisfy the bean store, as long as the class is reachable in the declaring package.

These are intentional simplifications: No circular-dependency resolver — cycles are caller-visible. No Scope SPI beyond @Singleton. Custom scopes are not supported in v1. No qualifier-attribute equality (Spring-style); qualifiers compare by annotation type and by @Named value. No AOP / proxying except the Provider<T> adapter described above. Field / method injection of @Inject is honored on framework-instantiated types (e.g. @Rest resources). The framework does not scan arbitrary user objects.
The org.apache.juneau.commons.lang package provides language utilities including value wrappers, version management, string formatting, state enums, and other common language constructs.

A generic mutable value wrapper. // Basic usage Holder<String> name = Holder.of("John"); name.set("Jane"); String result = name.get(); // Returns "Jane" // Use in lambda (effectively final variable) Holder<String> result = Holder.empty(); list.forEach(x -> { if (x.matches(criteria)) { result.set(x); } }); // With default values Holder<String> optional = Holder.empty(); String value = optional.orElse("default"); // Returns "default" // Mapping values Holder<Integer> number = Holder.of(5); Holder<String> text = number.map(Object::toString); // Holder of "5" // With listener for change notification Holder<String> monitored = Holder.of("initial") .listener(newValue -> log("Value changed to: " + newValue)); monitored.set("updated"); // Triggers listener

Mutable integer with additional convenience methods. IntegerHolder counter = IntegerHolder.of(0); counter.increment(); // 1 counter.decrement(); // 0 int value = counter.getAndIncrement(); // Returns 0, then sets to 1

Mutable long with additional convenience methods. LongHolder counter = LongHolder.of(0L); counter.increment(); // 1L counter.decrement(); // 0L long value = counter.getAndIncrement(); // Returns 0L, then sets to 1L

Mutable byte with additional convenience methods. ByteHolder counter = ByteHolder.create(); // Initialized to 0 counter.increment(); // 1 counter.decrement(); // 0 byte value = counter.incrementAndGet(); // Returns 1

Mutable short with additional convenience methods. ShortHolder counter = ShortHolder.create(); // Initialized to 0 counter.increment(); // 1 short value = counter.getAndIncrement(); // Returns 1, then sets to 2

Mutable character with convenience methods for incrementing/decrementing and matching against a set of characters. CharHolder ch = CharHolder.of('A'); ch.increment(); // 'B' boolean found = ch.isAny("XYZB"); // true - matches a character in the string

Mutable double/float with precision-based equality checks, since exact == comparisons on floating-point values are unreliable. DoubleHolder pi = DoubleHolder.of(3.14159); boolean close = pi.is(3.14, 0.01); // true - within 0.01 boolean anyClose = pi.isAny(0.01, 1.0, 3.15, 5.0); // true - matches 3.15 within 0.01

Nullable boolean with convenience methods. BooleanHolder flag = BooleanHolder.of(true); flag.isTrue(); // true flag.isNotTrue(); // false BooleanHolder nullable = BooleanHolder.empty(); nullable.isTrue(); // false (null is not true) nullable.isNotTrue(); // true (null is not true)
Non-nullable boolean flag (true/false only, no null state). Flag flag = Flag.of(true); flag.isTrue(); // true flag.isFalse(); // false flag.toggle(); // Switches to false

Mutable string with convenience methods for equality testing. StringHolder name = StringHolder.of("John"); // Check equality if (name.is("John")) { System.out.println("Name is John"); } // Check multiple values if (name.isAny("John", "Jane", "Bob")) { System.out.println("Name found"); }

Accumulates a running weighted average of numbers, re-weighting on each call to add(int, Number). WeightedAverage avg = new WeightedAverage(); avg.add(2, 10.0); // weight 2, value 10.0 avg.add(1, 40.0); // weight 1, value 40.0 double result = avg.getValue(); // (10.0*2 + 40.0*1) / 3 = 20.0

Cacheable printf-style string formatter (backed by String.format semantics). // Printf-style formatting StringFormat fmt = StringFormat.ofPrintf("Hello %s, you have %d items"); String result = fmt.format("John", 5); // Returns: "Hello John, you have 5 items" // Printf with explicit argument indices StringFormat fmt2 = StringFormat.ofPrintf("%1$s loves %2$s, and %1$s also loves %3$s"); String result2 = fmt2.format("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"); // Returns: "Alice loves Bob, and Alice also loves Charlie" // A one-shot helper is also available for non-cached use String result3 = StringFormat.formatPrintf("%s has %d items", "Alice", 10); // Returns: "Alice has 10 items" note StringFormat is printf-only — MessageFormat-style {0} placeholders are not recognized and render literally ({ and ' are treated as ordinary text). This applies consistently across the terse helpers too: Shorts.f() / Shorts.fs() and StringUtils.format(...) are also printf-only. If you need MessageFormat-style {0} / ''-quoting, use Shorts.mf() / Shorts.mfs() / StringUtils.mformat(...) (backed directly by java.text.MessageFormat) instead — there is no single class that mixes both grammars in one pattern. See the 10.0.0 release notes for migration details. Which String-Formatting Entry Point Should I Use?​ StringFormat, StringUtils.format(...)/mformat(...), and Shorts.f()/mf() all coexist deliberately — they're three different call-site shapes over the same two underlying grammars (printf and MessageFormat), not three competing implementations. Use this table to pick the right one: Use... When... Shorts.f(pattern, args) / Shorts.mf(pattern, args) You want the terse, one-off, static-import-friendly call — most call sites (logging, exception messages, assertions). f = printf-style, mf = MessageFormat-style. Shorts.fs(pattern, args) / Shorts.mfs(pattern, args) Same as above, but the formatting cost should be deferred — e.g. a logging API that takes a Supplier<String> and only calls it when the log level is enabled. StringUtils.format(pattern, args) / mformat(pattern, args) You're already in juneau-commons code that avoids the Shorts static-import convention, or you want the fully-qualified name for clarity in a public API signature. Shorts.f/mf are thin aliases over these two methods — behavior is identical either way. StringFormat.ofPrintf(pattern) The same pattern is reused repeatedly (e.g. in a loop, or as a static final field) and you want to pay the pattern-parsing cost once via the built-in cache, rather than re-parsing on every call. Printf-style only — there is no StringFormat MessageFormat counterpart. note StringFormat is the odd one out shape-wise (a stateful/cacheable class, not a static one-shot method) — reach for it only when reuse/caching matters. For everything else, Shorts.f/mf/fs/mfs are the recommended entry point; StringUtils.format/mformat are the methods they delegate to and remain public for callers that prefer explicit, non-abbreviated names.
Utility class for generating integer hash codes. int hashCode = HashCode.create() .add("foobar") .add(myObject) .add(123) .get();

Version management utility. Version version = Version.of("1.2.3"); version.getMajor(); // Optional.of(1) version.getMinor(); // Optional.of(2) version.getMaintenance(); // Optional.of(3) int major = version.getMajor().orElse(0); // 1 // Compare versions Version v1 = Version.of("1.2.3"); Version v2 = Version.of("1.2.4"); int comparison = v1.compareTo(v2); // -1 (v1 < v2)
Version range utility for checking if a version string falls within an OSGi-style range. VersionRange range = VersionRange.of("[1.0.0,2.0.0)"); boolean inRange = range.matches("1.5.0"); // true

Enumeration of state machine states for use in parsing operations. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.lang.StateEnum.*; // Use in state machine var state = S1; if (state == S1) { // Handle state S1 } else if (state == S2) { // Handle state S2 }

Three-state enum (TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN). TriState state = TriState.TRUE; state.isTrue(); // true state.isFalse(); // false state.isUnknown(); // false TriState unknown = TriState.UNKNOWN; unknown.isTrue(); // false unknown.isFalse(); // false unknown.isUnknown(); // true

Utilities for working with ASCII character sets and maps. AsciiSet asciiSet = AsciiSet.of("abc"); boolean contains = asciiSet.contains('a'); // true AsciiMap<String> asciiMap = AsciiMap.of(); asciiMap.put('a', "alpha"); String value = asciiMap.get('a'); // "alpha"

// Use Holder to create effectively final mutable variables Holder<String> result = Holder.empty(); list.stream() .filter(x -> x.matches(pattern)) .forEach(x -> result.set(x)); String found = result.orElse("not found");
String current = "1.2.3"; VersionRange supported = VersionRange.of("[1.0.0,2.0.0)"); if (supported.matches(current)) { // Version is supported }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.lang.StateEnum.*; StateEnum state = S1; while (state != null) { switch (state) { case S1: // Process S1 state = S2; break; case S2: // Process S2 state = S3; break; // ... } }
Juneau Commons Basics Juneau Commons Utils JavaDoc: Lang Package

The org.apache.juneau.commons.logging package now centers on RichLogger, a JUL-compatible logger wrapper with configurable message rendering, hierarchical capture propagation, and deterministic test-capture ergonomics.

RichLogger wraps an underlying java.util.logging.Logger and keeps a stable canonical logger identity per name while allowing independently configured builder-produced views. RichLogger logger = RichLogger.getLogger(MyClass.class); logger.info("Started"); logger.warning("Low disk space"); You can customize message rendering per view using MessageGenerator while preserving canonical listener/capture identity. RichLogger mfLogger = RichLogger .getLogger(MyClass.class) .builder() .generator(MessageGenerator.MESSAGE_FORMAT) .build(); mfLogger.info("User {0} logged in", userId); The RichLogger javadocs link above is expected to 404 until the next docs/javadocs publish picks up the renamed class page.

LogContext is a thread-confined, MDC-style key/value context. While a scope is open, every java.util.logging.LogRecord emitted by any RichLogger on the same thread automatically carries the context's entries — attachment happens once, centrally, in RichLogger.log(LogRecord), not per logger instance. The API home is RichLogger.context(). try (LogContext.Scope c = RichLogger.context().with("requestId", id)) { // Every record logged on this thread in this scope automatically carries requestId. logger.info("processing"); } Semantics: Classic MDC save/restore nesting. with(key, value) records the key's previous value (or "absent") before overwriting, and Scope.close() restores exactly that prior state — never a blanket clear. Nested scopes on the same key are safe. with(Map) sets a batch atomically and restores all of it in one close(). Null policy. A null key is rejected; a null value means "remove this key for the scope's duration" (a null is never stored). snapshot() returns an immutable copy of the current thread's entries (the shared empty Map.of() singleton when empty, so no allocation on the common empty path). Scope discipline. A Scope must be closed on the same thread that opened it — use try-with-resources. A forgotten close() leaves the entry live on that thread; the leak is the caller's, not the framework's. Not SLF4J MDC LogContext is thread-confined only in v1. It is not inherited by child threads, not propagated across executor or CompletableFuture boundaries, and it is not SLF4J MDC and is not restored by MdcAsyncListener. Apps that rely on SLF4J MDC on an async-completion thread keep it; apps that rely on LogContext do not — with one deliberate exception: the REST debug pipeline's completion record carries the request-thread snapshot across the async hop explicitly (see REST Logging / Debugging). General async propagation is intentionally out of scope for v1.

LogRecordContext is the identity-keyed side table that holds the LogContext snapshot attached to a given LogRecord. It is how a captured record exposes its correlation fields after the fact: Object requestId = LogRecordContext.of(record).get("requestId"); RichLogger.log(LogRecord) calls attachIfAbsent(record) as its first action, so a record that already carries a pre-seeded context (for example, one carried across an async boundary) is never overwritten by the live thread context.

MessageGenerator is the message-format strategy seam used by RichLogger and LogRecord. MessageGenerator.PRINTF uses StringUtils.format(...) (printf-style placeholders). MessageGenerator.MESSAGE_FORMAT uses StringUtils.mformat(...) (MessageFormat-style placeholders). Custom generators can be supplied through RichLogger.Builder.generator(...).
LogRecord remains a java.util.logging.LogRecord subtype and now carries generator-aware lazy formatting so rendered text is produced only when needed.

LogRecordCapture captures emitted JUL records in memory for assertions and includes helper accessors (messages(), last(), byLevel(...), matching(...), and assert helpers). RichLogger logger = RichLogger.getLogger(MyClass.class); try (LogRecordCapture capture = logger.captureEvents()) { doSomethingThatLogs(); capture.assertMessage("Started"); } Capture listeners are anchored to canonical logger identity and can observe descendant loggers through parent-chain propagation.
A listener interface receiving java.util.logging.LogRecord notifications, used by capture and custom test probes.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.reflect package provides comprehensive reflection utilities for working with classes, methods, fields, constructors, and annotations in a more convenient and type-safe way than the standard Java reflection APIs.

Utility class providing convenient static methods for creating reflection info objects. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.reflect.ReflectionUtils.*; // Convert Class to ClassInfo ClassInfo ci = info(MyClass.class); // Convert Method to MethodInfo Method m = MyClass.class.getMethod("myMethod"); MethodInfo mi = info(m); // Convert Field to FieldInfo Field f = MyClass.class.getField("myField"); FieldInfo fi = info(f); // Convert Constructor to ConstructorInfo Constructor<?> c = MyClass.class.getConstructor(); ConstructorInfo ci2 = info(c);

Lightweight utility class for introspecting information about a class. // Wrap a class in ClassInfo ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get all methods in parent-to-child order, sorted alphabetically per class for (MethodInfo methodInfo : classInfo.getAllMethods()) { // Do something with it } // Get all class-level annotations in parent-to-child order for (MyAnnotation annotation : classInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class)) { // Do something with it } // Get all fields for (FieldInfo fieldInfo : classInfo.getAllFields()) { // Do something with it } // Get all constructors for (ConstructorInfo constructorInfo : classInfo.getConstructors()) { // Do something with it }

Wrapper around java.lang.reflect.Method with additional convenience methods. ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get a specific method MethodInfo methodInfo = classInfo.getMethod("myMethod", String.class, int.class); // Get method name String name = methodInfo.getName(); // Get return type Class<?> returnType = methodInfo.getReturnType(); // Get parameters List<ParameterInfo> parameters = methodInfo.getParameters(); // Get annotations List<MyAnnotation> annotations = methodInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class); // Invoke method Object result = methodInfo.invoke(instance, "arg1", 42);

Wrapper around java.lang.reflect.Field with additional convenience methods. ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get a specific field FieldInfo fieldInfo = classInfo.getField("myField"); // Get field name String name = fieldInfo.getName(); // Get field type Class<?> type = fieldInfo.getType(); // Get annotations List<MyAnnotation> annotations = fieldInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class); // Get value Object value = fieldInfo.get(instance); // Set value fieldInfo.set(instance, newValue);

Wrapper around java.lang.reflect.Constructor with additional convenience methods. ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get a specific constructor ConstructorInfo constructorInfo = classInfo.getConstructor(String.class, int.class); // Get parameters List<ParameterInfo> parameters = constructorInfo.getParameters(); // Get annotations List<MyAnnotation> annotations = constructorInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class); // Create instance MyClass instance = constructorInfo.newInstance("arg1", 42);

Wrapper around java.lang.reflect.Parameter with additional convenience methods. MethodInfo methodInfo = classInfo.getMethod("myMethod", String.class); // Get parameters List<ParameterInfo> parameters = methodInfo.getParameters(); for (ParameterInfo param : parameters) { String name = param.getName(); Class<?> type = param.getType(); List<MyAnnotation> annotations = param.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class); }

Wrapper around java.lang.Package with additional convenience methods. // Get package info PackageInfo packageInfo = PackageInfo.of(MyClass.class.getPackage()); // Get package name String name = packageInfo.getName(); // Get annotations List<MyAnnotation> annotations = packageInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class);

Common interface for all annotatable wrapper classes. // All info classes implement Annotatable Annotatable annotatable = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); annotatable = MethodInfo.of(method); annotatable = FieldInfo.of(field); annotatable = ConstructorInfo.of(constructor); annotatable = ParameterInfo.of(parameter); annotatable = PackageInfo.of(package); // Get annotations from any annotatable List<MyAnnotation> annotations = annotatable.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class);

ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get all public methods for (MethodInfo method : classInfo.getPublicMethods()) { System.out.println(method.getName()); } // Get all declared methods (including private) for (MethodInfo method : classInfo.getDeclaredMethods()) { System.out.println(method.getName()); } // Get all methods including inherited for (MethodInfo method : classInfo.getAllMethods()) { System.out.println(method.getName()); }

ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get all annotations of a specific type List<MyAnnotation> annotations = classInfo.getAnnotations(MyAnnotation.class); // Check if annotation is present boolean hasAnnotation = classInfo.hasAnnotation(MyAnnotation.class); // Get single annotation (first one found) MyAnnotation annotation = classInfo.getAnnotation(MyAnnotation.class);

ClassInfo classInfo = ClassInfo.of(MyClass.class); // Get superclass ClassInfo superclass = classInfo.getSuperclass(); // Get all superclasses List<ClassInfo> superclasses = classInfo.getSuperclasses(); // Get interfaces List<ClassInfo> interfaces = classInfo.getInterfaces(); // Check if class is assignable from another boolean assignable = classInfo.isAssignableFrom(OtherClass.class);

The org.apache.juneau.commons.runtime package provides lean accessors for two common runtime inputs: command-line arguments and JAR manifest files.

A lean parser for command-line arguments passed to a main(String[]) method. It supports positional arguments, -key value, --key, --key=value, and -Dkey=value grammars (all enabled by default), returning values via an Optional-based API. public static void main(String[] argv) { Args args = new Args(argv); Optional<String> config = args.get("config"); // --config value List<String> files = args.positional(); // bare arguments } Grammar options can be toggled via Args.Builder obtained from Args.create().

A lean accessor for the contents of a JAR manifest. Wraps a java.util.jar.Manifest and exposes main-attribute and per-section entries via an Optional-returning API — constructable from a Class, File, Path, InputStream, Reader, or Manifest. ManifestFile mf = new ManifestFile(MyClass.class); Optional<String> version = mf.get("Implementation-Version");

The org.apache.juneau.commons.settings package provides a thread-safe way to access system properties with support for global and per-thread overrides, making it useful for unit tests and configuration management.

Encapsulates Java system properties with support for global and per-thread overrides. // Get the singleton Settings instance once and reuse it Settings settings = Settings.get(); // Get a system property as a StringSetting StringSetting setting = settings.get("my.property"); String value = setting.get(); // Get the string value // Get with type conversion using StringSetting methods Setting<Integer> intSetting = settings.get("my.int.property").asInteger(); Setting<Long> longSetting = settings.get("my.long.property").asLong(); Setting<Boolean> boolSetting = settings.get("my.bool.property").asBoolean(); Setting<Double> doubleSetting = settings.get("my.double.property").asDouble(); Setting<Float> floatSetting = settings.get("my.float.property").asFloat(); Setting<File> fileSetting = settings.get("my.file.property").asFile(); Setting<Path> pathSetting = settings.get("my.path.property").asPath(); Setting<URI> uriSetting = settings.get("my.uri.property").asURI(); Setting<Charset> charsetSetting = settings.get("my.charset.property").asCharset(); // Use custom type conversion Setting<MyCustomType> customSetting = settings.get("my.custom.property") .asType(MyCustomType.class); // Reset a setting to force recomputation setting.reset();

// Override for current thread (useful in unit tests) Settings.get().setLocal("my.property", "test-value"); // ... test code that uses the override ... Settings.get().unsetLocal("my.property"); // Remove specific override // OR Settings.get().clearLocal(); // Clear all thread-local overrides

// Set global override (applies to all threads) Settings.get().setGlobal("my.property", "global-value"); // ... code that uses the global override ... Settings.get().unsetGlobal("my.property"); // Remove specific override // OR Settings.get().clearGlobal(); // Clear all global overrides

// Create a custom Settings instance with custom sources MapStore springSource = new MapStore(); springSource.set("spring.datasource.url", "jdbc:postgresql://localhost/db"); Settings custom = Settings.create() .addSource(springSource) .addSource(FunctionalPropertySource.of(System::getProperty)) .build(); The springSource above is just a generic illustrative example (a plain MapStore populated with a Spring-style key) — it is not the actual Spring adapter. See Spring Property Integration below for the real integration.

When retrieving a property value, the lookup order is: Per-thread store (if set via setLocal()) Global store (if set via setGlobal()) Sources in reverse order (last source added is checked first) System property source (default, always second-to-last) System environment variable source (default, always last)

Provides read-only access to property values. // Functional source PropertySource source = FunctionalPropertySource.of(System::getProperty); // Map-based source MapStore store = new MapStore(); store.set("key", "value"); PropertySource source2 = store; // Stores extend PropertySource

Provides read/write access to property values. // Map store MapStore store = new MapStore(); store.set("key", "value"); String value = store.get("key"); // Functional store FunctionalPropertyStore store2 = FunctionalPropertyStore.of( key -> getValue(key), // Getter (key, value) -> setValue(key, value), // Setter key -> removeValue(key), // Unsetter () -> clearAll() // Clear );

Beyond the generic FunctionalPropertySource/MapStore shown above, juneau-commons ships several purpose-built PropertySource implementations, each with a *Provider companion for ServiceLoader-driven auto-registration: DotenvPropertySource — reads key-value pairs from a .env-style file. Defaults to ./.env; override the path via the juneau.dotenv.path system property or JUNEAU_DOTENV_PATH environment variable. RelaxedPropertySource — a decorator that wraps a delegate source and retries a miss with canonical name variants (upper-underscore and lower-dotted), so MySection/myKey, my.key, myKey, and MY_SECTION_MY_KEY can all resolve the same logical property. The verbatim name is always tried first. ArgsPropertySource — backed by parsed command-line Args, supporting lookups by flag name or positional index. ArgsPropertySource.createDefault() derives the args from sun.java.command (falling back to the juneau.args system property). ManifestFilePropertySource — backed by a classpath META-INF/MANIFEST.MF (via ManifestFile), memoized so the classpath is scanned at most once per source instance. ManifestFilePropertySource.createDefault() uses default classloader scanning. // Wrap the system-env source so env vars bind relaxedly (e.g. MY_PROP satisfies my.prop). Settings settings = Settings.create() .addSource(new RelaxedPropertySource(Settings.SYSTEM_ENV_SOURCE)) .addSource(new DotenvPropertySource()) .addSource(ArgsPropertySource.createDefault()) .build();

juneau-commons itself has no Spring dependency — the Settings framework only defines the pluggable PropertySource/PropertyStore SPI shown above; the first-class Spring integration lives in the juneau-rest-server-springboot module. SpringEnvironmentPropertySource — adapts a Spring Environment into the Settings singleton as a PropertySource. SpringBeanStore — auto-installs/removes it so Juneau's @Value("${...}") injection resolves against Spring's property space (application.yaml/properties, env vars, command-line args, etc.). For details, see juneau-rest-server-springboot.

A specialized Setting for string values that provides convenience methods for type conversion. StringSetting setting = Settings.get().get("my.property"); // Type conversions Setting<Integer> intValue = setting.asInteger(); Setting<Long> longValue = setting.asLong(); Setting<Boolean> boolValue = setting.asBoolean(); Setting<Double> doubleValue = setting.asDouble(); Setting<Float> floatValue = setting.asFloat(); Setting<File> fileValue = setting.asFile(); Setting<Path> pathValue = setting.asPath(); Setting<URI> uriValue = setting.asURI(); Setting<Charset> charsetValue = setting.asCharset(); // Custom type conversion Setting<MyType> customValue = setting.asType(MyType.class); // Reset to force recomputation setting.reset();

@Test void testWithOverride() { // Override system property for this test Settings.get().setLocal("my.property", "test-value"); try { // Test code that uses the property String value = Settings.get().get("my.property").get(); assertEquals("test-value", value); } finally { // Clean up Settings.get().clearLocal(); } }

// Create settings with multiple sources MapStore configFile = new MapStore(); // Load from config file configFile.set("app.name", "MyApp"); configFile.set("app.version", "1.0.0"); Settings settings = Settings.create() .addSource(configFile) // Check config file first .addSource(FunctionalPropertySource.of(System::getProperty)) // Then system properties .build(); String appName = settings.get("app.name").get();

juneau.settings.disableGlobal (system property) or JUNEAU_SETTINGS_DISABLEGLOBAL (system env) - If set to true, prevents new global overrides from being set via setGlobal(). Existing global overrides will still be returned until explicitly removed. juneau.enableVerboseExceptions - Controls the opt-in ThrowableUtils.log(exception) helper — it is never invoked automatically by any exception factory (iaex, brex, exex, etc.). If set to true, calling log(exception) logs the throwable's stack trace as a warning (not automatically printed to stderr) and returns the same throwable unchanged, so it can be used inline, e.g. throw log(iaex("...")); when false (the default), log(...) is a no-op passthrough. This is useful during development and debugging to pinpoint exactly where an exception originates, even if it is later caught and swallowed. See JuneauCommonsUtils for details.

Where a PropertySource is a read-only source of ordinary configuration values, a SecretStore (package org.apache.juneau.commons.secret, @since 10.0.0) is its secure, mutable sibling — it adds write/delete plus sensitivity semantics. Secret values are held as char[] (never String, so they can be explicitly zeroed and do not linger in the string pool) and are never toString()'d, logged, or dumped. SecretStore store = new InMemorySecretStore(); store.store("db.password", "hunter2".toCharArray()); boolean present = store.exists("db.password"); // presence, without materializing the value Optional<char[]> secret = store.find("db.password"); // the value, when present boolean removed = store.delete("db.password"); // whether a value was present The four operations model a clean three-state presence distinction: find(key) — returns the secret value when present, Optional.empty() when absent. The only method that materializes the value. exists(key) — reports presence without retrieving (or, for backends that decrypt on read, decrypting) the value. absent — find returns empty and exists returns false.

InMemorySecretStore — the zero-config default: a ConcurrentHashMap-backed, process-local store. It is not persistent and not cross-node — a convenience default and test double, not a production secret backend. It defensively copies values in and out so callers can zero their own arrays. EnvVarSecretStore — a read-only store satisfying find/exists from System.getenv. store/delete throw UnsupportedOperationException. Gives 12-factor deployments a zero-dependency secret source. Both are JDK-only. Anything that reaches an OS keychain, a remote vault, or a cloud secret manager lives in a separate opt-in module (see OS keychain below), never in juneau-commons.

Mirroring the rest of Juneau's framework-owned wiring, the active store resolves from a BeanStore, defaulting to an InMemorySecretStore when none has been contributed: SecretStore store = SecretStores.resolve(beanStore); // contributed bean wins, else InMemorySecretStore To contribute a store, add it to the BeanStore under the SecretStore type: BeanStore beanStore = new BasicBeanStore().addBean(SecretStore.class, new EnvVarSecretStore()); SecretStore store = SecretStores.resolve(beanStore); // the EnvVarSecretStore Passing a null bean store to resolve(...) also returns a new InMemorySecretStore.

SecretStore is a four-method interface. To back secrets with your own system (a database, a vault, a cloud secret manager), implement it: Method Contract void store(String key, char[] secret) Store or replace the secret. The caller keeps ownership of secret and may zero it afterward, so an implementation that retains the value must copy it. Read-only stores throw UnsupportedOperationException. Optional<char[]> find(String key) Return the value, or Optional.empty() if absent. The returned array belongs to the caller (it must not be a live view of internal state) and the caller should zero it when done. boolean exists(String key) Presence check that must not materialize the value. boolean delete(String key) Remove the secret. Returns true if one was present and removed, false if the key was already absent. Read-only stores throw UnsupportedOperationException. An implementation must never toString(), log, or otherwise dump a secret value. A key that is simply absent is a normal result, not a failure. For backends that can be unreachable, let the consumer choose the policy through a FailMode rather than baking one into the store: FAIL_OPEN treats a backend failure as an absent secret (find returns empty, exists/delete return false), while FAIL_CLOSED propagates the error. public class MyVaultSecretStore implements SecretStore { private final VaultClient client; // your backend client private final FailMode failMode; public MyVaultSecretStore(VaultClient client, FailMode failMode) { this.client = client; this.failMode = failMode; } @Override public void store(String key, char[] secret) { client.put(key, secret); } @Override public Optional<char[]> find(String key) { try { return Optional.ofNullable(client.get(key)); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (failMode == FailMode.FAIL_OPEN) return Optional.empty(); throw e; } } @Override public boolean exists(String key) { try { return client.contains(key); } catch (RuntimeException e) { if (failMode == FailMode.FAIL_OPEN) return false; throw e; } } @Override public boolean delete(String key) { return client.remove(key); } }

For classpath contribution there is a parallel SecretStoreProvider SPI, mirroring PropertySourceProvider: SecretStore create() — build the store, or return null to skip registration (for example on an unsupported OS). default int order() — sort key, lowest first. The default is 0. Register the provider class name in a META-INF/services/org.apache.juneau.commons.secret.SecretStoreProvider file. Discovery is the opt-in SecretStores.fromServiceLoader() — it is deliberately not consulted by resolve(...), so the no-contribution default stays a deterministic InMemorySecretStore rather than silently becoming whatever store happens to be on the classpath. It sorts the providers by order(), calls create() on each in that order, and returns the first non-null store as an Optional<SecretStore> (empty if there is none). To use a classpath-contributed store, seed your bean store from it: SecretStore store = SecretStores.fromServiceLoader().orElseGet(InMemorySecretStore::new); BeanStore beanStore = new BasicBeanStore().addBean(SecretStore.class, store); The providers shipped with Juneau are: Provider Store order() KeychainSecretStoreProvider (juneau-secret-macos-keychain) KeychainSecretStore (macOS only; returns null elsewhere) 10 EnvVarSecretStoreProvider (juneau-commons) EnvVarSecretStore 30 So when both are on the classpath on macOS, the keychain store is chosen; otherwise the environment-variable store. There is no provider for InMemorySecretStore.

By design a SecretStore is not part of the general config/SVL namespace — that is what keeps a secret one careless Settings dump or debug log away from disclosure. Where you do want a secret resolvable as a property, SecretStorePropertySource exposes a chosen store as a PropertySource — a conscious, greppable opt-in (for example wired as a session-scoped PropertySource[] bean). It implements SensitivePropertySource, a marker that dump/log/toString() paths honor to redact bridged values.

The opt-in juneau-secret-macos-keychain module ships a KeychainSecretStore backed by the macOS security keychain CLI. Because it shells out to an external OS process, it lives outside juneau-commons (which holds the line on zero-runtime-deps / no-OS-integration). It honors a FailMode (fail-open vs fail-closed, modeled on ReplayCache's FailMode) for backend-unavailable behavior, and registers a KeychainSecretStoreProvider for ServiceLoader discovery on macOS. Dependency​ Artifact org.apache.juneau:juneau-secret-macos-keychain (it depends on juneau-commons), package org.apache.juneau.secret.macos.keychain: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-secret-macos-keychain</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> How it maps to the keychain​ Each operation runs /usr/bin/security for a generic password item. The item's service (-s) is the service name you pass to the constructor, and its account (-a) is the secret key: SecretStore method security subcommand store(key, secret) add-generic-password -U (create or update) find(key) find-generic-password -w exists(key) find-generic-password (no password retrieval) delete(key) delete-generic-password Choose a stable, collision-resistant service name (for example a reverse-DNS string) so unrelated applications do not overwrite each other's entries. Creating a store​ // Default: FailMode.FAIL_CLOSED and a 15 second per-call timeout (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS). SecretStore store = new KeychainSecretStore("com.example.myapp"); // Choose the failure policy. SecretStore lenient = new KeychainSecretStore("com.example.myapp", FailMode.FAIL_OPEN); // Also set the per-call timeout, in seconds (must be > 0). SecretStore custom = new KeychainSecretStore("com.example.myapp", FailMode.FAIL_CLOSED, 30); The service name must not be null or blank. store.store("api.token", "s3cr3t".toCharArray()); if (store.exists("api.token")) { char[] token = store.find("api.token").orElseThrow(); try { // use the token... } finally { Arrays.fill(token, '\0'); // zero it when done } } store.delete("api.token"); Behavior notes​ Platform. Only macOS is supported. On any other OS, or if /usr/bin/security cannot be run, a call is a backend failure and is resolved by the FailMode. Absent is not a failure. A key that is not in the keychain makes find return empty and exists/delete return false regardless of FailMode. Failures. A missing tool, an unexpected non-zero exit, or a timeout is a backend failure. With FAIL_CLOSED (the default) it is thrown as an exception; with FAIL_OPEN, find returns empty, exists/delete return false, and store silently does nothing. Secret values. A secret passed to store must not contain a newline (\n) or carriage return (\r); the call throws an IllegalArgumentException before invoking any process. find returns a char[] that the caller owns and should zero. ServiceLoader discovery​ KeychainSecretStoreProvider is registered in META-INF/services/org.apache.juneau.commons.secret.SecretStoreProvider with order() 10. Its create() returns null unless the os.name system property contains "mac"; otherwise it creates a KeychainSecretStore with FAIL_CLOSED. The service name is taken from the juneau.secret.macos.keychain.service system property (KeychainSecretStoreProvider.SERVICE_PROPERTY), defaulting to org.apache.juneau (KeychainSecretStoreProvider.DEFAULT_SERVICE). // With juneau-secret-macos-keychain on the classpath (and running on macOS): System.setProperty("juneau.secret.macos.keychain.service", "com.example.myapp"); SecretStore store = SecretStores.fromServiceLoader().orElseGet(InMemorySecretStore::new); Because discovery is opt-in, SecretStores.resolve(beanStore) never picks this store up by itself; add it to the BeanStore explicitly as shown above.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.time package provides a precision-aware date/time type for granular time operations. It currently contains a single class, GranularZonedDateTime.

GranularZonedDateTime pairs a java.time.ZonedDateTime with a java.time.temporal.ChronoField precision that records how fine-grained the value is. A value parsed from "2011" is a year-precision value, one parsed from "2011-01-15T12:30" is minute-precision, and so on. The precision then determines what "one step forward" means when you roll the value. The class is immutable and thread safe. It exposes two public final fields, zdt and precision, and matching getters getZonedDateTime() and getPrecision(). // Parse a partial timestamp - precision is inferred from the input. GranularZonedDateTime g = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2026-07"); // MONTH_OF_YEAR precision ZonedDateTime zdt = g.getZonedDateTime(); // 2026-07-01T00:00 in the default zone ChronoField precision = g.getPrecision(); // ChronoField.MONTH_OF_YEAR

Method Description of(String) Parse an ISO 8601 timestamp. of(String, Clock) Parse, taking the zone and the "current date" (for time-only input) from the given Clock. of(String, ZoneId, Clock) Parse with a default zone used only when the string has no offset, plus a Clock. of(ZonedDateTime, ChronoField) Wrap an existing ZonedDateTime with an explicit precision. of(Date, ChronoField) Convert a java.util.Date using the system default zone. of(Date, ChronoField, ZoneId) Convert a java.util.Date using the given zone. new GranularZonedDateTime(ZonedDateTime, ChronoField) Public constructor. copy() Returns a new instance with the same values. // From an existing ZonedDateTime at an explicit precision. GranularZonedDateTime day = GranularZonedDateTime.of(ZonedDateTime.now(), ChronoField.DAY_OF_MONTH); // From a Date in a specific zone. GranularZonedDateTime fromDate = GranularZonedDateTime.of(new Date(), ChronoField.SECOND_OF_MINUTE, ZoneId.of("UTC")); The ZonedDateTime and Date factories do not validate the precision; a null precision is stored as-is and only fails later (for example in roll(int)). A null Date or ZoneId throws NullPointerException.

of(String) accepts these forms, and infers the precision from the finest component present: Input Precision 2011 YEAR 2011-01 MONTH_OF_YEAR 2011-01-15 DAY_OF_MONTH 2011-01-15T12 HOUR_OF_DAY 2011-01-15T12:30 MINUTE_OF_HOUR 2011-01-15T12:30:45 SECOND_OF_MINUTE 2011-01-15T12:30:45.123 (1-3 fractional digits) MILLI_OF_SECOND 2011-01-15T12:30:45.123456789 (4-9 fractional digits) NANO_OF_SECOND Additional rules: The year is exactly four digits. Missing date components default to 01 (month and day) and missing time components default to 0. The fractional-seconds separator may be . or ,. A time zone may follow any time component: Z, +HH, +HH:mm or +HHmm (and the - equivalents). An offset in the string always wins. When the string has no offset, the zone is the defaultZoneId argument if given, otherwise the Clock's zone (the system default zone when no clock is given). A string that begins with T (T12, T12:30, T12:30:45) is time-only. The date is taken from the current date according to the Clock in the resolved zone. A null string throws IllegalArgumentException. A malformed string throws java.time.format.DateTimeParseException. // Explicit UTC offset in the string. GranularZonedDateTime a = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2011-01-15T12:30:45Z"); // No offset - use New York as the default zone. GranularZonedDateTime b = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2011-01-15T12:30:45", ZoneId.of("America/New_York"), null); // Time-only with a fixed clock for deterministic results (useful in tests). Clock clock = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2000-01-01T12:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC); GranularZonedDateTime c = GranularZonedDateTime.of("T12:30:45", clock); // 2000-01-01T12:30:45Z

roll(int amount) returns a new instance moved by amount units of the value's own precision (negative moves backward). roll(ChronoField field, int amount) moves by amount units of an explicit field instead. In both cases the precision of the result is unchanged. GranularZonedDateTime year = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2011"); GranularZonedDateTime next = year.roll(1); // 2012-01-01T00:00, still YEAR precision GranularZonedDateTime hour = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2011-01-15T12Z"); GranularZonedDateTime later = hour.roll(ChronoField.HOUR_OF_DAY, 2); // 2011-01-15T14:00Z, still HOUR_OF_DAY precision The supported roll fields are YEAR, MONTH_OF_YEAR, DAY_OF_MONTH, HOUR_OF_DAY, MINUTE_OF_HOUR, SECOND_OF_MINUTE, MILLI_OF_SECOND and NANO_OF_SECOND. Any other ChronoField makes roll(ChronoField, int) throw IllegalArgumentException. Because the underlying operation is ZonedDateTime.plus(amount, unit), the normal java.time rules apply (for example month-end clamping and daylight-saving transitions). Rolling by one unit of the precision is a convenient way to compute the exclusive end of the period a partial timestamp denotes: GranularZonedDateTime start = GranularZonedDateTime.of("2026-07"); // 2026-07-01T00:00 GranularZonedDateTime end = start.roll(1); // 2026-08-01T00:00 (exclusive end of July)
toString() formats the value as ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME followed by the precision in parentheses, for example 2011-01-15T12:00:00Z(HourOfDay). It is intended for diagnostics, not for round-tripping.

The org.apache.juneau.commons.utils package provides general-purpose utility classes for common operations including string manipulation, collection operations, class utilities, file operations, and more. It contains the most frequently used utility classes in the codebase — most notably Shorts (a terse one-import alias facade) and StringUtils, which are imported statically across the Juneau ecosystem. tip Juneau deliberately favors short, memorable static method names (for example a(...), l(...), m(...), eq(...), nn(...), f(...)) over long descriptive ones. Beyond keeping call sites terse and readable, this conciseness has a practical benefit for AI-assisted development: shorter identifiers cost fewer tokens for a model to generate, so terse APIs are cheaper and faster to produce equivalent code with. They're also easier for LLMs to recall correctly, since a small, consistent vocabulary of names is simpler to memorize than a large set of verbose ones. The static-import style shown throughout this page keeps that vocabulary front-and-center.

A terse alias facade. A single wildcard static import exposes short one/two-letter aliases for the most-used helpers; each alias is a one-line delegation to a canonical, fully-descriptive method on a domain class (ObjectUtils, StringUtils, CollectionUtils, ClassUtils, ThrowableUtils, …). This class replaces the former Utils grab-bag (now deleted). import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; // Object equality with null handling eq("Hello", "Hello"); // true eq(null, null); // true eq("Hello", null); // false // Null-safe operations nn(obj); // Returns true if obj is not null n(obj); // Returns true if obj is null // Empty/not-empty checks ie(""); // true (empty string) ie(null); // true (null is empty) ie("Hello"); // false ine("Hello"); // true (not empty) ine(""); // false // Hash code generation int hash = h("Hello", 123, true); // Object identity String id = id(obj); // Returns "ClassName@hashcode" // Optional utilities Optional<String> opt = o("value"); Optional<String> empty = oe(); More commonly-used helpers: import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; // First non-null value / defaulting String name = or(nickname, username, "anonymous"); String port = or(configuredPort, "8080"); // 2-arg form of the same varargs coalesce // Formatting shorthand (printf-style placeholders — String.format semantics) String msg = f("User %s has %s items", "Alice", 10); // For MessageFormat-style {0} placeholders (e.g. i18n / .properties patterns), use mf(): String msg2 = mf("User {0} has {1} items", "Alice", 10); // Comparisons cmp("apple", "banana"); // < 0 lt(1, 2); // true gte(5, 5); // true btw(5, 1, 10); // true (isBetween) // Case conversion (null-safe) uc("hello"); // "HELLO" lc("HELLO"); // "hello" // Readable string / class name rendering String s = s(obj); // Null-safe toString() String r = r(obj); // Readable/debug representation String cn = cn(obj); // Fully-qualified class name String sn = cns(obj); // Simple class name // Run code that throws checked exceptions without try/catch boilerplate // (safe/safeOpt are canonical ThrowableUtils methods, not Shorts aliases — see below) String contents = ThrowableUtils.safe(() -> Files.readString(path)); Optional<String> maybe = ThrowableUtils.safeOpt(() -> Files.readString(path)); // Collapse empty values to null String x = nie(""); // null note min/max/abs (ObjectUtils) and isArray (ClassUtils) have no Shorts alias — call the domain method directly. Supplier memoization moved to org.apache.juneau.commons.function.Suppliers (Suppliers.memoize(...) / Suppliers.memoizer(...), no Shorts alias). The safe* family (safe, safeCatch, safeOpt, safeOptCatch, safeOrNull, safeSupplier) are likewise not Shorts aliases — they're canonical ThrowableUtils methods.

Reusable string utility methods for formatting, parsing, and manipulation. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.StringUtils.*; // Format strings (printf-style — String.format semantics) format("Hello %s, you have %d items", "John", 5); // For MessageFormat-style {0} placeholders, use mformat(): mformat("Hello {0}, you have {1} items", "John", 5); // Case-insensitive comparison equalsIgnoreCase("Hello", "hello"); // true // String splitting and joining split("a,b,c", ','); // Returns ["a", "b", "c"] join(List.of("a", "b", "c"), ","); // Returns "a,b,c" // Trimming and padding trim(" hello "); // Returns "hello" padLeft("42", 5, '0'); // Returns "00042" padRight("42", 5, '0'); // Returns "42000" padCenter("42", 6, '.'); // Returns "..42.." More string helpers: import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.StringUtils.*; // Empty/blank checks isEmpty(""); // true isNotEmpty("x"); // true isBlank(" "); // true (whitespace-only) isNotBlank(" x "); // true // Defaulting firstNonEmpty(null, "", "found"); // "found" defaultIfEmpty("", "fallback"); // "fallback" defaultIfBlank(" ", "fallback"); // "fallback" // Splitting (char delimiter) and joining List<String> parts = split("a,b,c", ','); // ["a", "b", "c"] String[] partsArr = splita("a,b,c", ','); // {"a", "b", "c"} String joined = join(List.of("a", "b", "c"), ","); // "a,b,c" // Substrings substringBefore("user@example.com", "@"); // "user" substringAfter("user@example.com", "@"); // "example.com" substringBetween("[value]", "[", "]"); // "value" left("hello", 3); // "hel" right("hello", 3); // "llo" // Transformations capitalize("hello"); // "Hello" camelCase("hello-world"); // "helloWorld" abbreviate("Hello World", 8); // "Hello..." repeat(3, "ab"); // "ababab" reverse("abc"); // "cba" // Searching / counting contains("hello world", "world"); // true countMatches("a.b.c.d", "."); // 3 // Validation isNumeric("12345"); // true isEmail("user@example.com"); // true isUri("https://juneau.apache.org"); // true // IDs and randomness String uuid = generateUUID(); String token = randomAlphanumeric(16); // Encoding String b64 = base64EncodeToString("Hello"); // "SGVsbG8=" String back = base64DecodeToString(b64); // "Hello" String hex = toHex("AB".getBytes()); // "4142"

Utility methods for working with collections, arrays, and maps. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.CollectionUtils.*; // Create collections List<String> list = listBuilder(String.class) .add("a", "b", "c") .build(); Map<String, Integer> map = mapBuilder(String.class, Integer.class) .add("one", 1) .add("two", 2) .build(); Set<String> set = setBuilder(String.class) .add("a", "b", "c") .build(); // Array utilities String[] arr = array("a", "b", "c"); List<Object> listFromArray = arrayToList(arr); Concise literal factories and accessors (the terse Shorts aliases for these are noted inline): import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.CollectionUtils.*; // Canonical literal factories — list()/map()/set() are all MODIFIABLE by default String[] arr = array("a", "b", "c"); // array (Shorts alias: a) List<String> list = list("a", "b", "c"); // modifiable ArrayList (Shorts alias: l) Map<String,Integer> map = map("one", 1, "two", 2, "three", 3); // modifiable LinkedHashMap, up to 10 pairs (Shorts alias: m) Set<String> set = set("a", "b", "c"); // modifiable, insertion-ordered LinkedHashSet (Shorts alias: st) SortedSet<String> sorted = sortedSet("a", "b", "c"); // TreeSet, nulls filtered (Shorts alias: ss) // Fixed-size / immutable variants have no short alias — call these explicitly List<String> fixed = fixedSizeList("a", "b", "c"); // Arrays.asList-backed, null-tolerant Map<String,Integer> immutable = immutableMap("one", 1, "two", 2); // Map.of-style, duplicate-key detection // Builders (Shorts aliases: lb/mb/stb) List<String> built = listBuilder(String.class).add("a", "b").build(); // Case-insensitive sorted set SortedSet<String> ci = treeSetCi(List.of("Banana", "apple", "Cherry")); // Safe element access (returns Optional) Optional<String> firstEl = first(list); String lastEl = last(list); String second = elementAt(list, 1); // Shorts alias: at // Reversing List<String> reversed = reverse(list); // Appending List<String> more = addAll(new ArrayList<>(list), "d", "e");

Utility methods for working with classes, including class-name rendering, type resolution, and reflection access. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.ClassUtils.*; // Readable class names for an object (null-safe) String fqn = className(myBean); // e.g. "com.example.MyBean" String simpleName = classNameSimple(myBean); // e.g. "MyBean" // Resolve a java.lang.reflect.Type to its raw Class Class<?> raw = toClass(myType); // Make a reflective member accessible (returns true on success) boolean ok = setAccessible(myMethod);

Utility methods for file operations. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.FileUtils.*; // Create a temp file (optionally seeded with contents) File tmp = createTempFile("data.txt", "content"); // Check whether a file exists within a directory boolean exists = fileExists(dir, "data.txt"); // Parse file-name components String ext = getFileExtension("file.txt"); // Returns "txt" String base = getBaseName("file.txt"); // Returns "file" String name = getFileName("/path/to/file.txt"); // Returns "file.txt"

Utility methods for I/O operations. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.IoUtils.*; // Read an input stream (or Reader/File/Path) as a string String content = read(inputStream); // Pipe (copy) bytes from an input stream to an output stream; returns bytes transferred long transferred = pipe(inputStream, outputStream); // Pipe characters from a reader to a writer pipe(reader, writer);

Utility methods for date and time operations. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.DateUtils.*; // Get a cached DateTimeFormatter for a pattern, then use the standard java.time API DateTimeFormatter fmt = getDateTimeFormatter("yyyy-MM-dd"); String formatted = LocalDate.now().format(fmt); LocalDate parsed = LocalDate.parse("2023-12-25", fmt);

Utility methods for working with annotations. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.AnnotationUtils.*; // Value-based equality and hashing for annotation instances boolean same = equals(annotation1, annotation2); int hashCode = hash(annotation1); // Expand a container/repeatable annotation into its repeated members Stream<Annotation> repeated = streamRepeated(containerAnnotation);

Membership assertion utility. The argument and state checks that used to live here moved to Shorts in 10.0 (see the example below); only assertOneOf stays in AssertionUtils. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; // Argument checks (throw IllegalArgumentException) String value = reqnn("value", obj); // non-null; returns the value String str = reqnb("str", input); // non-null and non-blank; returns the value req(count > 0, "count must be positive, was %s", count); // arbitrary condition (printf-style) // State checks (throw IllegalStateException) chk(isOpen, "Not open"); Connection c = chknn(connection, "Not connected: %s", name);

Utility methods for working with predicates and functional pipelines. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.PredicateUtils.*; // Null-safe predicate evaluation (returns false if the predicate is null) boolean matched = test(myPredicate, value); // Conditionally consume a value consumeIf(v -> v > 0, v -> System.out.println(v), value); // Filter a stream to distinct elements by a derived key List<Person> unique = people.stream() .filter(distinctByKey(Person::getEmail)) .collect(toList());

Utilities for inspecting, wrapping, and safely invoking code that may throw. import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.ThrowableUtils.*; // Wrap any throwable as a RuntimeException RuntimeException e = toRex(cause); // Search the cause chain Optional<IOException> ioEx = findCause(e, IOException.class); IOException cause2 = getThrowableCause(IOException.class, e); // Get stack trace as a string / print with a depth limit (safe for StackOverflowError) String trace = getStackTrace(throwable); printStackTrace(e, 100); // Run code that throws checked exceptions without try/catch boilerplate String contents = safe(() -> Files.readString(path)); // rethrows as RuntimeException Optional<String> maybe = safeOpt(() -> Files.readString(path)); // empty Optional on failure String orNull = safeOrNull(() -> Files.readString(path)); // null on failure note Exception factories (creating a new exception, as opposed to inspecting one) live directly on Shorts as terse, self-contained methods — they do not delegate to ThrowableUtils: import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; throw iaex("Value '%s' is not valid", value); // IllegalArgumentException throw isex("Component must be initialized before %s", m); // IllegalStateException throw rex("Unexpected error processing %s", input); // RuntimeException throw uoex("Method not supported for type %s", type); // UnsupportedOperationException throw brex(MyBean.class, "Failed to create instance"); // BeanRuntimeException throw exex(cause, "Error invoking method %s", method); // ExecutableException throw ioex("Failed to read file %s", path); // IOException

ThrowableUtils.log(exception) is an opt-in helper — it is never invoked automatically by any exception factory. When the juneau.enableVerboseExceptions setting is true, calling it logs the throwable's stack trace as a warning and returns the same throwable unchanged (so it can be used inline, e.g. throw log(iaex("..."))); when the setting is false (the default), it's a no-op passthrough: # In system properties or Juneau config file juneau.enableVerboseExceptions = true // Or programmatically via Settings Settings.get().setGlobal("juneau.enableVerboseExceptions", "true"); // Wrap a factory call with log(...) at sites where verbose logging is desired import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.ThrowableUtils.log; throw log(iaex("Value '%s' is not valid", value)); This is particularly useful when debugging swallowed exceptions or unexpected code paths where you need to identify exactly where an exception was created. tip To enable this only for a single test thread without affecting other threads, use a per-thread override: Settings.get().setLocal("juneau.enableVerboseExceptions", "true"); try { // ... code under test ... } finally { Settings.get().clearLocal(); }

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.StringUtils.*; // printf-style formatting (String.format semantics) String result = format("User %s has %d items", "Alice", 10); // Returns: "User Alice has 10 items" // For MessageFormat-style {0} placeholders (i18n / .properties), use mformat(): String result2 = mformat("User {0} has {1} items", "Alice", 10); // Returns: "User Alice has 10 items"

import static org.apache.juneau.commons.utils.Shorts.*; // Safe equality check if (eq(obj1, obj2)) { // Objects are equal (handles nulls) } // Safe null checks if (nn(obj)) { // Object is not null } if (n(obj)) { // Object is null } // Empty checks if (ie(collection)) { // Collection is null or empty } if (ine(collection)) { // Collection is not null and not empty }

The juneau-config library contains a powerful API for creating and using INI-style config files. Key Capabilities: Support for storing and retrieving any of the following data types: Primitives POJOs Beans Arrays, Maps, and Collections of anything Binary data Transactional modifications with commit/rollback capabilities A listener API Filesystem watcher integration allowing changes on the file system to be reflected in real-time Modifications through the Config class (e.g. add/remove/modify sections and keys, add/remove comments and whitespace, etc...) DO NOT cause loss of formatting in the file - all existing whitespace and comments are preserved Value encoding for added security Support for SVL variables Directly populate beans from config sections Accessing config sections through Java interface proxies An extensible storage API allows you to write your own config storage (e.g. storage in databases or the cloud)

Example configuration file # A set of entries [Section1] # An integer key1 = 1 # A boolean key2 = true # An array key3 = 1,2,3 # A POJO key4 = http://bar Config files are accessed through the Config class which are created through the Config.Builder class. The config language may look simple but it is a very powerful feature with many capabilities. See Config Overview for a walk-through of creating a Config and reading values.
Apache Juneau™ is a single cohesive Java ecosystem for marshalling Java objects to a wide variety of data formats and creating annotation-based REST end-to-end server and client APIs.

Universal Serialization - Marshal POJOs to 38+ formats from a single API: JSON (plus JSON5, JSONL, JSON5L, and JCS), XML, SOAP, HTML, URL-Encoding, UON, OpenAPI, MessagePack, CBOR, BSON, YAML, TOML, HOCON, HJSON, CSV, INI, Markdown, Parquet, Protobuf, Prototext, SSE, and PlainText — plus 12 RDF variants (RDF/XML, RDF/XML-Abbrev, RDF/JSON, N-Triples, Turtle, N3, N-Quads, TriG, TriX, JSON-LD, RDF/Thrift, and RDF/Proto) via juneau-marshall-rdf End-to-End REST - Annotation-driven REST server and client that share a single API, with automatic Swagger/OpenAPI generation and self-documenting UIs Transport-Agnostic REST Client - Pluggable adapters for Apache HttpClient 4.5/5.x, OkHttp, and Jetty 12, including HTTP/2 request/response multiplexing and server push DTO Beans - Ready-made bean models for HTML5, Atom, HAL, JSON:API, JSON Patch, JSON Schema, OpenAPI v3, Swagger v2, RFC 7807 Problem Details, and MCP Microservices - Lightweight, standalone microservices with embeddable Jetty 12 or Tomcat 10+, or Spring Boot integration Configuration Management - Sophisticated configuration-file API (INI and YAML) with variable resolution Bean-Centric Testing & Fluent Assertions - Powerful fluent-style assertion framework plus JUnit 5 extensions and test-time bean injection Large-Dataset Streaming - BeanSupplier/BeanConsumer/BeanChannel and token/record streaming APIs for processing large datasets without loading all elements into memory; direct database integration via lifecycle methods (begin/acceptThrows/onError/complete) Type Conversion - Lightweight, MarshallingContext-free converter framework with caching and broad type support Model Context Protocol (MCP) - Built-in MCP server support for exposing REST resources to AI agents Security - Content Security Policy (CSP) support, plus opt-in JWT, SAML 2.0, OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect authentication Zero / Minimal Dependencies - Core marshalling requires no external dependencies, making it ideal for uber-jars

Fast & memory-efficient - High-throughput serialization and parsing with a low memory footprint Safe by default - Parsers are not susceptible to deserialization attacks Lightweight - juneau-commons (~850KB) + juneau-marshall (~2.1MB) with no required external dependencies No magic (KISS) - No auto-wiring, no code generation, no dependency injection — just add it to your classpath and use it Exhaustively tested - Extensive test coverage with lots of up-to-date documentation and examples Modern & portable - Requires Java 17+; all components are also packaged as stand-alone OSGi bundles

The easiest way to pull in the library is through the following maven dependency: <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-shaded-all</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> Or for Bazel: maven_jar( name = "juneau_all", artifact = "org.apache.juneau:juneau-shaded-all:${juneau.version}", ) For more specific use cases, consider using one of the other shaded artifacts listed above, or individual modules from juneau-core and juneau-rest. If you would like to work with the bleeding-edge code, you can access the 10.0.0-SNAPSHOT version through the following repository: <pluginRepositories> <pluginRepository> <id>apache.snapshots</id> <url>http://repository.apache.org/snapshots/</url> <snapshots> <enabled>true</enabled> <updatePolicy>always</updatePolicy> </snapshots> </pluginRepository> </pluginRepositories> Each of the components are also packaged as stand-alone OSGi modules.

The juneau-examples-core module is a collection of small, standalone main() programs that demonstrate Apache Juneau's core marshalling APIs — serializing Plain Old Java Objects (POJOs) to a format and parsing them back — plus a few extension points (a custom serializer/parser and a custom config store). Each example is self-contained: run it directly and read the inline comments showing the expected output. Looking for a full application? The examples here are small main() programs for marshalling and MCP. For a complete, runnable REST application with browsable HTML views, Mustache and FreeMarker view resources, a React single-page UI, and typed clients, see the Petstore. For a minimal deployable app, see the Starter Projects.

The examples build from the Juneau reactor. To exercise the same APIs in your own project, add the marshall dependency (the examples also pull in the bean and config modules used by specific examples): <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The example module additionally depends on juneau-commons, juneau-bean-atom, juneau-bean-common, juneau-bean-html5, juneau-bean-jsonschema, juneau-bean-swagger-v2, and juneau-config for the DTO and configuration examples.

Each format example serializes the shared Pojo/PojoComplex bean and parses it back, asserting round-trip equality. Format Example class(es) Demonstrates JSON core/json/JsonSimpleExample, JsonComplexExample, JsonConfigurationExample JsonSerializer/JsonParser and Json5Serializer, generic-map parsing, and building serializers/parsers with custom configuration. XML core/xml/XmlSimpleExample, XmlComplexExample, XmlConfigurationExample XmlSerializer/XmlParser over simple and nested/collection POJOs, plus custom configuration. HTML core/html/HtmlSimpleExample, HtmlComplexExample HtmlSerializer/HtmlParser and HtmlDocSerializer (full-document output). UON core/uon/UonExample, UonComplexExample UonSerializer/UonParser round-trips. OpenAPI core/oapi/OapiExample OpenApiSerializer/OpenApiParser plus HttpPartSchema-driven HTTP-part serialization.

Example class Demonstrates bean/BeanExample Building HTML5 tables/forms with HtmlBuilder, an ATOM feed with AtomBuilder, and a Swagger document with SwaggerBuilder, then serializing them to HTML/JSON. bean/atom/AtomXmlExample, AtomJsonExample, AtomHtmlExample Serializing the shared AtomFeed bean to ATOM/XML, JSON, and HTML.

Example class Demonstrates core/svl/SvlExample Resolving $E{}/$S{} variables and #{...} functions with VarResolver.DEFAULT. core/config/store/SqlStore A skeleton ConfigStore backed by a relational database (a builder + polling watcher; the JDBC read methods are left as // Implement me! exercises). serializer/ImageSerializer A custom OutputStreamSerializer that writes BufferedImage objects as image/png / image/jpeg. parser/ImageParser A custom InputStreamParser that reads image/png / image/jpg byte streams back into BufferedImage.

Every example class exposes a public static void main(String[] args) entry point and can be launched directly from an IDE or with java once the module is on the classpath. There is no shared launcher or server — pick a class and run it. Most print their output via java.util.logging, and each class documents its expected output in inline comments.

The shared sample bean shows the pattern most format examples rely on — an immutable POJO whose constructor is annotated so Juneau can reconstruct it during parsing: public class Pojo { private final String id; private final String name; @BeanCtor public Pojo(@Name("id") String id, @Name("name") String name) { this.id = id; this.name = name; } public String getId() { return id; } public String getName() { return name; } } Because the constructor is marked @BeanCtor with @Name-annotated parameters, the same bean round-trips through every format (JSON, XML, HTML, UON, OpenAPI) without setters, letting your domain objects stay immutable.
