The Sold pets page, served at /console/pets/sold, is the smallest table page in the petstore: every pet that has been marked sold, with a species filter. It exists to show the contrast with the main Pets page. Same bean, but a different data mode and a much shorter template.

A table in client mode. The endpoint returns all the rows in one response and the browser does the filtering, sorting and paging. There is no server-side query, so the endpoint is a plain GET returning a list. A ribbon option group that filters on the species column in the browser, with no request to the server. A minimal page template: no tab attribute, no URL state, no row actions. Client mode is the right choice when the full row set is small. When it is not, use server mode, as the Pets page does.

The template is pets-sold.ftlh. The card body is trimmed here to its essentials. <@page toolkit="views"> <@card type="datatables" id="sold" title="Sold pets"> { rowType: 'Pet', dataMode: 'client', dataUrl: '/console/pets/sold/rows', columns: [ { key: 'id', label: 'Id' }, { key: 'name', label: 'Name' }, { key: 'species', label: 'Species' } ], ribbon: [ { type: 'optionGroup', id: 'species', title: 'Species', options: [ { id: 'dogs', title: 'Dogs', column: 'species', value: '$eq(DOG)' }, { id: 'cats', title: 'Cats', column: 'species', value: '$eq(CAT)' } ] }, { type: 'refresh' } ] } </@card> </@page> The filter values use the BeanQuery search syntax ($eq(DOG)). In client mode the table applies them locally; in server mode the same strings are sent to the server.

PetsPageBuilders.sold builds the same page. Request /console/pets/sold?builder to render it. PageSpec.create().toolkit("views") .table(TableSpec.create("sold").rowType("Pet").dataMode(DataMode.CLIENT).dataUrl("/console/pets/sold/rows") .columns(Column.create("id").label("Id"), Column.create("name").label("Name")) .ribbon( RibbonItem.optionGroup("species", RibbonItem.option("dogs").title("Dogs").column("species").value("$eq(DOG)"), RibbonItem.option("cats").title("Cats").column("species").value("$eq(CAT)")).title("Species"), RibbonItem.refresh()), "Sold pets");

GET /console/pets/sold/rows is served by PetsRest.soldRows. It returns every pet whose status is SOLD, sorted by id. Marking a pet sold is a separate action on the Pets page (POST /console/pets/{id}/sell), after which the pet appears here on the next refresh.

Source: juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core, classes PetsRest and PetsPageBuilders (in the pages package) and the template pets-sold.ftlh. Tests: PetsRest_Test (the sold/rows endpoint), PetstorePages_ContractTest (the page contract) and PetstoreTwins_Test (template equals builder).

Twin pattern: see 19.17. Template and Builder Twins. Petstore: Pets: the server-mode counterpart. Data Tables: client mode versus server mode. Rich Table Views: what a table card can do. Building a Console Page: the end-to-end tutorial.

The Store page is the console landing page, served at /console/store. It is a dashboard: a welcome card, a "Recent orders" table whose header carries a strip of quick-stat tiles, a revenue tile, four charts and a store-hours card. Every card reads its data from a small JSON endpoint on the same resource, so the page is a good first look at how a console page is wired together. For the pattern in general, see Building a Console Page.

A datatables card in client mode with a quickStats strip: three status tiles, a segmented order breakdown and an inventory meter. The tile values are computed once per request and handed to the template. A kpi card for "Revenue today". Four chart cards: a line chart, a donut, a bar chart and a treemap. The treemap opens the same edit dialog as the Pets table when you click a tile. An html card whose body is loaded from a fragment endpoint, so the opening hours are plain markup with no chrome.

The template is store.ftlh. Each card is a <@card> element inside one <@page>; chart cards carry their data URL in src and their options as a small JSON-style body. <@page tab="store" toolkit="views" init=["/console/dev/cards/petstore-cards.js"]> <@card type="chart" id="by-status" title="Pets by status" src="/console/store/stats/status"> { kind: 'bar', x: { field: 'status' }, series: [ { field: 'count', label: 'Pets' } ] } </@card> <@card type="chart" id="orders-trend" title="Orders, last 30 days" src="/console/store/stats/daily"> { kind: 'line', x: { field: 'day', label: 'Day' }, series: [ { field: 'placed', label: 'Placed' }, { field: 'delivered', label: 'Delivered', tone: 'ok' } ], onClick: { href: '/console/orders?state=day({day})' } } </@card> <@card type="html" id="hours" title="Store hours" src="/console/store/fragments/hours"/> </@page> The init script is a petstore-specific card script that the chrome loads after the toolkit. The trend chart links each point to the Orders page filtered to that day, which is why the href uses a {day} placeholder.

The same page can be built in Java. StorePageBuilders.store returns a PageSpec, and request the page with ?builder to render it through that path instead of the template. PageSpec.create().tab("store").toolkit("views").init("/console/dev/cards/petstore-cards.js") .card(ChartDef.bar("by-status").title("Pets by status").src("/console/store/stats/status") .x("status").series("count", "Pets").toCardSpec()) .card(ChartDef.line("orders-trend").title("Orders, last 30 days").src("/console/store/stats/daily") .x("day", null, "Day").series("placed", "Placed").series("delivered", "Delivered", "ok") .onClickHref("/console/orders?state=day({day})").toCardSpec()) .htmlSrc("hours", "Store hours", "/console/store/fragments/hours"); The two renderings are required to produce the same page contract. That is what the twin test pins; see Building a Console Page for the contract itself.

StoreRest serves everything under /console/store. Endpoint Returns GET /console/store The page. GET /console/store/recent-orders The ten newest orders, newest first. GET /console/store/stats/daily {day, placed, delivered} for each of the last 30 days. GET /console/store/kpi/revenue {label, value, unit}: the summed prices of pets whose orders were delivered today. GET /console/store/stats/species {species, count} per species, zero counts included. GET /console/store/stats/status {status, count} per pet status. GET /console/store/stats/pets {id, name, species, status} per pet, for the treemap. GET /console/store/fragments/hours The opening hours as markup only.

Source: juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core, classes StoreRest, StorePageBuilders (in the pages package) and the templates store.ftlh and fragments/store-hours.ftlh. Tests: StoreRest_Test, StoreRest_EmptyStore_Test, PetstoreTwins_Test and PetstorePages_ContractTest.

The Themes page (/console/dev/themes) shows the console's stock themes and one custom token theme, switchable with a ?theme= query parameter. It has a swatch card that names the active theme, a picker card that links every choice, and a card that prints the <@theme> and <@token> markup that produces the custom theme. Theming lives in the chrome template, not in the page, so this page is mostly a switch that feeds base.ftlh.

ThemesRest validates ?theme=. The default is the first stock theme, open. A name outside the choices is a 400 that lists them. The choice reaches base.ftlh as the petstoreTheme view attribute, which feeds <@console theme=...>: <@console brand="Juneau Petstore" title=(pageTitle!"") theme=(petstoreTheme!"open") schemeToggle=true> Every other petstore page leaves the attribute unset, so they all draw in open.
documents.s: How the choice reaches the chrome

documents.t: The choices are the framework's built-in names followed by custom: Name Meaning open, light-red, light-brown, red, gray The stock themes from ConsoleChromeMixin.BUILTIN_THEME_NAMES custom The light-brown theme plus three token overrides For ?theme=custom the page sets petstoreTheme to light-brown and petstoreCustomTheme to true. The page in each choice: open light-red light-brown red gray custom
documents.s: Stock themes and the custom one

documents.t: base.ftlh turns on a <@theme> block with no name, only when petstoreCustomTheme is set. A nameless block inherits the page theme (here light-brown) and layers its tokens on top, so you override a few tokens without redefining a palette. A token takes either a value or an alias that follows another token, and scheme="dark" limits it to the dark scheme.

The override block as it appears in base.ftlh: <#if petstoreCustomTheme!false> <@theme> <@token name="--jc-pill-red-bg" value="#fdeceb"/> <@token name="--jc-tab-bar-bg" alias="var(--jc-card-bg)"/> <@token name="--jc-link" value="#d9a65c" scheme="dark"/> </@theme> </#if>

The builder page does not emit the chrome itself. It carries the same two attributes the template page does, and the chrome (base.ftlh) draws the theme from them: return PageSpec.create().tab("dev/themes") .attr("petstoreTheme", theme).attr("petstoreCustomTheme", custom) .html("swatches", "This theme", ...) .html("picker", "Pick a theme", ...) .html("authoring", "Writing a custom theme", ...); ThemesRest passes light-brown as the theme and custom as true for ?theme=custom, so GET /console/dev/themes?theme=custom&builder and the template page render the same custom theme. Source: ThemesRest in juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core/src/main/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/dev/; DevPageBuilders.themes in .../console/pages/; themes.ftlh and base.ftlh under .../console/templates/. Every page in the petstore console is written twice. One copy is a FreeMarker template (.ftlh) that uses the console directives. The other is a Java method that builds the same page with PageSpec and TableSpec. The two are called twins, and a test proves they stay the same page. This page explains why the petstore keeps both, shows one pair side by side, and ends with a recipe for your own console.

The console renders a page from a page contract: a JSON document in #juneau-page plus one <template> per card. A template and a builder are two ways to produce that same contract. A template reads like the page. The card body is JSON5, so what you write is what the browser gets. It is the right default for a page whose shape you know when you write it. A builder composes the page in Java. It can loop, call helpers, share a table definition between two pages, and check column names against a bean at compile time. It is the right tool when the page is computed. The petstore writes both for every page so that each form has a worked, tested example, and so the tests can prove the builder covers everything a template can say. Each page on the tour has a "Builder twin" section with its own pair. The template is what a normal request serves. Adding ?builder to the URL renders the builder twin instead, and the response carries the header X-Petstore-Page: builder so a test can tell the two paths apart. ?mixed renders a third form, covered below.

The Audit page (Petstore: Audit) is the smallest pair. The template is audit.ftlh: <@page tab="ops/audit" toolkit="views"> <@card type="datatables" id="audit">{ dataMode: 'server', dataUrl: '/console/ops/audit/query', defaultOrder: [{ key: 'at', dir: 'desc' }], columns: [ { key: 'at', label: 'When', render: { id: 'timestamp' }, searchType: 'timestamp' }, { key: 'actor', label: 'Actor', searchType: 'text' } ], ribbon: [ { type: 'export', buttons: ['copy', 'csv'] }, { type: 'refresh', id: 'refresh' } ] }</@card> </@page> The builder is OpsPageBuilders.audit: PageSpec.create().tab("ops/audit").toolkit("views") .table(TableSpec.create("audit").dataMode(DataMode.SERVER).dataUrl("/console/ops/audit/query") .operators(SearchOperatorSet.standard()) .defaultOrder("at", Sort.DESC) .columns( Column.create("at").label("When").render("timestamp").searchType(SearchType.TIMESTAMP), Column.create("actor").label("Actor").searchType(SearchType.TEXT)) .ribbon(RibbonItem.export("copy", "csv"), RibbonItem.refresh().id("refresh"))); Both excerpts trim four of the six columns. The mapping is mechanical: Template Builder <@page tab="ops/audit" toolkit="views"> PageSpec.create().tab("ops/audit").toolkit("views") <@card type="datatables" id="audit"> .table(TableSpec.create("audit") dataMode: 'server' .dataMode(DataMode.SERVER) defaultOrder: [{ key: 'at', dir: 'desc' }] .defaultOrder("at", Sort.DESC) { key: 'at', render: { id: 'timestamp' } } Column.create("at").render("timestamp") { type: 'export', buttons: [...] } RibbonItem.export("copy", "csv")
documents.s: The audit page, side by side

documents.t: The Pets page (Petstore: Pets) is the large pair. pets.ftlh is one datatables card with about fifty lines of JSON5, and PetsPageBuilders.pets builds the same table from petsTable(). The pieces that repay a close look: Ribbon. The two optionGroup entries (pet status, species) become RibbonItem.optionGroup(...) calls whose options carry column and a $eq(...) or $in(...) value. The + Add pet dialog is RibbonItem.dialog(...). Export and refresh are RibbonItem.export(...) and RibbonItem.refresh(). Row rules. rowClassRules becomes .rowClass("status", Op.EQ, "SOLD", "is-muted"). The status column's render: { id: 'pill' } is .render("pill"). Selection and bulk actions. The template spells selection and bulk as plain objects. The builder builds a SelectionDef once and hands it to BulkMutateDef.create(...), so the bulk action cannot name a selection the table does not have. Badges. The pending-changes badge in the page header is declared once, in base.ftlh, with <@badge>. Both twins inherit it. A page may also declare a badge on its PageSpec with .badge(BadgeDef...), but declaring the same id in both places fails loud; see Petstore: FailLoud Catalogue, test a10. The other builder types you will meet across the tour are ChartDef (the Store charts), JobLogCardType (the Jobs page) and VisibilityRule (conditional row actions on the orders, pet and pending-changes pages). Each is the builder spelling of a card type or a key that the template writes as JSON5.

?mixed renders the third form. pets-mixed.ftlh is a four-line template: <@page tab="pets" toolkit="views"> <@card ref="pets"/> </@page> <@card ref="pets"/> does not define a card. It places the card named pets that the Java side supplies. PetsPageBuilders.petsMixed() is PageSpec.create().template("pets-mixed.ftlh").table(petsTable(), "Pets"): the layout is FreeMarker and the table is Java. Because pets() and petsMixed() both call petsTable(), the table cannot drift between the two. Use this form when the page frame is hand-written but one card is too large or too dynamic to write as JSON5. Add ?builder&mixed to render the mixed spec through the builder path.

PetstoreTwins_Test renders every page both ways and compares the results with PageContractAssert.assertTwins. The comparison is deliberately about the contract, not the HTML around it: the contract JSON is compared with its keys sorted, but list order is kept, because card, nav and option order is part of the page; the <template> ids must match, and each template's markup is compared with whitespace stripped. The pages come from PetstorePages_ContractTest.PAGE_PATHS, so a page added to that list gets a twin check without any change to the twin test. Extra tests (b01 to b06) cover the pages with the most moving parts: Store, the HTML, FreeMarker and Mustache flavors, a pet's Orders tab and Jobs. a03_mixedEqualsFtl checks that ?mixed and ?builder&mixed both equal the plain template. The test class also has a GAPS list: pages whose twin cannot equal the template yet, each with a reason and the card or key that only one side renders. GAPS is empty. Every builder page matches its template, and the list is kept so a future known difference has a place to be written down, with a reason, instead of a skipped test. The three builder-only developer pages (Charts, Data, Dashboard; see Petstore: Developer Pages) have no template and are not part of this check.

Start with the template. Write the page as an .ftlh file with <@page> and <@card>. It is the shortest path, and the JSON5 is easy to read. Add the twin when you need to compose. When two pages share a table, when a card list depends on data, or when you want compile-time checks, move the page into a PageSpec method. Keep the template and the builder together until the builder is trusted. Share the pieces. Put a table in a method like petsTable() and call it from both the full builder and the mixed one. Pin parity. Add the page path to one list that a twin test reads, and use assertTwins, so a change to one side fails the build until the other follows. Retire a side deliberately. Once the builder is the source of truth, delete the template and the ?builder switch. The petstore keeps both only because it is a teaching example. Source: PetstoreConsolePage (the ?builder switch and the page header), PetsRest, PetsPageBuilders and OpsPageBuilders under juneau-petstore/juneau-petstore-core/src/main/java/org/apache/juneau/petstore/console/, and the templates audit.ftlh, pets.ftlh and pets-mixed.ftlh under the matching resources directory. Tests: PetstoreTwins_Test and PetstorePages_ContractTest.
Petstore: FailLoud Catalogue Petstore: Audit Petstore: Pets Building a Console Page: the template directives and the page contract. Rich Table Views: the table card and its builder.

The Users page (/console/users) is the petstore's server-mode CRUD example: a table of user accounts with a status filter, an add dialog in the ribbon, and Edit and Delete row actions. Its one lesson beyond the plain table is the password. It is write-only: it can be set from the form, but nothing the server sends ever contains it.

The table pages, sorts and filters on the server. UsersRest.query runs the DataTables request through DataTablesQuery.run and answers a malformed search expression with a 200 error envelope, as the other server-mode pages do. The ribbon has a deselectable "User status" option group ($eq(ACTIVE) and $eq(INACTIVE) on the userStatus column), the "+ Add user" dialog button and a refresh button. The row actions are Edit, which opens the same form in a dialog, and Delete, which confirms first and is styled as dangerous.

Every read goes through a UserView record that has username, first name, last name and status, and no password field. The query runs over UserView through its own InMemoryBeanQueryContext, so the password is neither searchable nor serialized. GET /console/users/{username} returns the same view. The result toast of a create or an update carries a UserView too. The dialog is built by GET /console/users/form as a ModalDef with a FormDef: Case Password field Add (no username query parameter) Required, with the help text "Write-only; it is never shown again" Edit (?username=) Optional, never pre-filled, with the help text "Leave blank to keep the current password" The field is a masked password input and never carries a value. On update, a field left out of the body keeps its stored value, and a null or blank password keeps the stored password. Both the plain body and the dialog envelope ({fields: {...}}) are accepted. Route Does Errors POST /console/users/query One page of UserView rows POST /console/users Creates a user 400 blank username, 409 username taken PUT /console/users/{username} Updates a user 404 unknown user, 400 unknown status DELETE /console/users/{username} Deletes a user 404 unknown user Each write calls ConsoleWrites.actor(req). With the petstore.secure setting on, a write without the demo bearer token is a 401, and the audit entry names the actor. See Petstore: Secure for the demo tokens.

rowActions: [ { id: 'edit', label: 'Edit', form: '/console/users/form?username={username}', present: 'dialog', endpoint: '/console/users/{username}', method: 'PUT', onSuccess: 'redraw' }, { id: 'delete', label: 'Delete', endpoint: '/console/users/{username}', method: 'DELETE', confirm: "Delete user '{username}'?", confirmLabel: 'Delete', tone: 'danger', onSuccess: 'redraw' } ]

Juneau supports converting POJOs to and from plain text. Serialization simply uses the object's toString() method (or an ObjectSwap<?,String> swap if one is defined for the class). Parsing converts text back into a POJO via a static fromString(String) / valueOf(String) method, or a constructor taking a single String argument (again, honoring any registered swap). PlainText support is included in juneau-marshall. Maven <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-marshall</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> The relevant classes are: PlainText - Marshaller pairing the serializer and parser.PlainTextSerializer - Converts POJOs to plain text.PlainTextParser - Converts plain text to POJOs.
Both the serializer and parser handle text/plain.

The PlainText marshaller provides one-line convenience methods over its default serializer and parser: // Serialize a POJO to plain text (uses toString()). String text = PlainText.DEFAULT.of(myPojo); // Parse plain text back into a POJO. MyPojo pojo = PlainText.DEFAULT.to(text, MyPojo.class);

Any class that provides a string representation and a way to reconstruct itself from a string can be round-tripped: public class Temperature { private final int celsius; // Used by the parser (single-String constructor). public Temperature(String value) { celsius = Integer.parseInt(value.replace("C", "")); } // Used by the serializer. @Override public String toString() { return celsius + "C"; } } String text = PlainText.DEFAULT.of(new Temperature("20C")); // "20C" Temperature t = PlainText.DEFAULT.to("20C", Temperature.class);

The underlying serializer and parser can also be used directly via their reusable DEFAULT instances: String text = PlainTextSerializer.DEFAULT.write(myPojo); MyPojo pojo = PlainTextParser.DEFAULT.read(text, MyPojo.class); See Also Marshallers for the common of(...) / to(...) marshaller API. Swaps for replacing non-string types with string equivalents. POJO Categories for the categories of objects that can be reconstructed from strings.

Juneau parsers can use builders to instantiate POJOs. This is useful in cases where you want to create beans with read-only properties. Note that while it's possible to do this using the @BeanCtor annotation, using builders can often be cleaner. A typical builder usage is shown below: MyBean bean = MyBean.create().foo("foo").bar(123).build(); The typical code for such a builder using a static inner class is shown below: public class MyBean { // Read-only properties. public final String foo; public final int bar; // Private constructor. private MyBean(Builder builder) { this.foo = builder.foo; this.bar = builder.bar; } // Static method that creates a builder. public static Builder create() { return new Builder(); } // Builder class. public static class Builder { String foo; int bar; // Method that creates the bean. public MyBean build() { return new MyBean(this); } // Bean property setters. @MarshalledProp public Builder foo(String foo) { this.foo = foo; return this; } @MarshalledProp public Builder bar(int bar) { this.bar = bar; return this; } } } The POJO class can be any type including beans. Builders MUST be beans with one or more writable properties. The bean properties themselves do not need to be readable (i.e. getters are optional). Builders require two parts: A way to detect and instantiate a builder using reflection. A way to instantiate a POJO from a builder. The first can be accomplished through any of the following: A static create() method on the POJO class that returns a builder instance. public static Builder create() {...} A public constructor on the POJO class that takes in a single parameter that implements the PojoBuilder interface. The builder class must have a public no-arg constructor. public MyBean(Builder builder) {...} A @Builder annotation on the POJO class to explicitly identify it. The builder class must have a public no-arg constructor. @Builder(Builder.class) public class MyBean {...} The second can be accomplished through any of the following: The existence of a build() method on the builder class. public MyBean build() {...} The existence of a public constructor on the POJO class that takes in the builder instance. public MyBean(Builder builder) {...} See Also org.apache.juneau.commons.Builderorg.apache.juneau.marshall.swap.spi.PojoBuilder
In general, Juneau allows for marshalling for a wide variety of POJO types including: The following chart shows POJOs categorized into groups and whether they can be serialized or parsed:

Type Description Can serialize? Can parse? Java primitives and primitive objects String Integer Float Boolean All primitive types and boxed equivalents Standard Java primitive types (int, long, float, double, boolean, byte, short, char) and their boxed equivalents, plus String. yes yes Java Collections Framework objects, Java arrays, Java Optionals HashSet<String,Integer> TreeMap<Integer,Bean> List<int[][]> Bean[] Optional<Bean> OptionalInt OptionalLong OptionalDouble With standard keys/values Map keys are primitive/string, swapped, or bean types. Map, Collection, Optional, and array values are primitive/string, collection, bean, or swapped types. OptionalInt, OptionalLong, and OptionalDouble are treated as first-class optional primitive types and serialize/parse identically to Optional<Integer>, Optional<Long>, and Optional<Double> respectively. yes yes HashSet<Bean,Integer> TreeMap<Integer,Reader> Optional<Reader> With non-standard keys/values Map keys are collection, non-standard bean, raw-streamed, or otherwise non-string types. Map, Collection, and array values are non-standard bean, raw-streamed, or toString-only types. yes no Iterator<String> Stream<Bean> Iterable<Integer> Enumeration<String> Streamable sequence types Iterator, Iterable (non-Collection), Enumeration, and java.util.stream.Stream. These are serialized directly as arrays. Elements are written lazily for text-based formats (JSON, XML, UON, URL Encoding, OpenAPI). MsgPack, HTML, and CSV may materialize to a list internally due to format constraints. Parsing is not supported since these are inherently one-way consumption types. yes no Instant ZonedDateTime Calendar Date Duration Period XMLGregorianCalendar Date/time and duration types Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes (Instant, ZonedDateTime, LocalDate, etc.), XMLGregorianCalendar, java.time.Duration, and java.time.Period. These are serialized and parsed natively as ISO 8601 strings without requiring swaps. Swap classes remain available as override mechanisms for custom formats. yes yes Java Beans Standard beans Beans with one or more properties defined by public getters or public fields. Properties can also be defined as final read-only fields and passed in as constructor args, or populated via a builder class (see Builder-based beans below). Property values must be other standard, collection, or swapped types. yes yes Non-standard or partial beans True beans that have one or more properties defined by getter and setter methods but whose property types include non-standard, raw-streamed, or toString-only values. Also includes classes that look like beans but aren't: getters without setters, or classes without no-arg constructors and no recognized constructor-arg mapping. yes no Virtual beans Unimplemented bean interfaces with properties of standard, collection, or swapped types. Parsers automatically create interface proxies on top of BeanMap instances. yes yes Read-only beans Beans with readable properties but no setters and no constructor-arg mapping. Equivalent to standard beans but parse-only via a swapped form is not recoverable. yes no Java Records Java record classes (record Foo(String bar, int baz) {}). Record components are treated as bean properties. The canonical all-args constructor is used for parsing, so all record components are round-trip capable without any additional annotations. The @BeanType, @BeanProp, @MarshalledIgnore, and @BeanCtor annotations are supported on record classes and their components. yes yes Builder-based beans Classes that are constructed via a separate builder class. The framework auto-detects a builder when the object class has a public static create() method returning a builder (that implements the Builder interface), and the builder has a build() method returning the target type, or when the object class has a constructor that accepts a Builder-typed argument. The @Builder annotation can also explicitly name the builder class. During parsing, the builder is instantiated, properties are populated on it, and build() is called to produce the final object. yes yes Swapped objects Objects that are not directly serializable but have ObjectSwaps associated with them. The purpose of a POJO swap is to convert an object to another object that is easier to serialize and parse. Note: As of 10.0.0, date/time types (Calendar, Date, Temporal subtypes, XMLGregorianCalendar, Duration, Period) are handled natively and no longer require swaps. Swap classes remain available as override mechanisms. 2-way swapped Swapped to a primitive/string, standard collection, or standard bean form — reconstruction from the wire form is possible. Custom user-defined swaps yes yes 1-way swapped Swapped to a simpler form where reconstruction from the wire form is not possible. Note: As of 10.0.0, Iterator and Enumeration are handled natively and no longer require swaps. yes no Readers and InputStreams Contents are serialized directly to the output stream or writer. Typically used for low-level language-specific replacement of POJOs using per-Media-Type POJO swaps. FileInputStream StringReader Raw Reader and InputStream objects. Contents are written directly; no structural wrapping. yes no Non-serializable objects with standard methods for converting to a serializable form 2-way convertible Classes with a method that converts it to a serializable form: public X swap(MarshallingSession); where X is a primitive/string, standard collection, or standard bean. public String toString(); where the string is any meaningful data. And a method that converts it back: public static T fromString(String); public static T valueOf(String); public static T parse(String); public static T parseString(String); public static T forName(String); public static T forString(String); public T(X); where X is a primitive/string, standard collection, or standard bean. public static T unswap(MarshallingSession,X); where X is a primitive/string, standard collection, or standard bean. Examples: java.lang.Class java.sql.Time java.sql.Timestamp java.text.MessageFormat java.text.NumberFormat java.util.UUID java.util.logging.Level javax.xml.bind.DatatypeConverter yes yes 1-way convertible Classes that only have a method to convert to a serializable form: public X swap(MarshallingSession); where X is any collection or bean type. public String toString(); where the string is any meaningful data. yes no All other objects Anything that doesn't fall into one of the groups above is simply converted to Strings using the toString() method. yes no info Serializers are designed to work on tree-shaped POJO models. These are models where there are no referential loops (e.g. leaves with references to nodes, or nodes in one branch referencing nodes in another branch). There is a serializer setting detectRecursions to look for and handle these kinds of loops (by setting these references to null) but it is not enabled by default since it introduces a moderate performance penalty.

A separate category exists for POJOs that can be converted to and from Strings. These are used in places such as: Serializing of POJOs to Strings in the REST client API when no serializers are registered. Parsing of POJOs from Strings in the REST server API for text/plain requests where text/plain is not already mapped to an existing serializer. As a general rule, all POJOs are converted to Strings using the toString() method. However, there is one exception: TimeZone - Uses TimeZone.getID() POJOs are convertible from Strings using any of the following (matched in the specified order): Any of the following public static non-deprecated methods: create(String) fromString(String) fromValue(String) valueOf(String) parse(String) parseString(String) forName(String) forString(String) Has a public constructor that takes in a String. Exceptions exist for the following classes: TimeZone - Uses TimeZone.getTimeZone(String)Locale - Uses Locale.forLanguageTag(String) after replacing _ with -.Boolean - Blank and "null" are interpreted as null values.Primitives (except for void.class) - Uses the primitive wrapper classes for instantiating from Strings.

POJOs are also converted to various other types in places such as the Open-API serializers and parsers. In this section, the type being converted to will be referred to as X. POJOs are considered convertible from X if it has any of the following (matched in the specified order): Any any of the following public static non-deprecated methods: create(X) from*(X) Has a public constructor that takes in an X. The X class has a public non-static no-arg non-deprecated method called to*(). POJOs are considered convertible from X if any of the reverse of above are true.

By default, JSON support is provided for HTTP request and response bodies. Other languages can be specified using any of the following builder methods: RestClient.Builderjson()json5()xml()html()plainText()msgPack()uon()urlEnc()openApi() Example // Create a basic REST client with JSON 5 support. // Typically easier to use when performing unit tests. RestClient client = RestClient.create().json5().build(); Clients can also support multiple languages: Example // Create a REST client with support for multiple languages. RestClient client1 = RestClient.create().json().xml().openApi().build(); // Create a REST client with support for all supported languages. RestClient client2 = RestClient.create().universal().build(); When using clients with multiple language support, the request language is selected by setting the Content-Type request header. // Create a REST client with support for multiple languages. RestClient client = RestClient.create().universal().build(); client.post(URI, myBean) .contentType("application/json") .complete() .assertStatus().asCode().is(200); Languages can also be specified per-request. // Create a REST client with no default languages supported. RestClient client = RestClient.create().build(); // Use JSON for this request. client.post(URI, myBean) .json() .complete() .assertStatus().asCode().is(200); The RestClient.Builder class provides convenience methods for setting common serializer and parser settings. Example // Create a basic REST client with JSON support. // Use single-quotes and whitespace. RestClient client1 = RestClient.create().json().sq().ws().build(); Other methods are also provided for specifying the serializers and parsers used for lower-level marshalling support: RestClient.Builderserializer(Serializer)parser(Parser)marshaller(Marshaller) HTTP parts (headers, query parameters, form data...) are serialized and parsed using the HttpPartSerializer and HttpPartParser APIs. By default, clients are configured to use OpenApiSerializer and OpenApiParser. These can be overridden using the following methods: RestClient.BuilderpartSerializer(Class<? extends HttpPartSerializer>)partParser(Class<? extends HttpPartParser>)

The Juneau REST client supports sending serializer and parser session properties via HTTP headers or query parameters. This allows controlling per-request marshalling behavior when the server has enabled it: RestClient client = RestClient.create() .rootUrl("http://localhost:8080/myapi") .build(); // Send serializer options via header (JSON5 format) client.get("/mybean") .serializerSessionOptionsHeader("{useWhitespace:true}") .run() .getContent().as(MyBean.class); // Send parser options via query parameter (UON format) client.post("/mybean", body) .parserSessionOptionsQuery("(trimStrings=true)") .run(); // Set default options for all requests via builder RestClient clientWithDefaults = RestClient.create() .rootUrl("http://localhost:8080/myapi") .serializerSessionOptionsHeader("{addBeanTypes:false}") .parserSessionOptionsQueryDefault("(trimStrings=true)") .build(); See Session Options via HTTP for complete documentation on server configuration and security.

Entries can also be read as POJOs. In theory, any parsable POJO type can be represented as a config value. However in practice, we're typically talking about the following: Objects convertible from Strings. Beans. An example of an object convertible from a String was already shown in an example above. In that case, it was a URL which has a public constructor that takes in a String: # A POJO key4 = http://bar // Read values from section #1 URL key4 = config.get("Section1/key4").as(URL.class).orElse(null); Beans are represented as JSON 5 by default: // Contact information [ContactInfo] address = { street: '123 Main Street', city: 'Anywhere', state: 'NY', zip: 12345 } // Example bean public class Address { public String street, city; public StateEnum state; public int zip; } // Example usage Config config = Config.create("MyConfig.cfg").build(); Address myAddress = config.get("ContactInfo/address").as(Address.class).orElse(null); The default serializer and parser is registered on the Config through the following methods: Config.Builderserializer(WriterSerializer)parser(ReaderParser)

The petstore console is a worked example. This page is the short version of "how do I bring these patterns into an admin UI I already have": which of the four patterns to take, what each one needs from your app, and how to choose which to adopt. It does not repeat the framework pages. Each section points at the page that owns the detail and at the petstore page that shows it running. Start with the tour overview and the Console Tour if you have not seen the console yet. If you are building a page from scratch rather than porting, read Building a Console Page instead.

Move the chrome first. The four patterns below all assume the console shell is in place: a <@console> base template, a <@navigation> tree and the shared assets from ConsoleChromeMixin. Without it there is no header to hang a badge on and no card runtime to mount a job log. The chrome is described in Admin-Console Chrome, and the petstore's version of it is on Console Tour. Then take the patterns one at a time. They are independent, so you can adopt any subset. A good order, from least to most design work: the async-job plumbing (mostly a swap of what you already have); the audit page (a read-only view); the header badge (one endpoint and one directive); staged edits (the one that changes how your app behaves).

A badge is a small counter in the page header that polls a JSON endpoint and links to the page that explains the number. The petstore uses it for the count of pending changes. What you need: a count endpoint that answers GET with a JSON object carrying a numeric total; one <@badge> directive in the base template, placed after </@navigation>, not inside the navigation block. Leave the badge unscoped unless you want it hidden on other sections. A nav scope would hide it on every page outside that scope. The petstore's badge sets refreshesAllowMissing, so applying or discarding an item refreshes a card on the pending page without failing on pages where that card is not mounted. The attributes and the polling, backoff and abort behaviour are on <@badge> and BadgeDef. The petstore example, including the exact directive, is on Pending Changes.

Staged edits turn "save writes immediately" into "save queues a change that someone applies or discards". The petstore queues edits to pets, with the photo field excluded. See the box on Pet Detail. What you need: a store that holds the pending change with its own lifecycle: queued, applied, failed, discarded; three actions on a page: apply one, retry one, discard a set (bulk discard should be idempotent); a server-mode table over the queue, so the page scales past what the browser holds. Porting this is the largest change because it alters write semantics. Decide first what "apply" means in your app, for example posting to an external system versus committing locally, and what a failed apply leaves behind. The action contract is on Row Actions and Bulk Mutation; the lifecycle and the discard outcome are on Pending Changes.

Long-running work should return a job reference at once and let the browser follow it. The petstore's restock action does that and shows the stock job-log card. What you need: your resource implements the async-jobs mixin and exposes a job registry bean; a start action that takes an idempotency key, and a limit that refuses new jobs with a 429 when too many are running; a job-log card on the page, with cancel. The one habit to change is key minting. If your app generates a random UUID per request as the idempotency key, a double-submitted form starts two jobs. Mint a self-targeted key when the form renders and carry it back on submit, so a replay resolves to the job that already exists. That is IdempotencyKey.mintSelfTargeted, and it needs no server-side key store. If your code carries a workaround for resolving a scheme the framework now handles, re-check it against the Juneau version you build with before copying it. The mixin, the registry and the limit are on Async Jobs; the card is on Job Log Card. The petstore example is Jobs. If the job streams output rather than a log, see also Terminal Region and Run View Region.
documents.s: Async jobs with the job-log card

documents.t: Many consoles grow a hand-written widget that starts a job for one table row: a form in the row's detail panel that posts a request, streams a log, and writes the answer back into the panel. These usually become declarations, with no custom JavaScript. A form plus a log in the detail panel becomes a job-log region on the table's detail, with populate: 'job-log' and the form in config.submit. A hidden id or value copied from the row becomes a field with type: 'hidden' and source: 'row.<field>'. A visible field prefilled from the row takes source too. Code that writes the result into a textarea or a cell becomes output, for example { target: { field: 'answer' }, from: 'row.answer' }, or target.selector for an element in the panel's detail grid. A button with its own fetch becomes helpers.jobButton inside a small populator, or a call to JuneauViews.jobs.run. Code that stops the table's polling while the panel is open can go: the poll already waits while an expanded panel runs a job, and a collapsed row's job keeps running and re-attaches on expand. The server side changes too. A widget that minted keys with a placeholder target, so any key worked on any row, moves to a key endpoint, POST .../{id}/key, returning JobKeyLedger.response(ledger.issue(action, rowId, actor)), and a submit endpoint that checks the path id against RowJobSubmit.parse(body).targetId() and calls verify. Apply the action's own authorization on the key endpoint, take the row only from the verified targetId, and keep the row endpoint separate from any self-targeted dialog endpoint. See Row Jobs and Job Log Card; the petstore example is the species table on Jobs.

An audit page is the cheapest way to see the console end to end. It is a leaf page with one table, filled by a POST /query endpoint that receives the paging, sort and filter state and returns one page of rows. What you need: a row type for what you record (who, what, when); a query method on the thing that records it, taking the table state; a page with a datatables card in server mode, and a /query endpoint that answers it. If you already write an event log or a history table, you probably have the data and need only the endpoint and the card. The petstore keeps this deliberately small, to the point that the builder twin is about ten lines. See Audit for the page and Data Tables for server mode.

Nobody needs all of these patterns. Take the ones that match something your app already does by hand, and leave the rest. If your app already has Adopt A count or status shown in a nav label, such as "Review (3)" The header badge, so the count leaves the label and updates on its own. In-memory drafts or pending replies The staged-edits shape: a pending-changes page with apply, retry and discard. Per-class random keys for POSTs, or a long-running action mintSelfTargeted for replay-safe keys, and the job-log card for the run. A write journal or an event history An audit page over a paged /query. A start-run POST that returns an error when the same request is sent twice A self-targeted key, so a replay returns the existing run. A hand-written per-row job form or button A job-log row-detail region or helpers.jobButton, with keys from JobKeyLedger. Skipping a pattern is normal: if the run engine already has its own staged preview, or a badge would add little, skip it.

The console chrome renders and every page sits in the navigation tree. Any badge comes after </@navigation> and its endpoint returns a numeric total. Async starts take a self-targeted key, and a limit refuses extra jobs with a 429. Chrome values reach the template through facts only; see Console Tour. Misconfiguration fails loudly. Pin your own cases the way the petstore does on FailLoud Catalogue. A template page has a builder twin, or a test that fails if the two drift; see Template and Builder Twins.

The following example represents the bare-minimum needed for deploying a top-level REST endpoint with basic JSON marshalling support: @Rest( path="/mypath", serializers=JsonSerializer.class, parsers=JsonParser.class ) public class MyResource extends RestServlet { @RestGet(path="/") public Object getPojo() { ... } } The RestServlet class provides all the logic for starting up your REST application when the servlet container calls init(ServletConfig). On startup, it scans your class for annotations and sets up all of your serializers and parsers. It then does this recursively for all child resources. Users will typically not extend directly from RestServlet. Instead, several classes are provided by the framework to provide additional functionality and to handle different use-cases. Users will typically extend from one of the Basic* classes in one of three families: the servlet family, the resource family, and the Spring Boot family. Cross-cutting endpoints (swagger docs, static files, stats, error, favicon, navigation) are supplied by single-responsibility mixin classes rather than by interfaces.

The servlet family extends HttpServlet and is the standard choice for top-level resources deployed in a servlet container (standalone Jetty, embedded Tomcat, Spring Boot via ServletRegistrationBean). HttpServletRestServletBasicRestServlet - Full-featured servlet with universal marshalling and op-mixin endpointsBasicRestServletGroup - Adds child-resource navigation (GET / via NavigationMixin)

The resource family does not extend HttpServlet. Use these for child resources mounted under a servlet-family parent, or in Spring Boot environments where you want to declare child resources as Spring beans without Spring Boot auto-detecting them as top-level servlets. RestResourceBasicRestResource - Full-featured resource with universal marshalling and op-mixin endpointsBasicRestResourceGroup - Adds child-resource navigation

The Spring Boot family extends the servlet family but hooks into the Spring ApplicationContext to resolve child resources and helper classes as Spring beans. SpringRestServletBasicSpringRestServlet - Spring-aware equivalent of BasicRestServletBasicSpringRestServletGroup - Spring-aware equivalent of BasicRestServletGroup

Cross-cutting endpoints are contributed by single-responsibility mixin classes in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.ops. Mixins are composed into a host via @Rest(mixins=...). BasicRestServlet composes all of them by default; you can opt out via @Rest(noInherit={"mixins"}) and re-declare only what you need. RestMixinHtdocMixin - GET /htdocs/* static-file endpointStatsMixin - GET /stats timing-statistics endpointNavigationMixin - GET / child-resource navigation page (used by *Group classes)ErrorMixin - * /error error-redirect endpoint The RestServlet class itself is not configured with any serializers or parsers. However, it does provide several convenience methods to be aware of: RestServletLogging methods:log(Level,String,Object...)log(Level,Throwable,String,Object...)log(String)log(String,Throwable)Other methods:getContext()getPath()getRequest()getResponse() The Basic* classes compose the op-mixin endpoints via @Rest(mixins=...). BasicRestServlet declares: @Rest(mixins={SwaggerUiMixin.class, RedocMixin.class, ErrorMixin.class, HtdocMixin.class, StatsMixin.class, FaviconMixin.class}) public abstract class BasicRestServlet extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } BasicRestServletGroup adds NavigationMixin on top: @Rest(mixins={NavigationMixin.class}) public abstract class BasicRestServletGroup extends BasicRestServlet { ... } The Basic* classes also implement BasicJsonConfig (or BasicUniversalConfig on BasicRestServlet) which provides marshalling support. Other config interfaces are available as well to quickly provide different types of marshalling support. Note that these interfaces do not define any methods but rather simply provide a set of commonly-used annotations so that you don't need to define them on all your classes. BasicJsonConfigBasicJsonHtmlConfigBasicJson5ConfigBasicOpenApiConfigBasicYamlConfigBasicUniversalConfig For example, if you want to provide a resource that supports all languages in Juneau, simply add the BasicUniversalConfig interface like so: @Rest(...) public class MyResource extends RestServlet implements BasicUniversalConfig { ... } The *Spring* classes are meant to be used in Spring Boot environments so that you can take full advantage of the Spring Framework for injecting dependencies on child resources and helper classes. The resource family (BasicRestResource, BasicRestResourceGroup) provides the same functionality as the servlet classes but does not extend from HttpServlet. This is important in Spring Boot environments where you may want to define child resources as Spring beans but don't want Spring Boot to auto-detect them as servlets to be deployed as top-level resources.

Use case Base class Notes Single REST resource (non-Spring) BasicRestServlet or BasicRestResource Use when you don't need Spring bean injection Single REST resource (Spring Boot) BasicSpringRestServlet Enables @Autowired in child resources Router page (non-Spring) BasicRestServletGroup Mounts child resources Router page (Spring Boot) BasicSpringRestServletGroup Mounts child resources with Spring bean resolution

Top level resources in a servlet container: BasicRestServletBasicRestServletGroup Top level resources in a Spring Boot environment: BasicSpringRestServletBasicSpringRestServletGroup Child resources: BasicRestResourceBasicRestResourceGroup

The following classes are reference/demo resources that illustrate common microservice admin patterns. They live in the unpublished juneau-microservice-examples module (package org.apache.juneau.microservice.examples), not in the shipped juneau-microservice/juneau-microservice-jetty jars, so they aren't a dependency you pull in directly — treat them as copy-and-adapt samples: Predefined Resource ClassesConfigResource - View and modify the external INI config fileDirectoryResource - View and modify file system directoriesLogsResource - View, parse, download and delete log filesSampleRootResource - A sample root resource class to get started fromShutdownResource - Shutdown and/or restart the JVM

ConfigResource, LogsResource and ShutdownResource change state: they rewrite the configuration, delete log files and stop the process. They have no authentication of their own, and they need a CSRF boundary wherever a browser can reach them, or any page the user visits could send those writes. AdminBoundary puts all three behind their own CsrfBoundary (see CSRF protection: loopback vs general). In a microservice whose root resource mounts them as children, contribute its registration as a bean: @Bean(name="adminBoundary") public ServletFilterRegistration adminBoundary() { return AdminBoundary.registration("", "app.example.com"); } The first argument is the path the three resources are mounted under ("" at the root, or a path such as "/admin"). The rest are the host names the server is reached under, without ports. A request under any other Host is refused with 421 HOST_NOT_ALLOWED, reads included; this is the DNS-rebinding defence, and it keeps a page on a rebound name from reading the configuration or the logs. With no host names, only the loopback names localhost, 127.0.0.1 and [::1] are answered (on any port, AdminBoundary.LOOPBACK_HOSTS). Host names you give replace the loopback names rather than adding to them, so list localhost too if you still reach the server that way. The resources have no HTML forms and no write links, so a write from a browser is always refused with 403 and an X-Request-Boundary header naming the reason. So is a write that a browser could send cross-site without a CORS preflight: a urlencoded, multipart or text/plain POST, or a GET claiming another method through ?method= or an override header. Writes come from the command line and REST clients: curl -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' --data-binary @my.cfg http://localhost:10000/config curl -X PUT -H 'Content-Type: text/plain' -d 'newValue' http://localhost:10000/config/MySection/myKey curl -X DELETE http://localhost:10000/logs/old.log curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: application/json' http://localhost:10000/shutdown The resources' generated API pages are refused too when they try a write from the browser; use curl or a REST client. Reads are plain GETs, including the log actions: GET /logs/view/{path}, GET /logs/parse/{path} and GET /logs/download/{path}. The boundary answers only CSRF and DNS rebinding. It does not authenticate, and a direct network caller passes it, so do not expose the admin resources on an untrusted network. The filter is mapped on the request path as the servlet container normalizes it, while Juneau routes on the path segments it receives. The two agree under the container's default URI handling (for Jetty 12, UriCompliance.DEFAULT, which rejects ambiguous paths such as encoded separators and dot segments). Keep that default: a container set to accept ambiguous paths could route a request to an admin resource without the filter seeing it. ShutdownResource stops the process with System.exit by default. To observe a shutdown instead, for example in a test, construct it with new ShutdownResource(exit), or put a ShutdownResource.Exit bean in the bean store its parent builds it from. SampleRootResource mounts ConfigResource with no boundary; register AdminBoundary when you adapt it. DirectoryResource accepts only the HEAD, OPTIONS, VIEW and DOWNLOAD overrides; its view and download links are reads, and its listing no longer offers a delete link (use curl -X DELETE). DebugResource's jetty-thread-dump link is a plain GET that shows the dump; writing the dump file needs a real POST. A link can't reach either resource's writes, because the router refuses any override of a GET to a write, but uploads, deletes and the dump file still change state, so put both behind a CSRF boundary if a browser can reach them. A boundary judges ?method=VIEW and ?method=DOWNLOAD links as writes, so behind one, send real VIEW or DOWNLOAD requests instead.

Property extractors define custom property access logic for objects that don't follow standard JavaBean patterns or require specialized property extraction. They provide a flexible way to access properties from any object structure.

Property extractors are used when: Objects don't follow JavaBean getter conventions You need to compute properties dynamically You want to provide custom property names or aliases Objects use non-standard property access methods You need to access properties from legacy systems
Define custom property access logic by implementing the PropertyExtractor interface:

// Database entity extractor PropertyExtractor entityExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof DatabaseEntity; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { DatabaseEntity entity = (DatabaseEntity) obj; switch (prop) { case "id": return entity.getPrimaryKey(); case "displayName": return entity.computeDisplayName(); default: return entity.getAttribute(prop); } } }; // Registration var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addPropertyExtractor(entityExtractor) .build();

// Map-based property extractor with type conversion PropertyExtractor mapExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof Map; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { Map<?, ?> map = (Map<?, ?>) obj; // Support special properties if ("size".equals(prop)) { return map.size(); } if ("isEmpty".equals(prop)) { return map.isEmpty(); } if ("keys".equals(prop)) { return new ArrayList<>(map.keySet()); } if ("values".equals(prop)) { return new ArrayList<>(map.values()); } // Standard key access return map.get(prop); } };

// Extractor that provides property aliases PropertyExtractor aliasExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { private final Map<String, String> aliases = Map.of( "fname", "firstName", "lname", "lastName", "email", "emailAddress", "phone", "phoneNumber" ); @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return aliases.containsKey(prop); } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { String actualProp = aliases.get(prop); try { String methodName = "get" + capitalize(actualProp); Method method = obj.getClass().getMethod(methodName); return method.invoke(obj); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to extract property: " + prop, e); } } private String capitalize(String s) { return s.substring(0, 1).toUpperCase() + s.substring(1); } }; // Usage setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(user, "fname,lname,email", "John,Doe,john@example.com"); } finally { resetConverter(); }

// Extractor for computed/derived properties PropertyExtractor computedExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof User && prop.startsWith("computed_"); } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { User user = (User) obj; switch (prop) { case "computed_fullName": return user.getFirstName() + " " + user.getLastName(); case "computed_age": return Period.between(user.getBirthDate(), LocalDate.now()).getYears(); case "computed_initials": return user.getFirstName().charAt(0) + "." + user.getLastName().charAt(0) + "."; default: throw new IllegalArgumentException("Unknown computed property: " + prop); } } }; // Usage setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(user, "computed_fullName,computed_age,computed_initials", "John Doe,30,J.D."); } finally { resetConverter(); }

// Extract properties from XML/JSON documents PropertyExtractor documentExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof JsonNode || obj instanceof XmlNode; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { if (obj instanceof JsonNode) { JsonNode node = (JsonNode) obj; return node.get(prop); } else if (obj instanceof XmlNode) { XmlNode node = (XmlNode) obj; return node.getAttribute(prop); } return null; } };

// Access private fields via reflection PropertyExtractor privateFieldExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return prop.startsWith("_"); // Private fields prefixed with underscore } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { try { String fieldName = prop.substring(1); // Remove underscore prefix Field field = obj.getClass().getDeclaredField(fieldName); field.setAccessible(true); return field.get(obj); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to access field: " + prop, e); } } }; // Usage setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(myBean, "_privateField1,_privateField2", "value1,value2"); } finally { resetConverter(); }

// Extract columns from ResultSet PropertyExtractor resultSetExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof ResultSet; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { ResultSet rs = (ResultSet) obj; try { // Support column index access if (prop.matches("\\d+")) { int index = Integer.parseInt(prop); return rs.getObject(index); } // Support column name access return rs.getObject(prop); } catch (SQLException e) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to extract column: " + prop, e); } } };

// Extract properties from configuration objects PropertyExtractor configExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof Configuration; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { Configuration config = (Configuration) obj; // Support dot-notation for nested properties if (prop.contains(".")) { String[] parts = prop.split("\\."); Object current = config; for (String part : parts) { current = ((Configuration) current).getProperty(part); if (current == null) return null; } return current; } return config.getProperty(prop); } }; // Usage setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(config, "database.host,database.port,app.name", "localhost,5432,MyApp"); } finally { resetConverter(); }

Non-standard property access patterns Legacy systems without JavaBean getters Computed or derived properties Property aliases or shortcuts Document/tree structures (XML, JSON) Database results or cursors Dynamic property systems
documents.s: When to Create Custom Property Extractors

documents.t: Always implement canExtract() to check object compatibility Handle null objects and properties gracefully Throw descriptive exceptions for invalid properties Document property naming conventions Consider performance for frequently accessed properties Keep extraction logic simple and focused Avoid side effects or state modifications

// Cache expensive computations PropertyExtractor cachedExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { private final Map<String, Object> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof ExpensiveObject; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { String cacheKey = System.identityHashCode(obj) + ":" + prop; return cache.computeIfAbsent(cacheKey, k -> { // Expensive computation here return ((ExpensiveObject) obj).computeProperty(prop); }); } };

// Robust error handling in property extractors PropertyExtractor safeExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof MyObject; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { try { MyObject myObj = (MyObject) obj; return myObj.getProperty(prop); } catch (PropertyNotFoundException e) { return "<not found>"; } catch (Exception e) { return "<error: " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ">"; } } };

// Ensure thread-safe property extraction PropertyExtractor threadSafeExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return obj instanceof ThreadSafeObject; } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { ThreadSafeObject tso = (ThreadSafeObject) obj; synchronized (tso) { return tso.getProperty(prop); } } };

// Multiple extractors chained together PropertyExtractor chainedExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { private final List<PropertyExtractor> extractors = Arrays.asList( entityExtractor, mapExtractor, computedExtractor ); @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return extractors.stream() .anyMatch(e -> e.canExtract(conv, obj, prop)); } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { for (PropertyExtractor extractor : extractors) { if (extractor.canExtract(conv, obj, prop)) { return extractor.extract(conv, obj, prop); } } throw new IllegalArgumentException("No extractor found for property: " + prop); } };

// Try multiple extraction strategies with fallback PropertyExtractor fallbackExtractor = new PropertyExtractor() { @Override public boolean canExtract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { return true; // Universal extractor } @Override public Object extract(BeanConverter conv, Object obj, String prop) { // Try getter method try { String methodName = "get" + capitalize(prop); Method method = obj.getClass().getMethod(methodName); return method.invoke(obj); } catch (Exception e1) { // Try field access try { Field field = obj.getClass().getDeclaredField(prop); field.setAccessible(true); return field.get(obj); } catch (Exception e2) { // Try map access if (obj instanceof Map) { return ((Map<?, ?>) obj).get(prop); } return null; } } } };

// Test database entity DatabaseEntity entity = loadEntity(123); setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(entity, "id,displayName,createdDate", "123,John Doe,2023-01-15"); // Test configuration Configuration config = loadConfig(); assertBean(config, "database.host,database.port,app.timeout", "localhost,5432,30000"); // Test computed properties User user = loadUser(456); assertBean(user, "computed_fullName,computed_age", "Alice Smith,28"); } finally { resetConverter(); }
// Use property extractor with nested access setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(order, "customer{computed_fullName},items{0{name}}", "{John Doe},{{Laptop}}"); } finally { resetConverter(); }
