Add the Juneau transport module and Apache HttpClient 4.5 to your project: <!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Apache HttpClient 4.5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents</groupId> <artifactId>httpclient</artifactId> <version>4.5.14</version> </dependency> The Juneau adapter module declares httpclient:4.5.14 as a dependency, so the second block can be omitted if you are happy with the version the adapter brings in.

juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-45 provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by Apache HttpClient 4.5.x (org.apache.httpcomponents:httpclient). Consider it when: Your project already pulls in Apache HttpClient 4.5 and you want a single shared client instance across the application. You need mature, battle-tested connection pooling, proxy support, cookie management, or NTLM / Kerberos authentication built into HC 4.5. You are migrating an existing HC 4.5 integration to the Juneau REST client API incrementally. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient45.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.create()) // wraps HttpClients.createDefault() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); ApacheHc45Transport.create() is shorthand for ApacheHc45Transport.builder().build(). It creates a default CloseableHttpClient via HttpClients.createDefault().

Simply add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: // The ApacheHc45TransportProvider registered via ServiceLoader takes over automatically. RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use ApacheHc45TransportBuilder.httpClient(CloseableHttpClient) to supply your own pre-configured CloseableHttpClient. The transport takes ownership of the client and closes it when RestClient.close() is called. import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; import org.apache.http.impl.conn.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient45.*; CloseableHttpClient apacheClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager()) .setMaxConnPerRoute(20) .setMaxConnTotal(100) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.builder() .httpClient(apacheClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Apache HttpClient 4.5 ships PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager, which reuses TCP connections across requests. Tune it to match your workload: import org.apache.http.impl.conn.*; var cm = new PoolingHttpClientConnectionManager(); cm.setMaxTotal(200); // total connections in the pool cm.setDefaultMaxPerRoute(20); // max connections per host:port pair CloseableHttpClient poolingClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

Pass a custom SSLContext or SSLConnectionSocketFactory when building the CloseableHttpClient: import javax.net.ssl.*; import org.apache.http.ssl.*; import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContexts.custom() .loadTrustMaterial(trustStore, null) .build(); CloseableHttpClient tlsClient = HttpClients.custom() .setSSLContext(sslContext) .build();

Configure connect and socket timeouts via RequestConfig: import org.apache.http.client.config.*; import org.apache.http.impl.client.*; RequestConfig config = RequestConfig.custom() .setConnectTimeout(5_000) // ms to establish a connection .setSocketTimeout(30_000) // ms waiting for data .setConnectionRequestTimeout(2_000) // ms to lease a connection from the pool .build(); CloseableHttpClient timedClient = HttpClients.custom() .setDefaultRequestConfig(config) .build();

The RestClient lifecycle maps directly to the underlying CloseableHttpClient: // Build once at application startup RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc45Transport.builder().httpClient(myClient).build()) .build(); // Use throughout the application lifetime; wrap each response in try-with-resources try (var resp = client.get("/items").run()) { return resp.body().as(ItemList.class); } // At application shutdown — closes the CloseableHttpClient client.close();

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Apache HttpClient 5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.httpcomponents.client5</groupId> <artifactId>httpclient5</artifactId> <version>5.6.1</version> </dependency>

juneau-rest-client-apache-httpclient-50 provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by Apache HttpClient 5.x (org.apache.httpcomponents.client5:httpclient5). Consider it when: You are starting a new project and want the latest Apache HttpComponents API. You need HTTP/2 support within the Apache HC ecosystem. You are migrating an existing HC 5 integration to the Juneau REST client API. The transport uses the classic (synchronous) CloseableHttpClient execution path from HC 5. Async-only HC 5 features (e.g., CloseableHttpAsyncClient) are not exposed; route calls through the transport interface as usual. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient50.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc5Transport.create()) // wraps HttpClients.createDefault() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); ApacheHc5Transport.create() is shorthand for ApacheHc5Transport.builder().build(). It creates a default CloseableHttpClient via org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.HttpClients.createDefault().

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use ApacheHc5TransportBuilder.httpClient(CloseableHttpClient) to supply your own CloseableHttpClient. The transport takes ownership of the client and closes it when RestClient.close() is called. import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.apachehttpclient50.*; CloseableHttpClient apacheClient = HttpClients.createDefault(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(ApacheHc5Transport.builder() .httpClient(apacheClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Apache HttpClient 5 ships PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder for pooled connection management: import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.io.*; var cm = PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder.create() .setMaxConnTotal(200) .setMaxConnPerRoute(20) .build(); CloseableHttpClient poolingClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

import javax.net.ssl.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.ssl.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.io.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContexts.custom() .loadTrustMaterial(trustStore, null) .build(); var cm = PoolingHttpClientConnectionManagerBuilder.create() .setSSLSocketFactory(SSLConnectionSocketFactoryBuilder.create() .setSslContext(sslContext) .build()) .build(); CloseableHttpClient tlsClient = HttpClients.custom() .setConnectionManager(cm) .build();

In HC 5, timeouts are set via RequestConfig: import org.apache.hc.client5.http.config.*; import org.apache.hc.core5.util.*; import org.apache.hc.client5.http.impl.classic.*; RequestConfig config = RequestConfig.custom() .setConnectTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(5)) .setResponseTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(30)) .setConnectionRequestTimeout(Timeout.ofSeconds(2)) .build(); CloseableHttpClient timedClient = HttpClients.custom() .setDefaultRequestConfig(config) .build();

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-jetty</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- Jetty 12 HTTP Client (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>org.eclipse.jetty</groupId> <artifactId>jetty-client</artifactId> <version>12.1.9</version> </dependency>

juneau-rest-client-jetty provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by the Jetty 12 HttpClient (org.eclipse.jetty:jetty-client). Consider it when: Your application already embeds a Jetty server (e.g., via juneau-microservice-jetty) and you want to share the same Jetty lifecycle for outbound HTTP calls. You want a Jetty-native HTTP client without pulling in Apache HttpComponents or OkHttp. The request body is streamed via OutputStreamRequestContent on a background thread, so large bodies do not require full in-memory buffering. Response body bytes are made available as an InputStream via Jetty's InputStreamResponseListener. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

Note JettyHttpTransport.create() and JettyHttpTransportBuilder.build() declare throws Exception because they may need to start the underlying Jetty HttpClient. import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.jetty.*; RestClient client; try { client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.create()) // starts a new HttpClient internally .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException("Failed to start Jetty transport", e); } try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); JettyHttpTransport.create() is shorthand for JettyHttpTransport.builder().build(). It creates and starts a new HttpClient with default settings and a 30-second response-header timeout.

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); Auto-discovery uses the same throws Exception build path internally; the exception is wrapped in an IllegalStateException if thrown.

Use JettyHttpTransportBuilder to supply a pre-configured HttpClient or to adjust the response-header timeout. import org.eclipse.jetty.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.jetty.*; // Build your own Jetty HttpClient HttpClient jettyClient = new HttpClient(); // ... configure jettyClient ... RestClient client; try { client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(jettyClient) .responseTimeoutMs(15_000) // wait up to 15 s for response headers .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); } catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); } If the HttpClient you supply has not been started, JettyHttpTransport starts it automatically.

JettyHttpTransportBuilder.responseTimeoutMs(long) sets the maximum time to wait (in milliseconds) for the HTTP status line and headers after the request has been sent. It does not limit how long the response body takes to stream. Value Behaviour > 0 (default: 30_000) Wait that many milliseconds; throw TransportException on timeout. 0 or negative Wait indefinitely. JettyHttpTransport transport = JettyHttpTransport.builder() .responseTimeoutMs(60_000) // 60 s for slow endpoints .build();

Configure SSL on the HttpClient before passing it to the builder: import org.eclipse.jetty.client.*; import org.eclipse.jetty.util.ssl.*; SslContextFactory.Client sslContextFactory = new SslContextFactory.Client(); sslContextFactory.setKeyStorePath("/path/to/keystore.jks"); sslContextFactory.setKeyStorePassword("secret"); HttpClient tlsClient = new HttpClient(sslContextFactory); JettyHttpTransport transport = JettyHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(tlsClient) .build();

JettyHttpTransport.close() calls HttpClient.stop(). Map this to RestClient.close(): RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(JettyHttpTransport.builder().build()) .build(); // ... application runs ... // At shutdown — stops the Jetty HttpClient client.close(); When embedding inside a JettyMicroservice, the transport's lifecycle aligns naturally with the server because both use the same Jetty runtime. If you pass your own HttpClient to the adapter, stopping the client via RestClient.close() also stops that shared instance — factor this in if other components depend on it.

The following methods provide logging of requests and responses: RestClient.Builderlogger(Logger)logToConsole()logRequests(DetailLevel,Level,BiPredicate) The following example shows the results of logging all requests that end with /bean. Examples // A simple bean we're going to round-trip. MyBean bean = new MyBean(); bean = RestClient .create() .json5() .logRequests(DetailLevel.FULL, Level.SEVERE, (req,res)->req.getUri().endsWith("/bean")) .logToConsole() .build() .post("http://localhost/bean", bean) .run() .getContent().as(MyBean.class); This produces the following console output: === HTTP Call (outgoing) ====================================================== === REQUEST === POST http://localhost/bean ---request headers--- Accept: application/json5 ---request entity--- Content-Type: application/json5 ---request content--- {f:1} === RESPONSE === HTTP/1.1 200 ---response headers--- Content-Type: application/json ---response content--- {f:1} === END =======================================================================", It should be noted that if you enable request logging detail level DetailLevel.FULL, response bodies will be cached by default which may introduce a performance penalty. Additionally, the following method is also provided for enabling debug mode: RestClient.Builderdebug() Enabling debug mode has the following effects: RestClient.Builder.logToConsole() is called. Classic REST client logging/debug APIs are unchanged and remain available through the classic builder: org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient.Builderlogger(Logger)logToConsole()logRequests(DetailLevel,Level,BiPredicate)debug()

The next-generation client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) uses JUL-level-driven debug logging through RichLogger. org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient.BuilderdebugLoggerName(String)debugFormatter(RestClientDebugFormatter)RestClientDebugFormatterBasicRestClientDebugFormatter Default logger name: RestClient.class.getName(). Debug detail is controlled solely by the resolved JUL logger level: INFO: basic summary line. FINE: basic + request/response headers. FINEST: basic + headers + bounded request/response body capture — only if body dumping has been explicitly opted in via the JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES environment variable (see Secure by default below); otherwise FINEST emits a suppression placeholder instead of body content. Exactly one LogRecord is emitted per request/error, always at JUL INFO — the resolved tier controls message detail only, so FINE/FINEST-selected detail still travels through INFO sinks. This applies uniformly to both places the pipeline emits from: the normal request-completion path and the transport-exception (synthetic error response) path.

BasicRestClientDebugFormatter mirrors the NG REST server's BasicRestDebugFormatter secret-hardening design (see REST server Logging/Debugging » Secure by default): raising a client's debug logger to FINE/FINEST can never, by itself, turn the log stream into a plaintext-credential dump or a log-forging channel.

Request/response bodies are never dumped by default — not at FINEST, not for any content type. Dumping is a deliberate operator opt-in behind the same environment-variable master gate the server uses: export JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES=true Semantics are byte-identical to the server's gate: environment variable only (no system-property fallback), read once per JVM and cached, trim-then-parse truthy (any non-empty trimmed value enables except case-insensitive false/0). With the gate unset, formatBody emits a suppression placeholder naming the environment variable plus the captured byte count and content-type — never body bytes in any representation (plaintext, hex, or otherwise), even if a scrubber is configured. With the gate set, bodies render only when the content is renderable (see below); non-renderable/binary content, or a non-identity Content-Encoding (e.g. gzip), yields a distinct "not rendered" placeholder instead. danger Setting JUNEAU_REST_DEBUG_ALLOW_DUMP_BODIES re-enables plaintext request/response body logging at FINEST for both the client and the server. Treat FINEST client logs as sensitive, and supply a bodyScrubber(...) if any secret-bearing bodies (tokens, PII, card data) are possible. Prefer leaving the gate unset in production. isBodyRenderable(String contentType) (on the RestClientDebugFormatter SPI) decides whether a body is text worth logging, using the same predicate as the server's RestDebugFormatter.isBodyRenderable: renderable for text/*, application/json, application/xml, any +json/+xml suffix type, and application/x-www-form-urlencoded; non-renderable for everything else, including multipart/form-data, absent, or blank content types. The decision is made independently per side — the request's own Content-Type governs the request body, the response's own governs the response body.
documents.s: No body dumps without an explicit opt-in

documents.t: When body dumping is opted in, transform body text before it's logged via the RestDebugBodyScrubber SPI, registered with bodyScrubber(...): new BasicRestClientDebugFormatter().bodyScrubber((contentType, body) -> body.replaceAll("\"password\":\"[^\"]*\"", "\"password\":\"***\"")); Gate-subordinate: the scrubber runs only after the master gate has already permitted dumping; it merely chooses scrubbed-vs-raw text and never causes a body to be emitted while the gate is unset. Fail-closed: if scrub(...) throws or returns null, the formatter emits a suppression placeholder instead of the body — it never falls back to the raw, unscrubbed body. Non-null output is still sanitized (control characters escaped) and length-capped before it reaches the log. No default scrubber ships: with the gate set and no scrubber, the raw body is dumped (sanitized + capped).

At the headers tier (FINE-or-finer), header values are masked with [REDACTED] against a widened, formatter-local set — a superset of the shared RedactedHeaders.DEFAULT (Authorization, Cookie, Set-Cookie, Proxy-Authorization, X-API-Key) plus X-Auth-Token, X-Authorization, WWW-Authenticate, Referer, and Location. Matching is separator-normalized: it case-folds and strips -/_, so X-Auth-Token, X_Auth_Token, and XAuthToken all match. The shared RedactedHeaders.DEFAULT itself is left unchanged; this widened set is client-formatter-local, matching the server's own decision to keep its widened set formatter-local rather than merged into the shared default. Configure the masked set with redactedHeaders(Collection<String>) (replaces the masked set).

The request method and URI, header names and values, and body text (raw or scrubber-produced) are passed through a sanitizer that escapes CR/LF and other control characters to visible, inert forms (\r, \n, \uXXXX). A remote server therefore cannot inject a newline into a response header/body to forge a second physical log line. The order applied to every emitted string is mask → escape → cap.

Captured body bytes are bounded at capture time by bodyCap(int) (default 8 KB), then …[truncated N bytes] marks what was omitted; a second character-level cap (bodyCap() * 6) is applied after sanitization so a scrubber that returns an oversized string is still bounded. Unlike the server's formatter, the client does not add separate header-count/header-scan/field-length/URI-length bounding knobs — the client's header source is already a finite, bounded list rather than an adversarial unbounded input stream, so those extra knobs have no client-side analog.

RestClient automatically participates in end-to-end request correlation. By default, every outgoing request carries an X-Request-Id header so a call can be traced through the server logs (which honor that inbound id — see REST server » Always-on request correlation): Auto-send / mint. If the request has no X-Request-Id header, the client mints a fresh time-ordered Uuid7 and sends it. A header the caller already set (globally on the builder or per-request) is honored, never overwritten. Pre-call setter. RestRequest.requestId(String) sets the id for a single call fluently; getRequestId() reads the id that was (or will be) sent. Echo capture. The client captures the X-Request-Id the server echoes on the response, exposed via RestResponse.getRequestId(). When correlating logs, the client uses the echoed id when present and falls back to the sent id otherwise (the effective id). Opt-out. RestClient.Builder.sendRequestId(false) disables auto-sending entirely; an explicitly caller-supplied X-Request-Id header still travels. The effective id flows into debug logging: RestClientDebugPipeline stamps each emitted LogRecord with a structured requestId field (via LogRecordContext.attachIfAbsent(...)), and BasicRestClientDebugFormatter prepends a human-readable [requestId=<id>] marker to the rendered message — mirroring the server's statusLine prefix so a single request reads identically on both sides. try (var client = RestClient.builder().build(); var res = client.get("http://localhost/widgets/123").run()) { // Server-honored, echoed back: var id = res.getRequestId(); } // Explicit per-call id (honored, not overwritten): client.get("/widgets/123").requestId("order-9f2c").run(); // Opt out of auto-sending entirely: var quiet = RestClient.builder().sendRequestId(false).build(); For tests, capture emitted records directly via RichLogger.captureEvents(...): var logger = RichLogger.getLogger("my.client.debug"); logger.setLevel(Level.FINEST); try (var capture = logger.captureEvents(Level.FINEST); var client = RestClient.builder() .debugLoggerName("my.client.debug") .debugFormatter(new BasicRestClientDebugFormatter().bodyCap(8 * 1024)) .build(); var res = client.post("http://localhost/bean").bodyString("{\"x\":1}").run()) { res.body().asString(); var record = capture.last(); // assert on record.getLevel() and record.getMessage() }

<!-- Juneau transport adapter --> <dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-client-okhttp</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- OkHttp 5 (transitive from the adapter, pinned here for clarity) --> <dependency> <groupId>com.squareup.okhttp3</groupId> <artifactId>okhttp-jvm</artifactId> <version>5.3.2</version> </dependency> OkHttp 5 artifact name The adapter targets OkHttp 5.x, whose Maven artifact is okhttp-jvm (not the older okhttp artifact used by OkHttp 4.x). Make sure your dependency manager resolves the correct artifact.

juneau-rest-client-okhttp provides an HttpTransport implementation backed by OkHttp 5.x (com.squareup.okhttp3:okhttp-jvm). Consider it when: You want transparent HTTP/2 with automatic HTTP/1.1 fallback. You are developing for Android, where OkHttp is the de-facto HTTP client. You want efficient request/response body streaming with minimal in-memory buffering (OkHttp streams the request body directly to the socket when the content length is known). You rely on OkHttp-native interceptors, authenticators, or cookie jars elsewhere in your application and want to share the same OkHttpClient instance. The transport is auto-discovered via ServiceLoader when the module is on the classpath. An explicit .transport(...) call always wins over auto-discovery.

import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.okhttp.*; RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.create()) // wraps new OkHttpClient() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build(); try (var resp = client.get("/users/123").run()) { var user = resp.body().as(User.class); } client.close(); OkHttpTransport.create() is shorthand for OkHttpTransport.builder().build(). It creates a new OkHttpClient with default settings.

Add the module to the classpath and omit the .transport(...) call: RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

Use OkHttpTransportBuilder.httpClient(OkHttpClient) to supply your own OkHttpClient. The transport will call dispatcher().executorService().shutdown() and connectionPool().evictAll() on it when RestClient.close() is called. import okhttp3.*; import org.apache.juneau.marshall.json5.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.okhttp.*; OkHttpClient okClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .connectTimeout(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(5)) .readTimeout(java.time.Duration.ofSeconds(30)) .build(); RestClient client = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder() .httpClient(okClient) .build()) .serializer(Json5Serializer.DEFAULT) .parser(Json5Parser.DEFAULT) .rootUrl("https://api.example.com") .build();

OkHttp's documentation strongly recommends sharing a single OkHttpClient instance across the application so that its connection pool and thread pool are reused. Pass the same instance to each adapter: OkHttpClient shared = new OkHttpClient(); RestClient users = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder().httpClient(shared).build()) .rootUrl("https://users.example.com") .build(); RestClient orders = RestClient.builder() .transport(OkHttpTransport.builder().httpClient(shared).build()) .rootUrl("https://orders.example.com") .build(); When sharing, managing the OkHttpClient lifecycle (shutdown) is the caller's responsibility.
documents.s: Sharing One OkHttpClient Across Multiple RestClients

documents.t: OkHttp manages its connection pool internally. You can tune it via ConnectionPool: import okhttp3.*; OkHttpClient pooled = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .connectionPool(new ConnectionPool( 20, // max idle connections 5, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit.MINUTES)) // keep-alive duration .build();

import javax.net.ssl.*; import okhttp3.*; SSLContext sslContext = SSLContext.getInstance("TLS"); sslContext.init(keyManagers, trustManagers, null); OkHttpClient tlsClient = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .sslSocketFactory(sslContext.getSocketFactory(), (X509TrustManager) trustManagers[0]) .build();

OkHttp-native interceptors can be wired through the OkHttpClient builder and are transparent to Juneau's own interceptor chain: OkHttpClient intercepted = new OkHttpClient.Builder() .addInterceptor(chain -> { Request request = chain.request().newBuilder() .addHeader("X-Correlation-Id", UUID.randomUUID().toString()) .build(); return chain.proceed(request); }) .build();

OkHttpTransport.close() drains the connection pool and shuts down the dispatcher's thread pool: // httpClient.dispatcher().executorService().shutdown(); // httpClient.connectionPool().evictAll(); If you supplied a shared OkHttpClient, call close() on the last RestClient to use it, or manage the OkHttpClient lifecycle yourself.
