Outdated examples (10.0) Examples on this page using RestContext.Builder (constructor injection or @RestInit parameter injection) is pre-10.0 and kept only for historical context. The Builder-injection protocol was removed; migrate to @Rest(...) / @RestOp(...) attributes, @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers, and new RestContext(RestContextInit) for programmatic bootstrap. See the V10 Migration Guide. The RestContext object is the workhorse class for all of the configuration of a single REST resource class. It's by-far the most important class in the REST API. Every class annotated with @Rest ends up with an instance of this object. The object itself is read-only and unchangeable and is initialized from the resource/method annotations plus injected beans in the resource bean store. In 10.0+, configuration is annotation-driven (@Rest(...), @RestOp(...), @RestGet(...), etc.) with optional @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers for programmatic overrides. This class is vast. Combined with RestOpContext (which is the equivalent per-method context), these classes define the entire configuration and workflow of the REST API. For direct programmatic bootstrap, use RestContext.Args with new RestContext(init). This replaces the legacy RestContext.create(...).init(...).build() factory chain. 10.0+ guidance Prefer these configuration surfaces: @Rest(...) for resource-level settings. @RestOp(...) / verb annotations for operation-level settings. @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers for programmatic overrides. note The builders or built objects above can also be defined as injected beans defined in a Spring Configuration if you wish to do all your app configuration Spring-style. This is described in detail in the juneau-rest-server-springboot documentation. The lifecycle methods are still annotation-driven via @RestInit, @RestPreCall, @RestPostCall, @RestStartCall, and @RestDestroy.

As of 10.0.0, the env-driven defaults behind most RestContext.* settings — the values consulted when a @Rest(...) attribute is left unset — are resolved as a single bound object, RestContextProperties, rather than as 15 separate @Value fields. RestContextProperties is declared @ConfigProperties(prefix = "RestContext") (see @ConfigProperties Annotation Basics for how the annotation and its underlying binder work), and it's the framework's own pilot for that feature. Practically, this changes nothing about how you configure these settings — a RestContext.* key is still resolved from the same places it always was: A resource's @Rest(config=...) file, via the config's PropertySource registration in the resource's BeanStore. Environment variables and system properties (relaxed key matching applies, so RestContext.clientVersionHeader, REST_CONTEXT_CLIENT_VERSION_HEADER, and rest.context.client.version.header-style dotted forms are all equivalent). Any other registered PropertySource. What's new is that the bound instance itself is directly accessible — either from the context: RestContextProperties props = ctx.getRestContextProperties(); or from the resource's bean store, since the bind auto-registers it (see Auto-registration in the BeanStore): RestContextProperties props = ctx.getBeanStore().getBean(RestContextProperties.class).orElseThrow(); Every existing public getter on RestContext (isRenderResponseStackTraces(), getClientVersionHeader(), getUriRelativity(), etc.) keeps its exact signature and blending behavior with @Rest-annotation overrides — they're unaffected thin wrappers; only the source of the default half of that computation moved from a private @Value field to RestContextProperties. Two settings are intentionally not part of RestContextProperties: RestContext.uriAuthority and RestContext.uriContext remain standalone @Value("${RestContext.uriAuthority}") / @Value("${RestContext.uriContext}") Optional<String> fields directly on RestContext, because they carry a null-vs-empty distinction that @ConfigProperties' current raw-type-only conversion can't express (see the current limitations of @ConfigProperties). Leniency improvement for present-but-empty booleans Under the pre-10.0.0 @Value boolean fields, a present-but-empty value (e.g. RestContext.eagerInit=) threw BeanCreationException. As of 10.0.0, RestContextProperties carries every boolean setting as a raw string and RestContext parses it leniently, so a present-but-empty value now resolves to false instead of throwing — for all 8 boolean settings (disableContentParam, renderResponseStackTraces, problemDetails, virtualThreads, responseTraceparent, mdcAsyncPropagation, eagerInit, lazyChildren). See the 10.0.0 release notes for details.

REST Java methods are identified on REST servlets using the @RestOp annotation. The annotation allows the framework to identify the available REST methods through reflection. RestOpallowedParserOptions allowedSerializerOptions asyncCompletionExecutor asyncTimeoutMillis clientVersion consumes converters defaultAccept defaultCharset defaultContentType defaultRequestAttributes defaultRequestFormData defaultRequestHeaders defaultRequestQueryData defaultResponseHeaders description encoders guards matchers maxInput metricName metricTags method noInherit observability parsers path problemDetails produces roleGuard rolesDeclared serializers summary swagger value virtualThreads Example @RestOp(method=GET, path="/") public String sayHello() { return "Hello world!"; } The following specialized annotations are also provided for specific HTTP methods: RestGet RestPut RestPost RestPatch RestDelete RestOptions Example @RestGet(path="/") public String sayHello() { return "Hello world!"; }

The RestOpContext object is the workhorse class for an individual RestOp-annotated method. Every class annotated with @RestOp ends up with an instance of this object. Similar to RestContext, the object is read-only and unchangeable and is initialized with all of the various annotations pulled from the method. Per-operation configuration is annotation-driven via @RestOp (and its method-specific cousins @RestGet, @RestPut, @RestPost, @RestDelete, @RestPatch, @RestOptions). Programmatic per-operation overrides are supplied via @Bean-named beans (use the methodScope= attribute to scope an override to specific operation methods). Both Builder-injection protocols — per-op @RestInit(RestOpContext.Builder) and class-level @RestInit(RestContext.Builder) — were removed in 10.0; see the V10 Migration Guide for replacement recipes. 10.0+ configuration model RestOpContext is now configured through: @RestOp(...) / @RestGet(...) / @RestPost(...) / @RestPut(...) / @RestPatch(...) / @RestDelete(...) / @RestOptions(...) attributes. @Bean(name="...") bean suppliers (optionally scoped with methodScope=). Resource-level defaults inherited from @Rest(...) (unless blocked by noInherit). See @Rest, @RestOp and @Mixin Attributes for every attribute that feeds into the context.

A RestOpContext is created once per @RestOp method when the owning RestContext is initialized, and is shared by all requests to that method. You can get at it in three ways: @RestGet("/info") public String info(RestOpContext opContext, RestRequest req) { // 1. As a Java method parameter (see JavaMethodParameters). // 2. From the request. RestOpContext same = req.getOpContext(); return opContext.getHttpMethod() + " " + opContext.getPathPattern(); } As a method parameter of type RestOpContext (resolved by RestOpContextArgs; see Java Method Parameters). The same resolver also supplies JsonSchemaGenerator, ParserSet and SerializerSet parameters taken from the operation context. RestRequest.getOpContext(). RestOpSession.getContext(). The owning resource-level context is available through RestOpContext.getContext(), which returns the RestContext (see RestContext).
The context exposes the effective, fully-resolved settings for the operation, i.e. the @RestOp value with anything unset inherited from @Rest.

Method Description getJavaMethod() The java.lang.reflect.Method implementing the operation. getHttpMethod() The resolved HTTP method (explicit, inferred from the Java method name, or *). getPathPattern() The first path pattern as a string. getPathMatchers() All UrlPathMatcher objects for the operation. getRequiredMatchers() / getOptionalMatchers() The RestMatcher objects that must / may match for the operation to be chosen. getRestOpAnnotations() The @RestOp-group annotations applied to the method.

Method Description getSerializers() / getParsers() The SerializerSet / ParserSet for the operation. getEncoders() The EncoderSet. getMarshallingContext() The MarshallingContext. getPartSerializer() / getPartParser() The HttpPartSerializer / HttpPartParser. getJsonSchemaGenerator() The JsonSchemaGenerator. getSupportedAcceptTypes() / getSupportedContentTypes() The MediaType lists derived from the serializers/parsers (or produces/consumes). getAllowedParserOptions() / getAllowedSerializerOptions() Session option keys clients may set. getMaxInput() Maximum number of input bytes. getResponseMeta(), getResponseBeanMeta(Object), getResponseHeaderMeta(Object) Response metadata for the return type / a given object.

Method Description getDefaultCharset() Default character set. getDefaultRequestHeaders() HttpHeaderList applied when the client does not send the header. getDefaultRequestAttributes() NamedAttributeMap of default request attributes. getDefaultRequestQueryData() / getDefaultRequestFormData() HttpPartList of default query / form-data values. getDefaultResponseHeaders() HttpHeaderList of default response headers.

Method Description isProblemDetails() Whether RFC 7807 problem-details responses are enabled; inherited from @Rest(problemDetails) when unset. isDebugMarshalling() Whether REST-driven marshalling debug is enabled. isVirtualThreadsEnabled() Whether per-request virtual-thread dispatch is enabled (Java 21+). isObservabilityEnabled() Whether observability is enabled for the operation. getMetricName() / getMetricTags() Metric name and tags from @RestOp(metricName, metricTags). getAsyncTimeoutMillis() / getAsyncCompletionExecutor() Timeout and completion executor for CompletableFuture-returning handlers. getLogger() The per-operation RichLogger. RestOpContext implements Comparable<RestOpContext>, which is what orders operations when a request is matched against them.

RestContext - the resource-level equivalent. Inferred HTTP Methods and Paths - how getHttpMethod() and getPathPattern() are derived when not stated. Overloading HTTP Methods - @Mutating reads getHttpMethod().

One of the most powerful features of the REST client class is the ability to turn a plain Java interface into a fully-working client for a 3rd-party REST resource. You describe the API with a Java interface and a handful of annotations — the HTTP method, the path, which arguments become headers, query parameters, form data, or the request body, and what the response should be parsed into. RestClient then hands you back a dynamic proxy that implements the interface, translating every method call into an HTTP request and every response back into a Java return value. The methods used to retrieve remote interfaces are: RestClientgetRemote(Class)getRemote(Class,Object)getRemote(Class,Object,Serializer,Parser)

Define an interface, annotate it, and get a proxy from a RestClient: Example @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemotePost("/pets") Pet addPet( @Content CreatePet createPet, @Header("E-Tag") UUID etag, @Query("debug") boolean debug ); @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId); } // Use a RestClient with default JSON 5 support. RestClient client = RestClient.create().json5().build(); // Instantiate our proxy interface. PetStore store = client.getRemote(PetStore.class, "http://localhost:10000"); // Use it to create a pet... CreatePet createPet = new CreatePet("Fluffy", 9.99); Pet pet = store.addPet(createPet, UUID.randomUUID(), true); // ...and fetch it back. Pet sameCat = store.getPet(pet.getId()); The addPet(...) call above translates to a real HTTP request under the hood: POST http://localhost:10000/petstore/pets HTTP/1.1 Accept: application/json Content-Type: application/json E-Tag: 475588d4-0b27-4f56-9296-cc683251d314 { name: 'Fluffy', price: 9.99 } No hand-written URL building, serialization, or response parsing required — the interface is the contract. See Also The @RemoteOp annotation (and its method/path) can often be skipped entirely if your Java method names follow a simple naming convention. See @RemoteOp for the inference rules.

Method behavior is driven entirely by annotations on the interface, its methods, and their parameters: Annotation Applies to Purpose @Remote Interface Marks the interface as a REST proxy; sets the base path, common headers, and client versioning. @RemoteOp (and @RemoteGet/@RemotePost/@RemotePut/@RemotePatch/@RemoteDelete) Method Maps a method to an HTTP verb + path. Often optional if the method name implies the verb. @Path Parameter URL path variables ({petId}-style placeholders). @Query Parameter Query-string parameters. @Header Parameter HTTP request headers — including dynamic, multi-value forms. @FormData Parameter application/x-www-form-urlencoded body parameters. @Content Parameter The HTTP request body. @Request Parameter or class Bundles multiple parts (content/headers/query/etc.) behind a single request bean. @Response Return type Bundles content/headers/status behind a single response bean. Every one of these supports both single-value forms (@Query("limit") int limit) and dynamic, multi-value forms (@Query Map<String,Object> params) — see the dynamic headers example below for the pattern in detail.
The sections below are short teasers of what's possible. Each links to a deep-dive page with the full set of supported types and edge cases.

Path variables (@Path) fill in {placeholders} in the URL: @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId); Query parameters (@Query) — and the equivalent for @FormData form posts: @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] findPets(@Query("species") String species, @Query("limit") int limit); Dynamic and multiple headers​ @Header (and @Query/@FormData/@Path) isn't limited to one header per parameter. Leave the name off (or use the explicit wildcard "*") and pass a Map, a HeaderList, or a bean — every entry or property is expanded into its own header: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { // Every map entry becomes its own header. @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets(@Header("*") Map<String,Object> headers); // Same idea via a pre-built HeaderList... @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPetsViaHeaderList(@Header HeaderList headers); // ...or a bean whose properties become individual headers. @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPetsViaBean(@Header PetHeaders headers); } Map<String,Object> headers = JsonMap.of("X-Client-Id", "acme", "X-Trace-Id", UUID.randomUUID()); Pet[] pets = store.getPets(headers); This is a great way to forward a variable, caller-supplied set of headers (correlation IDs, feature flags, tenant context, etc.) without adding a new interface parameter every time one shows up. See @Header for the full list of supported dynamic forms. Request bodies (@Content) accept any serializable POJO, or raw Reader/InputStream: @RemotePost("/pets") Pet addPet(@Content CreatePet pet); Request beans (@Request) bundle several of the above behind one argument, so callers pass a single object instead of a long parameter list: @RemotePost String postPet(CreatePetRequest bean); @Request public class CreatePetRequest { @Content public CreatePet getContent() { ... } @Query public Map<String,Object> getQueryParams() { ... } @Header("E-Tag") public UUID getUUID() { ... } }

Return types are flexible — parsed POJOs, raw streams, async wrappers, or just the status code: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets(); // Parsed POJO @RemoteGet(path="/pets", returns=STATUS) int getPetsStatus(); // Just the HTTP status @RemoteGet("/pets") Future<Pet[]> getPetsAsync(); // Async @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") InputStream getPetRaw(@Path("petId") int petId); // Raw stream } See @RemoteOp for the complete list of supported return types. Response beans (@Response) do the same thing in reverse — bundle the body, headers, and status code of a response behind one typed object: @RemotePost CreatePetResponse postPet(@Content CreatePet pet); @Response public interface CreatePetResponse { @Content Pet getContent(); @Header("E-Tag") UUID getUUID(); @StatusCode int getStatus(); } Error handling happens automatically through checked exceptions. Declare a throws clause using any of the roughly 60 predefined HTTP response exceptions (or your own), and Juneau throws the matching one when the server returns that status code: @RemoteGet("/pets/{petId}") Pet getPet(@Path("petId") int petId) throws NotFound; try { Pet pet = store.getPet(999); } catch (NotFound e) { // HTTP 404 was returned - Juneau matched the status to the declared exception type. }

Default values let you specify fallbacks for null arguments right on the annotation, so callers don't have to pass every parameter every time: @RemoteGet("/pets") Pet[] getPets( @Header(name="Accept-Language", def="en-US") String language, @Query(name="limit", def="10") Integer limit ); // Uses default language="en-US" and limit=10. Pet[] pets = store.getPets(null, null); def is supported on @Header, @Query, @FormData, @Path, and @Content, at either the parameter or method level (parameter wins when both are set).

The same Java interface can define both the client proxy and the server implementation, so a signature change is caught by the compiler on both sides instead of drifting apart at runtime: @Remote(path="/petstore") public interface PetStore { @RemoteGet("/pet") Collection<Pet> getPets() throws NotAcceptable; } @Rest(path="/petstore") public class PetStoreResource extends BasicRestServlet implements PetStore { @Override @RestOp(method=GET, path="/pet") public Collection<Pet> getPets() throws NotAcceptable { return store.getPets(); } } See Dual-purpose (end-to-end) interfaces for the full walkthrough, including how parameter-level annotations like @Header and @Path are inherited from the interface for free. See Also @Remote - Interface-level configuration: base path, common headers, versioning. @RemoteOp - HTTP method/path mapping, naming-convention inference, return types. @Content - The request body. @FormData - Form post parameters. @Query - Query-string parameters. @Header - Request headers, including dynamic/multi-value forms. @Path - URL path variables. @Request - Bean-style bundling of request parts. @Response - Bean-style bundling of response parts. Dual-purpose (end-to-end) interfaces - Sharing one interface between client and server.

The REST/RPC (RPC over REST) API allows the creation of client-side remote proxy interfaces for calling methods on server-side POJOs using entirely REST. note This is not to be confused with REST Proxies which are entirely client-side driven Java interfaces against arbitrary backend REST interfaces.

The following example shows a remote interface built on the petstore sample's real Pet bean and PetStore service (juneau-petstore). (The petstore samples don't currently expose a remote interface via RRPC; this walkthrough builds one on top of those currently-shipping petstore types purely to illustrate the RRPC mechanism.) @RemoteInterface // Annotation is optional public interface IPetStore { Collection<Pet> getPets(); Pet getPet(long id); Pet createPet(Pet pet); Pet updatePet(Pet pet); void deletePet(long id); } The requirements for a remote interface method are: Must be public. Can be called anything. Can have any number of serializable and parsable parameters. Can return a serializable and parsable value. Can throw any Throwables. Throwables with public no-arg or single-arg-string constructors are automatically recreated on the client side when thrown on the server side.

note REST/RPC is a classic-client-only feature. It is implemented on org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient (the Apache HttpClient 4.5-based client); the next-generation, transport-agnostic NG REST client (org.apache.juneau.rest.client.RestClient) has no getRrpcInterface(...) method and no equivalent. If you're building against the NG client, use standard REST calls with the server-side @RestOp(method=RRPC)/RrpcServlet endpoints instead of a generated proxy. Remote Interface proxies are instantiated on the client side using one of the following methods: RestClientgetRrpcInterface(Class)getRrpcInterface(Class,Object)getRrpcInterface(Class,Object,Serializer,Parser) Since we build upon the existing classic RestClient API, we inherit all of it's features. For example, convenience methods for setting POJO filters and properties to customize the behavior of the serializers and parsers, and the ability to provide your own customized Apache HttpClient for handling various scenarios involving authentication and Internet proxies. Here's an example of the above interface being used: import org.apache.juneau.rest.client.classic.RestClient; // Create a classic RestClient using JSON for serialization, and point to the server-side remote interface servlet. RestClient client = RestClient.create() .json() .rootUrl("http://localhost:10000/remote") .build(); // Create a proxy interface. IPetStore petStore = client.getRrpcInterface(IPetStore.class); // Invoke a method on the server side and get the returned result. Pet pet = petStore.createPet( new Pet() .setName("Fluffy") .setSpecies(Species.CAT) .setPrice(200f) .setStatus(PetStatus.AVAILABLE) ); Under the covers, this method call gets converted to a REST POST. HTTP POST http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/createPet(org.apache.juneau.petstore.dto.Pet) Accept: application/json Content-Type: application/json [ { "name":"Fluffy", "species":"CAT", "price":200.0, "status":"AVAILABLE" } ] Note that the body of the request is an array. This array contains the serialized arguments of the method. The object returned by the method is then serialized as the body of the response.

There are two ways to expose remote interfaces on the server side: Extending from RrpcServlet. Using a @RestOp(method=RRPC) annotation on a Java method. In either case, the proxy communications layer is pure REST. Therefore, in cases where the interface classes are not available on the client side, the same method calls can be made through pure REST calls. This can also aid significantly in debugging, since calls to the remote interface service can be made directly from a browser with no coding involved.

The RrpcServlet class is a simple specialized servlet with an abstract getServiceMap() method to define the server-side POJOs. Note that getServiceMap() maps each interface Class to a POJO instance that implements it — since the petstore's real PetStore service doesn't itself implement IPetStore, a small anonymous adapter delegates each IPetStore method to the underlying store: @Rest( path="/remote" ) public class SamplePetStoreRrpcServlet extends RrpcServlet { // Our server-side POJO. private final transient PetStore store = new PetStore(); @Override /* RrpcServlet */ protected Map<Class<?>,Object> getServiceMap() throws Exception { Map<Class<?>,Object> map = new LinkedHashMap<>(); // In this simplified example, we expose the same underlying store under two different interfaces. // One is IPetStore which only exposes methods defined on that interface, and // the other is PetStore itself which exposes all public methods defined on the class itself (dangerous!). map.put(IPetStore.class, new IPetStore() { @Override public Collection<Pet> getPets() { return store.getPets(); } @Override public Pet getPet(long id) { return store.getPet(id); } @Override public Pet createPet(Pet pet) { return store.createPet(pet); } @Override public Pet updatePet(Pet pet) { return store.updatePet(pet); } @Override public void deletePet(long id) { store.deletePet(id); } }); map.put(PetStore.class, store); return map; } }

The @RestOp(method=RRPC) approach is easier if you only have a single interface you want to expose. You simply define a Java method whose return type is an interface, and return the implementation of that interface: // Our exposed interface. @RestOp(method=RRPC, path="/petstoreproxy/*") public IPetStore getProxy() { return new IPetStore() { @Override public Collection getPets() { return store.getPets(); } @Override public Pet getPet(long id) { return store.getPet(id); } @Override public Pet createPet(Pet pet) { return store.createPet(pet); } @Override public Pet updatePet(Pet pet) { return store.updatePet(pet); } @Override public void deletePet(long id) { store.deletePet(id); } }; }

If you point your browser to the servlet above, you get a list of available interfaces: http://localhost:10000/remote Clicking the hyperlinks on each shows you the list of methods that can be invoked on that service. Note that the IPetStore link shows that you can only invoke methods defined on that interface, whereas the PetStore link shows ALL public methods defined on that class.
http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore Only the five methods declared on the IPetStore interface are listed here.

http://localhost:10000/remote/PetStore Since this second entry maps the concrete PetStore class directly, every public method declared on PetStore — not just the five on IPetStore — is listed and invocable, including getOrders(), createOrder(Order), getUsers(), and the rest of the petstore service surface. This is why exposing a concrete class this way is dangerous in a real application; prefer exposing a narrow interface like IPetStore instead. Let's see how we can interact with this interface through nothing more than REST calls to get a better idea on how this works. We'll use the same method call as in the introduction. First, we need to create the serialized form of the arguments: Object[] args = new Object[] { new Pet() .setName("Fluffy") .setSpecies(Species.CAT) .setPrice(200f) .setStatus(PetStatus.AVAILABLE) }; String asJson = Json5Serializer.DEFAULT_READABLE.write(args); System.err.println(asJson); That produces the following JSON output: [ { name: 'Fluffy', species: 'CAT', price: 200.0, status: 'AVAILABLE' } ] Note that in this example we're using JSON. However, various other content types can also be used such as XML, URL-Encoding, UON, or HTML. In practice however, JSON will preferred since it is often the most efficient. Next, we can use a tool such as Poster to make the REST call. Methods are invoked by POSTing the serialized object array to the URI of the interface method. In this case, we want to POST our JSON to the following URL: http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/createPet(org.apache.juneau.petstore.dto.Pet) Make sure that we specify the Content-Type of the body as text/json. We also want the results to be returned as JSON, so we set the Accept header to text/json as well. When we execute the POST, we should see the following successful response whose body contains the returned Pet bean serialized to JSON: From there, we could use the following code snippet to reconstruct the response object from JSON: String response = "output from above"; Pet pet = JsonParser.DEFAULT.read(response, Pet.class); RRPC methods are invoked with POST only. A browser link can't call them: GET .../getPets?method=POST is refused with 405, because the router never lets an override turn a GET into a POST. Use a client that can send a POST, for example curl: curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/json' -H 'Accept: text/json' -d '[]' http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/getPets curl -X POST -H 'Content-Type: text/json' -H 'Accept: text/json' -d '[3]' 'http://localhost:10000/remote/IPetStore/getPet(long)' The body is the JSON array of method arguments. The hyperlinks on the method names above lead you to a simple form-entry page where you can test passing parameters in UON notation as URL-encoded form posts.

Denial of service attacks can be alleviated through the maxInput() setting. Arbitrarily-large input will trigger an exception before causing out-of-memory errors. The default value for this setting is 100MB. Since the parsers do not use intermediate DOMs and instead parse directly into Java objects, deeply nested data structures will almost always trigger stack overflow errors long before memory consumption becomes an issue. However, this is NOT true of the RDF parsers, which build an intermediate DOM. If parsing RDF, you may want to consider lowering the max-input value above.

Juneau ships two request boundaries in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter. Both decide whether a state-changing request came from a page your application served (or from a non-browser client) and refuse it when it came from some other site's page. Neither one authenticates the caller, and neither proves the user meant the action; those need their own mechanisms. Boundary Use it when LoopbackBoundary The app is bound to the loopback interface and is reached under one pinned Host (for example 127.0.0.1:8790) over plain HTTP. It pins that single origin and is the stricter of the two. CsrfBoundary Everything else: an app reached under a real host name, over HTTPS, behind a proxy, or under more than one name. Nothing is pinned; the request's own scheme and host are the expected origin. Both are applied by RequestBoundaryFilter. A rejected request is answered directly with a JSON body, a Cache-Control: no-store header, and an X-Request-Boundary header naming the reason (for example ORIGIN_MISMATCH or CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING). The request never reaches application code. Even without a boundary, the router refuses an override of a safe method (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) to an unsafe one with 405. A boundary still judges any custom-method claim as a write, including one declared @RestOp(read=true).

On every state-changing request (the method is judged after any ?method= or X-Method, X-HTTP-Method-Override, X-HTTP-Method or X-Method-Override override, so an override cannot carry a write past the checks): Origin, with Sec-Fetch-Site as a fallback, must match the request's own scheme, host and port. A literal null origin is refused. A browser request must also carry a synchronizer token in a request header (X-Csrf-Token by default). The token is read from that header and nowhere else: never a query parameter, never a form field. Origins are compared as normalized scheme, host and port. Default ports are equated (https://app.example.com and https://app.example.com:443 match). IPv6 literals are compared in bracketed form exactly as sent, and nothing else is re-canonicalized, so two spellings of the same address do not match each other. That is deliberate: it fails closed.

CsrfBoundary boundary = CsrfBoundary.create() .allowedHosts("app.example.com") .build(); servletContext.addFilter("csrf", new RequestBoundaryFilter(boundary)) .addMappingForUrlPatterns(EnumSet.of(DispatcherType.REQUEST), false, "/*"); Map the filter at /* so nothing can be reached around it. Register it for REQUEST dispatches only. An ERROR dispatch of a refused write can arrive without the token header and be refused in turn, replacing the error page with a 403, and a FORWARD to an HTML view looks like a page load and can create a session. The default registration in a servlet container, and Spring Boot's FilterRegistrationBean, is already REQUEST only. Register it ahead of any filter that acts on the request on the application's behalf. The one exception is described under proxies below. By default the filter creates an HTTP session on a safe request that looks like a page load, so that the page it serves can carry a session-scoped token. Turn that off with createSessions(false).

By default (OriginSource.HOST_HEADER) the request's own origin is request.getScheme() plus the Host header. X-Forwarded-* and Forwarded are never read, so a client cannot spoof them past the boundary. HTTP/2 has no Host header: the :authority pseudo-header plays that part, and servlet containers surface it only as getServerName() and getServerPort(). A request with no Host whose protocol is exactly HTTP/2.0 is therefore judged on its server name and port in Host's place, under both OriginSources and allowedHosts. A request without Host on any other protocol is still refused with HOST_MISSING. HOST_HEADER is consequently protocol-dependent: it reads the raw Host on HTTP/1.1 and the container's server name on HTTP/2, and the server name is what a container's forwarded-header support rewrites (Tomcat's RemoteIpValve with a host header, Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter, Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer). On HTTP/2 an X-Forwarded-Host that such support honors is therefore trusted under HOST_HEADER too. Behind a proxy that terminates TLS, the scheme the app sees is http while the browser's Origin is https. Use OriginSource.CONTAINER and configure the container's own forwarded-header support, so the container rewrites the request before the boundary sees it: Stack Setting Jetty Add a ForwardedRequestCustomizer to the connector's HttpConfiguration. Tomcat Add a RemoteIpValve. Spring Boot server.forward-headers-strategy=native rewrites before any filter runs, so filter order does not matter. Spring Boot server.forward-headers-strategy=framework registers ForwardedHeaderFilter at Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE. Register the boundary's filter strictly later, never at HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE itself. nginx proxy_set_header Host $host; and proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme; The boundary cannot see its own filter order. A misordered or misconfigured deployment shows up as ORIGIN_MISMATCH refusals and a one-time warning in the log naming the likely cause (scheme-only or port-only mismatch). Enable a forwarded-header customizer only behind a proxy that overwrites, rather than appends to, X-Forwarded-*. A browser cannot send those headers, but anything that can reach the connector directly can, and the container then trusts the forwarded host.

A WebSocket upgrade is a GET, so the filter lets it through; the bus WebSocket endpoint applies the boundary to the handshake itself. BusWebSockets.register accepts a bus whose BusPolicy boundary is a LoopbackBoundary or a CsrfBoundary, and refuses to register for any other boundary type (it fails closed). Under a CsrfBoundary: No token can be sent on a handshake, so the control is Origin plus Sec-Fetch-Site. The container's checkOrigin hook runs first. A missing, blank or null Origin, or one that is not a well-formed http or https origin, is refused with HTTP 403 before the upgrade. A well-formed Origin that is cross-site, or does not match the handshake's own origin, is refused after the upgrade: the connection is closed with code 4403 before any frame is sent and before any bus session is touched. The handshake has no server name, so the check judges the raw Host header plus the scheme of the handshake's request URI, whatever OriginSource is set to. ws counts as http and wss as https. A WebSocket over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441, an extended CONNECT) has no Host. When a handshake carries neither Host nor Sec-WebSocket-Key or Upgrade (which mark an RFC 6455 request, and which the container enforces), the authority of its request URI, which is the :authority, stands in for Host. Jetty advertises RFC 8441 by default whenever HTTP/2 is enabled; Tomcat does not support it, so on Tomcat there is no HTTP/2 handshake to judge. Behind a reverse proxy that rewrites Host to an internal name, with no container-side host rewriting, same-origin upgrades are refused. That is accepted behavior. Preserve the original Host at the proxy (in nginx, proxy_set_header Host $host;). If the proxy cannot preserve Host, see Trusting a forwarded origin. Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer rewrites the Host that both ordinary requests and the WebSocket handshake see, using X-Forwarded-Host. With it enabled the forwarded host is trusted for both, so the overwrite-not-append rule above applies to the WebSocket endpoint too. For an HTTP/2 handshake on Jetty this customizer is the only forwarded-header support that applies: it runs at the connector, while the WebSocket upgrade filter runs ahead of any servlet filter, so Spring's ForwardedHeaderFilter never sees the handshake. On Tomcat the handshake's request URI reports ws or wss, normalized as above. RemoteIpValve rewrites that scheme from X-Forwarded-Proto, so a TLS-terminating proxy works. It does not rewrite the Host header the handshake reads, even with the valve's hostHeader set to X-Forwarded-Host. Unlike Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer, a forwarded host is therefore never trusted for the WebSocket endpoint, and the preserve-Host advice above applies.

By default the boundary never reads X-Forwarded-* or Forwarded itself. A deployment whose proxy rewrites Host and whose container does no forwarded-host handling (no ForwardedRequestCustomizer, or Tomcat without a host-rewriting valve) can opt in on CsrfBoundary: CsrfBoundary.create() .trustedForwarding(CsrfBoundary.ForwardedSource.X_FORWARDED) // or FORWARDED (RFC 7239) .trustedHops(1) // proxies you operate, 1 to 16 .trustedProxies("10.0.12.0/24") // your proxies' addresses; optional .build(); This is a trust decision, so it is fail-closed throughout: Reachability. Only turn it on when every request reaches the app through proxies that you operate, or set trustedProxies so that peers that are not your proxies are not believed. A peer that can reach the app directly can send any forwarded host it likes. Proxy hygiene. Every proxy you operate must overwrite or append to the forwarded header the way trustedHops assumes, and strip any client-supplied copy. trustedProxies does not replace this: an allow-list cannot detect a proxy that passes a client's header through. One header family is read, never both. The forwarded host and protocol are both required (X-Forwarded-Host plus X-Forwarded-Proto, or Forwarded elements carrying host= and proto=). X-Forwarded-Port is never read: put the port in the host value. A missing, repeated-in-conflict or malformed value is refused with a FORWARDED_* reason (HTTP 403) and a handshake is closed with 4403. A forwarded header whose lines cannot be put in wire order (a handshake that presents the same header under more than one spelling) is refused as FORWARDED_HOST_MALFORMED or FORWARDED_PROTO_MALFORMED. The entry that counts is the one added by your outermost proxy: the nth from the right, with n set by trustedHops. Entries to its left are client-controlled and ignored. Set trustedHops to the number of proxies you run. Too small is safe (the request is refused, or the wrong hop mismatches); too large reaches into client-supplied entries and is not safe. Picking the nth entry from the right assumes the container hands the handshake's repeated header lines to the endpoint in the order they arrived. Jetty and Tomcat both do (each is covered by an integration test); with any other container, confirm this before turning trusted forwarding on. The forwarded origin replaces the container's view; it is never added to it. allowedHosts is checked against the forwarded host. If the container also rewrites forwarded headers, the two must agree: under OriginSource.CONTAINER a disagreement is refused with FORWARDED_CONTAINER_MISMATCH, and a rewritten host that equals an ignored left-hand entry, or that might be one that does not parse (a container may normalize it), is refused too. The cross-check compares hosts only, not ports or schemes. A safe request (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) on a boundary with no allowedHosts is not judged, so direct health probes without forwarded headers still pass. Optionally, name the proxies. trustedProxies("10.0.12.0/24", "fd00:12::/64") makes the boundary believe the forwarded header only from a connection whose peer address is in one of the ranges. A request from any other peer that carries the header is refused (FORWARDED_PEER_NOT_TRUSTED, 403, or 4403 on a WebSocket). One without the header is judged on its own Host, as if forwarding were off, so allowedHosts still applies. List the addresses your proxies connect from, not your whole network. Host bits below the prefix are ignored (10.0.12.7/24 means 10.0.12.0/24), and a /0 entry (0.0.0.0/0 or ::/0) trusts every peer of that address family. Only the last proxy before the server is checked. trustedHops still decides which entry counts, and an allow-list does not make an overstated trustedHops safe. Requires OriginSource.HOST_HEADER. The peer is the address the container reports. The setting is meaningless, or unsafe, where the container rewrites it: Jetty's ForwardedRequestCustomizer (which takes X-Forwarded-For from anyone), Tomcat's RemoteIpValve and Spring Boot's forward-headers-strategy=native, or the PROXY protocol. Use it only where the server sees your proxy's own address. WebSockets. A WebSocket handshake carries no peer address in the standard API. On Jetty the boundary reads the one Jetty supplies. On Tomcat there is none, so with trustedProxies set a handshake that carries a forwarded host is always refused, and one without it is judged on its own Host and scheme. Bus sockets then work on Tomcat only if TLS ends at Tomcat (or nothing uses TLS), the proxy preserves Host, and it sends no X-Forwarded-Host on the socket route. Otherwise leave trustedProxies unset on Tomcat. Direct callers. With allowedHosts set, a caller that bypasses the proxy is checked on its own Host, so add the backend name it uses (backend) to allowedHosts if it must write. That is safe: a rebound page's Host is the attacker's name.

An unsafe request with neither Origin nor Sec-Fetch-Site is not from a browser page, and the policy set with nonBrowser(...) decides what happens to it. With the default, NonBrowser.ADMIT_NON_SIMPLE, it is admitted without a token only when a browser could not have sent it cross-site without a CORS preflight, which this boundary never answers. For client authors the rule is: send JSON, or send Origin plus the token. Concretely, an unsafe request with no Origin is admitted if its method is not GET, HEAD or POST, or if it carries exactly one Content-Type that is not application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain. Everything else is refused. The alternatives are NonBrowser.REJECT (refuse every such request) and NonBrowser.REQUIRE_TOKEN (treat it like a browser request and require the token). requireJson(true) additionally requires a single application/json content type on every admitted write. This relies on browsers sending Origin on every non-simple request they issue. Current browsers do, and the Origin check is the real control for them.

A plain HTML <form> cannot set a request header, so every HTML form POST, including your own app's, is refused with CSRF_TOKEN_MISSING. CsrfBoundary is for applications whose writes go through script that sends the token header (the Juneau views toolkit already does). The token is not accepted as a form field or query parameter on purpose: that would put it in URLs, logs and Referer headers.

The default token strategy, CsrfTokens.perSession(), derives one token per session id (an HMAC of the id under a per-process key), so a visitor who loads the page learns only their own token. CsrfTokens.perProcess() uses one token for the whole process; any visitor can read it, so in a multi-user app it adds little beyond the Origin check. In a cluster, give every node the same key so any node accepts any node's token. Because a per-session token follows the session id, the application must: call request.changeSessionId() on login, or a token seen before login stays valid after it; mark the session cookie HttpOnly and SameSite, and not scope it to a parent Domain; not use URL rewriting for session ids. The boundary never changes a session id and never sets cookie attributes; those stay the application's. The value written into a page is masked under a fresh pad on every embed. Masking defends only against BREACH-style compression oracles; anyone who can see the wire value can unmask it. Never log the token header.

Any code that stamps a token into a response must call RequestBoundaryFilter.markTokenBearing(response) before it writes the first byte of the body. It replaces Cache-Control with private, no-store; without it a shared cache can serve one session's token to another session. This applies to a view host that uses ViewTable.CSRF_ATTR or RegionTable.of(region, csrfToken), and to PageSpec.csrf(...). The console page chrome does it for you. A token is never embedded into a response that is already committed, because the response can no longer be marked. That includes csrf attributes an author put on the page's body element. The page still loads, and its writes then fail visibly for want of a token.

A rebound page's Origin and Host agree, so origin checking alone does not stop DNS rebinding. TLS defeats it. A plain-HTTP intranet app should list its host names with allowedHosts(...); the boundary then refuses any request, safe ones included, whose own host is not listed, with 421. CsrfBoundary does not support cross-origin callers and adds no Access-Control-Allow-* headers. Do not put an origin-reflecting CORS layer in front of it: reflecting every Origin back undoes the check.

The Apache HttpClient 4.5 transport (ApacheHc45Transport) never sends credentials to a different origin as the result of a redirect. This applies the same way to a client the transport built and to one you supplied with httpClient(...). When a redirect leads to a different scheme, host or port (including an https to http downgrade), every credential header is removed from that request. Every request is compared with the first origin of the exchange (exact scheme, host and port), not with the previous request. That covers the headers you set on the request (Authorization, Cookie, X-API-Key and the rest of the standard credential set) and the ones HttpClient adds itself: the Cookie from the client's cookie store, and the Authorization from its credentials provider, its preemptive authentication, or the answer to a 401 challenge. A cross-origin server that challenges the redirected request therefore gets no answer, and the caller sees the 401. Proxy-Authorization is not removed, because it is addressed to the proxy and not to the origin. Headers that are not credentials, such as those from setDefaultHeaders(...), are left alone. A same-origin redirect keeps everything. A chain that returns to the first origin (an SSO round trip, A to B to A, or A to B to C to A) gets that origin's credentials back on the returning request, exactly as an unredirected request to it would: the headers you set, the cookie-store Cookie, and the credentials-provider or preemptive Authorization. Any request that is not at the first origin is stripped, so A to B to A to B strips the second B. The comparison is exact: the same host on a different port or scheme, an IP address instead of the host name, or a different spelling of the name is a different origin and stays stripped. There is no option to turn the stripping off. Details worth knowing: A hop that returns to the first origin gets the credentials back only when its method is GET or HEAD. If the chain has left the first origin and then comes back with any other method (a 307/308 replay of a POST, say), that hop stays stripped. A 302 that turns a POST into a GET is restored. A request that never left the first origin keeps everything whatever its method. The SSRF-guarded @Remote redirect path is shared by every transport (JDK, OkHttp, Apache HttpClient 4.5 and 5, and the mock transport), so the same first-origin and GET/HEAD rules apply to all of them there. A redirect Location that carries user info (https://user:pw@host/) is refused, because HttpClient would use it to replace the client's stored credentials for that host. The guarded path and a transport-built HC4.5 client enforce this. A client you supplied with httpClient(...) keeps its own redirect strategy, which is not changed. On a 307/308 redirect of a non-GET request, HttpClient 4.5 replays the previous hop's headers rather than the original request's, so the headers you set are not brought back on a return to the first origin, and Host carries over from the previous hop. Proxy-Authorization is not removed, except on a tunnelled route (an https target through a proxy): inside the tunnel the proxy never sees the request, so it is removed like any other credential. A legacy DefaultHttpClient (any AbstractHttpClient) is refused by httpClient(...): it never lets the guard run just before the request is written, so its cookie-store Cookie followed a cross-origin redirect. Build the client with HttpClients.

Content Security Policy — locking down Juneau's auto-generated HTML pages. Marshalling Security — parser-level security characteristics. Views Security Model — how the views toolkit uses the CSRF boundary.

@RestOp handler methods may return CompletableFuture<T> (or any CompletionStage<T>); the framework unwraps the value through the standard response-processor chain when the future resolves. A separate, opt-in @Rest(virtualThreads=true) flag dispatches handler invocation onto Java 21+ virtual threads with graceful degradation on Java 17. The two features compose: a CompletableFuture return on a virtualThreads=true resource gives you the high-throughput "no-thread-blocked" pattern without changing the rest of the request pipeline.

Returning a CompletableFuture<T> or CompletionStage<T> is recognized by a new AsyncResponseProcessor slotted ahead of SerializedPojoProcessor in the default processor chain. Synchronous handlers — methods returning String, MyDto, byte[], Reader, Throwable, etc. — keep their existing path with zero behavioral change. @Rest(path="/orders") public class OrderResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Inject OrderService orders; @RestGet("/{id}") public CompletableFuture<Order> get(@Path long id) { return orders.lookupAsync(id); // resource thread is not blocked } @RestGet("/{id}/timeline") public CompletionStage<Timeline> timeline(@Path long id) { return orders.timelineAsync(id); // CompletionStage works too } }
documents.s: Async returns (on by default — return-type opt-in)

documents.t: The handler returns a CompletionStage<T> (any concrete subclass — CompletableFuture<T> is the common one). AsyncResponseProcessor calls req.startAsync() to obtain an AsyncContext. If the underlying servlet container does not support async dispatch (e.g. unit-test mock environments), the processor falls back to a bounded CompletableFuture.get(timeout) and re-feeds the unwrapped value through the rest of the chain on the calling thread. A whenComplete((value, error) -> ...) callback on the future: Success — sets the unwrapped value back onto the RestResponse and re-invokes the response-processor chain (skipping AsyncResponseProcessor itself to avoid recursion). The standard SerializedPojoProcessor then handles serialization just like a synchronous return. Failure — routes the throwable through the existing exception pipeline (ThrowableProcessor / ProblemDetailsProcessor). RFC 7807 / 9457 problem-details rendering works unchanged for failed futures when @Rest(problemDetails="true") is set. AsyncContext.complete() runs exactly once (state-machined behind an AtomicBoolean).

Bare java.util.concurrent.Future<T> (i.e. NOT CompletableFuture or CompletionStage) is explicitly rejected with HTTP 500 and a clear message: Bare java.util.concurrent.Future is not supported as a return type from @RestOp methods. Return CompletableFuture or CompletionStage instead, or block on the result yourself before returning. This was a deliberate choice: honoring it via a blocking submit(future::get) was weighed against rejecting it, and rejection won because callers who want async should already be reaching for CompletableFuture, and silently blocking a request thread on a Future.get() is a footgun.

The default async-completion timeout is 30 seconds — chosen to match typical proxy timeouts. On timeout, the response is 504 Gateway Timeout and the AsyncContext is aborted. Override per-resource or per-op: @Rest(asyncTimeoutMillis = "60000") // 60s for every op on this resource public class LongRunningResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestOp(method = "GET", path = "/quick", asyncTimeoutMillis = "5000") public CompletableFuture<Quote> quick() { ... } // overrides resource-level to 5s @RestOp(method = "GET", path = "/poll", asyncTimeoutMillis = "0") public CompletableFuture<Job> poll() { ... } // 0 disables the timeout } The value is in milliseconds; 0 means no timeout (rely on the container's default); negative values are treated as "use the default 30s". SVL is supported (asyncTimeoutMillis = "${TIMEOUT_MS:30000}").

Cancellation is best-effort — when the servlet container reports a connection drop via AsyncListener.onError or onTimeout, the underlying CompletableFuture is cancelled with mayInterruptIfRunning=true. The framework does not attempt to cancel the future on every client disconnect (containers vary in how reliably they surface that signal).

As of 10.0, SLF4J MDC context is propagated automatically across CompletableFuture async hops via MdcAsyncListener. Any diagnostic context set on the request thread (e.g. requestId, userId) is visible to log statements emitted inside the whenComplete callback, even though that callback runs on a different thread. How it works: At dispatch time, AsyncResponseProcessor snapshots the request thread's MDC via MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(). The snapshot is carried into the completion callback via MdcAsyncListener.wrap(callback, snapshot). On the completion thread: the pre-existing MDC (if any) is saved, the request-thread snapshot is installed, the callback body runs, and the completion thread's MDC is restored (or cleared) in a finally block. If the request thread had no MDC (snapshot is null or empty), or SLF4J is absent from the classpath, the original callback is returned unchanged — zero overhead. The listener is on by default when SLF4J is on the classpath. To opt out programmatically: // In a RestContext builder or AbstractRestBuilder subclass: builder.mdcAsyncPropagation(false); Note: this class bridges SLF4J MDC only. Users of Log4j2's ThreadContext directly (without the SLF4J facade) are not covered and should propagate context manually. RequestAttributes, VarResolverSession, Locale, and the resolved JUL logger reference/level snapshot that drives REST debug capture are all request-scoped (carried on RestSession / RestOpSession), not ThreadLocal-backed — they survive the async hop without any extra wiring. Security contexts that rely on ThreadLocal directly (e.g. classic SecurityContextHolder) are not propagated by MdcAsyncListener; for those, use OpenTelemetry's Context.makeCurrent() which is async-friendly by design.

By default, the whenComplete callback runs on whatever thread completes the CompletableFuture — often an I/O-driver or database-callback thread. When that is undesirable (for example, response serialization is expensive and should not block the driver thread), you can route the callback through a named application-owned Executor: @Rest(path="/api", asyncCompletionExecutor="myCompletionPool") public class ApiResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean(name="myCompletionPool") public Executor completionPool() { return Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8); } @RestGet("/orders/{id}") public CompletableFuture<Order> getOrder(@Path String id) { return orderService.fetchAsync(id); // callback runs on myCompletionPool } } The value is the @Bean(name=...) lookup key for an Executor registered in the resource's bean store. An empty string (the default) means no override — completion callbacks run on the future's natural thread. Per-operation override is available via @RestOp(asyncCompletionExecutor=...) (and the verb annotations); op-level wins over resource-level. A reference to a bean name that does not resolve in the bean store causes a startup failure with a clear error. MDC propagation still works when this executor is set — MdcAsyncListener wraps the callback before it is routed through the executor, so the MDC snapshot is restored on whichever thread the executor picks.

Return CompletableFuture / CompletionStage when the work you're doing already produces one natively — Java 11+ HttpClient.sendAsync(...), Project Reactor's Mono.toFuture(), the reactive Mongo / Cassandra drivers, R2DBC, or CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) against an explicit application-owned Executor. The request thread is freed immediately and the response is written on whatever thread completes the future. Block in the handler when the work is synchronous-only (JDBC, classic Apache HttpClient blocking API, file I/O, JMS) AND virtualThreads=true is NOT enabled. Wrapping a blocking call in CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) against the common fork-join pool is an anti-pattern — you've moved the block from one platform-thread pool to another and added scheduling overhead. The two patterns compose with virtual-thread dispatch: with virtualThreads=true you can return a CompletableFuture AND block inside the handler safely, because the handler is running on a virtual thread and the future just defers the response write. The decision is per-op, not service-wide — mix freely. @RestGet("/external/{id}") public CompletableFuture<Quote> external(@Path long id) { return http.sendAsync(req(id), ofString()) // already async — return the future .thenApply(r -> Quote.parse(r.body())); } @RestGet("/db/{id}") public Order db(@Path long id) throws SQLException { return jdbcRepo.lookup(id); // JDBC is blocking — just block; } // pair with virtualThreads=true if hot
documents.s: When to return CompletableFuture vs. block in the handler

documents.t: Virtual-thread dispatch is opt-in and disabled by default — the same non-negotiable contract used for Jakarta Bean Validation and Observability. A fresh RestContext built with no virtualThreads attribute set never instantiates a virtual-thread executor, even on Java 21+. Opt in per-resource or per-op: @Rest(path="/orders", virtualThreads = "true") // every op on this resource public class OrderResource extends BasicRestServlet { ... } @Rest(path="/mixed") public class MixedResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestOp(method = "GET", path = "/heavy", virtualThreads = "true") // just this op public Report heavy() { ... } } When enabled (and the runtime is Java 21+), RestOpInvoker dispatches the entire handler call — parameter binding, the user method body, and the standard exception-mapping path — onto a virtual thread submitted to a per-resource Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). The platform "carrier" thread that received the request is parked on CompletableFuture.get() until the virtual thread finishes, then resumes to write the response.
documents.s: Virtual-thread dispatch (Java 21+, opt-in, off by default)

documents.t: The Juneau runtime floor is Java 17. On Java 17 / 18 / 19 / 20, the virtualThreads=true flag is detected at first use, a one-shot WARNING is logged via Logger.getLogger("org.apache.juneau.rest.server.RestContext.async"), and the framework falls back to caller-thread dispatch — exactly the existing pre-10.0.0 behavior. No runtime error. The implementation uses runtime reflection for the executor creation: if (Runtime.version().feature() < 21) { log.warning("virtualThreads=true configured but runtime is Java <21 — falling back to caller-thread dispatch."); return null; } return (Executor) Executors.class.getMethod("newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor").invoke(null); This means the framework compiles cleanly on Java 17 (no <source>21</source> needed) and the virtual-thread path simply does nothing on older JVMs. Tests are guarded with @EnabledForJreRange(min = JAVA_21) for the virtual-thread-active path and @DisabledForJreRange(min = JAVA_21) for the warning-and-fallback path.

The two features are independent but compose naturally — a CompletableFuture return on a virtualThreads=true resource gives you both the structured-concurrency benefits of virtual threads AND a non-blocking response path: @Rest(path="/users", virtualThreads = "true") public class UserResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Inject UserRepo repo; @RestGet("/{id}") public CompletableFuture<User> get(@Path long id) { return repo.findAsync(id); // VT runs the handler; } // future resumes the response on whatever // thread completes it. }

synchronized blocks and JNI calls pin a virtual thread to its underlying carrier thread for their duration, which defeats the point of going virtual in the first place. If you opt in to virtualThreads=true, prefer java.util.concurrent.locks.ReentrantLock over synchronized in handler-side code, especially around shared resources held during blocking I/O.

The headline win is scaling I/O-bound endpoints without thread-pool exhaustion — anything where each request spends most of its wall-clock time blocked on someone else's I/O. Scenario Why VTs help JDBC / JPA-backed CRUD JDBC is blocking by spec. A platform-thread Tomcat caps at ~200 in-flight requests; with VTs the same JVM serves thousands of concurrent DB-bound requests because blocked VTs cost ~KB of heap each, not ~1 MB of OS stack. Fan-out aggregator endpoints (GET /dashboard calling 5 downstream services) Write straight-line synchronous code with a blocking HTTP client and still get massive concurrency. No CompletableFuture.allOf(...) choreography required if you don't want it. Webhook receivers / spiky workloads Stripe / GitHub / Slack can hammer the service with 10k concurrent POSTs during an event. VTs absorb the spike without queue rejection. Long-polling / SSE / WebSocket-upgrade handshakes Connections that block for many seconds. With VTs, holding 100k open is feasible on a single JVM. Slow third-party API integrations (payment / identity / geocoding) When an upstream brownout pushes p99 to 8 seconds, platform threads exhaust the pool and unrelated endpoints start failing too. With VTs the blocked threads are essentially free — degradation stays localized to the slow endpoint. Mixed workloads on one resource Per-op @RestOp(virtualThreads="true") opts in only the I/O-heavy ops (e.g., the JDBC-backed search) while keeping cheap ops (admin / health / metrics) on platform threads. Think of virtualThreads=true as "this endpoint is going to spend most of its wall-clock time blocked on someone else's I/O, and I want each request to be as cheap as a coroutine." That's why the flag is opt-in per-resource and per-op rather than a global default — the framework can't know whether your handler is JDBC-blocked or CPU-bound, but you do.

CPU-bound endpoints — image resizing, crypto, big serialization. You're still bounded by cores; VTs just add scheduler overhead. Already non-blocking code — if the handler returns CompletableFuture and calls HttpClient.sendAsync(...), the platform thread is freed at await time anyway. VTs are redundant; the async-returns half of this feature is enough on its own. Hot paths with heavy synchronized — on Java 21, synchronized blocks pin the carrier thread (see Virtual-thread pinning caveat). If a hot path has contended synchronized around expensive work, throughput can actually drop. Pinning is fully fixed in JDK 24 / JEP 491. Frameworks that hard-bind state to ThreadLocal with assumptions of bounded thread count — legacy MDC / session code can balloon memory under millions of virtual threads. When in doubt, leave it off. The default is correct for CPU-bound services and for services that already use a non-blocking client end-to-end.
documents.s: When NOT to enable virtual-thread dispatch

documents.t: The MetricsRecorder / TracerHook boundary is preserved across both async returns and virtual-thread dispatch — see Observability: Virtual-thread dispatch sits ABOVE the observability hooks. When virtualThreads=true, the entire invoke(...) body — including tracerHook.startSpan(...) and metricsRecorder.record(...) — runs on the virtual thread. OpenTelemetry's Context.makeCurrent() works as expected because the OTel Scope is opened and closed on the same (virtual) thread. Async returns defer observability completion to future-resolution time. When the handler returns a CompletionStage, the framework attaches a whenComplete callback that closes the OTel Scope and records the Micrometer Timer sample at the moment the future resolves — not the synchronous "future returned" moment. The metric / span describes the actual end-to-end latency including the async wait, and the resolved HTTP status / exception is captured correctly even when the future fails.

Setting Type Default Effect @Rest(virtualThreads) String ("true" / "false" / "") "" (off) Enable virtual-thread dispatch for every op on the resource. @RestOp(virtualThreads) String ("true" / "false" / "") "" (inherit from @Rest) Per-op override. "false" opts out of a resource-level enablement. @Rest(asyncTimeoutMillis) String (long, ms) "" (use 30000ms default) Async-completion timeout for every async-returning op on the resource. @RestOp(asyncTimeoutMillis) String (long, ms) "" (inherit from @Rest) Per-op timeout override. "0" disables the timeout for this op. All four attributes accept SVL (${...}) so values can flow from system properties, env vars, or Config.

The contract is verified end-to-end in juneau-integration-tests: Behavior Test CompletableFuture<String> happy path AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#a01_completableFutureString_happyPath CompletableFuture<MyDto> serializes through the standard processor chain AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#a04_completableFuturePojo_serializesBean Failed future propagates through ThrowableProcessor (404, 500, etc.) AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#b0*_*_completableFuture Never-completing future → 504 Gateway Timeout AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#c01_neverCompletingFuture_504OnTimeout Per-op asyncTimeoutMillis overrides resource-level AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#d01_perOpTimeoutOverridesResourceLevel Bare Future rejected with InternalServerError AsyncResponseProcessor_Test#e01_bareFutureRejected virtualThreads=true on Java 21+ → handler runs on a virtual thread VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#a01_java21Plus_virtualThreadDispatch virtualThreads=true + CompletableFuture returns combine VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#a02_java21Plus_virtualThreadDispatch_combinedWithCompletableFuture Java 17 graceful degradation — handler still works, warning emitted VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#b01_degradation_handlerStillWorks + b02_java17_logsWarningOnce Per-op virtualThreads="false" overrides resource-level "true" VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#c01_perOpOptOutOverridesResourceLevel Per-op virtualThreads="true" works without resource-level enablement VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#c02_perOpOptInWithoutResourceLevel Default off-by-default — no annotation, no virtual-thread dispatch even on Java 21+ VirtualThreadDispatch_Test#d01_offByDefault

Juneau REST servers ship two opt-in authentication (AuthN) guards in org.apache.juneau.rest.server.auth plus an @Auth Principal argument resolver. A separate, optional sub-module — juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt — adds JWT verification on top via nimbus-jose-jwt. The core juneau-rest-server jar stays JWT-free; teams that don't want JWT pay zero classpath cost. All three pieces are purely additive — they are wired in through the existing @Bean / RestGuardList extension point and do not change the behavior of any pre-existing handler.

Component Module Purpose BearerTokenGuard juneau-rest-server Parse Authorization: Bearer <token>, delegate to a TokenValidator, stash a Principal. ApiKeyGuard juneau-rest-server Read an API key from a header / query / cookie, delegate to an ApiKeyStore, stash a Principal. TokenValidator (SPI) juneau-rest-server Pluggable token validator (opaque, JWT, custom). ApiKeyStore (SPI) juneau-rest-server Pluggable API-key lookup (in-memory, database, Vault, etc.). @Auth Principal juneau-rest-server Inject the authenticated Principal into @RestOp method parameters. ClaimsPrincipal juneau-rest-server Principal subclass with typed claim access (used by JWT validators). AuthenticationException juneau-rest-server 401 with a fluent WWW-Authenticate setter. JwtTokenValidator juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt JWKS-backed JWT validator with algorithm allowlisting, mandatory claim checks, and clock-skew tolerance.

BearerTokenGuard extracts a bearer token from the Authorization header, hands it to a TokenValidator, and stashes the resulting Principal on the request attributes under RestServerConstants.PRINCIPAL_ATTR. On failure it throws a 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer realm="<realm>" set on the response (RFC 7235 §4.1).

TokenValidator opaqueValidator = token -> { var principal = revocationCheckedLookup(token); if (principal == null) throw new AuthenticationException("Token revoked or unknown"); return principal; }; @Rest(path="/api") public class ApiResource extends RestServlet { @Bean public RestGuardList guards(BeanStore bs) { return RestGuardList.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenGuard.create().realm("api").validator(opaqueValidator).build()) .build(); } @RestGet(path="/me") public String me(@Auth Principal p) { return p.getName(); } } The validator is allowed to throw AuthenticationException with a richer WWW-Authenticate value (e.g. Bearer error="invalid_token", error_description="...") — the guard preserves it.

ApiKeyGuard reads an API key from a configurable source (header / query / cookie), delegates lookup to an ApiKeyStore, and stashes the resolved Principal. The default source is the X-API-Key request header. ApiKeyStore store = key -> { var principal = lookupByKey(key); return Optional.ofNullable(principal); }; @Bean public RestGuardList guards(BeanStore bs) { return RestGuardList.create(bs) .append(ApiKeyGuard.create().store(store).build()) // default: X-API-Key header .build(); } // Alternatives: ApiKeyGuard.create().store(store).fromHeader("X-Acme-Token").build(); // custom header ApiKeyGuard.create().store(store).fromQuery("apiKey").build(); // query string ApiKeyGuard.create().store(store).fromCookie("api_key").build(); // cookie Security note — query-string keys leak into proxy / access logs and browser history. Prefer header or cookie sources for production traffic; the query-string source exists for legacy / debugging use only. ApiKeyStore implementations should compare keys in constant time (java.security.MessageDigest#isEqual(byte[],byte[])) to defeat timing side-channels.

Once a guard has stashed a principal, you can inject it into any @RestOp method via the @Auth annotation, or simply by declaring a Principal-typed parameter: @RestGet(path="/me") public String me(@Auth Principal p) { return p.getName(); } @RestGet(path="/bare") public String bare(Principal p) { return p.getName(); } // type-driven; no annotation needed @RestGet(path="/claims") public String claims(@Auth ClaimsPrincipal cp) { return cp.getClaim("scope", String.class).orElse("none"); } AuthArg is registered in DefaultConfig, so no extra wiring is required to enable type-driven resolution.

The optional juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt sub-module adds JwtTokenValidator — a TokenValidator that fetches keys from a JWKS endpoint, verifies signatures, and enforces iss / aud / exp / nbf with secure defaults.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <dependency> <groupId>com.nimbusds</groupId> <artifactId>nimbus-jose-jwt</artifactId> <version>10.3</version> <!-- consumer-supplied; provided scope on juneau-rest-server-auth-jwt --> </dependency> The nimbus dependency is declared provided on the sub-module by design, so it does not bleed transitively into upstream juneau-rest-server consumers. Pick the nimbus version you want.

var validator = JwtTokenValidator.create() .jwksUrl(URI.create("https://issuer.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json")) .issuer("https://issuer.example.com/") .audience("https://api.example.com") .build(); var guard = BearerTokenGuard.create().realm("api").validator(validator).build(); Builder method Purpose jwksUrl(URI) JWKS endpoint URL. Mutually exclusive with jwkSource(...). jwkSource(JWKSource) Plug in a custom key source (HSM, federation, tests). Mutually exclusive with jwksUrl(...). issuer(String) Required exact-match iss claim. audience(String) Required aud claim (token's aud must contain this value). algorithms(JWSAlgorithm...) Algorithm allowlist. Default: RS256, ES256. HS256 opt-in only; "none" is permanently rejected. clockSkew(Duration) exp / nbf tolerance. Default: 60s. Capped at 5 minutes by the builder. jwksCacheTtl(Duration) JWKS cache TTL. Default: 5 minutes. Past TTL the cache serves stale keys on fetch failure (warn logged). jwksEagerRefreshOnKidMiss(boolean) Trigger an out-of-band JWKS refresh when a fresh-cache key selection returns no results (key-rotation kid miss). Default: true. Set false to restore pre-10.0.0 behavior. Applies only to jwksUrl(...)-backed caches; see below. jwksEagerRefreshCooldown(Duration) Minimum spacing between eager refreshes. Default: 10 seconds. Must be positive, ≤ jwksCacheTtl, and ≤ 60 seconds. clock(Clock) Inject a deterministic clock for tests.

JwtTokenValidator ships with deliberately strict defaults: No alg: none — unsigned JWTs are rejected unconditionally. There is no opt-in. Algorithm allowlisting — defaults to [RS256, ES256]. HS256 is rejected unless the caller explicitly opts in. This defeats the algorithm-confusion attack where a JWT is signed with HS256 using the RSA public key as the HMAC secret. Mandatory claims — iss, aud, exp, nbf are required by default. Missing-claim tokens are rejected. Clock-skew cap — the builder will refuse a clockSkew(...) value larger than 5 minutes. JWKS rotation — keys are re-fetched after the configured TTL (default 5 minutes). On JWKS fetch failure the cache continues serving the last-known-good key set with a WARNING-level log entry, avoiding correlated auth outages from transient network blips. JWKS eager refresh on kid miss — when a fresh-cache key selection returns no matching keys (typically because an IdP rotated its signing key mid-TTL), the cache performs one out-of-band JWKS refresh before failing the request. Bounded by a 10-second cooldown and a single-in-flight guard. Enabled by default; opt out with jwksEagerRefreshOnKidMiss(false). Applies only to jwksUrl(...)-backed caches — a caller-supplied jwkSource(...) is unaffected.

AdminMixin ships with DenyAllGuard as its default — the secure default is "no admin access until you wire something up." Swapping in BearerTokenGuard (or any other guard) is a zero-mixin-source-change migration: @Rest(path="/myapp", mixins=AdminMixin.class) public class MyAppResource extends BasicRestServlet { @Bean(name="guards") // overrides the mixin's DenyAllGuard. public RestGuardList guards(BeanStore bs) { return RestGuardList.create(bs) .append(new BearerTokenGuard(myTokenValidator)) .build(); } } The mixin honors whatever guard the host registers via the bean-store override seam; nothing inside AdminMixin needs to change. (A routed-child flavor, AdminResource, and a standalone-servlet flavor, AdminServlet, are also available and follow the same default-deny-plus-@Bean-override pattern.)

When stacking RateLimitGuard and AuthN guards, run AuthN first so unauthenticated requests don't consume a rate-limit budget intended for legitimate clients. RestGuardList runs guards in declaration order: @Bean public RestGuardList guards(BeanStore bs) { return RestGuardList.create(bs) .append(BearerTokenGuard.create().validator(myValidator).build()) // 1. AuthN .append(RateLimitGuard.create().permitsPerSecond(50).build()) // 2. throttle .build(); }

Always require iss, aud, exp, nbf when accepting JWTs. JwtTokenValidator enforces this by default — don't disable it. Allowlist algorithms explicitly. Never accept none. Treat HS256 as the special case it is (shared-secret signing); avoid mixing it with asymmetric keys in the same validator. Pin a JWKS rotation strategy. Even with JwtTokenValidator's graceful-degradation, you want real-world clients to roll new keys before old ones expire. TLS everywhere. Bearer tokens and API keys are credentials — never log them and never echo them in response bodies. Constant-time comparison. API-key stores that compare strings naively are vulnerable to timing attacks. Use MessageDigest#isEqual. Replay-attack mitigation. Bearer tokens and JWTs are bearer tokens by definition. Pair short exp values with TLS pinning and (when feasible) DPoP / mutual-TLS for sensitive endpoints. See also: Guards, REST Authenticator — Resource-Level Authentication, Rate-Limiting and Request-Id Propagation, AuthN Filter Framework, SAML 2.0 AuthN Support, OAuth 2.0 / OIDC AuthN Support, AdminMixin.

The RestAuthenticator SPI provides an ergonomic, in-resource way to resolve a request's Principal and roles for @Rest resources — so roleGuard, RoleBasedRestGuard, @Auth Principal injection, and req.isUserInRole(...) all "just work" without container-managed security or a servlet-layer filter. It complements the AuthN Filter Framework: that framework authenticates at the servlet-container layer (before Juneau routing); RestAuthenticator authenticates at the resource layer (per matched operation). Both reuse the same underlying auth implementations (SAML, OAuth, JWT, API-key, bearer-token), so a single bean can serve either layer.

Aspect Servlet-filter layer (AuthFilterChain) Resource layer (RestAuthenticator) Where it runs A jakarta.servlet.Filter, before the RestServlet is reached. A dedicated framework step inside Juneau dispatch, after the operation is matched and before guards. Registration @Bean AuthFilterChain auto-mounted by JettyServerComponent. Resource bean / @Rest(authenticator=) / @Bean method / RestServlet.createAuthenticator(...). Scope URL patterns across the whole servlet. Per @Rest resource, inherited down the child-resource tree. Unmatched (404) paths Filter still runs. Authenticator runs only for matched operations. Underlying contract Authenticator (AuthFilter, AuthFilterChain). RestAuthenticator (adapts any Authenticator). Both layers ultimately produce the same thing — a resolved Principal + role set surfaced through getUserPrincipal() / isUserInRole(String) / getRemoteUser() and the RestServerConstants.PRINCIPAL_ATTR request attribute — so downstream guards and @Auth resolution don't care which layer authenticated the request.

The lowest-level contract is shared by both layers: @FunctionalInterface public interface Authenticator { Optional<AuthResult> authenticate(HttpServletRequest req) throws AuthenticationException; } The same three-state return contract as AuthFilter: State Meaning Optional.empty() Does not apply — no recognizable credentials. Optional.of(AuthResult) Authentication succeeded. throw AuthenticationException Credentials present but invalid (→ 401). AuthFilter and AuthFilterChain both implement Authenticator, so every existing filter (BearerTokenAuthFilter, ApiKeyAuthFilter, SamlAuthFilter, OAuthFilter, OidcSessionAuthFilter, custom impls) is reusable verbatim at the resource layer.

RestAuthenticator is the resource-level front door.
