documents.t: @RestOp-annotated methods automatically get rendered as Swagger operations. The following shows the annotations defined on the GET /pets operation. The real PetStoreResource (juneau-petstore-core) doesn't currently add @OpSwagger tags to this method, so tags="pet" below is illustrative of how you'd add them:

@RestGet( path="/pets", summary="All pets in the store", swagger=@OpSwagger( tags="pet", ... ), ... ) public Collection<Pet> getPets() { return store.getPets(); } Methods marked as deprecated will show up as deprecated in the Swagger UI:
@RestGet( path="/pets/legacySearch", summary="Legacy pet search (use query parameters on GET /pets instead)", ... ) @Deprecated public Collection<Pet> legacySearch(...) { ... }

Expanding operations shows you a list of parameters. Parameter information can be defined in a couple of ways. The typical way is through annotations on parameters being passed to your @RestOp-annotated method, like so: @RestGet public Collection<Pet> getPets( @Query( name="s", schema=@Schema( description={ "Search.", "Key/value pairs representing column names and search tokens.", "'*' and '?' can be used as meta-characters in string fields.", "'>', '>=', '<', and '<=' can be used as limits on numeric and date fields.", "Date fields can be matched with partial dates (e.g. '2018' to match any date in the year 2018)." }, type="array", collectionFormat="csv" ) ) String[] s, @Query( name="v", schema=@Schema( description={ "View.", "Column names to display." }, type="array", collectionFormat="csv" ) ) String[] v, ... ) { ... } note The @Schema annotation can also be attached directly to the parameter or parameter type as well. The type and collectionFormat values above are optional and auto-detected based on the parameter class type if omitted. They're included here for clarity. The examples will be explained in the next section. Another option is to specify your parameter information in the parameters annotation as free-form JSON 5. The Queryable converter class ships a canned SWAGGER_PARAMS constant with this exact information pre-built, so resources that use Queryable don't have to hand-write it. LogsResource (juneau-microservice-examples) does exactly this:

@RestOp( method="PARSE", path="/*", summary="View parsed contents of file", converters=Queryable.class, swagger=@OpSwagger( parameters={ Queryable.SWAGGER_PARAMS } ) ) public LogParser viewParsedEntries(...) { ... }

public class Queryable implements RestConverter { public static final String SWAGGER_PARAMS = """ { in:'query', name:'search', description:'Search expression: comma-separated column=expression clauses, e.g. name=$contains(smith),age=$gte(18). See the BeanQuery search language docs: https://juneau.apache.org/docs/topics/JuneauCommonsBeanQuery', type:'string', examples:{example:'?search=name=$contains(smith),age=$gte(18)'} },{ in:'query', name:'view', description:'Comma-separated columns to return, in order.', type:'string', examples:{example:'?view=name,age'} },{ in:'query', name:'sort', description:'Comma-separated sort columns. Append \\':desc\\' (or \\'-\\') for descending. The default is ascending order.', type:'string', examples:{example:'?sort=name,age:desc'} },{ in:'query', name:'position', description:'0-based index of the first row.', type:'integer', minimum:0, examples:{example:'?position=20'} },{ in:'query', name:'limit', description:'Maximum rows to return. Defaults and caps are set by the server.', type:'integer', examples:{example:'?limit=10'} },{ in:'query', name:'opts', description:'Options as key=value clauses, e.g. counts=true.', type:'string', examples:{example:'?opts=counts=true'} }"""; } This information could have also been defined in the Swagger JSON for the resource as well. note If you take a BeanQueryRequest method argument instead of using Queryable, you do not need this constant: each getter on BeanQueryRequest already carries a @Schema description (and position carries minimum=0), so the same six parameters appear in the generated Swagger automatically. The parameter section contains information about the request body as well for PUT and POST methods, as shown here: @RestPost( path="/pets", summary="Add a new pet to the store", swagger=@OpSwagger( tags="pet" ) ) public Pet createPet( @Content @Schema(description="Pet object to add to the store") Pet pet ) { return store.createPet(pet); } Note that the schema information on the body parameter is automatically detected if not provided.

Under the input parameters are listed the possible responses for the resource. The 200 response is determined by the return type on the method, in this case a collection of Pet objects: @RestGet( path="/pets", summary="All pets in the store", ... ) public Collection<Pet> getPets() { return store.getPets(); } Note that additional responses can be specified by throwing exceptions annotated with the @Response annotation such as this one: @Response @StatusCode(406) @Schema(description="Not Acceptable") public class NotAcceptable extends BasicHttpException {...} Like input parameters, the Swagger for responses can be define in multiple locations such as: @Response annotated classes, methods, and parameters.@Rest(swagger) / @RestOp(swagger) annotations. See Also Response Beans

The look-and-feel of the Swagger UI is controlled via a single CSS file: SwaggerUI.css. In the microservice template, this file is located in the files/htdocs/styles directory. It's a simple straightforward file consisting of less than 350 lines. This file can be modified to change the look-and-feel of your Swagger UI.

Tags allow you to group operations into general categories. In the user interface, these can be expanded/collapsed by clicking on the tag sections. The Petstore sample groups its operations under pet, store and user tags. In the example below, the three tag sections and the Models section have been collapsed, leaving the untagged operations at the top: Tags are also defined in the @Swagger annotation. The following continues the illustrative MyResource example from the previous section. The real PetStoreResource (juneau-petstore-core) declares the same three tags with the annotation-only approach shown further down:

"tags": [ { "name": "pet", "description": "Everything about your Pets", "externalDocs": { "description": "Find out more", "url": "http://juneau.apache.org" } }, { "name": "store", "description": "Access to Petstore orders" }, { "name": "user", "description": "Operations about user", "externalDocs": { "description": "Find out more about our store", "url": "http://juneau.apache.org" } } ], The annotation-only approach is shown here:

swagger=@Swagger( ... tags={ @Tag( name="pet", description="Everything about your Pets", externalDocs=@ExternalDocs( description="Find out more", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ) ), @Tag( name="store", description="Access to Petstore orders" ), @Tag( name="user", description="Operations about user", externalDocs=@ExternalDocs( description="Find out more about our store", url="http://juneau.apache.org" ) ) } ), Tags are associated with operations using the @OpSwagger(tags) annotation:

@RestGet( path="/users", summary="Petstore users", swagger=@OpSwagger( tags="user" ) ) public Collection<User> getUsers() {...} Operations can be mapped to multiple tags. Tags are optional. Operations not mapped to tags are listed in the UI before tagged operations, so they show up at the top of the page. In the Petstore these are the built-in endpoints (such as /api/* and /stats) inherited from BasicRestServlet:

@Swap can be used to associate a swap class using an annotation. This is often cleaner than using the builder swaps() method since you can keep your swap class near your POJO class. @Swap(MyObjectSwap.class) public class MyPojo { ... } // Sample swap for converting MyPojo classes to a simple string. public class MyObjectSwap extends ObjectSwap { @Override /* ObjectSwap */ public String swap(MarshallingSession session, MyPojo pojo) { return pojo.toSomeSerializableForm(); } } Multiple swaps can be associated with a class using multiple @Swap annotations: @Swap(MyJsonSwap.class) @Swap(MyXmlSwap.class) @Swap(MyOtherSwap.class) public class MyPojo {} Readers get serialized directly to the output of a serializer. Therefore it's possible to implement a swap that provides fully-customized output. public class MyJsonSwap extends ObjectSwap { public MediaType[] forMediaTypes() { return MediaType.forStrings("*/json"); } public Reader swap(MarshallingSession session, MyPojo pojo) throws Exception { return new StringReader("{message:'Custom JSON!'}"); } } The @Swap annotation can also be used on getters and setters as well to apply a swap to individual property values: public class MyBean { private MyPojo myPojo; // Swap applied to bean property. @Swap(MyPojoSwap.class) public MyPojo getMyPojo() { return myPojo; } } When applied to bean properties, the swap annotation need only be applied to either the getter, setter, or field. The swap annotation can also be applied to the private field of a bean property, like so: public class MyBean { @Swap(MyPojoSwap.class) private MyPojo myPojo; public MyPojo getMyPojo() { return myPojo; } public MyBean setMyPojo(MyPojo myPojo) { this.myPojo = myPojo; return this; } }

Swappers transform objects before they are processed by BCT assertions. They provide a way to unwrap, evaluate, or transform objects into more testable forms. Swappers are particularly useful for wrapper types like Optional, Supplier, and Future.

BCT comes with built-in swappers for common wrapper and lazy-evaluation types: // Optional types Optional<String> optional = Optional.of("Hello"); assertString("Hello", optional); // Uses optionalSwapper() - unwraps to "Hello" Optional<String> emptyOptional = Optional.empty(); assertString("<null>", emptyOptional); // Uses optionalSwapper() - unwraps to null // Supplier types Supplier<String> supplier = () -> "World"; assertString("World", supplier); // Uses supplierSwapper() - calls get() to get "World" Supplier<String> expensiveSupplier = () -> { // Simulate expensive computation return "Expensive Result"; }; assertString("Expensive Result", expensiveSupplier); // Uses supplierSwapper() - calls get() // Future types CompletableFuture<String> completedFuture = CompletableFuture.completedFuture("Done"); assertString("Done", completedFuture); // Uses futureSwapper() - gets completed result CompletableFuture<String> pendingFuture = new CompletableFuture<>(); assertString("<pending>", pendingFuture); // Uses futureSwapper() - shows pending status

optionalSwapper() - Unwraps Optional values to their contained value or null supplierSwapper() - Calls Supplier.get() to evaluate lazy values futureSwapper() - Extracts completed Future results or shows "<pending>" for incomplete futures
Define custom swappers for your domain-specific wrapper types:

// Lazy wrapper swapper Swapper<LazyValue> lazySwapper = (conv, lazy) -> { if (lazy == null) return null; return lazy.getValue(); // Evaluate the lazy value }; // Result wrapper swapper Swapper<Result> resultSwapper = (conv, result) -> { if (result == null) return null; if (result.isSuccess()) { return result.getValue(); } else { return "Error: " + result.getError(); } }; // Registration var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addSwapper(LazyValue.class, lazySwapper) .addSwapper(Result.class, resultSwapper) .build();

// Either/Union type swapper Swapper<Either<String, Integer>> eitherSwapper = (conv, either) -> { if (either == null) return null; return either.isLeft() ? either.getLeft() : either.getRight(); }; // Validation result swapper Swapper<ValidationResult> validationSwapper = (conv, validation) -> { if (validation == null) return null; if (validation.isValid()) { return validation.getValue(); } else { // Return list of error messages return validation.getErrors(); } }; // Proxy object swapper Swapper<ProxyObject> proxySwapper = (conv, proxy) -> { if (proxy == null) return null; // Unwrap the proxy to get the real object return proxy.getTarget(); }; // Registration var converter = BasicBeanConverter.builder() .defaultSettings() .addSwapper(Either.class, eitherSwapper) .addSwapper(ValidationResult.class, validationSwapper) .addSwapper(ProxyObject.class, proxySwapper) .build();

// Swap based on object state Swapper<CachedValue> cachedValueSwapper = (conv, cached) -> { if (cached == null) return null; if (cached.isExpired()) { return "<expired>"; } else if (cached.isPending()) { return "<pending>"; } else { return cached.getValue(); } }; // Usage assertString("myValue", cachedValue); // "myValue" if valid assertString("<expired>", expiredValue); // "<expired>" if expired

// Swapper that performs multiple transformations Swapper<ComplexWrapper> complexSwapper = (conv, wrapper) -> { if (wrapper == null) return null; // Step 1: Extract inner value Object inner = wrapper.getInner(); // Step 2: Apply transformation if (inner instanceof Optional) { inner = ((Optional<?>) inner).orElse(null); } // Step 3: Apply conversion if (inner instanceof Supplier) { inner = ((Supplier<?>) inner).get(); } return inner; };

// Test Optional values Optional<User> optUser = userService.findById(123); assertBean(optUser, "name,email", "John,john@example.com"); // Test Supplier values Supplier<Config> configSupplier = () -> loadConfig(); assertBean(configSupplier, "timeout,retries", "30000,3"); // Test Future values CompletableFuture<Order> futureOrder = orderService.getOrderAsync(456); futureOrder.join(); // Wait for completion assertBean(futureOrder, "id,total", "456,99.99");

// Test Result wrapper with custom swapper Result<User> result = userService.createUser(userData); setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(result, "name,email", "Alice,alice@example.com"); // Test validation results ValidationResult<Order> validation = orderValidator.validate(order); assertBean(validation, "id,total", "123,99.99"); // Test error case ValidationResult<Order> invalidValidation = orderValidator.validate(invalidOrder); assertList(invalidValidation, "Missing required field: customer", "Invalid total: -10"); } finally { resetConverter(); }

// Test lazy computation LazyValue<Report> lazyReport = new LazyValue<>(() -> generateReport()); setConverter(converter); try { assertBean(lazyReport, "title,itemCount", "Monthly Report,150"); } finally { resetConverter(); } // Swapper ensures the lazy value is evaluated before testing

Use Swappers when: You need to unwrap or transform objects before property extraction The object is a wrapper type (Optional, Supplier, Result, etc.) You want to change the object structure for testing Property access needs to work on the unwrapped value Use Stringifiers when: You only need to change the string representation The object structure is fine, just needs better formatting You want to customize how the object appears in assertions
documents.s: When to Use Swappers vs. Stringifiers

documents.t: Swappers are applied before any other processing: // 1. Swapper unwraps the Optional Optional<User> optUser = Optional.of(new User("Alice", 25)); // 2. PropertyExtractor accesses properties on the unwrapped User // 3. Stringifier formats the property values assertBean(optUser, "name,age", "Alice,25");
// Ensure thread-safe swappers for concurrent testing Swapper<ThreadSafeLazy> threadSafeSwapper = (conv, lazy) -> { if (lazy == null) return null; synchronized (lazy) { return lazy.getValue(); } };

// Robust swapper with error handling Swapper<AsyncValue> safeAsyncSwapper = (conv, async) -> { if (async == null) return null; try { return async.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } catch (TimeoutException e) { return "<timeout>"; } catch (Exception e) { return "<error: " + e.getMessage() + ">"; } };
Domain-specific wrapper types Lazy evaluation containers Result/Either/Try types Async/Future-like types Proxy objects Validation wrappers

Always handle null input appropriately Return null for null input (maintain null semantics) Keep swappers simple and focused on unwrapping/transformation Avoid expensive operations in swappers when possible Document any side effects (e.g., evaluating lazy values) Consider thread safety for shared swappers Handle exceptions gracefully with meaningful error messages

Swappers are called for every object being tested Avoid expensive operations (database calls, network requests) Consider caching for expensive transformations Be careful with lazy evaluation - ensure it's what you want Use timeouts for async operations

// Use descriptive names that indicate the transformation optionalSwapper() // Unwraps Optional supplierSwapper() // Evaluates Supplier futureSwapper() // Extracts Future result resultSwapper() // Unwraps Result type eitherSwapper() // Extracts Either value validationSwapper() // Unwraps ValidationResult

// Optional/Maybe Swapper<Optional> optionalSwapper = (conv, opt) -> opt != null ? opt.orElse(null) : null; // Try/Result Swapper<Try> trySwapper = (conv, tryValue) -> tryValue != null ? (tryValue.isSuccess() ? tryValue.get() : tryValue.getError()) : null; // Either Swapper<Either> eitherSwapper = (conv, either) -> either != null ? (either.isLeft() ? either.getLeft() : either.getRight()) : null;

// CompletableFuture Swapper<CompletableFuture> futureSwapper = (conv, future) -> { if (future == null) return null; if (future.isDone()) { try { return future.get(); } catch (Exception e) { return "<error>"; } } return "<pending>"; };

// Validation result with errors Swapper<Validation> validationSwapper = (conv, validation) -> { if (validation == null) return null; return validation.isValid() ? validation.getValue() : validation.getErrors(); };

Bean-Centric Testing Basics - Main BCT documentation Customization - Configuration via @BctConfig and BctConfiguration Stringifiers - Converting objects to strings Listifiers - Converting collection-like objects to lists PropertyExtractors - Custom property access logic

Swaps are a critical component of Juneau. They allow the serializers and parsers to handle Java objects that wouldn't normally be serializable. Swaps are, simply put, 'object swappers' that swap in serializable objects for non-serializable ones during serialization, and vis-versa during parsing. Some examples of non-serializable objects are File, Reader, Iterable, etc... These are classes that aren't beans and cannot be represented as simple Maps, Collections, or primitives. In the following example, we introduce a ObjectSwap that will swap in a bean of a particular type with a map containing customized key-value pairs: // Sample swap for converting a bean to a specialized map of key-value pairs. public class MyBeanSwap extends ObjectSwap<MyBean,JsonMap> { // Converts a bean to a generic map. @Override /* ObjectSwap */ public JsonMap swap(MarshallingSession session, MyBean bean) { return JsonMap.of("foo", bean.getBar()); } // Converts the generic map back into a bean. @Override /* ObjectSwap */ public MyBean unswap(MarshallingSession session, JsonMap map, ClassMeta<?> hint) throws Exception { MyBean bean = new MyBean(); bean.setBar(map.getString("foo")); return bean; } } The swap can then be associated with serializers and parsers like so: // Create a new JSON serializer with our swap. WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().simple().swaps(MyBeanSwap.class).build(); String json = serializer.write(new MyBean()); // Create a JSON parser with our swap. ReaderParser parser = JsonParser.create().swaps(MyBeanSwap.class).build(); MyBean bean = parser.read(json, MyBean.class); Another example of a ObjectSwap is one that converts byte[] arrays to BASE64-encoded strings: public class ByteArrayBase64Swap extends StringSwap { @Override /* StringSwap */ public String swap(MarshallingSession session, byte[] bytes) throws Exception { ByteArrayOutputStream baos = new ByteArrayOutputStream(); OutputStream b64os = MimeUtility.encode(baos, "base64"); b64os.write(bytes); b64os.close(); return new String(baos.toByteArray()); } @Override /* StringSwap */ public byte[] unswap(MarshallingSession session, String string, ClassMeta<?> hint) throws Exception { byte[] bytes = string.getBytes(); ByteArrayInputStream bais = new ByteArrayInputStream(bytes); InputStream b64is = MimeUtility.decode(bais, "base64"); byte[] tmp = new byte[bytes.length]; int n = b64is.read(tmp); byte[] res = new byte[n]; System.arraycopy(tmp, 0, res, 0, n); return res; } } The following example shows the BASE64 swap in use: // Create a JSON serializer and register the BASE64 encoding swap with it. WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer.create().simple().swaps(ByteArrayBase64Swap.class).build(); ReaderParser parser = JsonParser.create().swaps(ByteArrayBase64Swap.class).build(); byte[] bytes = {1,2,3}; String json = serializer.write(bytes); // Produces "'AQID'" bytes = parser.read(json, byte[].class); // Reproduces {1,2,3} byte[][] bytes2d = {{1,2,3},{4,5,6},null}; json = serializer.write(bytes2d); // Produces "['AQID','BAUG',null]" bytes2d = parser.read(json, byte[][].class); // Reproduces {{1,2,3},{4,5,6},null} The MarshallingContextable.Builder.swap(Class,Class,ThrowingFunction) and MarshallingContextable.Builder.swap(Class,Class,ThrowingFunction,ThrowingFunction) methods are another way to define swaps by using functions. // Use a function to convert beans to strings. WriterSerializer serializer = JsonSerializer .create() .simple() .swap(MyBean.class, String.class, x -> myBeanStringifier(x)) .build();

Each config file contains zero or more sections containing zero or more entries: [Section1] key1 = 1 [Section2] key1 = 2 Unicode escapes can be used in values. key1 = \u0070\u0075\u0062\u006c\u0069\u0063 Comment lines start with the '#' character and can be placed on lines before sections and entries: # A comment about this section [Section1] # A comment about this entry key1 = 1 Comments can also be placed on the same line as entries: key1 = 1 # A comment about this entry Values containing '#' must be escaped to prevent identification as a comment character: valueContainingPound = Value containing \u0023 character Likewise, '' should be escaped to prevent confusion with unicode escapes. Values containing newlines can span multiple lines. Subsequent lines start with a tab character. multiLineValue = line 1, line 2, line 3 When retrieved, the above translates to "line1,\nline2,\nline3". Leading and trailing whitespace on values are ignored. Whitespace is not ignored within multi-line values (except for the leading tab character on each line). Blank lines can be used anywhere in the file. # A comment line # Another comment line [Section1] ... Values located before any sections are considered part of the no-name section, meaning they are accessed simply by key and not section/key. # Top of file # Use config.getString("key1") to retrieve. key1 = val1 # The first section [Section1] # Use config.getString("Section1/key2") to retrieve. key2 = val2 Section and key names must be at least one character long and not consist of any of the following characters: / \ [ ] = # Whitespace in section and key names is technically allowed but discouraged.

Each JVM has a system default config. This is a configuration file that serves as the default configuration for the system. It's accessed using the following static methods: ConfiggetSystemDefault()setSystemDefault(Config) If you do not specify a system default config, one will be automatically searched for, using the candidate names returned by Config.getCandidateSystemDefaultConfigNames(). Each candidate name is looked up first as a file in the current/working directory (the directory the JVM was launched from), and then as a classpath resource; the first candidate that resolves to either is used as the system default. The candidate names are built in the following order: If the system property (or environment variable) juneau.configFile is set, it is the only candidate — no other names are considered. Otherwise: If the JVM was launched from a jar file (i.e. sun.java.command ends in .jar), two jar-name-derived candidates are added first: the jar's base file name with a .cfg extension (e.g. myapp-1.0.cfg), followed by that same base name with any trailing ./_-delimited version suffix stripped (e.g. myapp.cfg). Every file in the current/working directory whose name ends in .cfg is added next, in whatever order the JVM's File.listFiles() returns them for that directory — this is filesystem/OS-dependent and is not guaranteed to be alphabetical. Finally, the following fixed fallback names are added, in this order: juneau.cfg, default.cfg, application.cfg, app.cfg, settings.cfg, application.properties. Later in the section on REST resources, we describe how to associate configurations with REST resources using the @Rest(config) annotation. The system default configuration can be referenced with the keyword SYSTEM_DEFAULT like so: // Always use system default. @Rest(config="SYSTEM_DEFAULT") // Use system property if set or the system default if not. @Rest(config="$S{juneau.configFile,SYSTEM_DEFAULT}") By default, all properties in the system default configuration are automatically set as system properties. This can be disabled by setting the system property juneau.disableAutoSystemProps to true.

As a convenience, the SystemProperties section of your configuration file can be used to define system properties to set during initialization of your microservice: #======================================================================================================================= # System properties #----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- # These are arbitrary system properties that are set during startup. #======================================================================================================================= [SystemProperties] # Configure Jetty for StdErrLog Logging # org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.class = org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.StrErrLog # Configure Jetty to log using java-util logging org.eclipse.jetty.util.log.class = org.apache.juneau.microservice.jetty.JettyLogger # Jetty logging level # Possible values: ALL, DEBUG, INFO, WARN, OFF org.eclipse.jetty.LEVEL = WARN derby.stream.error.file = $C{Logging/logDir}/derby-errors.log

The @Swap(template) annotation allows you to associate arbitrary contextual strings with swaps. The primary purpose is for providing template names, such as for Apache FreeMarker, therefore the name 'template'. However, the usage of the string is open-ended. For example, you could pair a template string like so: @Swap(impl=FreeMarkerSwap.class, template="MyPojo.div.ftl") public class MyPojo {} The implementation of the FreeMarker swap would look something like this: // Our templated swap class. public class FreeMarkerSwap extends ObjectSwap { public MediaType[] forMediaTypes() { // Make sure this only applies to the HTML serializer. return MediaType.forStrings("*/html"); } public Reader swap(MarshallingSession session, Object object, String template) throws Exception { // Call some method that uses FreeMarker to convert 'o' to raw HTML using // the 'MyPojo.div.ftl' template. return getFreeMarkerReader(template, object); } }

The terminal region shows a command's output the way a terminal would: colours, bold, cursor movement, progress bars that redraw in place, and full-screen boxes. The server sends the command's raw bytes, unchanged, and xterm.js renders them in the browser. Use it when the output only makes sense on a terminal. The region lives in its own module, juneau-rest-server-terminal (package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.terminal). It is opt-in: add the module and nothing else changes. It depends on juneau-rest-server-views and on the xterm.js WebJar (org.webjars.npm:xterm__xterm, pinned at 6.0.0).

<@card type="terminal" id="build" title="Build"> { contractVersion: '1', terminal: { bytesUrl: '/runs/juneau-terminal/r42/bytes', eventsUrl: '/runs/juneau-run-view/r42/events', refreshMs: 1000, title: 'mvn test', tailBytes: 2097152 } } </@card> Key Rules bytesUrl Required. A same-origin path, with no scheme, no leading //, no .. segment and no {. eventsUrl Optional. A run-view events endpoint over the same run. It gives the steps their offsets and the badge its exit code. refreshMs Optional. The poll interval while the command runs. Values below 1000 are raised to 1000; a value of 0 or less is an error. title Optional. Shown in the toolbar. tailBytes Optional, 1 to 1 GiB, default 2 MiB. On first load only the last tailBytes are fetched; Load all fetches the rest. The card takes its options as the body only; src= and template= are rejected. The page needs no toolkit=: the card pulls the terminal toolkit pack, which brings views and xterm with it. From Java, TerminalDef.forMixin("build", "/runs", "r42") builds the same options.

Implement TerminalMixin on a REST resource. Its one abstract method resolves an id to a source, and is where your access rules live: @Rest public class RunsResource extends BasicRestServlet implements TerminalMixin, RunViewMixin { @Override public Optional<TerminalSource> terminalSource(String id, RestRequest req) { return runs.find(id).map(Run::terminal); } } TerminalEndpoints gives the same logic for custom paths. Path Answers GET …/juneau-terminal/{id}/bytes?from=<offset>&max=<n> Raw bytes from from (default 0), at most 256 KiB per call. GET …/juneau-terminal/{id}/raw Every byte still held, as an attachment named <id>.log. GET …/juneau-terminal.js, …/juneau-terminal.css The runtime and its stylesheet. The bytes endpoint sets these headers: Header Meaning Term-Next The offset to ask for next. Term-End The current end of the log. Term-Cols, Term-Rows The terminal size the command ran at. Term-Done true once the command has finished and every byte has been read. Term-Truncated true when the bytes before from are no longer held. Term-Error gone when the log has been deleted. Ids match ^[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,128}$; anything else is 400. An unknown or forbidden id is 404. A from past the end is 416, with Term-End. A from or max that is not a plain non-negative integer is 400, as is a from above 2^53-1. Both endpoints send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. When the source has gone, bytes still answers 200 with no bytes, Term-Done: true and Term-Error: gone, and Term-Next and Term-End equal to from. raw answers 200 with an empty body and the same Term-Error: gone.

Source Use FileTerminalSource.create(path) A growing log file. The size comes from a <log>.size sidecar ({"cols":C,"rows":R}), default 120×40. MemoryTerminalSource.create(capacity, cols, rows) A ring buffer your code writes into. Readers that fall behind see Term-Truncated. Implement TerminalSource for anything else.

TerminalProcess.start(tool, cmd, cols, rows, dir) runs cmd under juneau_run.py --pty at a fixed size. tool names the output parser and must be maven, pytest, playwright or generic; anything else throws. The command sees a real terminal, so tools that colour or redraw behave as they do in a shell. The process writes the log, the size sidecar and a run-view events file into dir. terminal() and events() give the two sources to serve, and both report done once the process has exited. cmd is a list of arguments, passed as they are: it is never joined into a string or run through a shell. Each run needs its own dir; a directory that already holds a run is refused. The script is found through the juneau.run.script system property or the JUNEAU_RUN_SCRIPT environment variable; python3 must be on the PATH. POSIX only. dir is also the command's working directory. The runner's own stdout and stderr go to runner.out in it, which is appended to and has no size cap; it is for diagnosis only and is never served. TerminalProcess.start(tool, cmd, cols, rows, dir, prompts) also opens a prompt channel: the runner gets --prompts stdio, each prompt line the script sends goes to TerminalPrompts.onLine, onEnd is called once when the channel ends, and answer(jsonLine) sends a reply. Neither a prompt nor an answer is logged. Prompts and input are mutually exclusive. close() ends the channel, and the runner then cancels the job. The line format is the prompt protocol.

Run-view step, suite and test events can carry rawOffset, the byte offset in the log where the line that produced the event starts. With an eventsUrl, the terminal records the line each step starts on. A run view next to it links each step to that line with rawHref: '#build-O{offset}', where build is the terminal card's id. The terminal scrolls when the page hash changes. rawHref takes exactly one {offset}. A deep link that points before the start of a trimmed tail loads everything once (as Load all does) and then scrolls.

The terminal keeps the command's columns and rows, and scales its font (8 to 20 px) to fit the panel. 100,000 lines of scrollback by default (see xterm options), a search box (Enter for next, Shift+Enter for previous) over the screen being shown, Copy, and Follow. A Raw link downloads the whole log. It is shown only when bytesUrl ends in /bytes and resolves to an http: or https: URL; the link is the same path with /raw. Polling backs off to 5 s after three empty polls, pauses while the tab is hidden, and retries errors at 1, 2, 5, then 10 s. Once the bytes are done, the events are still polled until one reports the run finished. After 5 empty polls in a row the client gives up on them and shows the final badge without an exit code. Links open only for http: and https:. Clipboard writes from the output (OSC 52) are ignored. The terminal takes no input unless both the card and the page wire it; see Input.

JuneauTerminal.mount(host, {bytesUrl, terminal: {convertEol: true}}) passes a few xterm options through to the terminal. Use convertEol for output with bare 
 line ends (anything not written through a PTY), which xterm otherwise draws as a staircase. Key Type Meaning convertEol boolean Treat 
 as 
. scrollback integer, 0 to 1,000,000 Lines of scrollback (default 100,000). fontFamily non-empty string The terminal font family. On the client, other keys and values of the wrong type are ignored. The size, input, link and font-size options stay with Juneau. A card carries the options nested as {bytesUrl, terminal: {convertEol: true}}, the same shape mount takes. Server-declared cards accept the same terminal key: in a <@card> FreeMarker body (terminal: {bytesUrl: '/runs/juneau-terminal/r42/bytes', terminal: {convertEol: true}}), through TerminalDef.fromMap, or from Java with the terminal(Map) builder method (TerminalDef.create(id)....terminal(Map.of("convertEol", true))). On the server, unlike the client, an unknown inner key or a value of the wrong type or range is an error rather than being ignored.

A terminal card can let the user type into a running job. Input is off by default and is opt-in at every layer: the process, the access check, the bus handler and the page contract each have to say yes. It lives in a second module, juneau-rest-server-terminal-bus (package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.terminal.bus), which adds TerminalInput and depends on the terminal module and the server bus.

var process = TerminalProcess.start("generic", List.of("./release.sh"), 120, 40, dir, true); TerminalAccess access = new TerminalAccess() { public boolean canWatch(TerminalCaller caller, String terminalId) { return mayWatch(caller, terminalId); } public Optional<TerminalSink> inputSink(TerminalCaller caller, String terminalId) { return mayType(caller, terminalId) ? Optional.of(process) : Optional.empty(); } }; var input = TerminalInput.create(access); var bus = ServerBus.create(BusPolicy.create() .upstream(TerminalInput.TOPIC, input) .downstream(TerminalInput.STATUS_TOPIC, false) .build()); input.bind(bus); TerminalProcess always implements TerminalSink. Started with input true it takes bytes through write; with input false (the default of the shorter start overloads) acceptsInput() is always false. TerminalAccess decides, per caller and terminal id, who may watch and who may type. inputSink returns empty by default, so a TerminalAccess that only implements canWatch allows no typing. A typist must also be allowed to watch. The handler answers through the bus, but the bus is built from the policy that holds the handler, so the handler is bound to the bus afterwards, once. The two policy lines register term.input as an upstream topic handled by TerminalInput, and term.input-status as a downstream topic that is not retained.

The card sets terminal.input and terminal.inputId. inputId is the terminal id sent in every frame; it must match the id grammar of the endpoints above, and input: true without it is an error. TerminalDef.forMixin fills inputId from the terminal id you pass it. The card then publishes term.input, subscribes to term.input-status in the input-status role (the only role a terminal card accepts), and the page declares the status topic and a WebSocket bridge: { "contractVersion": "1", "title": "T", "nav": [], "activeNav": [], "topics": [ {"topic": "term.input-status", "retain": false, "publisher": "server"} ], "bridges": [ {"id": "term", "transport": "websocket", "session": "/c/juneau-bus/session", "downstream": ["term.input-status"], "upstream": ["term.input"]} ], "cards": [ {"id": "term", "type": "terminal", "terminal": {"bytesUrl": "/t/juneau-terminal/t1/bytes", "input": true, "inputId": "t1"}, "publishes": [{"topic": "term.input", "retain": false}], "subscribes": [{"topic": "term.input-status", "as": "input-status"}]} ] } Upstream topics are only allowed on a WebSocket bridge, so an SSE bridge cannot carry input. A FreeMarker page wires input the same way. input and inputId go in the card body's terminal object, publishes and subscribes are attributes on <@card>, and the topic and bridge are declared with <@topic> and <@bridge>: <@topic name="term.input-status" retain=false publisher="server"/> <@bridge id="term" transport="websocket" session="servlet:/juneau-bus/session" downstream="term.input-status" upstream="term.input"/> <@card type="terminal" id="term" title="Release" publishes="term.input" subscribes=[{"topic": "term.input-status", "as": "input-status"}]> { contractVersion: '1', terminal: { bytesUrl: '/t/juneau-terminal/t1/bytes', input: true, inputId: 't1' } } </@card> A frame on term.input is {"id": <terminal id>, "data": <string>}, and an empty data is a probe. Every probe, and every refused data frame, is answered on term.input-status to the sending session only, as {"id", "state"}. The state is one of: State Meaning live A probe succeeded: this caller may type and the job is taking input. denied The caller may not watch the terminal or has no input sink for it. closed The sink no longer accepts input (the job ended, or a write failed). busy The sink's pending-input buffer was full and the bytes were dropped. bad The frame was malformed: a bad or missing id, a missing or non-string data, or any key besides id and data. An accepted data frame gets no answer. The answer repeats the id only when it is a valid terminal id; for an invalid one the answer has no id key at all (it is omitted, not null).

Without input, the region is a transcript with a search box, Copy, a Follow toggle, a status badge and a Raw link, as in the petstore jobs page: With input enabled: A toggle in the toolbar, Enable input. It appears only with input: true, an inputId and a WebSocket bridge carrying term.input upstream and term.input-status downstream; otherwise the card looks as before. It is the only way to arm: pressing it sends a probe, and the terminal accepts keystrokes only after a live answer. A status chip next to it: Input live while armed, Input unavailable when the probe got no answer within 2 s, Input not permitted after denied, Job ended after closed, Input throttled: some keys not sent after busy, and Disconnected: input not sent while the bridge is down. For denied and closed the toggle is disabled and relabelled Input not permitted or Job ended. A denied or closed that arrives after the 2 s probe timeout still disables the toggle. Pressing Esc twice within 500 ms disarms and swallows the second Esc, so it never reaches the job. The first Esc is sent as usual. The terminal also disarms on a denied or closed answer while armed, when the bridge disconnects (chip Disconnected: input not sent), and when the run finishes (chip Job ended). Keystrokes are batched: the browser sends at most one frame every 100 ms, and a frame carries at most 4096 UTF-8 bytes of what was typed (longer input is split across frames on code point boundaries).

Default-deny. No input without input on the process, a canWatch that returns true, a present inputSink, and a sink that still accepts input. Each failure is answered as denied or closed; the answer carries no reason beyond that state, and never says why access was refused. Rate limit. The bus's maxUpstreamPerSecond policy (20 frames per second per session by default) bounds the frame rate; the client's 100 ms batching stays well under it. Each frame is limited to the bus frame size (64 KiB by default). The process holds at most 64 KiB of pending input; beyond that write returns false and the caller gets busy. The write is queued and never blocks the WebSocket thread. Two layers. The bus authorizer (BusPolicy.Builder.authorizer) runs once, when the session opens, as a coarse per-page switch. TerminalAccess runs on every frame and is the only per-user gate. Do not strip the input topics for some users. The browser refuses the whole session when its grants do not match the contract, so a watch-only user would lose watching too. Deny them in TerminalAccess instead. CSRF and origin. There is no per-frame token. Frames rely on the CSRF check on the session POST and the exact-origin check on the WebSocket upgrade. A sink is a keyboard. Never return one for every viewer. Audit. Each accepted non-empty write is logged at INFO on the juneau.terminal.input logger: principal=alice terminal=t1 bytes=10 keys=^C,ESC,CR,TAB,BS,^D,^Z keys names the control bytes present, comma-separated, in order of first appearance, at most 8. ^C, ^D, ^Z, ESC, CR, TAB and BS are named (both 0x08 and DEL, 0x7F, are BS); any other C0 byte uses caret notation (^A, ^J for LF, ^@, and so on). The typed text is never logged. An anonymous caller is principal=-. Any other principal has every character at or below 0x20, every ISO control, U+2028, U+2029, =, \ and % written as %XX for each of its UTF-8 bytes (upper-case hex), so a name can neither split the line nor forge a field. Refusals are logged at FINE only, as principal=

terminal= state=, with - for an invalid id.

A card with terminal.input: true must carry the whole wiring: the term.input publish, the term.input-status subscription in the input-status role, a topics entry declaring term.input-status with publisher: "server", and a WebSocket bridge carrying term.input upstream and term.input-status downstream. The page validator reports each missing piece as E-58, for example terminal card 'term' has input: true but its publishes lacks 'term.input'. The browser runs the same check as E-JS-52. The problem is not tied to a card, so the console logs it to the browser console and shows it in the page banner. E-58 is a page-validator code and is unrelated to the bus runtime's E-JS-58 (a bad frame). A FreeMarker or PageSpec page fails to render with the first such problem.

There is no paste guard beyond the batching and rate limit above: pasted text goes to the job as keystrokes, in frames of up to 4096 bytes. Input is bytes written into the job's pseudo-terminal, the runner's PTY, unfiltered. The terminal's line discipline acts on control characters: ^C interrupts the foreground process (an unhandled interrupt ends the job with exit 130), and ^D ends a read, or ends input at the start of a line. ^Z does not suspend a plain job, because nothing could resume it; a shell with job control of its own, such as bash -i, still suspends its foreground job. What the job does after that is the job's business. Text the job does not echo, such as a password, never reaches the log. The audit line records which control keys were sent, not what was typed.

By default a card polls bytes?from=<offset> every second, or every 5 s once it has gone idle. When the page has a bus, the server can instead send a nudge: a small hint that terminal t1 now ends at offset N. The card fetches straight away, so output appears with low latency while the page polls far less. A nudge carries only end (the offset one past the last byte) and, once no more bytes will be appended, done: true. It never carries terminal bytes. Polling stays the fallback and the safety net: a page with no bus, or with no nudge wiring, behaves exactly as described above.

TerminalNudges lives in juneau-rest-server-terminal-bus next to TerminalInput. The terminal module itself has no bus dependency; it only knows the TerminalNudgePublisher interface, void nudge(String terminalId, long end, boolean done), which TerminalNudges implements. var nudges = TerminalNudges.create(access); var bus = ServerBus.create(BusPolicy.create() .downstream("term.nudge:*", false) .build()); nudges.bind(bus); The topic is term.nudge:<terminalId>. The downstream line must be present and unretained; bind throws IllegalStateException otherwise. A retained nudge would replay a stale offset to every new session. bind can be called once, and close stops the scheduler. A nudge before bind or after close is dropped. Nudges are coalesced: at most one per terminal per 250 ms, always carrying the latest end. A done whose delivery fails is picked up by polling. The publisher must not block or throw. TerminalNudges.nudge only records state and schedules; the delivery runs on its own daemon thread. Attach a source to the publisher with the id it is served under: var memory = MemoryTerminalSource.create(1 << 20, 120, 40).nudges("t1", nudges); var process = TerminalProcess.start("generic", List.of("./release.sh"), 120, 40, dir, true).nudges("t1", nudges); var file = FileTerminalSource.create(dir.resolve("run.log")).build().nudges("t1", nudges); MemoryTerminalSource.nudges publishes after every write and a final done from finish. The publisher is called outside the source's lock, and an exception from it is swallowed so a write never fails because of a nudge. TerminalProcess.nudges starts a daemon thread that checks the size of the runner's log every 100 ms and publishes when it has grown. It publishes done once the job has finished, and close stops it promptly. FileTerminalSource.nudges starts a daemon thread that checks the size of the log file every 100 ms and publishes when it has grown. A missing or shrinking file publishes nothing and the thread keeps going. It never publishes done, because a plain file source does not know when the producer finishes; the card's polling sees done through the terminal supplier. FileTerminalSource is AutoCloseable: close stops the thread promptly. All three nudges methods can be called once, and reject an id that is not a valid terminal id.

Name the exact topic everywhere. For terminal t1 the page needs three things: { "contractVersion": "1", "title": "T", "nav": [], "activeNav": [], "topics": [ {"topic": "term.nudge:t1", "retain": false, "publisher": "server"} ], "bridges": [ {"id": "nudges", "transport": "sse", "session": "/c/juneau-bus/session", "downstream": ["term.nudge:t1"]} ], "cards": [ {"id": "term", "type": "terminal", "terminal": {"bytesUrl": "/t/juneau-terminal/t1/bytes"}, "subscribes": [{"topic": "term.nudge:t1", "as": "nudge"}]} ] } The card's subscribes entry uses the nudge role; a terminal card now accepts input-status and nudge. Nudges are downstream only, so an SSE or WebSocket bridge both work. In a FreeMarker page the pieces are the same <@topic>, <@bridge> and subscribes attribute shown under Input. BusWiringValidator already checks partial wiring, so a missing piece is reported rather than silently ignored. How the exact and wildcard forms combine: topics entry Bridge downstream Result term.nudge:t1 term.nudge:t1 Passes and delivers. This is the supported wiring. term.nudge:t1 term.nudge:* Rejected with E-51: the exact declaration does not cover the wildcard downstream. term.nudge:* term.nudge:t1 Rejected with E-52: the exact bridge entry does not cover the wildcard declaration. term.nudge:* term.nudge:* Passes the validator but delivers nothing. The last row is the one silent trap. Delivery needs a session to hold the exact topic, and a session granted only the wildcard is skipped, so wildcard on both sides validates and then never nudges. Always wire the exact topic.

A page that calls JuneauTerminal.mount(host, {id, bytesUrl}) itself, with no card, has no roles.nudge to route a bus message through. It delivers its own nudges instead: mount puts nudge(payload) on the handle JuneauTerminal.handle(id) returns, and on the cleanup function mount returns (for a mount without an id). const stop = JuneauTerminal.mount(host, {id: 'lane_x', bytesUrl: '/t/juneau-terminal/lane_x/bytes'}); bus.subscribe('term.nudge:lane_x', function (payload) { JuneauTerminal.handle('lane_x').nudge(payload); }); The payload is the same {end, done?} as a card receives, with the same rules: a nudge at or behind the bytes already read is ignored, a malformed payload is ignored, and a nudge after the cleanup has run does nothing. Polling stays the safety net.

A nudge whose end is ahead of what the card has already read triggers an immediate fetch. A nudge at or behind the current offset is ignored, as is a malformed one. A nudge carrying done fetches once if the bytes are not yet finished. While nudges are arriving, the card polls at max(refreshMs, 5000) ms instead of its normal interval. The mode starts with the first nudge, not when the bridge connects, so a connected bridge that never sends a nudge does not slow the poll. When the bridge disconnects, including a slow-consumer detach, the card goes back to its normal interval at once. This is idle-aware: a card that was already idle returns to 5 s, not 1 s. A failing fetch is retried on the usual 1, 2, 5, 10 s schedule. A nudge never bypasses that backoff while fetches are failing, and never starts a second concurrent fetch. Nudge mode does not time out. If nudges stop while the bridge stays up, the 5 s poll still runs, so output is at most 5 s late.

canWatch runs for every delivery. For each nudge, TerminalNudges asks TerminalAccess.canWatch about every connected session that was granted that exact topic, and publishes only to the sessions that pass. That is at most 4 deliveries per terminal per second times the number of sessions, so canWatch must be cheap. An exception from it counts as a denial. Base the rule on the principal plus live state. The TerminalCaller that canWatch sees is built from the bus session, so its principal and attributes were fixed when the session opened. A long-lived session can carry stale attributes, bounded by the bus's maxSessionAge. Decide from the principal and from server state read at call time. Use the same rule as the bytes endpoint. A nudge carries no bytes, but it tells a viewer that a terminal grew. The content gate is terminalSource(id, req) in TerminalMixin, a separate check. Keep the two consistent, but do not expect to copy one into the other: terminalSource sees the live RestRequest, while canWatch sees a TerminalCaller frozen at session open. Express the rule over the principal plus live server state so either can evaluate it. If they disagree, the worst case is that a user learns terminal X grew but cannot read it. Revocation takes effect on the next delivery. canWatch runs before the frame is published, so a revocation that races a delivery can let that one nudge through. The next one is denied. Terminal ids cannot be enumerated. Nudges are never retained, a session granted only term.nudge:* receives nothing, and whether a topic is granted at session open never depends on whether the terminal exists. A session can list up to 256 exact term.nudge:<guess> topics (the bus's topic cap), but it still receives only what canWatch allows. Do not strip term.nudge topics in the authorizer. The browser refuses a whole session whose grants differ from its request, so a watch-restricted user would lose the page's bus. Deny them in canWatch instead.

Search highlights by UTF-16 index, so a line with wide (double-cell) characters can highlight the wrong span. Step and checkpoint links use buffer line numbers. Once the scrollback (100,000 lines by default; see xterm options) is full and old lines drop, they go stale.
TerminalSmoke_BrowserTest in the module drives the region in a real browser. It binds a socket, so it is opt-in: run it with -Pjs-tests -Dtest='TerminalSmoke_BrowserTest' -Djuneau.terminalSmoke=true.

Run View Region juneau-run: the PTY runner behind TerminalProcess Admin-Console Chrome Input: the juneau-rest-server-terminal-bus module and TerminalInput Bus nudges: TerminalNudges and TerminalNudgePublisher

The juneau-rest-server-view-thymeleaf module adds Thymeleaf view-rendering to juneau-rest-server without bleeding the Thymeleaf engine dependency into the core. This page covers the Thymeleaf-specific bridge. For the engine-agnostic View interface itself, see the 10.0.0 release notes under the juneau-rest-server section. The sibling JSP View Support, Mustache View Support, and FreeMarker View Support pages cover the JSP, Mustache, and FreeMarker bridges with the same shape.

Thymeleaf is the default web view technology for Spring Boot — it's the engine Spring Boot autoconfigures when spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf is on the classpath, and it's the template engine Spring's reference docs recommend over JSP for embedded servlet containers. It also has zero servlet-container dependencies: the core engine renders directly to a java.io.Writer and works under MockRest, Jetty microservices, and Spring Boot equally well.

Class Role View (in juneau-rest-server core) Engine-agnostic contract: getTemplateName(), getAttributes(), getResponseHeaders(). ThymeleafMixin Mixin. Mounts /thymeleaf/* for raw .html template requests; registers ThymeleafViewRenderer on the response-processor chain. Builder: basePath(String) (default /), cacheTemplates(boolean) (default true), templateMode(TemplateMode) (default HTML). Builder implements the shared ViewMixinBuilder contract. ThymeleafView View implementation. Immutable; fluent: ThymeleafView.of("hello").attr("name", name).header("Cache-Control", "no-store"). ThymeleafViewRenderer ResponseProcessor that detects ThymeleafView returns and asks the configured org.thymeleaf.TemplateEngine to process(templateName, context, writer) directly onto the response.
juneau-rest-server-view-thymeleaf ships only org.thymeleaf:thymeleaf in provided scope. No engine is bundled with the bridge module. Consumers add the engine matching their deployment.

Deployment Recommended setup Maven coordinates Spring Boot Spring Boot autoconfigured SpringTemplateEngine (extends TemplateEngine) org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf Juneau microservice / Jetty Bridge-default TemplateEngine (built on first use, anchored on the importer's classloader) org.thymeleaf:thymeleaf Custom resolvers / dialects User-supplied @Bean TemplateEngine (e.g. FileTemplateResolver, custom Spring MessageSource, Spring Security dialect) Whatever you need on top of org.thymeleaf:thymeleaf The bridge picks up a TemplateEngine bean from the request's BeanStore via BeanStore.getBean(TemplateEngine.class) first; if no engine bean is registered, it constructs a default TemplateEngine with a single ClassLoaderTemplateResolver configured with prefix=basePath, suffix=".html", templateMode=HTML, and cacheable=true. When no Thymeleaf engine is on the classpath, the renderer surfaces a clear diagnostic naming the missing dependency: No Thymeleaf engine is available on the classpath. Add one of: - org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf (Spring Boot autoconfig) - org.thymeleaf:thymeleaf (Juneau microservice / Jetty) Or register a custom @Bean TemplateEngine that picks up your preferred resolvers. See https://juneau.apache.org/docs/topics/ThymeleafViewSupport for the full matrix.

<dependency> <groupId>org.apache.juneau</groupId> <artifactId>juneau-rest-server-view-thymeleaf</artifactId> <version>${juneau.version}</version> </dependency> <!-- pick ONE engine setup --> <dependency> <groupId>org.thymeleaf</groupId> <artifactId>thymeleaf</artifactId> <version>3.1.3.RELEASE</version> </dependency>
src/main/resources/ templates/ hello.html
Hello, name!

import org.apache.juneau.http.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.servlet.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.thymeleaf.*; @Rest(path="/app", mixins=ThymeleafMixin.class) public class AppResource extends RestServlet { @Bean ThymeleafMixin thymeleaf() { return ThymeleafMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .cacheTemplates(false) // dev convenience; default true is production-safe .build(); } @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return ThymeleafView.of("hello").attr("name", name); } } GET /app/hello/world returns Hello, world! — ThymeleafViewRenderer intercepts the ThymeleafView return, populates a Thymeleaf Context from the view's attributes, and asks the active TemplateEngine to render /templates/hello.html directly onto the response.

To use ThymeleafView from a host-class @RestGet without adopting the full mixin, add ThymeleafViewRenderer.class directly to the host's responseProcessors: @Rest(responseProcessors={ThymeleafViewRenderer.class}) public class AppResource extends BasicRestServlet { @RestGet("/hello/{name}") public View hello(@Path String name) { return ThymeleafView.of("templates/hello.html").attr("name", name); } } The ResponseProcessorList partition pass (added in 10.0.0) automatically repositions ThymeleafViewRenderer to run before SerializedPojoProcessor. Because Thymeleaf renders directly to a Writer with zero servlet-container dependencies, attribute interpolation works under MockRest — verified end-to-end by ThymeleafView_TypedHandler_Test#a04_renderInterpolatesAttributesFromTypedHandler.

The mixin also installs a default /thymeleaf/* mount that renders raw .html templates under the configured base path. With basePath("/templates/"), a request for GET /app/thymeleaf/about renders /templates/about.html directly — no Java handler required. The handler strips a trailing .html so /app/thymeleaf/about.html works too. The greedy /* handler is excluded from the generated Swagger / OpenAPI spec via @OpSwagger(ignore=true) since the path isn't API-meaningful.

The default mount /thymeleaf/* can be overridden via the SVL variable ${juneau.thymeleaf.path:thymeleaf} — set via system property (-Djuneau.thymeleaf.path=views), environment variable (JUNEAU_THYMELEAF_PATH=views), or Config key (juneau.thymeleaf.path = views) to change the runtime mount without subclassing.

The raw-template handler funnels every user-supplied @Path("/*") String path through FileUtils.resolveVirtualPathSafely(String, String) and rejects any .. traversal that escapes the configured basePath with HTTP 403. Both direct (/thymeleaf/../secret) and nested (/thymeleaf/a/b/../../../secret) traversal attempts are blocked at the handler boundary before reaching the engine resolver. This is the same hardening the JSP bridge applies; see ThymeleafMixin_PathTraversal_Test for the canonical coverage.

Spring Boot's reference docs explicitly recommend Thymeleaf as the default web view technology — there is no awkward fat-jar resource-layout dance (Thymeleaf doesn't depend on servlet semantics; the engine just resolves classpath:/templates/*.html directly), and Spring Boot autoconfigures a SpringTemplateEngine (which extends TemplateEngine) that the bridge picks up automatically through BeanStore.getBean(TemplateEngine.class).

@Configuration public class AppConfig { @Bean public ThymeleafMixin thymeleaf() { return ThymeleafMixin.create() .basePath("/templates/") .build(); } } The Spring BeanStore adapter resolves the bean through ApplicationContext.getBean(ThymeleafMixin.class); no additional plumbing is required.

ThymeleafViewRenderer implements ViewRenderer and is automatically positioned before SerializedPojoProcessor by the ResponseProcessorList partition pass. A @RestOp method returning ThymeleafView reaches the renderer without any extra configuration — the mixin registers the renderer and the framework ensures ordering. MockRest-level typed-handler integration is verified by ThymeleafView_TypedHandler_Test (attribute interpolation asserted end-to-end).

Some apps want /views/ for the public site and /admin/views/ for the admin console. Register two ThymeleafMixin beans, each in its own subclass with its own paths override: @Rest(paths={"/views/*"}) public class PublicViewsResource extends ThymeleafMixin { public PublicViewsResource() { super(ThymeleafMixin.create().basePath("/templates/public/")); } } @Rest(paths={"/admin/views/*"}) public class AdminViewsResource extends ThymeleafMixin { public AdminViewsResource() { super(ThymeleafMixin.create().basePath("/templates/admin/")); } } Both subclasses mount independently and each resolves templates against its own basePath.

ThymeleafMixin.Builder implements ViewMixinBuilder, the minimal contract shared by all four view-engine mixin builders (basePath(String) + cacheTemplates(boolean)). Code written against the interface works unchanged if you later swap engines: import org.apache.juneau.rest.server.view.*; ViewMixinBuilder<?> anyEngineBuilder = ThymeleafMixin.create(); anyEngineBuilder.basePath("/templates/").cacheTemplates(false);

thymeleaf-spring6 is not a direct dep of the bridge module. The bridge depends only on org.thymeleaf:thymeleaf (the engine core). Spring Boot users pull thymeleaf-spring6 in transitively via spring-boot-starter-thymeleaf; the bridge picks up the resulting SpringTemplateEngine through the standard BeanStore lookup. Thymeleaf 2.x is not supported. Thymeleaf 3.x is the LTS line and ships with Spring Boot 3.x. Apps still on Thymeleaf 2.x should migrate before adopting the bridge. Custom dialects (Spring Security, Layout, etc.) are users' responsibility — register them on your own @Bean TemplateEngine and the bridge will use it instead of the default.

Juneau exposes a public low-level streaming API that complements the POJO databind path (Serializer.write(...) / Parser.read(...)) with cursor-based push and pull primitives. Two surfaces, layered:

Surface Returns Methods When to use RecordReader / RecordWriter one whole-value record per call canRead() / read(Class), write(Object) Format-neutral whole-value access; works on every Juneau format. TokenReader / TokenWriter one fine-grained event per call next(), startObject() / fieldName(...) / string(...) / etc. Structural events for formats whose wire encoding is already token-shaped (JSON family, CBOR, MsgPack). TokenReader extends RecordReader and TokenWriter extends RecordWriter, so FULL-capability formats inherit record-stream semantics for free. PARTIAL-capability formats expose only the record surface — calling structural methods on them is a compile error (the type system enforces "no nested structure visible at the cursor").

A format declares what streaming surfaces it supports by implementing role interfaces in org.apache.juneau.marshall.stream. Capability is detected with a plain instanceof check — there is no capability enum: Role Granted method Implemented by RecordReadable / RecordWritable readRecords(input) / writeRecords(output) every streaming format TokenReadable / TokenWritable readTokens(input) / writeTokens(output) json, json5, jsonl, cbor, msgpack ArrayRecordReadable / ArrayRecordWritable readArrayRecords(input) / writeArrayRecords(output) json, json5, cbor, msgpack, bson, parquet, yaml (readers + writers); xml, html (readers only — no array-record writer) TokenReadable extends RecordReadable (and TokenWritable extends RecordWritable), so a format that exposes the token cursor automatically gets the record cursor for free: its readRecords(...) default returns the readTokens(...) cursor. Formats that only expose the record surface implement RecordReadable/RecordWritable alone — there is no readTokens(...) method to call, so structural access is a compile-time impossibility. A format exposes the token cursor only when its wire encoding admits a clean structural mapping to the normalized token vocabulary. For example, jsonl is TokenReadable because each line is itself a complete JSON value that maps directly onto the token model, whereas csv and sse are RecordReadable-only because a CSV row and an SSE event carry no nested structure the cursor could surface. Writer-only formats (jsonschema, jcs, soap-xml) have no parser, so they implement only the *Writable roles. Negotiate a parser/serializer at runtime with instanceof, and use the cursor-quality signal isRecordStreaming() to tell a true O(1) streaming cursor from a buffered one: boolean json = JsonParser.DEFAULT instanceof TokenReadable; // true (FULL) boolean yaml = YamlParser.DEFAULT instanceof TokenReadable; // false (record-only) boolean rec = YamlParser.DEFAULT instanceof RecordReadable; // true if (JsonParser.DEFAULT instanceof RecordReadable p) boolean streaming = p.isRecordStreaming(); // true = O(1) streaming, false = buffered

The table below is the authoritative, code-derived summary of what each format supports. Reading columns reflect the roles implemented by the format's Parser; writing columns reflect the roles implemented by its Serializer. The Streaming column is the cursor-quality signal (isRecordStreaming() / isArrayRecordStreaming() / cursor-level isStreaming()). Rec / Tok / Arr — the record (RecordReadable/RecordWritable), token (TokenReadable/TokenWritable), and array-record (ArrayRecordReadable/ArrayRecordWritable) surfaces. Tier — FULL = exposes the structural token cursor (TokenReadable/TokenWritable), so it also gets the record cursor for free; PARTIAL = record cursor only (calling structural token methods is a compile error). Cursor streaming — O(1) = a true streaming cursor (constant memory per record/token); buffered = the whole value is materialized (RecordAdapter-backed). "Supported" (✓) and "streams in O(1)" are independent: a format can support a surface yet still buffer it. Notes jsonl is naturally multi-record — read/write it with the record cursor (its token cursor doubles as the record cursor), one value per line. Its array-record roles (readArrayRecords / writeArrayRecords) are overridden at the session level to alias that line record stream — each top-level line is one element, emitted/consumed without a surrounding [...] array, streaming O(1). (This corrects the inherited JSON behavior, which targets a single [...]-wrapped document and is invalid for line-delimited JSONL.) msgpack streams its record/token cursors in O(1), but the array-record cursor is buffered (isArrayRecordStreaming() == false). The writer additionally offers a streaming writeArrayRecords(output, expectedCount) count overload that writes the length-prefix header up front. jsonschema and jcs are writer-only and token-writable, but their serialize(...) path buffers (isRecordStreaming() == false) because the schema / canonical form is computed over the whole value. The array-record writer is inherited from JSON, and the token writer emits ordinary JSON (the object(Object) databind bridge is disabled — use serialize(...) for schema / canonical output). xml and html expose the array-record reader (readArrayRecords, buffered, with a caller-specified-root overload) but have no array-record writer. csv is record-capable but currently buffered (isRecordStreaming() == false); O(1) row streaming is a deferred enhancement.

The POJO databind path (Serializer.write(...) / Parser.read(...)) remains the primary, recommended API. Reach for the streaming surfaces when: You're processing very large or unbounded inputs and don't want to materialize the whole graph. You need to skip parts of a document without binding them. You're composing output from heterogeneous data sources without an intermediate POJO model. You need wire-byte exactness that the POJO path can't guarantee. The streaming surface is purely structural — object swaps and @Schema annotations apply only on the POJO databind path, never at the token layer.
documents.s: When to use streaming vs databind

documents.t: Record Streaming — whole-value record cursor (all formats). Token Streaming — fine-grained structural cursor (FULL formats). Array-Record Streaming — opt-in element streaming for top-level arrays. REST Streaming Integration — using the cursors as @RestOp parameters.

The TokenReader / TokenWriter surface exposes structural events one at a time — START_OBJECT, FIELD_NAME, VALUE_STRING, END_OBJECT, etc. — for formats whose wire encoding is already token-shaped. Available on formats that implement the TokenReadable / TokenWritable role: json, json5, jsonl, cbor, msgpack (read + write), plus jsonschema and jcs (writer-only). See the per-format capability matrix for the full breakdown of which formats expose the token cursor for reading vs writing.

try (TokenReader r = JsonParser.DEFAULT.readTokens("{\"a\":1,\"b\":[true,null]}")) { while (r.next() != TokenType.END_OF_STREAM) { switch (r.getCurrentToken()) { case FIELD_NAME -> handleKey(r.getFieldName()); case VALUE_STRING -> handleString(r.getString()); case VALUE_NUMBER -> handleNumber(r.getNumber()); case VALUE_BOOLEAN -> handleBool(r.getBool()); case VALUE_NULL -> handleNull(); default -> { /* structural */ } } } } Key methods: next() — advances and returns the new current token type. getCurrentToken() — current token without advancing. getDepth() — nesting depth (0 at root). getString() / getNumber() / getNumberLexeme() / getBool() / getBinary() — accessors for the current scalar. getFieldName() — when current token is FIELD_NAME. skipChildren() — fast-forward past the current container's body to its matching end. read(Class) — bridge from token cursor to the format's databind path: consumes one whole value at the cursor's current position and binds it to a POJO. For numeric values both the original lexeme and the parsed Number are available — use getNumberLexeme() for big-decimal / precision-sensitive consumers.

StringWriter sw = new StringWriter(); try (TokenWriter w = JsonSerializer.DEFAULT.writeTokens(sw)) { w.startObject(); w.fieldName("a"); w.number(1); w.fieldName("b"); w.startArray(); w.bool(true); w.nil(); w.endArray(); w.endObject(); } // sw is now: {"a":1,"b":[true,null]} The output target must be a Writer or OutputStream (for byte-based formats). To capture output as a string, use a StringWriter and read sw.toString() afterward. Method families: startObject() / endObject() / startArray() / endArray() — structural framing. fieldName(String) — emits a field name (must precede the value). string(String) / number(...) / bool(boolean) / nil() / binary(byte[]) — scalar values. object(Object) — bridge from token writer to the format's databind path: emits a whole POJO at the current cursor position via PojoWalker. It's the caller's responsibility to emit a well-formed event sequence (every startObject() matched by an endObject(), every field name followed by exactly one value or container, etc.). Implementations are not required to validate.

Each token-capable format exposes its own concrete subtype for callers that want compile-time specificity: JsonTokenReader r = (JsonTokenReader) JsonParser.DEFAULT.readTokens(input); CborTokenWriter w = (CborTokenWriter) CborSerializer.DEFAULT.writeTokens(output); Or declare them as @RestOp parameters — the framework picks the matching parser automatically (see REST Streaming Integration).

Cursor-level settings are derived from the parser/serializer's builder. The following families are honored on token cursors: Reader (from Parser.Builder): autoCloseStreams, unbuffered, trimStrings, streamCharset. Writer (from JsonSerializer.Builder): useWhitespace, maxIndent, quoteChar / quoteCharOverride, escapeSolidus, trimStrings. These are explicitly NOT honored at the token layer — they're databind-path-only: addBeanTypes*, addRootType, keepNullProperties, trimEmptyMaps, trimEmptyCollections, sortMaps, sortCollections, swap configuration, @Schema annotations.
